title: Contributing to MLSys·im
text:
MLSys·im improves with every new hardware spec, solver, tutorial, and bug report. This guide explains how to contribute, whether the contributor is a student who spotted a wrong datasheet number, an instructor designing a teaching scenario, or a researcher who needs a new analytical solver.
Read the modeling and documentation conventions before changing equations, solver interfaces, or shared scenarios. They describe the code organization, generated API documentation, and textbook compatibility checks. The code walkthrough traces an existing serving scenario from its named inputs to its solver, equations, and result schema. Use it to find the file that owns a change.

title: Contributing to MLSys·im
text:
1. Reporting Issues
The fastest way to contribute: open an issue on GitHub.
Good bug reports include:

Which spec is wrong (e.g., “A100 peak TFLOP/s in Hardware.Cloud.A100”)
The correct value and its source (official datasheet URL preferred)
The installed version of MLSys·im (python -c "import mlsysim; print(mlsysim.__version__)")

Good feature requests include:

The hardware, model, or solver to add, and why
A link to the official specification or paper

title: Contributing to MLSys·im
section: 2. Adding Hardware to the Silicon Zoo
text:
2. Adding Hardware to the Silicon Zoo
Every chip in the Silicon Zoo lives in one of five categories: Cloud, Workstation, Mobile, Edge, or Tiny. Each entry follows a strict format with mandatory provenance metadata.






TipBackground reading



The Hardware Acceleration and Compute Infrastructure slide decks cover the accelerator landscape and datasheet specs that feed into MLSys·im’s hardware registry.



Step 1: Add a YAML spec under hardware/data/
Chip and board specs live in the Silicon Zoo; there is no shared constants file to park them in (units live in core/units.py, physical constants in physics/constants.py). Add one YAML file under the right tier, for example mlsysim/hardware/data/cloud/MyAccelerator.yaml. The loader validates the file against HardwareNode at import time and exposes it through the same Python API (Hardware.Cloud.MyAccelerator).
__key__: MyAccelerator
name: Example Accelerator
release_year: 2026
compute:
  peak_flops: 312 TFLOPs / s
  precision_flops:
    fp32: 19.5 TFLOPs / s
    int8: 624 TOPS
memory:
  capacity: 80 GiB
  bandwidth: 2039 GB / s
interconnect:
  name: PCIe Gen4 x16
  bandwidth: 32 GB / s
tdp: 400 W
metadata:
  provenance:
    kind: datasheet
    ref: Example accelerator datasheet
    url: https://...
    verified: "2026-05-30"
Reuse shared records from mlsysim/core/provenance_catalog.py when several entries share one external paper, benchmark, or report. For component-specific hardware or server nodes, define provenance colocated with the item (or inherit from the accelerator’s metadata.provenance). See mlsysim/PROVENANCE.md and run python -m mlsysim.tools.audit_provenance --scope all --strict before opening a PR.
The YAML data layer is intentionally strict: duplicate YAML keys, duplicate __key__ values, missing data directories, and unknown schema fields fail loading. If the value is a technology-class reference, use @tech: rather than copying a shared fact into many devices, for example latency: "@tech:Interconnect.NVLink.latency".


Step 2: Verify with the registry contract tests
The loader contract and duplicate-spec gates run automatically: tests/test_registry_loader_contract.py and tests/test_registry_no_duplicate_specs.py. The legacy core/constants.py catch-all module was deleted outright; tests/test_constants_allowlist.py enforces that neither it nor a compat shim for it ever comes back.


Step 3: Use the canonical path in downstream examples
Examples import Hardware.Cloud.A100, not A100_FLOPS_FP16_TENSOR. Downstream content should use the same canonical registry paths as package tutorials.


Provenance rules
Every registry entry requires metadata.provenance (Provenance model in core/provenance.py). Use kind honestly: datasheet, literature, estimate (needs notes), convention, or illustrative.

Link to an official primary source (manufacturer datasheet, not a blog post)
Set verified (YYYY-MM-DD) on datasheet and literature entries
State which variant in ref or notes (e.g., SXM5 vs. PCIe)
When a spec varies across SKUs, use the most conservative published value unless the variant is specified in the node name



Formatting for QMD and LEGO cells
Display helpers live in mlsysim.fmt, separate from the physics in mlsysim.physics.*:







Helper
Use when




fmt(q, precision=1)
Human-readable quantities in prose


fmt_int(n)
Integer counts without spurious decimals


check(condition, message)
Assert invariants in tutorials and LEGO cells


MarkdownStr
Inline QMD values that must not be LaTeX-escaped



Registry operands come from zoos; derived values from mlsysim.physics.calc_* or solvers.

title: Contributing to MLSys·im
section: 3. Adding Models to the Model Zoo
text:
3. Adding Models to the Model Zoo
Models live in category YAML files under mlsysim/models/data/: language.yaml, vision.yaml, tiny.yaml, recommendation.yaml, statespace.yaml, and generativevision.yaml. Each entry includes a __type__ tag selecting the validated workload class (TransformerWorkload, CNNWorkload, SSMWorkload, DiffusionWorkload, SparseTransformerWorkload, or plain Workload).






TipBackground reading



The Network Architectures and Neural Network Computation slide decks explain the architectural parameters (layers, heads, hidden dimensions) that define each workload.



Transformer workloads
Llama3_8B:
  __type__: TransformerWorkload
  name: Llama-3.1-8B
  architecture: Transformer
  metadata:
    provenance:
      kind: literature
      ref: 'Dubey et al. (2024), The Llama 3 Herd of Models'
      url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783
      verified: '2026-03-06'
      id: prov:dubey-llama3-2024
  parameters: 8030000000 param
  inference_flops: 16060000000 flop
  layers: 32
  hidden_dim: 4096
  heads: 32
  kv_heads: 8
For inference_flops, the standard approximation is \(2P\) FLOPs per token for transformer forward passes (multiply-accumulate counted as 2 operations). When a more precise count is available from the paper, use it and note the source in a comment.


CNN workloads
ResNet50:
  __type__: CNNWorkload
  name: ResNet-50
  architecture: CNN
  metadata:
    provenance:
      kind: literature
      ref: 'He et al. (2016), Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition'
      url: https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385
      verified: '2026-03-06'
      id: prov:he-resnet-2015
  parameters: 25600000 param
  inference_flops: 8200000000 flop
  layers: 50

title: Contributing to MLSys·im
text:
4. Adding Systems and Infrastructure
MLSys·im models the full deployment stack: individual accelerators compose into nodes, nodes compose into racks and fleets, and fleets connect via network fabrics. Infrastructure captures the grid, datacenter environment, pricing, and capacity facts that those systems run within.






TipBackground reading



The Network Fabrics and Fleet Orchestration slide decks explain the network topologies and cluster compositions that MLSys·im models analytically.



Adding a fleet or fabric (systems/registry.py)
# A new reference node (inheriting or defining colocated provenance)
DGX_B200 = Node(
    name="DGX B200",
    accelerator=Hardware.Cloud.B200,
    accelerators_per_node=8,
    intra_node_bw=1800 * ureg.GB / ureg.second,
    nics_per_node=8,
    psus_per_node=6,
    psu_redundancy=1,
    psu_rating=3.3 * kilowatt,
    max_power=14.3 * kilowatt,
    metadata=Metadata(
        provenance=pc.DGX_B200_USER_GUIDE_POWER,
        description="Official NVIDIA DGX B200 server: 8x B200 180GB SXM6, six 3.3 kW PSUs in 5+1 redundancy (14.3 kW max).",
    ),
)

# A new cluster built from that node
Training_2K = Fleet(
    name="Training Cluster (2048 GPUs)",
    node=DGX_B200,
    count=256,  # 256 nodes x 8 GPUs = 2048
    fabric=Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR,
    metadata=Metadata(
        provenance=pc.CLUSTER_TIER_CONVENTIONS,
        description="2,048-GPU training cluster tier on InfiniBand NDR.",
    ),
)


Adding a grid profile (infrastructure/data/grids.yaml)
Grid profiles capture the carbon intensity, cooling efficiency (PUE), and water usage (WUE) of a datacenter region.
Iceland:
  name: Iceland (Geothermal)
  carbon_intensity_g_kwh: 28
  pue: 1.06
  wue: 0.0
  primary_source: geothermal
  metadata:
    provenance: "@prov:IEA_WEO_2023"






TipBackground reading



The Sustainable AI slide deck covers PUE, WUE, and carbon intensity, the exact quantities that GridProfile captures.

title: Contributing to MLSys·im
text:
5. Writing a Tutorial
The best tutorials teach one insight through one concrete example. Before writing, answer three questions:

What is the one thing the reader will understand after this tutorial?
What would they have guessed incorrectly before reading it?
What surprising number will they compute?


Tutorial structure
Follow the pattern established in Hello, Roofline, Geography is a Systems Variable, Two Phases of Inference, and Scaling to 1000 GPUs:
---
title: "Short, specific title"
subtitle: "Payoff sentence: core lesson in 10 words."
---

[2-3 sentence hook: what problem does this solve?]

This tutorial covers:
- [Concept 1]
- [Concept 2]
- [Concept 3]

::: {.callout-tip}
## Background concept
[1-paragraph intuition before any code]
:::

## 1. Setup
[import block -- path hack MUST be hidden with #| echo: false]

## 2. First Example
[minimal working code + output]

## 3-N. Build Understanding
[progressive complexity, callouts explaining surprising results]

## Next Steps
[2-3 links to related content]


Code style in tutorials

Use clean imports: Start with import mlsysim. The package is pip install-ed in the docs build environment (see .github/workflows/mlsysim-preview-dev.yml), so no path manipulation is needed.
Use Zoo entries: Pull from mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100, mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B, etc.; tutorial code contains no hardcoded constants
Print with units: Always use pint’s ~ format spec: f"{value.to('ms'):~.2f}"
Comment sparingly: Code should be readable without comments; add a callout if explanation is needed



Linking to slide decks
When a tutorial covers a topic that has an existing slide deck, link to the deck so readers can deepen their understanding. Relevant slide decks for common tutorial topics:



Tutorial topic
Slide deck




Roofline analysis
Hardware Acceleration


Benchmarking & MFU
Benchmarking, Performance Engineering


LLM serving (TTFT/ITL)
Model Serving, Inference at Scale


Distributed training
Model Training, Distributed Training


Collective communication
Collective Communication


Fault tolerance
Fault Tolerance


Sustainability & carbon
Sustainable AI


Model compression
Model Compression


Network architectures
Network Architectures

title: Contributing to MLSys·im
text:
6. Adding or Improving a Solver
MLSys·im ships 32 analytical solvers (see mlsysim.solvers), each grounded in peer-reviewed literature. All inherit from the 3-Tier base classes (ForwardModel, BaseSolver, BaseOptimizer) and implement solve(**kwargs). The six foundational ones:








Solver
What it computes
Key references




SingleNodeModel
Roofline bounds, MFU/HFU
Williams et al. (2009)


DistributedModel
3D/4D parallelism, all-reduce, pipeline bubbles
Shoeybi et al. (2019), Narayanan et al. (2019)


ReliabilityModel
MTBF, failure probability, Young-Daly checkpointing
Young (1974), Daly (2006)


SustainabilityModel
Energy, carbon, water (PUE, WUE)
Patterson et al. (2021)


EconomicsModel
CapEx, OpEx, TCO
Barroso et al. (2018)


ServingModel
TTFT, ITL, KV-cache pressure
Pope et al. (2023), Patel et al. (2024), Agrawal et al. (2024)









TipBackground reading



The Performance Engineering and Distributed Training slide decks cover the analytical models (roofline, all-reduce cost, pipeline bubbles) that the solvers implement.



Solver contribution checklist

Place canonical equations in mlsysim/physics/: every solver equation must be independently callable and unit-tested
Inherit from BaseSolver and implement solve(**kwargs) -> dict
Use pint units throughout: all inputs and outputs must carry physical units
Cite the source paper in a docstring on the solver class
Add tests (e.g. in tests/test_solver_invariants.py or a new test file) covering at least one known-good result from the paper
Document the solver by adding a page under docs/api/



Example: extending a solver
All formulas live in mlsysim/physics/ so they can be tested in isolation:
# In mlsysim/mlsysim/physics/
def ring_allreduce_time(message_bytes, num_nodes, bandwidth):
    """Ring all-reduce latency: 2(N-1)/N * M/B.

    Reference: Thakur et al. (2005), "Optimization of Collective
    Communication Operations in MPICH."
    """
    return 2 * (num_nodes - 1) / num_nodes * message_bytes / bandwidth

7. Running Tests
Before submitting a pull request, ensure the test suite passes:
# Install development dependencies
pip install -e ".[dev]"

# Run the full test suite (from the mlsysim package root)
pytest tests/ -v

# Run a specific test file
pytest tests/test_solver_invariants.py -v
Key areas of the test suite:







Test file
What it validates

Single-node inference, OOM exceptions, precision switching


test_hardware.py
Registry access, ridge point calculation, JSON serialization

Solver behavior and the public mlsysim.solvers surface


test_empirical.py
Empirical validation against published numbers


test_registry_loader_contract.py / test_constants_allowlist.py
YAML loader contract and the retired-constants gate

8. Submitting a Pull Request

Fork the repository on GitHub
Create a branch with a descriptive name: git checkout -b feat/add-b200-hardware
Make the changes following the patterns in this guide
Run tests to confirm nothing is broken
Open a PR against the dev branch with:

A clear description of what changed and why
A link to the source document for any new spec values
Output showing the change working (python -c "..." snippet)

title: Contributing to MLSys·im
text:
9. Architecture Overview
Knowing the module layout makes it easier to find the right file to edit.
mlsysim/
  core/
    constants.py    # Retired shim: re-exports units only (CI allowlist enforced)
    loader.py       # YAML loading, duplicate-key checks, registry generation
    provenance.py   # Sourced values and provenance helpers
    registry/       # Base Registry pattern
    types.py        # Shared schema types
    units.py        # Unit registry and exported Pint units
  engine/           # Solvers, scenario evaluation, calibration, explainers
  physics/          # Canonical calc_* implementations (roofline, all-reduce, TCO, …)
  hardware/data/    # Hardware.* YAML zoo
  models/data/      # Models.* YAML zoo
  datasets/data/    # Datasets.* YAML zoo
  systems/registry.py    # Systems.Nodes / Racks / Fabrics / Clusters / Storage / Pods
  infrastructure/   # Infrastructure.* grids and pricing
  scenarios/        # Runnable Scenarios.* bundles and ReferenceStats.* anchors
  platforms/registry.py  # Platforms.* zoo
  tests/            # pytest suite (includes registry migration gates)
  examples/         # Standalone scripts
  docs/             # Quarto documentation site

title: Contributing to MLSys·im
text:
Community Standards
MLSys·im is a pedagogical tool used in courses at Harvard and beyond. Contributions should:

Prioritize accuracy over completeness: a wrong spec is worse than a missing one
Cite sources: every number needs a URL to an official datasheet or peer-reviewed paper
Explain the analytical reasoning: a tutorial that teaches why is better than one that shows how
Use units everywhere: pint prevents dimensional errors; do not bypass it with raw floats

Every contribution makes MLSys·im more accurate and more useful for the next generation of ML systems engineers.

title: The MLSys·im Philosophy
text:
MLSys·im was built to solve a specific problem in machine learning systems education and engineering: the gap between abstract intuition and cycle-accurate simulation.
When reasoning about ML infrastructure, whether sizing a serving fleet for LLaMA-3 or estimating the carbon footprint of a 10,000-GPU training run, engineers often rely on spreadsheets filled with hidden assumptions, unit-conversion errors, and unexplained constants. Conversely, cycle-accurate simulators require weeks of setup, deep proprietary knowledge, and hours to run a single workload.
MLSys·im provides a third path: First-Principles Analytical Modeling.
The framework follows four design principles.

title: The MLSys·im Philosophy
text:
1. Every Number Has a Source
A language model asked to “estimate the latency of ResNet-50 on an A100” will return a number, but it has no source for it and the number is often wrong.
MLSys·im computes every estimate from stated equations and sourced inputs.






%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%%
flowchart LR
    A[<b>Primary Source</b><br/><i>Datasheet / Paper</i>] -->|provenance| B(<b>Registry</b><br/><i>e.g., Hardware.Cloud.H100</i>)
    B -->|Sourced Value<br/>+ SI Units| C{<b>Solver Engine</b>}
    C --> D[<b>Trusted Estimate</b><br/><i>No Unexplained Constants</i>]

    style A fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#cbd5e1
    style B fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#94a3b8
    style C fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0284c7,stroke-width:2px
    style D fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#10b981






Every number in the MLSys·im ecosystem is mathematically derived from explicit, vetted constants. If a solver needs the memory bandwidth of an H100 GPU, it does not use a hardcoded float 3000.0. It queries the Hardware registry, which returns a Sourced object containing 3.35 TB/s, complete with a Provenance struct linking directly to the NVIDIA H100 datasheet.
If a student or engineer asks, “Where did this number come from?”, the framework provides the exact URL, the academic paper, or the empirical methodology used to derive it. No unexplained constants are hidden in the source code.

title: The MLSys·im Philosophy
text:
2. Dimensional Strictness (SI Units Everywhere)
The most common source of error in back-of-the-envelope systems analysis is unit mismatch (e.g., dividing gigabytes by gigabits per second without a factor of 8).
To physically prevent these errors, MLSys·im enforces strict dimensional analysis at runtime using the pint unit library.

A workload of 140 GB (Llama-2 70B in FP16) is represented with explicit units (ureg.GB), not as a bare number.
A network link of 400 Gbps (InfiniBand NDR) is represented with explicit units (ureg.Gbps), not as a bare number.
If a user accidentally attempts to add a latency (ms) to a throughput (1/s), the Python interpreter will instantly raise a DimensionalityError.

By forcing every input, intermediate variable, and output to carry physical SI units, the framework rejects any calculation whose units do not match.

title: The MLSys·im Philosophy
text:
3. Analytical Speed over Cycle-Accurate Simulation
MLSys·im is an analytical engine, not a discrete-event simulator.
We do not track individual packets across a network switch, nor do we simulate warp-scheduler occupancies inside a GPU streaming multiprocessor. Instead, we use closed-form equations (like the Roofline model, the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) communication model, and Erlang-C queueing theory) to establish the hard physical bounds of a system.
By relying on analytical math (\(Y = f(X)\)): * Evaluation is instantaneous: A full-stack analysis of a 100,000-GPU cluster takes less than 0.3 seconds on a standard laptop. * Bottlenecks are explicit: Closed-form equations make it easy to take gradients (Sensitivity Analysis) or invert an equation to find the required hardware (Synthesis Analysis). * Intuition is preserved: Analytical models expose why a system behaves as it does (e.g., comparing the H100 to the A100 shows that FP16 peak compute rises 3.2× from 312 to 989 TFLOP/s while HBM bandwidth rises 1.6× from 2.04 to 3.35 TB/s, shifting the ridge point from 153 to 295 FLOP/byte), whereas detailed simulations only show that a workload is slow.
To bridge the gap between theoretical peaks and realized performance, MLSys·im introduces a single, explicit Efficiency Coefficient (\(\eta\)) into compute-bound solvers (such as MFU). This clearly separates the raw physics of the hardware from the software friction of the framework.

title: The MLSys·im Philosophy
text:
4. Separation of Demand and Supply
A recurring anti-pattern in systems modeling is tightly coupling a model to the hardware it runs on (e.g., writing a script specifically for “GPT-3 on A100”).
MLSys·im enforces a strict Demand vs. Supply abstraction:






%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%%
flowchart TB
    subgraph Demand["<b>Demand (Workloads)</b>"]
        direction TB
        W["<i>Transformer / CNN</i><br/>Parameters & FLOPs"]
    end

    subgraph Supply["<b>Supply (Hardware & Systems)</b>"]
        direction TB
        H["<i>Compute & Memory</i><br/>TFLOP/s & Bandwidth"]
    end

    Demand -->|Lower to graph| S["<b>Solvers (Layer E)</b>"]
    Supply -->|Physical Constraints| S
    S --> R["<b>Analytical Prediction</b><br/><i>Latency, Bottleneck, Cost</i>"]

    style Demand fill:#fef08a,stroke:#d97706
    style Supply fill:#ddd6fe,stroke:#7c3aed
    style S fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0284c7,stroke-width:2px







Demand (Workloads): A TransformerWorkload only knows about its parameters, sequence length, and arithmetic intensity. It has no concept of what a GPU is.
Supply (Hardware/Systems): A HardwareNode only knows about its peak TFLOP/s, memory hierarchy, and power draw. It has no concept of what a Transformer is.

Demand and supply meet in the Solvers (Layer E). A solver takes the abstract Demand, maps it onto the physical Supply, and applies the governing equations to predict the outcome.
Because of this decoupling, a workload defined once can be swept instantly across every hardware device in the Silicon Zoo, from a 1-Watt microcontroller to a 100-MegaWatt supercomputer.

title: The MLSys·im Philosophy
text:
Conclusion
MLSys·im is the executable companion to the Machine Learning Systems textbook. It replaces informal estimates and ad hoc spreadsheets with a composable tool that checks units and states its equations.
When MLSys·im reports that a system will bottleneck on memory bandwidth, an engineer can trust the math, check the units, and audit the datasheets.

title: Accuracy & Validation
text: MLSys·im is a first-order analytical model. It predicts performance from closed-form equations, not from cycle-accurate simulation or empirical measurement. This page documents where those predictions are accurate, where they diverge, and what drives the gap.

title: Accuracy & Validation
text:
Design Philosophy
MLSys·im follows the same trade-off that Hennessy & Patterson’s MIPS simulator made for computer architecture: give up cycle accuracy to cover more kinds of system and to run faster. A gem5 simulation of a single LLaMA-70B inference step can take hours; MLSys·im solves it in milliseconds. The goal is not to replace empirical benchmarks but to enable rapid, principled reasoning about system design trade-offs before committing to expensive experiments.
This philosophy maps directly to the core analytical models in the Math Foundations page. Each model implements a specific approximation grounded in published research, with a characterized accuracy envelope documented below.

title: Accuracy & Validation
text:
Validation Hardening Checklist
The implementation now enforces strict precision names, explicit unit-family validation, and exact distributed topology divisibility before solver math runs. The remaining validation work is about evidence quality rather than basic input safety:

Golden textbook examples. Preserve representative chapter calculations as small, named regression tests with expected values and tolerances. This catches drift when formulas or registry specs change.
Formula-by-formula solver review. For each solver, document the source equation, assumptions, units, and calibration constants next to a focused test fixture. Start with DistributedModel, ServingModel, TrainingMemoryModel, EconomicsModel, and SustainabilityModel.
Registry provenance audit. Check every hardware, model, system, and infrastructure entry for source URL, SKU/variant specificity, verified date, and whether the value is measured, estimated, illustrative, or conventional.
Empirical calibration refresh. Re-run the benchmark comparisons in empirical-calibration.md against current registry values and current published benchmark reports. Published benchmark scalar values live in Literature.Benchmarks; the code contract for reviewed sanity ranges lives in mlsysim.engine.empirical.
Property and edge-case tests. Add invariants such as monotonic memory growth with sequence length, non-increasing feasible batch size with model size, non-negative latency components, and stable unit conversions across SI/binary byte units.
CLI plan semantics cleanup. hardware.accelerators is the total accelerator count. Use node_count plus accelerators_per_node when the physical topology matters.
Solver module decomposition. Solver implementations now live in engine/solvers/ by domain, while mlsysim.solvers is the stable public import path; the export list derives mechanically from engine/solvers/__init__.py, so the two cannot drift.

title: Accuracy & Validation
text:
The Accuracy Hierarchy
MLSys·im predictions differ in how far they can be trusted. The table below ranks prediction types from most to least accurate.








Prediction Type
Typical Accuracy
Why




KV-cache sizing
Exact
Definitional formula, not approximated


Checkpoint sizing
Exact
Direct calculation: \(N \times \text{bytes\_per\_param}\)


Training memory components
Exact for state tensors; approximate for activations
Weights, gradients, and optimizer states are direct byte counts; activation memory follows checkpointing coefficients


Bottleneck classification (compute vs. memory)
>95% correct
The roofline ridge point is a structural property of the hardware


Relative configuration ranking (which config is faster?)
>90% correct
Errors cancel when comparing two configurations on the same hardware


Scaling efficiency direction (how does MFU change with DP/TP/PP?)
±10% on MFU
Communication models are bandwidth-optimal lower bounds


Single-node throughput (absolute latency)
±15–30%
Sensitive to the efficiency parameter η


Serving replica count
Directionally useful
Composes roofline, batching capacity, and M/M/c queueing; validate final SLAs empirically


TCO and carbon estimates
±20%
Dominated by PUE and grid carbon intensity assumptions


ITL in production serving
−25% to −50%
Missing KV-cache paging, batch scheduling, and quantization kernel overhead









TipThe golden rule



Trust MLSys·im for direction and classification. Be cautious with absolute numbers. The model identifies which resource is the bottleneck and which configuration is better. It does not promise the exact millisecond.

WarningITL underprediction is expected



MLSys·im predicts the roofline lower bound for inter-token latency. It does not model quantization kernel overhead, KV-cache paging latency (PagedAttention), or batch scheduling overhead in production serving systems. Real ITL is typically 1.5–2× the roofline bound. Use ITL predictions as the theoretical floor, not as a production estimate.
For the full treatment of serving-system overheads (continuous batching, PagedAttention, SLO compliance), see the Inference at Scale slides (Vol II, Ch 10).



Interpreting the error column
All errors are relative to the measured value: \(\text{Error} = (\text{Predicted} - \text{Measured}) / \text{Measured}\). For latency, a positive error means MLSys·im overpredicts latency (conservative), and a negative error means it underpredicts (optimistic). Overprediction on latency is safer for capacity planning; underprediction is dangerous for SLA commitments.

title: Accuracy & Validation
text:
Where MLSys·im is Most Accurate

Bottleneck classification (roofline)
The model is most reliable for determining which resource limits performance. If MLSys·im predicts a memory bottleneck, the actual workload will almost always be memory-bound too, even if the exact latency differs. This classification is typically >95% correct across documented workloads because the roofline ridge point is a structural property of the hardware that does not depend on software efficiency.
The underlying roofline model is documented in the Hardware Acceleration slides (Vol I, Ch 11) and applied to real H100 workloads in the Compute Infrastructure slides (Vol II, Ch 2).


Scaling efficiency direction (distributed training)
The model correctly predicts how scaling efficiency changes as the DP/TP/PP configuration varies. The relative ranking of configurations is reliable even when absolute MFU values are off by ±10%. This is because the communication cost models (Ring AllReduce, Tree AllReduce, Hierarchical AllReduce) implement bandwidth-optimal lower bounds from Patarasuk & Mueller (2009), so the relative costs scale correctly.
See the Distributed Training slides (Vol II, Ch 6) for the 3D parallelism framework and scaling efficiency analysis.


KV-cache and checkpoint sizing
The KV-cache formula (\(\text{KV} = 2 \times L \times H_{\text{kv}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times S \times B \times \text{bpe}\)) is definitional, not approximated. It computes the exact number of bytes the K and V tensors occupy. Similarly, checkpoint sizing (\(N \times \text{bytes\_per\_param}\)) is a direct count. Memory feasibility checks (feasible: True/False) are accurate because they compare against the same HBM capacity reported in manufacturer datasheets.


Training memory breakdown
TrainingMemoryModel separates weights, gradients, optimizer state, activations, and communication buffers. The first three terms are direct byte counts from the model size, precision, optimizer, and ZeRO stage. Activations are the approximate term: they depend on the selected checkpointing strategy and use coefficients from transformer activation-recomputation analysis [1]. Treat the model as a memory feasibility and attribution tool: it identifies which term is responsible for pressure, and empirical framework profiling can then refine the activation term for a specific implementation.


Serving capacity planning
ServingCapacityModel is a composition model. It uses ServingModel for TTFT/ITL, ContinuousBatchingModel for per-replica token capacity, and TailLatencyModel for queueing pressure. This is useful for first-pass sizing and sensitivity sweeps: if QPS doubles, or generated length doubles, the model shows how many replicas are implied. Capacity depends on the request-length assumption. By default every request fills max_seq_len, the conservative case; passing mean_request_tokens sizes paged allocation for a workload of shorter, exponentially distributed requests (KV Allocation and Batch Capacity). Do not use the result as a production SLA guarantee. Production serving must still be validated with the target scheduler, traffic mix, batching policy, and percentile measurement.


MoE routing imbalance
MoERoutingModel captures a single effect: hot experts make a top-k MoE behave as though more experts are active, increasing effective active parameters and expert-parallel all-to-all traffic. The routing_imbalance_factor is intentionally exposed. Use 1.0 for balanced routing, then sweep higher values to understand sensitivity. A real router’s load distribution should be measured from token counts per expert and fed back into this parameter.


Carbon and TCO estimates
Sustainability and economics estimates are usually dominated by a few explicit assumptions: PUE, energy price, regional carbon intensity, cluster occupancy, and amortization period. The main source of error is often the assumed PUE (power usage effectiveness), which varies from ~1.12 (hyperscaler) to ~1.58 (coal-region enterprise). The carbon accounting methodology aligns with the lifecycle framework in the Sustainable AI slides (Vol II, Ch 15).

text:
Where MLSys·im Diverges From Measurement








Source of Error
Typical Impact
When It Matters

~37–42% of KV memory
Comparing paging against exact-size or power-of-two contiguous allocators [2]




The efficiency parameter (η)
MLSys·im uses efficiency (η, default 0.5) as a single scalar representing the sustained fraction of peak hardware throughput. This is the largest source of absolute error. The table below provides calibrated ranges from published benchmarks.








Workload Type
Recommended η
Reference




Training (fp16/bf16, Megatron-LM / PaLM)
0.30--0.50
Shoeybi et al. (2019), Chowdhery et al. (2022)


Inference (fp16, vLLM/TRT-LLM)
0.25--0.40
MLPerf Inference, Pope et al. (2023)


Inference (int8, quantized)
0.20–0.40
Community benchmarks


Edge inference (TFLite, ONNX RT)
0.15–0.30
MLPerf Tiny



The default efficiency=0.5 (0.5) models a well-optimized training job on datacenter hardware (sustained reference MFU is 0.40). For inference, pass efficiency=0.35 for more conservative estimates. For edge devices, use efficiency=0.2. All solvers whose compute term depends on η expose it as a parameter; defaults are starting points from the literature and benchmarks, not hidden constants.
Cross-check η against cited bands in the Literature Zoo (Literature.Training.MfuHigh, Literature.Training.MfuInferenceBatched) and engine knobs in mlsysim.engine.calibration.REFERENCE_MFU_SUSTAINED.
For a rigorous treatment of precision engineering and its impact on performance, see the Performance Engineering slides (Vol II, Ch 9).


What is not modeled
MLSys·im deliberately omits the following effects. Each omission is a design decision, not an oversight:

Cache hierarchy behavior. L1/L2/SRAM tiling effects can swing latency by 5–30% for small batch sizes. Modeling them would require operator-level simulation, which conflicts with the goal of millisecond solve times.
NVLink contention under tensor parallelism. For TP ≤ 4 (within a single NVSwitch domain), contention is negligible. For TP > 4 (cross-switch), contention can add 5–15% overhead that MLSys·im does not capture.
Pipeline schedule variants. MLSys·im implements the standard GPipe bubble formula: \(\text{bubble} = (P - 1) / (V \cdot M + P - 1)\). Advanced schedules (zero-bubble, interleaved 1F1B with \(V > 1\)) can reduce bubbles by 10–20% beyond what the formula predicts.
Quantization kernel efficiency. INT8/INT4 kernels achieve a lower fraction of peak throughput than FP16 Tensor Core kernels because of dequantization overhead and less mature compiler support. MLSys·im treats precision as a pure ops-per-byte ratio.
KV allocation dynamics. ServingModel sizes the KV cache densely for a known sequence length. ContinuousBatchingModel compares max-length reservation with paged allocation under an assumed exponential request-length distribution, sized at peak occupancy. It does not model how reserved slots fill over a request’s lifetime, external fragmentation in exact-size or power-of-two contiguous allocators, preemption and swapping, or paged-attention kernel latency. Kwon et al. measure 96.3% of vLLM’s KV memory holding token states, against 20.4% to 38.2% for contiguous pre-allocation [2].

BYTES_FP16














Name
Type
Description





ComputationGraph
Work in FLOPs, resident weight bytes, parameter count, arithmetic intensity in FLOP/byte, and the available layer count.






Equation: F = inference_flops if supplied, otherwise 2 * P_active; W = size_in_bytes(precision) uses P_total; I = F / W.
Assumptions: all expert weights remain resident even when only a subset executes for a token. A declared inference_flops value overrides the active-parameter approximation.
Excludes: expert routing, inter-device dispatch, load imbalance, sparse memory fetch efficiency, attention-context work, and KV state.



Derivation: multiply parameter count by storage width to obtain weight bytes, then divide the declared or approximated work by those bytes. This is a demand-accounting projection; it does not predict device time.



>>> from mlsysim.models.types import SparseTransformerWorkload
>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
>>> model = SparseTransformerWorkload(name='MoE', architecture='moe', parameters=Q_(100, 'count'), active_parameters=Q_(25, 'count'), layers=1, experts=4)
>>> graph = model.lower('fp16')
>>> graph.total_ops == 2 * model.active_parameters.magnitude * Q_(1, 'flop')
True
>>> graph.weight_bytes == model.size_in_bytes('fp16')
True

title: ContactDeadlineScenario

Robotics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/robotics/learning.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A constant-speed drive into site’s latch plate: when the force ramp k v t reaches the tripwire and the limit, when braking can begin, and the time left, at both approaches.


Equation: Linear contact ramp F(t)=stiffness*speed*t; force-limit deadline=force_limit/(stiffness*speed).

Bandwidth is the SoC memory’s peak; the row-conflict time is memory_tech’s t_RP + t_RCD. Addresses interleave across every channel unless one_channel confines the backlog and the read to one, which divides the bandwidth by the channel count (bus width over channel width).

text:
Robotics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/robotics/learning.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
An illustrative linear drive regulating target_force against a surface, in simulation and on hardware, with one stated discrepancy in each reality-gap channel: dynamics (force-rise rate and drive delay), timing (p99 actuation delay against the simulator’s), sensing (range bias and dropout), and appearance (pixel difference hiding a contact-patch shift).


Equation: Target time is force/rise_rate; missed travel is speed times the extra actuation delay.
Assumptions: Constant force-rise rates and approach speed over the compared delay windows.
Excludes: Closed-loop dynamics, statistical fitting of the supplied p99, and coupled reality-gap channels.

title: engine.solvers.mapping
text:
engine.solvers.mapping
Volumetric-map solvers: clearance-query reads, map storage, update traffic, and encoder rate (added 2026-10-20).
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers. The equations live in physics/robotics/perception.py; these models compose them for one stated permission controller, workcell, depth stream, or encoder.





Name
Description




ClearanceQueryModel
Reads a sphere-hull clearance query needs per map representation, against the permission tick’s read budget.


EncoderRateModel
A per-frame encoder of flop_per_frame run at frame_rate, against a peak rate.


HostMapSizingModel
A dense voxel grid of a workcell against a hashed narrow band around its surfaces.


RaymarchTrafficModel
Naive ray-marching map-update traffic f N_rays (d / r) S against a memory bandwidth.





engine.solvers.mapping.ClearanceQueryModel()
Reads a sphere-hull clearance query needs per map representation, against the permission tick’s read budget.
The collision allocation divided among the hulls gives the time per query; SRAM bandwidth over that time, in cells, is the read budget. An occupancy scan reads calc_sphere_scan_cells cells; an octree pays calc_octree_depth dependent reads for each; an ESDF reads the corners of one trilinear interpolation. A snapshot of slab_volume stores V / r^3 cells, and a cell’s center misplaces a point by up to calc_voxel_quantization_error.





Name
Description




solve
Compare map-query reads and storage at each voxel pitch.





engine.solvers.mapping.ClearanceQueryModel.solve(
    tick_rate,
    collision_allocation,
    hulls,
    hull_radius,
    protective_clearance,
    sram_bandwidth,
    esdf_cell_bytes,
    occupancy_cell_bytes,
    map_edge,
    slab_volume,
    pitches,
    trilinear_reads,
    wcet=None,
)
Compare map-query reads and storage at each voxel pitch.

Description

required

required

required

required

required

required

required

Positive storage per occupancy cell, in bytes.
required

required


slab_volume

required

sequence of Quantity
Positive voxel widths in meters. Result rows are keyed by rounded centimeters, so pitches must have distinct keys to retain every row.
required

int
Nonnegative number of corner-cell reads for one ESDF interpolation.
required


wcet
Quantity
Positive reference worst-case execution time, in seconds. If supplied, report allocation divided by this value; no WCET is inferred.
None














Name
Type
Description





ClearanceQueryResult
Tick and per-query times in microseconds, read budgets as counts, and pitch-indexed storage in kilobytes and spatial error in meters. Budget ratios describe this accounting model, not collision safety.






mlsysim.physics.robotics.perception.calc_sphere_scan_cells : Sphere-grid scan count. mlsysim.physics.robotics.perception.calc_octree_depth : Dependent octree levels. mlsysim.physics.robotics.perception.calc_voxel_quantization_error : Cell-center spatial error.



Equation: t_query = collision_allocation / hulls; reads_budget = t_query * sram_bandwidth / esdf_cell_bytes. Dense storage counts slab_volume / pitch**3 cells; octree reads multiply sphere-scan cells by tree depth, while the ESDF reads trilinear_reads corners. Assumptions: one equal time allocation per hull, uniform cubic voxels, fully sustained SRAM bandwidth, and a fixed interpolation read count. Excludes: cache reuse, dependency stalls, tree traversal instructions, scene reconstruction error, and certification of a collision checker.



Derivation: divide time and byte budgets by per-query and per-cell costs; the spatial counts and quantization bound are supplied by the linked sphere-scan, octree-depth, and voxel-quantization functions.



A constructed controller gives each of two hulls half its collision budget.
>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = ClearanceQueryModel().solve(
...     Q_(100, 'Hz'), Q_(2, 'ms'), 2, Q_(0.1, 'm'), Q_(0.05, 'm'),
...     Q_(1, 'GB/s'), Q_(4, 'byte'), Q_(1, 'byte'), Q_(1, 'm'),
...     Q_(1, 'm^3'), [Q_(0.1, 'm')], 8)
>>> result.query_time == Q_(1, 'ms')
True

Name
Description




solve
Compare frame-encoder work demand with an available compute rate.





engine.solvers.mapping.EncoderRateModel.solve(flop_per_frame, frame_rate, peak)
Compare frame-encoder work demand with an available compute rate.











Name
Type
Description
Default




flop_per_frame
Quantity
Nonnegative arithmetic work for one frame, in FLOPs.
required


frame_rate
Quantity
Nonnegative frame arrival rate, in Hz.
required


peak
Quantity
Positive compute capacity, in FLOPs per second. Supply an effective rate instead if utilization losses should already be included.
required














Name
Type
Description





EncoderRateResult
Required and supplied rates in the units of peak, and their ratio. The field shortfall is demand/capacity, not a percentage or latency.






Equation: required = flop_per_frame * frame_rate; shortfall = required / peak. Assumptions: every frame executes the same work, and throughput can be compared with the supplied compute rate. Excludes: memory traffic, queueing, launch overhead, and deadline guarantees.



Derivation: work per frame multiplied by frames per second is work per second; division by supply gives dimensionless capacity demand.



A constructed stream whose demand equals supply has unit demand ratio.
>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = EncoderRateModel().solve(Q_(10, 'flop'), Q_(2, 'Hz'), Q_(20, 'flop/s'))
>>> result.shortfall == 1
True






engine.solvers.mapping.HostMapSizingModel()
A dense voxel grid of a workcell against a hashed narrow band around its surfaces.
Dense storage is V / r^3 voxels; the band of half-width delta around surface area A has volume 2 delta A and fills V_band / (B r)^3 blocks of B^3 voxels each.





Name
Description




solve
Count dense-grid storage and ideal narrow-band block storage.





engine.solvers.mapping.HostMapSizingModel.solve(
    extent,
    pitch,
    voxel_bytes,
    surface_area,
    band_half_width,
    block_edge,
)
Count dense-grid storage and ideal narrow-band block storage.











Name
Type
Description
Default




extent
sequence of Quantity
Three positive workspace side lengths, in meters.
required


pitch
Quantity
Positive cubic voxel width, in meters.
required


voxel_bytes
Quantity
Positive bytes stored per voxel, excluding hash-table metadata.
required


surface_area
Quantity
Positive mapped surface area, in square meters.
required


band_half_width
Quantity
Positive distance stored on each side of the surface, in meters.
required


block_edge
int
Positive voxels per side of each cubic block.
required














Name
Type
Description





HostMapSizingResult
Workspace and band volumes in cubic meters, ideal cell/block counts, dense storage in GB, band storage in MB, and dimensionless ratios. Fractional block counts are retained; memory admission is not checked.






Equation: V = extent[0] * extent[1] * extent[2]; N_dense = V / pitch**3; V_band = 2 * band_half_width * surface_area. N_blocks = V_band / (block_edge * pitch)**3 and each block stores block_edge**3 * voxel_bytes. Assumptions: flat locally independent surface bands, identical voxel payloads, and continuously divisible block occupancy. Excludes: band overlap, workspace clipping, partial-block rounding, hash keys, allocator overhead, and GPU residency constraints.



Derivation: volume divided by cubic-cell volume gives cell count; multiplying a surface area by its two-sided band thickness gives the narrow-band volume used in this geometric approximation.



A constructed cubic workspace exposes the volume accounting directly.
>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = HostMapSizingModel().solve(
...     [Q_(1, 'm')] * 3, Q_(0.1, 'm'), Q_(4, 'byte'),
...     Q_(1, 'm^2'), Q_(0.05, 'm'), 4)
>>> result.workspace_volume == Q_(1, 'm^3')
True

    height_px,
    frame_rate,
    ray_length,

    bandwidth,
)
Estimate uncached voxel-update traffic for a depth-image stream.











Name
Type
Description
Default




width_px
int
Positive image width, in pixels.
required


height_px
int
Positive image height, in pixels.
required


frame_rate
Quantity
Positive depth-frame rate, in Hz.
required


ray_length
Quantity
Nonnegative traversed distance per ray, in meters.
required


pitch
Quantity
Positive distance between ray samples, in meters.
required


bytes_per_step
Quantity
Nonnegative bytes transferred per ray sample, in bytes.
required


bandwidth
Quantity
Positive available memory bandwidth, in bytes per second.
required














Name
Type
Description





RaymarchTrafficResult
Ray count per frame, steps per ray, traffic in GB/s, and traffic divided by available bandwidth. A share above one identifies a bandwidth deficit under the stated access model.






Equation: rays = width_px * height_px; steps = ray_length / pitch; traffic = frame_rate * rays * steps * bytes_per_step. Assumptions: every pixel emits one equal-length ray and every step causes the supplied byte transfer. Fractional step counts are retained. Excludes: repeated-voxel reuse, culling, empty-space skipping, compression, contention with other clients, and integer step rounding.



Derivation: multiply frames per second, rays per frame, steps per ray, and bytes per step; the units reduce to bytes per second.



Doubling the constructed frame rate doubles the traffic.
>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> model = RaymarchTrafficModel()
>>> args = (2, 2, Q_(1, 'Hz'), Q_(1, 'm'), Q_(0.1, 'm'),
...         Q_(4, 'byte'), Q_(1, 'GB/s'))
>>> first = model.solve(*args)
>>> second = model.solve(*args[:2], args[2] * 2, *args[3:])
>>> second.traffic == first.traffic * 2
True

title: solvers.BatchingOptimizer
text:
solvers.BatchingOptimizer()
Finds the maximum batch size that satisfies a P99 latency SLA.
Searches the continuous batching design space using an M/M/c queueing model to find the optimal balance between throughput and tail latency.





Name
Description




solve
Determine the maximum batch size that satisfies a P99 latency SLA.





solvers.BatchingOptimizer.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    seq_len,
    sla_latency_ms,
    arrival_rate_qps,
    num_replicas=1,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
    max_search_batch=256,
)
Determine the maximum batch size that satisfies a P99 latency SLA.
Exhaustively scans batch sizes 1..max_search_batch. For each candidate b, the per-batch service latency is TTFT + ITL * seq_len from ServingModel, and the batch arrival rate is arrival_rate_qps / b (requests are grouped into batches). Among feasible candidates the largest batch wins by the chosen objective; this is not a separate optimization of saturation throughput.

title: KernelFusionScenario
text:
Optimization scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/optimization.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A chain of chain_length element-wise operations, run as one kernel each or fused into one.
Unfused, every operation reads its input from device memory and writes its output back (two trips each) and pays dispatch plus launch; fused, the chain reads once, keeps intermediates on chip, writes once, and pays one launch. For N elements of b bytes the traffic is 2kNb against 2Nb.


Equation: Unfused traffic makes 2*k whole-array trips; fused traffic makes two while launch count falls from k to one.
Assumptions: All intermediates fit on chip and the complete chain can be fused.
Excludes: Register pressure, extra arithmetic, occupancy changes, and end-to-end speedup prediction.



Derivation: Separate kernels write each intermediate to memory and read it for the next operation, giving two whole-array transfers per operation. A fused chain retains intermediates on chip and transfers only its external input/output, while paying one dispatch/launch pair.



>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> s = Scenarios.ElementwisePairFusion
>>> s.traffic_ratio == s.chain_length
True

title: OperationalLoadScenario
text:
Economics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/economics.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
Assumed operational-load shapes for N models: alerts a N, deployments N ln N, and pairwise conflicts c N^2 against one team’s team_capacity.
The shapes are a sketch, not measurements; crossing_models is the first model count whose total reaches the capacity.


Equation: The constructed load is a*n + n*ln(n) + c*n**2, compared with team_capacity on an integer grid.
Assumptions: Common abstract work units and a capacity crossing within 1..max_models.
Excludes: Empirical staffing forecasts and confidence intervals; if no crossing exists the current argmax selection returns the first grid point.



Derivation: The linear alert term, n*ln(n) deployment term, and quadratic conflict term are deliberately constructed workload shapes, not fitted laws. Adding them is meaningful only because the caller places them in common work units; the integer grid then locates a crossing of the supplied team capacity.



>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> s = Scenarios.OperationalLoadSketch
>>> len(s.model_counts()) == s.max_models
True

title: engine.solvers.harness
text:
engine.solvers.harness
Agent-harness solvers: what the runtime holds, shares, and admits (added 2026-10-20).
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers. Each model is arithmetic on stated inputs: approval escrow sized by Little’s law, weighted deficit round-robin between request classes, bounded-liability admission of the next model call, one trajectory metered against its budget vector, and call or step ceilings read from public agent runs. None models a particular serving engine, provider quota, or queueing burst.





Name
Description




ApprovalEscrowModel
What approval escrow holds for a long-running workload and an urgent one.


BoundedLiabilityAdmissionModel
Bounded-liability admission of the next model call, against a check of settled spend.


DeficitRoundRobinModel
Weighted deficit round-robin between backlogged request classes.


TrajectoryBudgetMeterModel
One append-only trajectory metered against a budget vector of turns, tokens, time, and dollars.





engine.solvers.harness.ApprovalEscrowModel()
What approval escrow holds for a long-running workload and an urgent one.
Little’s law gives the trajectories waiting for a decision, L = lambda W. For the repair workload each keeps its workspace lease, so escrow binds on retained memory; for the remediation workload fewer than one waits, and the decision binds on time to mitigate, T = diagnose + decide + apply. Means only: bursts and batch review hold more for as long as they last.





Name
Description




solve
Estimate retained workspaces and remediation delay during approval.





engine.solvers.harness.ApprovalEscrowModel.solve(
    repair_rate,
    repair_wait,
    lease,
    remediation_rate,
    diagnosis,
    remediation_wait,
    apply_verify,
)
Estimate retained workspaces and remediation delay during approval.











Name
Type
Description
Default




repair_rate
Quantity
Nonnegative repair arrivals per unit time.
required


repair_wait
Quantity
Mean nonnegative approval waiting time per repair.
required


lease
Quantity
Memory retained by each waiting repair, convertible to GiB.
required


remediation_rate
Quantity
Nonnegative remediation arrivals per unit time.
required


diagnosis
Quantity
Diagnosis duration, convertible to minutes.
required


remediation_wait
Quantity
Mean remediation approval wait, convertible to minutes.
required


apply_verify
Quantity
Application and verification duration, convertible to minutes.
required














Name
Type
Description





ApprovalEscrowResult
Mean counts held, retained memory in GiB, mitigation time in minutes, and dimensionless approval share of mitigation time.






Equation: held = repair_rate * repair_wait; retained = held * lease. Mitigation time is diagnosis + remediation_wait + apply_verify. Assumptions: stationary mean arrivals and waits, one lease per repair, and positive total mitigation duration. Excludes: bursts, batching of reviews, lease sharing, and queue transients.



Derivation: Little’s occupancy identity multiplies arrival rate by mean residence time. Retained memory multiplies occupancy by memory per resident. The mitigation phases are disjoint durations and therefore add.



>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = ApprovalEscrowModel().solve(Q_(2, '1/hour'), Q_(1, 'hour'),
...     Q_(3, 'GiB'), Q_(1, '1/hour'), Q_(1, 'minute'),
...     Q_(2, 'minute'), Q_(1, 'minute'))
>>> result.retained_memory.m_as('GiB') == 6
True






engine.solvers.harness.BoundedLiabilityAdmissionModel()
Bounded-liability admission of the next model call, against a check of settled spend.
A spend check admits when the call’s liability fits allowance - settled. The reservation test admits only when settled spend, outstanding reservations, the call’s liability, and the protected finalization reserve together fit the allowance. Liability prices every input token at the undiscounted rate and the whole output allowance (calc_bounded_liability). Dollars throughout.





Name
Description




solve
Reserve the next call’s maximum token charge before admitting it.

    allowance,
    settled,
    reserved,
    finalization_reserve,
    input_tokens,
    output_allowance,
    input_price,
    output_price,
    probe,
)
Reserve the next call’s maximum token charge before admitting it.











Name
Type
Description
Default

required

Quantity

required

Quantity

required

Quantity

required

required

int

required

required

required

Quantity

required














Name
Type
Description





BoundedLiabilityAdmissionResult
Dollar liabilities and headrooms as floats, admission booleans, token ceilings, and dimensionless spending shares.






Equation: liability = input_tokens * input_price + output_allowance * output_price. Headroom = allowance - settled - reserved - finalization_reserve. Admission requires liability <= headroom. Assumptions: prices are fixed, all input is undiscounted, and output cannot exceed its allowance. Negative headroom represents an exhausted budget. Excludes: tool fees, taxes, provider rounding, and reconciliation of actual bills.



Derivation: reserve each token’s maximum charge before spending. Subtract settled, outstanding, and protected amounts from the same budget once each.



>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = BoundedLiabilityAdmissionModel().solve(Q_(10, 'USD'),
...     Q_(2, 'USD'), Q_(3, 'USD'), Q_(1, 'USD'), 100, 100,
...     Q_(0.01, 'USD/token'), Q_(0.01, 'USD/token'), Q_(1, 'USD'))
>>> result.admitted and result.headroom == 4
True






engine.solvers.harness.DeficitRoundRobinModel()
Weighted deficit round-robin between backlogged request classes.
Each round a class earns w q charge units and spends c per call (input tokens plus the full output allowance), carrying unspent credit forward. Weights fix the token-charge shares, w / sum(w); the call shares follow w q / c and so depend on call size. A direct simulation of rounds rounds checks the long-run formula.





Name
Description




solve
Compare token-charge shares and call shares under deficit round-robin.





engine.solvers.harness.DeficitRoundRobinModel.solve(quantum, classes, rounds)
Compare token-charge shares and call shares under deficit round-robin.











Name
Type
Description
Default




quantum
float
Positive token-charge credit allocated per unit weight per round.
required


classes
Mapping[str, Mapping[str, float]]
Backlogged classes, each with positive weight and nonnegative input and output token charges. Their sum must be positive.
required


rounds
int
Positive number of simulated rounds, sufficient to serve a call.
required














Name
Type
Description





DeficitRoundRobinResult
Credit and token charges, calls per round, rounds per call, dimensionless limiting shares, and finite-run simulated shares.






Equation: calls_per_round = weight * quantum / (input + output). Charge share is weight / sum(weights); call share normalizes calls_per_round. Assumptions: permanently backlogged classes, fixed per-call charge, and credit carried between rounds without a cap. Excludes: arrival processes, variable output length, latency, and GPU capacity.



Derivation: each round adds weight times quantum credit and each completed call consumes its input-plus-output charge. Dividing credit by charge gives the long-run call rate; the loop retains integer-call residual credit.



>>> result = DeficitRoundRobinModel().solve(10,
...     {'short': {'weight': 1, 'input': 5, 'output': 5},
...      'long': {'weight': 1, 'input': 10, 'output': 10}}, 4)
>>> result.call_ratio == 2
True






engine.solvers.harness.TrajectoryBudgetMeterModel()
One append-only trajectory metered against a budget vector of turns, tokens, time, and dollars.
With prefix reuse every turn’s earlier prompt is billed at the cached rate and only the newly appended tokens (and the whole first prompt) at the input rate; without reuse every input token is billed uncached. The token meter counts cached input in full, so only the dollar meter sees a cache miss. Each used fraction is used / allowance; the leading meter is the largest.

Description

engine.solvers.harness.ApprovalEscrowModel()
What approval escrow holds for a long-running workload and an urgent one.
Little’s law gives the trajectories waiting for a decision, L = lambda W. For the repair workload each keeps its workspace lease, so escrow binds on retained memory; for the remediation workload fewer than one waits, and the decision binds on time to mitigate, T = diagnose + decide + apply. Means only: bursts and batch review hold more for as long as they last.

)

ApprovalEscrowResult
Mean counts held, retained memory in GiB, mitigation time in minutes, and dimensionless approval share of mitigation time.






Equation: held = repair_rate * repair_wait; retained = held * lease. Mitigation time is diagnosis + remediation_wait + apply_verify. Assumptions: stationary mean arrivals and waits, one lease per repair, and positive total mitigation duration. Excludes: bursts, batching of reviews, lease sharing, and queue transients.



Derivation: Little’s occupancy identity multiplies arrival rate by mean residence time. Retained memory multiplies occupancy by memory per resident. The mitigation phases are disjoint durations and therefore add.



>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = ApprovalEscrowModel().solve(Q_(2, '1/hour'), Q_(1, 'hour'),
...     Q_(3, 'GiB'), Q_(1, '1/hour'), Q_(1, 'minute'),
...     Q_(2, 'minute'), Q_(1, 'minute'))
>>> result.retained_memory.m_as('GiB') == 6
True

Equation: liability = input_tokens * input_price + output_allowance * output_price. Headroom = allowance - settled - reserved - finalization_reserve. Admission requires liability <= headroom. >>> result.admitted and result.headroom == 4
True






engine.solvers.harness.DeficitRoundRobinModel()
Weighted deficit round-robin between backlogged request classes.
Each round a class earns w q charge units and spends c per call (input tokens plus the full output allowance), carrying unspent credit forward. Weights fix the token-charge shares, w / sum(w); the call shares follow w q / c and so depend on call size. A direct simulation of rounds rounds checks the long-run formula.

Description

Type

Default

required

Name
Type
Description





DeficitRoundRobinResult
Credit and token charges, calls per round, rounds per call, dimensionless limiting shares, and finite-run simulated shares.






Equation: calls_per_round = weight * quantum / (input + output). Charge share is weight / sum(weights); call share normalizes calls_per_round. Assumptions: permanently backlogged classes, fixed per-call charge, and credit carried between rounds without a cap. Excludes: arrival processes, variable output length, latency, and GPU capacity.



Derivation: each round adds weight times quantum credit and each completed call consumes its input-plus-output charge. Dividing credit by charge gives the long-run call rate; the loop retains integer-call residual credit.



>>> result = DeficitRoundRobinModel().solve(10,
...     {'short': {'weight': 1, 'input': 5, 'output': 5},
...      'long': {'weight': 1, 'input': 10, 'output': 10}}, 4)
>>> result.call_ratio == 2
True

title: solvers.ZeroFailureModel
text:
solvers.ZeroFailureModel()
Upper bound on the per-trial failure rate after a failure-free campaign.
Poisson (rule of three):  p_upper = -ln(1 - C) / n
exact binomial:           p_upper = 1 - (1 - C)^(1/n)
With target_rate, also the clean trials that bound the rate at the target: ceil(ln(1 - C) / ln(1 - target)), and its rule-of-three estimate -ln(1 - C) / target (exact form and target added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




solve
Upper bound on the per-trial failure rate after a failure-free campaign.





solvers.ZeroFailureModel.solve(trials, confidence, target_rate=None)
Upper bound on the per-trial failure rate after a failure-free campaign.











Name
Type
Description
Default




trials
int
Positive number of independent failure-free trials.
required


confidence
float
One-sided confidence level in (0, 1).
required


target_rate
Optional[float]
Optional target per-trial failure probability in (0, 1).
None














Name
Type
Description





ZeroFailureResult
Dimensionless approximate/exact failure bounds and trial counts; optional target counts are None when no target is supplied.






Equation: For n trials and confidence C, approximate upper failure probability is -ln(1-C)/n; exact upper probability is 1-(1-C)^(1/n). A target p requires ceil(ln(1-C)/ln(1-p)) failure-free trials.
Assumptions: Independent identically distributed Bernoulli trials; approximate rate uses the zero-event Poisson bound.
Excludes: Nonstationarity, correlated failures, and proof of absence of failures.



Derivation: For independent Bernoulli trials, the probability of zero failures is (1-p)^n. Invert this probability at tail mass 1-C to obtain the exact one-sided bound. Replacing ln(1-p) by -p yields the Poisson approximation; see mlsysim.physics.robotics.assurance.calc_zero_failure_sample_size.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_ as Q
>>> ZeroFailureModel().solve(100, 0.95).rate_upper_exact < 1
True

title: ConvLayerScenario
text:
Training scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/training.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
One kernel-by-kernel convolution, stride one, over a height-by-width-by-in_channels input to out_channels feature maps; values of bytes_per_value each.
same_padding keeps the output the size of the input; without it the window stays inside the input (“valid”), as an unpadded unfold does.


Equation: Each output position reuses k*k*Cin*Cout weights; batch FLOPs are twice positions*weights*batch.
Assumptions: Stride one, same or valid padding, and one-pass traffic at the declared precisions.
Excludes: Dilation, groups other than the separate depthwise illustration, workspace, and measured kernel traffic.



Derivation: A convolution filter contains k*k*Cin weights for each output channel. Applying that filter at each output location repeats its MACs without adding new parameters. The separate depthwise-plus-pointwise construction uses one spatial filter per input channel followed by channel mixing.



>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> s = Scenarios.MnistFirstConvLayer
>>> s.variant(batch_size=2*s.batch_size).flops == 2*s.flops
True

title: QuantizedAcceptanceGatesScenario
text:
Statistics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/statistics.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A float model and its quantized copy against acceptance gates set before compression.
Accuracies are percent; ECE is a fraction. Edge cases are edge_share of inputs, so a test_images test set holds edge_share * test_images of them, and the float edge-case accuracy is known only to the binomial half-width at confidence on that count.


Equation: The calculation members below define top1_loss, top5_loss, edge_drop, ece_ratio, edge_images, edge_half_width.
Assumptions: Accuracy inputs use percentage points; subgroup precision uses an independent-binomial normal approximation.
Excludes: Multiple-testing correction, paired disagreement, and certification from point estimates.



Derivation: A float model and its quantized copy against acceptance gates set before compression. Each member records the corresponding algebra or named physics function.

>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> case = Scenarios.MobileNetV2Int8CameraTrapGates
>>> value = case.edge_half_width
>>> print(f"{value:.3g}")
12.9

title: engine.engine.Engine
text:
engine.engine.Engine()
The core analytical engine for single-node Roofline performance modeling.
Maps a (Workload, HardwareNode) pair to a PerformanceProfile by applying the Roofline model: the workload is “lowered” into a hardware-agnostic ComputationGraph, then bounded by the hardware’s compute ceiling and memory bandwidth ceiling.


Compute-dominated training time can be organized as:
Time = FLOPs / (N × Peak_FLOPS × MFU × η_scaling × Goodput)
where N is device count, MFU is Model FLOPs Utilization, η_scaling is scaling efficiency, and Goodput accounts for failures and checkpointing. This accounting view requires mutually consistent definitions of the efficiency factors. Engine.solve evaluates compute and memory bounds on one device; DistributedModel adds fleet coordination terms. Neither this expression nor a single efficiency factor replaces those bounds.
Source: Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Floating-Point Programs and Multicore Architectures.”






Name
Description




solve
Estimate one device’s compute, memory, and capacity limits.


sweep
Evaluate feasible inference configurations over a Cartesian product.

    model,
    hardware,
    batch_size=1,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
    raise_errors=False,
    is_training=False,
    seq_len=2048,
    zero_stage=0,
    dp_size=1,
    is_lora=False,
    activation_recomputation=False,
)

Raise OOMError for a footprint above device capacity. Otherwise retain feasible=False and estimate offload-limited latency.

bool
Include backward work and training state. Inference capacity checks weights only; use ServingModel for KV-aware capacity.

int
ZeRO stage 0, 1, 2, or 3, passed to Transformer training memory.

int
Positive data-parallel count used for ZeRO state sharding. Does not add distributed execution or communication to this solver.
1


is_lora
bool
Use the training-memory adapter approximation. The generic non-Transformer fallback uses a separate 1.1-times-weights heuristic.
False


activation_recomputation
bool
Recompute a forward pass during training: four rather than three forward-equivalent work units, paired with full activation recompute.
False














Name
Type
Description





PerformanceProfile
Modeled batch latency in milliseconds, throughput in samples/s, energy in joules, byte footprint, utilization fractions, selected resource bound, and feasibility trace. A false capacity flag remains false even when an offload-latency estimate is returned.






mlsysim.physics.performance.calc_bottleneck : Compute and memory bounds. mlsysim.solvers.ServingModel : KV-aware prefill and decode estimates. mlsysim.models.types.TransformerWorkload.training_memory : Training state.



Equation: T = max(F_batch / (eta * F_peak), W * (1 + 0.1 * B) / BW) + T_dispatch + L * T_layer * launch_multiplier. Here W is weight bytes, B is batch size, and launch_multiplier is three for training and one for inference. Training work is three forward passes, or four with full recomputation. Throughput is B / T; energy is average_power * T.
Assumptions: activation traffic is the declared 0.1 * W per-sample heuristic, not an architecture trace. Compute and memory bounds overlap ideally. The bandwidth path selects host offload, resident SRAM, flash, or primary memory. Offload charges all traffic at the limiting link rate, not only the spilled fraction. Power is TDP times an idle-plus-HFU model with fractions in engine.calibration; missing TDP yields zero estimated energy. Fixed dispatch and layer taxes are modeling defaults.
Excludes: KV-cache capacity, attention-context work in generic inference, allocator reserve, kernel workspaces, queueing, serving concurrency, and communication between devices. Feasibility is a footprint check, not a deployment guarantee. The bottleneck label compares compute and memory terms; overhead_dominated separately flags a larger additive tax.



Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785 (bibliography key: williams2009). The activation traffic, layer tax, and power coefficients are separate implementation assumptions, not constants established by Roofline.



>>> from mlsysim import Engine, Hardware, Models
>>> result = Engine.solve(Models.Vision.ResNet50, Hardware.Cloud.H100)
>>> result.feasible
True
>>> result.latency >= max(result.latency_compute, result.latency_memory)
True

    model,
    hardware_list,
    batch_sizes=None,
    precisions=None,
    efficiency=0.5,
)

Name
Type
Description
Default




model
Workload
Fixed workload to lower for each device and precision.
required


hardware_list
list of HardwareNode
Devices to evaluate in their supplied order; an empty list gives no results.
required


batch_sizes
list of int
Positive sample counts. None or an empty list uses [1].
None


precisions
list of str
Registered numeric formats. None or an empty list uses [‘fp16’].
None


efficiency
float
Declared compute efficiency in [1e-9, 1], shared by all configurations.
0.5














Name
Type
Description





list of dict
One entry per capacity-feasible combination, containing hardware name, batch_size, precision, and a PerformanceProfile with units. Capacity failures are omitted rather than returned as failed rows.






mlsysim.engine.engine.Engine.solve : Per-configuration model and limits.



Equation: results = [solve(model, h, b, p) for h, b, p in hardware_list x batch_sizes x precisions if the footprint fits]. The latency and energy equations are those of Engine.solve.
Assumptions: every point uses generic inference and the same efficiency; input order determines result order. OOMError alone is caught; invalid parameters and other errors still propagate.
Excludes: training configuration sweeps, optimization, queueing, measured hardware execution, and a record of omitted infeasible configurations. No runtime bound follows from the number of configurations alone.



Derivation: enumeration of the Cartesian product delegates each point to Engine.solve and filters its capacity failures. There is no separate performance equation or cross-configuration scheduling model.



>>> from mlsysim import Engine, Hardware, Models
>>> rows = Engine.sweep(Models.Vision.ResNet50, [Hardware.Cloud.H100], [1, 2])
>>> [row['batch_size'] for row in rows]
[1, 2]
>>> all(row['profile'].feasible for row in rows)
True

Equation: -_math.log(1.0 - confidence) / (rates[event] / 100.0).



engine.scenario_types.RoadExposureScenario.requirements(event)
Supplied zero-failure, precision, and improvement exposure requirements for event, each in millions of miles.
RAND’s three rows for one event class: zero failures, precision, improvement (millions).
Equation: tuple((float(t[event]) for t in (zero_failure, precision, improvement))).



engine.scenario_types.RoadExposureScenario.shortfall(event)
Dimensionless zero-failure exposure requirement divided by the reported fleet exposure for event.
Equation: zero_failure[event] / fleet_miles.

title: core.provenance.Sourced
text:
core.provenance.Sourced()
Scalar with mandatory Provenance. Subclasses float so notebooks and generated calculations can divide and format values without extra coercion.
.. warning:: Provenance does NOT survive arithmetic. Any operation on a Sourced (x * 2, x / y, -x, round(x) …) returns a plain float — Python numeric dunders construct float results, and nothing re-attaches .provenance/.name/.description. (copy.copy raises TypeError because __new__ requires a provenance argument.) The audit trail therefore lives only on the registry leaf value itself. Derived quantities that need their own audit trail must be wrapped explicitly with sourced(derived_value, Provenance(kind=DERIVED, ...)).

Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A training run of run_duration on fleet, on demand against spot capacity.
Spot adds checkpoint_overhead_fraction of the run for checkpoints and restart_per_interruption for each of interruptions_per_day per day of the run.


Equation: spot bill = device count * (useful hours + checkpoint hours + restart hours) * spot price.
Assumptions: The run keeps a fixed fleet. Interruption counts use complete baseline days; restart overhead does not generate more interruptions.

Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A silent click-through regression from ctr_before to ctr_after at request_rate, caught after detection_time; each click is worth value_per_click.


Equation: Exposed requests are rate*time; lost clicks are exposed_requests*(ctr_before-ctr_after).
Assumptions: Constant request rate, click-through rates, and value per click during the delay.
Excludes: Seasonality, click dependence, recovery effects, and causal revenue validation.



Derivation: At constant request rate, the observation window contains rate*time requests. Multiplying by the absolute click-through decrease yields expected lost clicks, and multiplying by value_per_click yields the assumed monetary loss.

title: CertifiedRadiusScenario
text:
Statistics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/statistics.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
Binary randomized smoothing at noise noise_sd, against an l-infinity budget on one input.
The l-infinity budget is linf_levels steps of an image whose pixels take pixel_levels values; its box corner has Euclidean length budget * sqrt(coordinates), the length the certificate must reach to cover the whole box.


Equation: The smoothing helper gives an L2 radius; the L-infinity corner has norm sqrt(coordinates) times its coordinate budget.
Assumptions: The supplied top-class probability is a valid smoothing probability bound under Gaussian noise.
Excludes: Estimating that probability from samples or certifying a different noise distribution.



Derivation: The smoothing helper gives an L2 radius; the L-infinity corner has norm sqrt(coordinates) times its coordinate budget. Individual property contracts identify the exact accounting expression or reusable calculation. Registry entries supply the scenario inputs; this class does not turn them into measured outcomes.



Evaluate a named scenario using its declared inputs.
>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> scenario = Scenarios.SmoothingRadiusCifar10
>>> round(float(scenario.radius), 4)
1.5451

Description

L2 norm of an L-infinity box corner over the declared number of coordinates.


coordinates

Whether the smoothing radius contains the entire L-infinity perturbation box.

linf_levels

physics.statistics.calc_arcsine_two_arm_sample_size(
    effect_h,
    alpha=0.05,
    power=0.8,
)
Plan equal arm sizes using an arcsine effect size.











Name
Type
Description
Default

float
Nonzero dimensionless Cohen h effect size; its sign does not affect sample size.
required

0.05

0.8

Equation: n = ceil(2*((Phi**(-1)(1-alpha/2)+Phi**(-1)(power))/h)**2).
Assumptions: Independent equal-size arms and the large-sample variance approximation for transformed proportions.
Excludes: Exact binomial power, unequal allocation, multiple testing, and input-domain validation.



Cohen (1988), Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, chapter 6. Derivation: Each transformed rate has variance 1/n; solve the two-arm normal power relation with variance 2/n.

Assumptions: Supervised imitation on expert states, bounded per-step cost, and possible persistent state-distribution shift after an error.
Excludes: Task-specific recovery, learned-policy guarantees, and finite-data estimation of epsilon.
Ross and Bagnell (2010), Theorem 2.1: a policy trained only on the demonstrator’s states compounds a per-step error eps quadratically.

Excludes: Verification of Gaussian residuals or covariance calibration, repeated-testing corrections, and bias modeling.



Bar-Shalom, Li, and Kirubarajan (2001), Estimation with Applications to Tracking and Navigation, section 5.4. SciPy chi-square distribution and inverse CDF: https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.chi2.html
