Equation (beta quantiles, alpha = 1 - confidence): lower = B^{-1}(alpha/2; k, n - k + 1) (0 when k = 0) upper = B^{-1}(1 - alpha/2; k + 1, n - k) (1 when k = n)
Source: Clopper and Pearson, “The Use of Confidence or Fiducial Limits Illustrated in the Case of the Binomial,” Biometrika 26(4), 1934.

Central confidence probability in (0, 1).

Lower and upper binomial probability limits.






Equation: Limits are beta quantiles at alpha/2 and 1-alpha/2 with endpoint conventions.
Assumptions: Independent identically distributed Bernoulli trials and fixed sample size.
Excludes: Sequential testing and dependent observations.

Compute the signed arcsine effect size for two proportions.

Default

required

float
Second probability on [0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Dimensionless signed Cohen h; positive when p_high exceeds p_low.






Equation: h = 2*asin(sqrt(p_high)) - 2*asin(sqrt(p_low)).
Assumptions: Probabilities describe comparable binary outcomes.
Excludes: Sampling uncertainty, a test decision, and validation of probability bounds.



Cohen (1988), Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, chapter 6. Derivation: Subtract the two variance-stabilizing arcsine-transformed probabilities.



>>> calc_cohens_h(0.5, 0.5) == 0

Normalize observed agreement relative to chance agreement.

Type
Description
Default

Observed matching-label fraction in [0, 1].
required

float
Chance agreement probability in [0, 1).
required














Name
Type
Description

Dimensionless kappa; negative values indicate agreement below chance.






Equation: kappa = (p_o-p_e)/(1-p_e).
Assumptions: Chance agreement is estimated from suitable annotator marginals.
Excludes: Confidence intervals, weighted ordinal disagreement, and prevalence adjustment.



Derivation: scale observed excess agreement p_o-p_e by the maximum possible excess 1-p_e. Cohen (1960) introduced this agreement coefficient.



>>> calc_cohens_kappa(0.75, 0.5)

physics.statistics.calc_conjunctive_confidence(premise_confidences)
Combine independent premise probabilities by conjunction.











Name
Type
Description
Default




premise_confidences
sequence of float
Nonempty probabilities p_i in [0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Dimensionless probability that every premise holds.






Equation: P(all premises) = product(p_i).
Assumptions: Independent premise events, each necessary for the conclusion.
Excludes: Common-cause dependence and validation of supplied confidence judgments.
Equation: P(claim) = prod_i p_i
The conjunction is no stronger than its weakest premise and, with more than one premise below 1, strictly weaker.
Source: probability of the intersection of independent events, as applied to conjunctive assurance arguments in Bloomfield and Littlewood 2003, “Multi-legged arguments: the impact of diversity upon confidence in dependability arguments” (DSN 2003).



Derivation: repeated multiplication of independent-event intersection probabilities.



>>> calc_conjunctive_confidence([0.5, 0.5])
0.25




physics.statistics.calc_consecutive_detection_frames(
    per_frame_detection,
    all_miss_probability,
)
Find the frame count for an all-miss probability target.
Consecutive frames a person must be in view before detection may be counted on.
Equation: N = ceil( ln p_miss / ln(1 - p_frame) )
the fewest frames for which the chance of missing the person in every one, (1 - p_frame)^N, is at most all_miss_probability, with misses independent from frame to frame (the best case; correlated misses need more frames). A tolerance of 1e-12 keeps an exact ratio from rounding up.











Name
Type
Description
Default




per_frame_detection
float
Detection probability per independent frame, in (0, 1).
required


all_miss_probability
float
Maximum all-miss probability in (0, 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





int
Minimum frame count under the independent-miss model.






Equation: N = ceil(log(all_miss_probability)/log(1-per_frame_detection)-1e-12).
Assumptions: Independent frame misses with a constant detection probability.
Excludes: Temporal correlation and uncertainty in detector performance.



Derivation: Multiply independent miss probabilities and invert the geometric decay.



>>> calc_consecutive_detection_frames(0.5, 0.25) == 2
True




physics.statistics.calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal(
    threshold,
    operational_mean,
    elite_share,
)
Trace population cross-entropy updates for an exponential tail.











Name
Type
Description
Default




threshold
float or Quantity
Positive target failure threshold gamma.
required


operational_mean
float or Quantity
Positive operational mean m0, in threshold units.
required


elite_share
float
Elite proposal fraction beta in (0, 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Levels contains thresholds in input units, n_levels is their count, and proposal_mean is the final mean in input units.






Equation: level_k = min(gamma, -m_k*log(beta)); m_(k+1) = level_k + m0, until level_k reaches gamma.
Assumptions: Population expectations replace empirical elites; the initial proposal mean equals the operational mean.
Excludes: Sampling variability, weight degeneracy, finite-sample stopping, and non-exponential families.
From q_0 = p = Exp(m0), each round sets the level to the (1 - beta) quantile of the current proposal, level = -m_k ln(beta) (capped at the threshold), and refits the proposal mean to the likelihood-weighted elite draws; for this family that is E_p[D | D > level] = level + m0. Stops when the level reaches the threshold, so the final mean is threshold + m0.
Returns a dict with levels (list, in the units of threshold), n_levels, and proposal_mean.
Source: Rubinstein and Kroese, The Cross-Entropy Method (Springer, 2004), multilevel rare-event algorithm; the exponential refit is in closed form.



Derivation: exponential memorylessness gives E[X | X > level] = level + m0; the proposal quantile supplies the next level. Rubinstein and Kroese (2004), The Cross-Entropy Method, motivates multilevel adaptation.



>>> result = calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal(2.0, 1.0, 0.5)
>>> result["levels"][-1] == 2.0 and result["proposal_mean"] == 3.0
True

required

Type

Equation: Excess cost bound = u*S*epsilon.
Assumptions: Expert labels on learner-visited states and a bounded recoverability constant u.
Excludes: Finite-iteration regret terms, policy optimization, and proof that a given system satisfies the assumptions.
Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell (2011), Theorem 3.2: linear in the horizon while the recoverability constant u stays bounded.

physics.statistics.calc_effective_sample_size(n_records, lag1_correlation)
Approximate the independent sample count of an AR(1) mean.











Name
Type
Description
Default




n_records
int or float
Nonnegative number of observations.
required


lag1_correlation
float
Stationary lag-one correlation rho in (-1, 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Effective count under the asymptotic AR(1) variance approximation.






Equation: N_eff = N*(1-rho)/(1+rho).
Assumptions: A stationary AR(1) autocorrelation rho**k and enough records for the infinite-lag approximation.
Excludes: Finite-sample edge corrections, nonstationary drift, and arbitrary dependence.
N_eff = N (1 - rho) / (1 + rho) for estimating the mean of a series whose adjacent records have lag-one correlation rho (Thiebaux and Zwiers 1984).



Derivation: sum 1+2*sum(rho**k, k>=1)=(1+rho)/(1-rho) as the variance inflation of the sample mean; divide N by that inflation.



>>> calc_effective_sample_size(100, 0.0)
100.0




physics.statistics.calc_equal_n_for_z(rate_a, rate_b, z_critical)
Solve the equal-group size for a specified pooled z statistic.

Type
Description
Default

Distinct probabilities on [0, 1] with their mean in (0, 1).
required

Distinct probabilities on [0, 1] with their mean in (0, 1).
required

required

Type

Equation: n = 2*p*(1-p)*(z_critical/(rate_a-rate_b))**2, p = (rate_a+rate_b)/2.
Assumptions: Equal-size independent Bernoulli groups and fixed hypothesized rates.
Excludes: Power beyond reaching a z threshold, rate-estimation uncertainty, and input validation.



Derivation: Rearrange z = gap/sqrt(2*p*(1-p)/n) for n.



>>> n = calc_equal_n_for_z(0.6, 0.4, 2.0)
>>> math.isclose(abs(calc_two_proportion_z(0.6, 0.4, n, n)), 2.0)

physics.statistics.calc_expected_calibration_error(bins)
Compute count-weighted absolute calibration error.
Expected calibration error of binned predictions: sum |B_i| / n * |acc_i - conf_i|.
bins is a sequence of (count, confidence, accuracy); the weight of each bin is its share of the predictions (Pakdaman Naeini et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2017, eq. 3).

Type
Description
Default




bins
sequence
Sequence of (count, confidence, accuracy) triples; rates in [0, 1].
required









Name
Type
Description

Dimensionless weighted absolute probability error.






Equation: ECE = sum(count_i/total * abs(accuracy_i-confidence_i)).
Assumptions: Nonnegative bin counts with positive total; rates on the same probability scale.
Excludes: Bin selection, debiasing, and confidence intervals.



Derivation: Guo et al. (2017), On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks: count-weighted bin accuracy-confidence differences.

True

Fit an exponential rate through two readings.

>>> fit_exponential_growth([0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 10.0])
(10.0, 1.0, 0.0)

physics.statistics.calc_arcsine_two_arm_sample_size(
    effect_h,
    alpha=0.05,
    power=0.8,
)
Plan equal arm sizes using an arcsine effect size.











Name
Type
Description
Default

float
Nonzero dimensionless Cohen h effect size; its sign does not affect sample size.
required

float
Two-sided significance probability in (0, 1); default 0.05.
0.05

Target power probability in (0, 1); default 0.80.
0.8

Type

Required observations per arm, rounded upward.






Equation: n = ceil(2*((Phi**(-1)(1-alpha/2)+Phi**(-1)(power))/h)**2).
Assumptions: Independent equal-size arms and the large-sample variance approximation for transformed proportions.
Excludes: Exact binomial power, unequal allocation, multiple testing, and input-domain validation.



Cohen (1988), Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, chapter 6. Derivation: Each transformed rate has variance 1/n; solve the two-arm normal power relation with variance 2/n.

required














Name
Type

Worst-case excess cumulative cost under normalized per-step costs.






Equation: Excess cost bound = S**2*epsilon.
Assumptions: Supervised imitation on expert states, bounded per-step cost, and possible persistent state-distribution shift after an error.
Excludes: Task-specific recovery, learned-policy guarantees, and finite-data estimation of epsilon.
Ross and Bagnell (2010), Theorem 2.1: a policy trained only on the demonstrator’s states compounds a per-step error eps quadratically.

required

required

required

Assumptions: Caller supplies aligned ordered CDF data; no interpolation is performed.
Excludes: CDF estimation, input normalization, interpolation, and uncertainty intervals.
values ascend with cumulative (a released CDF); past the end the last value is returned.

Type

Equation: p_e = sum(s_k**2).
Assumptions: Annotators independently sample labels from the same marginal distribution.
Excludes: Distinct annotator marginals, label dependence, and estimation uncertainty.
class_shares is each annotator’s label mix (fractions summing to 1); both annotators are assumed to share it.



Derivation: matching on class k has probability s_k*s_k; sum mutually exclusive matches.

required

Type

Equation: gate = F_chi2(dof)**(-1)(confidence).
Assumptions: The normalized squared statistic has a central chi-square distribution with the specified degrees of freedom.
Excludes: Verification of Gaussian residuals or covariance calibration, repeated-testing corrections, and bias modeling.



Bar-Shalom, Li, and Kirubarajan (2001), Estimation with Applications to Tracking and Navigation, section 5.4. SciPy chi-square distribution and inverse CDF: https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.chi2.html

Assumptions: Independent central chi-square statistics with a common dimension d; their sum has N*d degrees of freedom.
Excludes: Serially correlated residuals, estimated effective sample size, and noncentral alternatives.

Equation (beta quantiles, alpha = 1 - confidence): lower = B^{-1}(alpha/2; k, n - k + 1) (0 when k = 0) upper = B^{-1}(1 - alpha/2; k + 1, n - k) (1 when k = n)
Source: Clopper and Pearson, “The Use of Confidence or Fiducial Limits Illustrated in the Case of the Binomial,” Biometrika 26(4), 1934.

Central confidence probability in (0, 1).

Lower and upper binomial probability limits.

Excludes: Sequential testing and dependent observations.

Compute the signed arcsine effect size for two proportions.

Type
Description
Default

float
First probability on [0, 1]; the name does not enforce ordering.
required


p_low
float
Second probability on [0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Dimensionless signed Cohen h; positive when p_high exceeds p_low.






Equation: h = 2*asin(sqrt(p_high)) - 2*asin(sqrt(p_low)).
Assumptions: Probabilities describe comparable binary outcomes.
Excludes: Sampling uncertainty, a test decision, and validation of probability bounds.



Cohen (1988), Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, chapter 6. Derivation: Subtract the two variance-stabilizing arcsine-transformed probabilities.



>>> calc_cohens_h(0.5, 0.5) == 0
True

Normalize observed agreement relative to chance agreement.











Name
Type
Description
Default

float
Observed matching-label fraction in [0, 1].
required


chance_agreement
float
Chance agreement probability in [0, 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Dimensionless kappa; negative values indicate agreement below chance.






Equation: kappa = (p_o-p_e)/(1-p_e).
Assumptions: Chance agreement is estimated from suitable annotator marginals.
Excludes: Confidence intervals, weighted ordinal disagreement, and prevalence adjustment.



Derivation: scale observed excess agreement p_o-p_e by the maximum possible excess 1-p_e. Cohen (1960) introduced this agreement coefficient.



>>> calc_cohens_kappa(0.75, 0.5)

physics.statistics.calc_conjunctive_confidence(premise_confidences)
Combine independent premise probabilities by conjunction.











Name
Type
Description
Default




premise_confidences
sequence of float
Nonempty probabilities p_i in [0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Dimensionless probability that every premise holds.






Equation: P(all premises) = product(p_i).
Assumptions: Independent premise events, each necessary for the conclusion.
Excludes: Common-cause dependence and validation of supplied confidence judgments.
Equation: P(claim) = prod_i p_i
The conjunction is no stronger than its weakest premise and, with more than one premise below 1, strictly weaker.
Source: probability of the intersection of independent events, as applied to conjunctive assurance arguments in Bloomfield and Littlewood 2003, “Multi-legged arguments: the impact of diversity upon confidence in dependability arguments” (DSN 2003).



Derivation: repeated multiplication of independent-event intersection probabilities.



>>> calc_conjunctive_confidence([0.5, 0.5])
0.25




physics.statistics.calc_consecutive_detection_frames(
    per_frame_detection,
    all_miss_probability,
)
Find the frame count for an all-miss probability target.
Consecutive frames a person must be in view before detection may be counted on.
Equation: N = ceil( ln p_miss / ln(1 - p_frame) )
the fewest frames for which the chance of missing the person in every one, (1 - p_frame)^N, is at most all_miss_probability, with misses independent from frame to frame (the best case; correlated misses need more frames). A tolerance of 1e-12 keeps an exact ratio from rounding up.











Name
Type
Description
Default




per_frame_detection
float
Detection probability per independent frame, in (0, 1).
required


all_miss_probability
float
Maximum all-miss probability in (0, 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





int
Minimum frame count under the independent-miss model.






Equation: N = ceil(log(all_miss_probability)/log(1-per_frame_detection)-1e-12).
Assumptions: Independent frame misses with a constant detection probability.
Excludes: Temporal correlation and uncertainty in detector performance.



Derivation: Multiply independent miss probabilities and invert the geometric decay.



>>> calc_consecutive_detection_frames(0.5, 0.25) == 2
True




physics.statistics.calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal(
    threshold,
    operational_mean,
    elite_share,
)
Trace population cross-entropy updates for an exponential tail.











Name
Type
Description
Default




threshold
float or Quantity
Positive target failure threshold gamma.
required


operational_mean
float or Quantity
Positive operational mean m0, in threshold units.
required


elite_share
float
Elite proposal fraction beta in (0, 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Levels contains thresholds in input units, n_levels is their count, and proposal_mean is the final mean in input units.






Equation: level_k = min(gamma, -m_k*log(beta)); m_(k+1) = level_k + m0, until level_k reaches gamma.
Assumptions: Population expectations replace empirical elites; the initial proposal mean equals the operational mean.
Excludes: Sampling variability, weight degeneracy, finite-sample stopping, and non-exponential families.
From q_0 = p = Exp(m0), each round sets the level to the (1 - beta) quantile of the current proposal, level = -m_k ln(beta) (capped at the threshold), and refits the proposal mean to the likelihood-weighted elite draws; for this family that is E_p[D | D > level] = level + m0. Stops when the level reaches the threshold, so the final mean is threshold + m0.
Returns a dict with levels (list, in the units of threshold), n_levels, and proposal_mean.
Source: Rubinstein and Kroese, The Cross-Entropy Method (Springer, 2004), multilevel rare-event algorithm; the exponential refit is in closed form.



Derivation: exponential memorylessness gives E[X | X > level] = level + m0; the proposal quantile supplies the next level. Rubinstein and Kroese (2004), The Cross-Entropy Method, motivates multilevel adaptation.



>>> result = calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal(2.0, 1.0, 0.5)
>>> result["levels"][-1] == 2.0 and result["proposal_mean"] == 3.0
True




physics.statistics.calc_dagger_cost_bound(
    horizon_steps,
    per_step_error,
    recoverability=1.0,
)
Evaluate linear horizon growth under recoverable imitation.

Type
Description
Default

int or float
Nonnegative decision horizon S.
required


per_step_error
float
Learner-state error epsilon in [0, 1].
required


recoverability
float
Nonnegative excess-to-go bound u per error; default 1.0.
1.0

Type
Description





float
Excess cumulative cost bound in the cost units of recoverability.






Equation: Excess cost bound = u*S*epsilon.
Assumptions: Expert labels on learner-visited states and a bounded recoverability constant u.
Excludes: Finite-iteration regret terms, policy optimization, and proof that a given system satisfies the assumptions.
Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell (2011), Theorem 3.2: linear in the horizon while the recoverability constant u stays bounded.



Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell (2011), A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v15/ross11a/ross11a.pdf



>>> calc_dagger_cost_bound(20, 0.01) == 2 * calc_dagger_cost_bound(10, 0.01)

physics.statistics.calc_effective_sample_size(n_records, lag1_correlation)
Approximate the independent sample count of an AR(1) mean.











Name
Type
Description
Default




n_records
int or float
Nonnegative number of observations.
required


lag1_correlation
float
Stationary lag-one correlation rho in (-1, 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Effective count under the asymptotic AR(1) variance approximation.






Equation: N_eff = N*(1-rho)/(1+rho).
Assumptions: A stationary AR(1) autocorrelation rho**k and enough records for the infinite-lag approximation.
Excludes: Finite-sample edge corrections, nonstationary drift, and arbitrary dependence.
N_eff = N (1 - rho) / (1 + rho) for estimating the mean of a series whose adjacent records have lag-one correlation rho (Thiebaux and Zwiers 1984).



Derivation: sum 1+2*sum(rho**k, k>=1)=(1+rho)/(1-rho) as the variance inflation of the sample mean; divide N by that inflation.



>>> calc_effective_sample_size(100, 0.0)
100.0




physics.statistics.calc_equal_n_for_z(rate_a, rate_b, z_critical)
Solve the equal-group size for a specified pooled z statistic.











Name
Type
Description
Default




rate_a
float
Distinct probabilities on [0, 1] with their mean in (0, 1).
required


rate_b
float
Distinct probabilities on [0, 1] with their mean in (0, 1).
required


z_critical
float
Positive target magnitude of the normal statistic.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Unrounded count per group; callers round up when planning whole observations.






Equation: n = 2*p*(1-p)*(z_critical/(rate_a-rate_b))**2, p = (rate_a+rate_b)/2.
Assumptions: Equal-size independent Bernoulli groups and fixed hypothesized rates.
Excludes: Power beyond reaching a z threshold, rate-estimation uncertainty, and input validation.



Derivation: Rearrange z = gap/sqrt(2*p*(1-p)/n) for n.



>>> n = calc_equal_n_for_z(0.6, 0.4, 2.0)
>>> math.isclose(abs(calc_two_proportion_z(0.6, 0.4, n, n)), 2.0)

physics.statistics.calc_expected_calibration_error(bins)
Compute count-weighted absolute calibration error.
Expected calibration error of binned predictions: sum |B_i| / n * |acc_i - conf_i|.
bins is a sequence of (count, confidence, accuracy); the weight of each bin is its share of the predictions (Pakdaman Naeini et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2017, eq. 3).











Name
Type
Description
Default




bins
sequence
Sequence of (count, confidence, accuracy) triples; rates in [0, 1].
required









Name
Type
Description





float
Dimensionless weighted absolute probability error.






Equation: ECE = sum(count_i/total * abs(accuracy_i-confidence_i)).
Assumptions: Nonnegative bin counts with positive total; rates on the same probability scale.
Excludes: Bin selection, debiasing, and confidence intervals.



Derivation: Guo et al. (2017), On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks: count-weighted bin accuracy-confidence differences.



>>> calc_expected_calibration_error([(10, 0.5, 0.5)]) == 0
True




physics.statistics.calc_exponential_decay_rate(initial, later, elapsed)
Fit an exponential rate through two readings.
Rate gamma of A(t) = A0 exp(-gamma t) through two readings: gamma = ln(A0 / A1) / t. elapsed may be a Quantity (the rate is then per its unit) or a plain number.

Type
Description
Default

float
Positive initial reading, in the same units as later.
required


later

Positive later reading, in the same units as initial.
required


elapsed
float
Nonzero elapsed time, as a float or Pint quantity.
required














Name
Type
Description





float or Quantity
Inverse-time rate, retaining the inverse units of elapsed when supplied.






Equation: gamma = log(initial/later)/elapsed.
Assumptions: Positive readings in matching units and nonzero elapsed time.
Excludes: Measurement noise and multiple-timescale decay.



Derivation: Take logarithms of later = initial*exp(-gamma*elapsed).

text:
hardware.HardwareNode()
Layer B (Hardware Supply): Represents a complete hardware accelerator.
This is the primary object that solvers evaluate against. It encapsulates the compute, memory, IO, and power constraints of a single physical device (e.g., an NVIDIA H100 GPU or a Jetson Orin Nano).





Name
Description

Attach mass units to the stored manufacturing-carbon estimate.









Name
Description

Calculate the peak Roofline arithmetic-intensity crossover.





hardware.HardwareNode.ridge_point(precision=None)
Calculate the peak Roofline arithmetic-intensity crossover.











Name
Type
Description
Default




precision
str
Precision key for compute.precision_flops, matched case-insensitively. None selects peak_flops; an unknown key warns and falls back to it.
None














Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Peak compute throughput divided by primary-memory bandwidth, in FLOP/byte. This is not derated by a solver’s efficiency input.






Equation: I_ridge = F_peak / BW_primary. At this intensity, the ideal compute and memory-time bounds coincide.
Assumptions: positive primary-memory bandwidth and the declared peak compute rate; peak compute and bandwidth can be compared for the same workload precision and memory traffic boundary.
Excludes: dispatch overhead, SRAM/flash/offload paths, achieved bandwidth, and compute efficiency. A solver’s effective ridge may differ.



Williams et al. (2009), “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785 (bibliography key: williams2009).



>>> from mlsysim import Hardware
>>> hw = Hardware.Cloud.H100
>>> hw.ridge_point() == (hw.compute.peak_flops / hw.memory.bandwidth).to('flop/byte')
True

title: engine.solvers.proposer
text:
engine.solvers.proposer
Learned-proposer solvers: what one fresh evaluation costs, and how long its evidence lasts.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__). The equations live in physics.transformer (the roofline latency of one vision-language-action evaluation) and physics.robotics (chunk streaming, the renewal schedule, the tracked evidence horizon); these models compose them for one stated machine or situation (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




DecoderFamiliesModel
One fresh H-step chunk from a VLA backbone, for each decoder family.


EvidenceHorizonModel
How long a chunk’s evidence stays true for a tracked target, against its renewal schedule.


ProposerTrafficModel
Weight traffic of a machine’s two learned proposers on its shared memory bus.


VlaEvaluationModel
One fresh evaluation of a decoder-only VLA backbone on one processor.





engine.solvers.proposer.DecoderFamiliesModel()
One fresh H-step chunk from a VLA backbone, for each decoder family.
Every family pays the backbone’s prefill. Binned autoregressive decoding emits horizon * action_dim tokens one sweep at a time; FAST emits fast_tokens compressed tokens one at a time; a parallel head folds the binned tokens into one longer prefill; a flow-matching expert runs expert_steps refinement steps, each max(compute, (expert weights + cached prefix KV) / B_sustained) (Black et al. 2024; Pertsch et al. 2025; Kim, Finn and Liang 2025).

Description

DecoderFamiliesResult
Modeled decoder times in ms, expert/prefix storage in MB, token counts, and dimensionless time ratios. No quality-equivalence or memory-capacity guarantee is implied by comparing these schedules.






VlaEvaluationModel.solve : Evaluate the shared backbone under one decoder schedule.



Equation: binned_tokens = horizon * action_dim. Each autoregressive schedule uses VlaEvaluationModel; the parallel schedule extends prefill. An expert pass takes max(2 * expert_params * horizon / effective_compute, (expert_weights + prefix_kv) / sustained_bandwidth), where prefix_kv = 2 * layers * hidden_dim * kv_bytes_per_value * input_tokens. Expert total = backbone_prefill + expert_steps * expert_pass_time. Assumptions: shared backbone inputs and rates, full-width keys and values, fixed token/refinement counts, and repeated prefix-cache reads per expert pass. Expert work uses parameter-linear FLOPs for each horizon position. Excludes: expert attention/activation traffic beyond the specified prefix reads, launch overhead, residency checks, and decoder-quality prediction.



Derivation: count one key and one value at each layer/hidden coordinate for each prefix token; combine its byte transfer with an expert weight sweep. The maximum of the computed resource times is the pass lower bound. Decoder token counts and expert iterations are scenario inputs, not measured performance or equal-quality guarantees.



A constructed chunk exposes its binned token count directly.
>>> from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, Q_
>>> result = DecoderFamiliesModel().solve(
...     Models.Language.Llama3_8B, Hardware.Edge.JetsonAGXOrin,
...     Q_(2, 'byte/param'), 8, 0.5, 0.5, 2, 3, 4,
...     Q_(1000, 'param'), 2, Q_(2, 'byte/param'), Q_(2, 'byte'),
...     Q_(1, 'second'))
>>> result.binned_tokens == 2 * 3
True






engine.solvers.proposer.EvidenceHorizonModel()
How long a chunk’s evidence stays true for a tracked target, against its renewal schedule.
Untracked, a target at speed v uses up the margin r_tol - e_0 in (r_tol - e_0) / v. Tracked, only a residual acceleration remains, so the evidence horizon is sqrt(2 (r_tol - e_0) / a_slip) (calc_tracked_evidence_horizon). The chunk policy’s renewal schedule (calc_chunk_renewal_schedule) gives the evidence age at replacement (renewal period plus inference), the setpoints one renewal needs, and the span one chunk supplies; drift over an age T is a_slip T^2 / 2.





Name
Description




solve
Compare tracking-error growth with a chunk-renewal schedule.

    initial_error,
    target_speed,
    slip_acceleration,

    chunk_step,
    chunk_horizon,
    inference_latency,
)

Name
Type
Description





ValueError
If the renewal period is not aligned to whole setpoint intervals, the inference misses its next renewal, or the chunk cannot bridge replacement.






mlsysim.physics.robotics.calc_tracked_evidence_horizon : Solve the constant-acceleration error horizon. mlsysim.physics.robotics.calc_chunk_renewal_schedule : Account for renewal alignment and replacement age.



Equation: margin = tolerance - initial_error. Untracked deadline = margin / target_speed; tracked horizon = sqrt(2 * margin / slip_acceleration). Replacement age = 1 / chunk_rate + inference_latency, and position drift at age T is slip_acceleration * T**2 / 2. A chunk spans chunk_horizon * chunk_step; fits compares replacement age with horizon. Assumptions: initial velocity error has been removed by tracking, residual acceleration is constant, and renewal aligns with the setpoint grid. Excludes: jerk, measurement noise growth, missed renewals, transport/admission delays, obstacle motion beyond the stated target model, and control stability.



Derivation: integrate constant residual acceleration twice to obtain position error a*T**2/2, then solve for the remaining margin. Compose this horizon with the linked periodic-renewal schedule; the comparison inherits both models’ assumptions and is not a certified safety envelope.



The constructed schedule’s replacement age includes inference latency.
>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = EvidenceHorizonModel().solve(
...     Q_(1, 'm'), Q_(0.1, 'm'), Q_(1, 'm/s'), Q_(1, 'm/s^2'),
...     Q_(10, 'Hz'), Q_(0.01, 's'), 20, Q_(0.02, 's'))
>>> result.age_at_replacement == result.renewal_period + Q_(0.02, 's')
True






engine.solvers.proposer.ProposerTrafficModel()
Weight traffic of a machine’s two learned proposers on its shared memory bus.
The intent model’s 16-bit sweep M / (B eta) bounds its fresh rate; spread over a chunk of H setpoints it is t / H per setpoint (calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization). One sweep per setpoint at the setpoint rate would demand f_setpoint M; one per chunk divides that by H. In operation the deployed intent model sweeps its weights once per action token per evaluation (D M_deployed f_intent) and the chunk policy once per renewal (M_chunk f_chunk); their sum against the sustained bandwidth is the proposers’ share of the bus (weight traffic only).





Name
Description




solve
Account for two learned proposers sharing a machine’s memory bus.





engine.solvers.proposer.ProposerTrafficModel.solve(
    machine,
    fp16_bytes_per_param,
)
Account for two learned proposers sharing a machine’s memory bus.











Name
Type
Description
Default




machine
MobileManipulatorPlatform
Platform providing intent/chunk models, stored intent weights, processor bandwidth, DRAM efficiency, chunk horizon/step, proposer rates, permission rate, and intent latency breakdown. Rates are in Hz and times in seconds; bandwidth, horizon, and step must be positive and efficiency in (0, 1].
required


fp16_bytes_per_param
Quantity
Positive reference storage per parameter, in byte/param. The FP16 comparison normally supplies two bytes; deployed intent storage comes separately from machine.intent_weight_memory.
required














Name
Type
Description





ProposerTrafficResult
Weight storage in GB, sweep times in ms, frequencies in Hz, traffic in GB/s, and dimensionless bus/duty ratios. A bus share above one indicates demand exceeding the supplied bandwidth model, not measured utilization.






mlsysim.physics.robotics.calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization : Divide sweep time among supplied chunk setpoints.



Equation: sustained_bandwidth = peak_bandwidth * dram_efficiency; sweep_time = weights / sustained_bandwidth. Intent traffic is action_dim * deployed_intent_weights * intent_rate, and chunk traffic is chunk_weights * chunk_rate. Their sum divided by sustained_bandwidth is proposer_share. The single-sweep chunk comparison divides reference weight traffic at the setpoint rate by chunk_horizon. Assumptions: a full intent-model weight sweep per action dimension and a full chunk-model sweep per renewal. The machine supplies deployed weight precision and latency assumptions independently of the FP16 comparison. Excludes: KV/activation traffic, vision encoding, other bus clients, cache reuse, compute contention, scheduling jitter, and physical safety claims.



Derivation: weight bytes per evaluation multiplied by evaluations per second give bandwidth demand; sum both proposer streams and divide by supplied sustained bandwidth. The linked chunk-streaming helper derives sweep amortization per setpoint. This is explicit traffic accounting, not a hardware benchmark or a model of application-level success.



The registered platform’s total traffic is the sum of its two streams.
>>> from mlsysim import Embodied, Q_
>>> machine = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
>>> result = ProposerTrafficModel().solve(machine, Q_(2, 'byte/param'))
>>> result.proposer_traffic == result.intent_traffic + result.chunk_traffic
True






engine.solvers.proposer.VlaEvaluationModel()
One fresh evaluation of a decoder-only VLA backbone on one processor.
Wraps calc_vla_inference_latency (compute/memory bounds for prefill, then action_tokens - 1 decode passes, or one longer prefill under parallel decoding) and adds the roofline coordinates of its two phases: the ridge R_peak / BW_peak at the 16-bit rate, the prefill intensity (linear FLOPs per weight byte, about S at 16-bit weights), and the decode intensity (2 N FLOP per weight sweep per weight byte, 1 at 16-bit weights).





Name
Description




solve
Estimate one decoder-backbone evaluation and its resource bounds.





engine.solvers.proposer.VlaEvaluationModel.solve(
    model,
    processor,
    weight_bytes_per_param,
    input_tokens,
    action_tokens,
    bus_efficiency,
    compute_utilization,
    parallel_decode=False,
)
Estimate one decoder-backbone evaluation and its resource bounds.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model
TransformerWorkload
Decoder geometry with parameter count in param, layer count, and hidden width. The supplied model represents the language/action backbone.
required


processor
HardwareNode
Processor with positive FP16 compute throughput and memory bandwidth. An explicit fp16 override takes precedence over canonical peak_flops.
required


weight_bytes_per_param
Quantity
Positive stored bytes per parameter, in byte/param. Weight quantization changes traffic while arithmetic still uses the processor’s fp16 rate.
required


input_tokens
int
Positive count of prompt and image-patch tokens entering the backbone.
required


action_tokens
int
Positive number of generated action tokens.
required


bus_efficiency
float
Caller-supplied sustained fraction of peak memory bandwidth in (0, 1].
required


compute_utilization
float
Caller-supplied sustained fraction of fp16 compute throughput in (0, 1].
required


parallel_decode
bool
If True, process input and action placeholders in one bidirectional pass; otherwise prefill produces the first token before serial decoding.
False














Name
Type
Description





VlaEvaluationResult
Weight storage in GB, work in FLOPs, intensities in FLOP/byte, phase times in ms, and reciprocal evaluation rates in Hz. These are modeled resource bounds; this result does not check model residency or control safety.






mlsysim.physics.transformer.calc_vla_inference_latency : Compose compute and weight-traffic bounds for each pass. mlsysim.physics.transformer.calc_transformer_prefill_flops : Count parameter-linear and attention prefill work.



Equation: weights = parameters * weight_bytes_per_param. Each pass takes max(compute_work / effective_compute, weights / effective_bandwidth). Serial decode repeats its pass action_tokens - 1 times; parallel decode instead extends prefill to input_tokens + action_tokens. Prefill work includes the helper’s attention term, while reported prefill_intensity intentionally uses only parameter-linear work. Assumptions: one full weight read per pass, compute/memory overlap within a pass, fp16 arithmetic, and fixed caller-provided utilization factors. The peak ridge uses peak rates, not efficiency-adjusted rates. Excludes: the vision encoder, decode attention and KV traffic, runtime workspaces, launch overhead, memory admission, and closed-loop dynamics.



Derivation: compose the prefill and serial-pass bounds implemented and sourced in calc_vla_inference_latency; divide work by weight bytes for arithmetic intensity and invert modeled time for the evaluation rate. The decoder-family choice is an assumed execution pattern, not a reproduction of a published robot’s latency measurement.



A one-token constructed request has no post-prefill decode pass.
>>> from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, Q_
>>> result = VlaEvaluationModel().solve(
...     Models.Language.Llama3_8B, Hardware.Edge.JetsonAGXOrin,
...     Q_(2, 'byte/param'), 8, 1, 0.5, 0.5)
>>> result.decode_steps == 0 and result.t_total == result.t_prefill
True

Weight storage in GB, work in FLOPs, intensities in FLOP/byte, phase times in ms, and reciprocal evaluation rates in Hz. These are modeled resource bounds; this result does not check model residency or control safety.






mlsysim.physics.transformer.calc_vla_inference_latency : Compose compute and weight-traffic bounds for each pass. mlsysim.physics.transformer.calc_transformer_prefill_flops : Count parameter-linear and attention prefill work.



Equation: weights = parameters * weight_bytes_per_param. Each pass takes max(compute_work / effective_compute, weights / effective_bandwidth). Serial decode repeats its pass action_tokens - 1 times; parallel decode instead extends prefill to input_tokens + action_tokens. Prefill work includes the helper’s attention term, while reported prefill_intensity intentionally uses only parameter-linear work. Assumptions: one full weight read per pass, compute/memory overlap within a pass, fp16 arithmetic, and fixed caller-provided utilization factors. The peak ridge uses peak rates, not efficiency-adjusted rates. Excludes: the vision encoder, decode attention and KV traffic, runtime workspaces, launch overhead, memory admission, and closed-loop dynamics.



Derivation: compose the prefill and serial-pass bounds implemented and sourced in calc_vla_inference_latency; divide work by weight bytes for arithmetic intensity and invert modeled time for the evaluation rate. The decoder-family choice is an assumed execution pattern, not a reproduction of a published robot’s latency measurement.

...     Models.Language.Llama3_8B, Hardware.Edge.JetsonAGXOrin,
...     Q_(2, 'byte/param'), 8, 1, 0.5, 0.5)
>>> result.decode_steps == 0 and result.t_total == result.t_prefill

title: DelegationCohortScenario
text:
Equation: Spend sums token counts times their prices and service duration times its price; accepted-task cost divides spend by accepted count.
Assumptions: Both policies share the same cohort, prices, deadlines, and acceptance contract; ratio denominators are nonzero.
Excludes: Prediction of acceptance rates or latency; supplied outcomes are inputs rather than results generated by the model.

title: DelegationCohortScenario
text: Derivation: Spend sums token counts times their prices and service duration times its price; accepted-task cost divides spend by accepted count. This is declared scenario accounting rather than a fitted empirical law.

title: physics.drivetrain
text:
physics.drivetrain
Braking-drive physics for a wheeled mobile base (Volume IV, added 2026-09-28, M6).
A credible deceleration is admissible only if three independent ceilings exceed it: tire-floor traction, tip-over about the leading support, and the torque the drives can deliver at their configured current limit. A fourth check asks whether the drive keeps current control at speed, which requires the motor’s back-EMF to stay below the bus.
Sources: Coulomb friction and the tipping moment balance are freshman rigid-body equilibrium (OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, Secs. 6.2 and 12.2); the reflected rotating mass m_eff = m + sum(N^2 J / r^2) follows Lynch and Park, Modern Robotics (2017), Sec. 8.9.2; the brushless DC terminal equation V = e + I R is Krishnan, Permanent Magnet Synchronous and Brushless DC Motor Drives (CRC Press, 2010).





Name
Description




calc_braking_limits
Compare a requested deceleration with independent braking ceilings.


calc_drive_torque_deceleration_limit
Calculate the braking ceiling from available wheel torque.


calc_drive_voltage_headroom
Evaluate direct-drive motor terminal voltages during drive and braking.


calc_max_cg_height_ratio
Invert the tip-over ceiling to bound the height-to-arm ratio.


calc_required_friction
Invert the traction ceiling to obtain required tire friction.


calc_tipover_deceleration_limit
Calculate the rigid-body braking ceiling before forward tip-over.


calc_traction_deceleration_limit
Calculate the tire-friction braking ceiling.





physics.drivetrain.calc_braking_limits(
    mass,
    deceleration,
    *,
    wheel_torque_max,
    wheel_radius,
    n_driven_wheels,
    friction_coefficient,
    drive_load_share=1.0,
    rotating_equivalent_mass=None,
    cg_height=None,
    tip_arm=None,
)
Compare a requested deceleration with independent braking ceilings.











Name
Type
Description
Default




mass
Quantity
Positive translating mass in kilograms.
required


deceleration
Quantity
Positive requested deceleration in meter/second squared.
required


wheel_torque_max
Quantity
Positive available braking torque per driven wheel in newton meters.
required


wheel_radius
Quantity
Positive wheel rolling radius in meters.
required


n_driven_wheels
int
Number of driven braked wheels, at least one.
required


friction_coefficient
float
Positive dimensionless tire-floor friction coefficient.
required


drive_load_share
float
Braked-wheel normal-load fraction in (0, 1].
1.0


rotating_equivalent_mass
Quantity
Nonnegative reflected rotating mass in kilograms; None supplies zero.
None


cg_height
Quantity
Positive center-of-gravity height in meters; required with tip_arm for a tip-over check.
None


tip_arm
Quantity
Positive horizontal tipping arm in meters; required with cg_height.
None














Name
Type
Description





dict
Individual ceilings a_traction, a_torque, a_tip and a_admissible in meter/second squared; force in newtons; m_eff in kilograms; dimensionless mu_required and cg_ratio_max; binding label and Boolean passes.






Equation: a_admissible = min(a_traction, a_torque, a_tip) over the available ceilings. The request passes only if every available ceiling meets it and the tip-over geometry was supplied. Assumptions: the component traction, torque, and static moment models apply simultaneously. Missing center-of-gravity geometry makes a_tip None and passes False, while still reporting the available ceilings and h/d bound. Excludes: drive-voltage limits, reaction latency, dynamic stability, and uncertain friction. Passing these algebraic ceilings is not a safety certification.



Derivation: intersect the admissible sets returned by :func:calc_traction_deceleration_limit, :func:calc_tipover_deceleration_limit, and :func:calc_drive_torque_deceleration_limit; the smallest ceiling binds.



>>> result = calc_braking_limits(1 * ureg.kg, 1 * ureg.m / ureg.s**2, wheel_torque_max=1 * ureg.N * ureg.m, wheel_radius=1 * ureg.m, n_driven_wheels=1, friction_coefficient=0.5)
>>> result['a_tip'] is None and result['passes'] is False
True




physics.drivetrain.calc_drive_torque_deceleration_limit(
    wheel_torque_max,
    wheel_radius,
    n_driven_wheels,
    mass,
    rotating_equivalent_mass=None,
)
Calculate the braking ceiling from available wheel torque.











Name
Type
Description
Default




wheel_torque_max
Quantity
Positive delivered torque per braked wheel, in newton meters.
required


wheel_radius
Quantity
Positive rolling radius, in meters.
required


n_driven_wheels
int
Number of torque-producing braked wheels, at least one.
required


mass
Quantity
Positive translating mass, in kilograms.
required


rotating_equivalent_mass
Quantity
Nonnegative sum of reflected rotational inertia divided by wheel radius squared, in kilograms; None means zero.
None














Name
Type
Description





dict
Force in newtons under force, effective mass in kilograms under m_eff, and deceleration in meter/second squared under a_max.






Equation: force = n * torque/r; m_eff = m + m_rot; a_max = force/m_eff, with m_rot = sum(J_reflected/r^2). Assumptions: equal torque and wheel radius at every driven wheel; the supplied torque already accounts for gearing, current limits, and transmission efficiency. Excludes: tire slip, aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance, and speed-dependent motor limits. A sourced upper bound on m_rot produces a lower torque ceiling.



Derivation: Newton’s law F = m_eff a with each wheel’s torque converted through F = torque/r. Reflected inertia follows energy equivalence between rotation and translation; see Lynch and Park, Modern Robotics (2017), Section 8.9.2.



>>> result = calc_drive_torque_deceleration_limit(1 * ureg.N * ureg.m, 1 * ureg.m, 1, 1 * ureg.kg)
>>> result['a_max'] == 1 * ureg.m / ureg.s**2
True




physics.drivetrain.calc_drive_voltage_headroom(
    back_emf_constant,
    velocity,
    wheel_radius,
    bus_voltage,
    current,
    line_resistance,
)
Evaluate direct-drive motor terminal voltages during drive and braking.











Name
Type
Description
Default




back_emf_constant
Quantity
Positive line-to-line back-EMF per shaft speed, e.g. volt/rpm.
required


velocity
Quantity
Nonnegative ground speed, in meter/second.
required


wheel_radius
Quantity
Positive rolling radius, in meters.
required


bus_voltage
Quantity
Positive available DC bus voltage, in volts.
required


current
Quantity
Nonnegative conducting phase current, in amperes.
required


line_resistance
Quantity
Positive line-to-line winding resistance, in ohms.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Wheel speed omega in rpm; e_bemf, v_drive, v_brake, and headroom in volts. Headroom is bus voltage minus back-EMF, not the loaded drive margin.






Equation: omega = v/r; e = K_e omega; V_drive = e + I R; V_brake = e - I R; headroom = V_bus - e. Assumptions: direct drive with two phases conducting and constant winding resistance; braking current opposes the back-EMF. If back-EMF exceeds the bus, inverter diode conduction can prevent controlled braking current. Excludes: inductive transients, inverter voltage drops, bus regeneration limits, and current-controller dynamics.



Derivation: apply the brushless DC steady terminal balance V = e + I R, reversing current polarity for braking. Krishnan, Permanent Magnet Synchronous and Brushless DC Motor Drives (CRC Press, 2010), supplies the motor-circuit basis; the headroom metric here is the unloaded bus-minus-EMF difference.



>>> result = calc_drive_voltage_headroom(1 * ureg.V / ureg.rpm, 0 * ureg.m / ureg.s, 1 * ureg.m, 24 * ureg.V, 0 * ureg.A, 1 * ureg.ohm)
>>> result['headroom'] == 24 * ureg.V
True




physics.drivetrain.calc_max_cg_height_ratio(deceleration)
Invert the tip-over ceiling to bound the height-to-arm ratio.











Name
Type
Description
Default




deceleration
Quantity
Positive requested deceleration in meter/second squared.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Largest dimensionless center-of-gravity height divided by tipping arm.






Equation: (h/d)_max = g/a. Assumptions: a fixed rigid-body center of gravity and planar static moment balance, as in :func:calc_tipover_deceleration_limit. Excludes: suspension and transient pitch dynamics; the ratio alone does not establish that a particular machine is stable.



Derivation: rearrange a h <= g d to h/d <= g/a for positive deceleration.



>>> calc_max_cg_height_ratio(1 * ureg.standard_gravity)
1.0




physics.drivetrain.calc_required_friction(deceleration, drive_load_share=1.0)
Invert the traction ceiling to obtain required tire friction.











Name
Type
Description
Default




deceleration
Quantity
Positive requested deceleration in meter/second squared.
required


drive_load_share
float
Braked-wheel normal-load share phi, in (0, 1].
1.0














Name
Type
Description





float
Minimum dimensionless friction coefficient under the load-share model.






Equation: mu_required = a/(g * phi). Assumptions: the same fixed-load Coulomb friction model as :func:calc_traction_deceleration_limit. Excludes: drive torque, tip-over, dynamic load transfer, and uncertainty in surface friction. A computed coefficient does not establish available traction.



Derivation: solve a = mu g phi for mu using the specified deceleration and braked-wheel load share.



>>> calc_required_friction(1 * ureg.standard_gravity, 1.0)
1.0




physics.drivetrain.calc_tipover_deceleration_limit(cg_height, tip_arm)
Calculate the rigid-body braking ceiling before forward tip-over.











Name
Type
Description
Default




cg_height
Quantity
Positive center-of-gravity height h above the floor, in meters.
required


tip_arm
Quantity
Positive horizontal distance d from the center of gravity to the leading support line, in meters.
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Deceleration ceiling in meter/second squared.






Equation: a_tip = g * d/h. Assumptions: planar rigid-body moment balance about the leading support line, with a fixed center of gravity for the arm pose being checked. Excludes: suspension motion, transient pitching, payload shifts, uneven floors, and dynamic stabilization. The result is not a tip-over safety certification.



Derivation: balance the inertial pitching moment m a h against the restoring weight moment m g d. Static moment balance is described in OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, Section 12.2.



>>> a = calc_tipover_deceleration_limit(1 * ureg.m, 1 * ureg.m)
>>> a == 1 * ureg.standard_gravity
True




physics.drivetrain.calc_traction_deceleration_limit(
    friction_coefficient,
    drive_load_share=1.0,
)
Calculate the tire-friction braking ceiling.











Name
Type
Description
Default




friction_coefficient
float
Positive dimensionless tire-floor friction coefficient mu.
required


drive_load_share
float
Fraction phi of machine weight carried by braked wheels, in (0, 1].
1.0









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Deceleration ceiling in meter/second squared.






Equation: a_traction = mu * g * phi. Assumptions: Coulomb friction with constant normal-load share on the braked wheels; unbraked casters contribute no retarding force. Excludes: transient load transfer, slip dynamics, surface variation, and traction-control behavior. The ceiling is conditional, not a safety guarantee.



Derivation: the available horizontal force is mu times the braked-wheel normal load phi m g; divide by translating mass m. This is the Coulomb friction model stated in OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, Section 6.2.



>>> a = calc_traction_deceleration_limit(0.5)
>>> (a / ureg.standard_gravity).m_as('') == 0.5
True

Excludes: transient load transfer, slip dynamics, surface variation, and traction-control behavior. The ceiling is conditional, not a safety guarantee.



Derivation: the available horizontal force is mu times the braked-wheel normal load phi m g; divide by translating mass m. This is the Coulomb friction model stated in OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, Section 6.2.



>>> a = calc_traction_deceleration_limit(0.5)
>>> (a / ureg.standard_gravity).m_as('') == 0.5
True

title: Economics Scenarios
text:
Scenario contracts

AdaptationPaybackScenario: A one-time adaptation that cuts each task’s model usage, against its incremental cost.
ArchitectureChoiceScenario: Single-call designs and a bounded loop under one check, with a human fallback for rejects.
BatchServingCostScenario: One accelerator rented at price, serving batches back to back: cost per request by batch size.
CanaryScheduleScenario: A staged rollout that needs samples_per_variant guardrail samples per stage at request_rate; stages is the configured ladder of (traffic share, duration).
ClickLossScenario: A silent click-through regression from ctr_before to ctr_after at request_rate, caught after detection_time; each click is worth value_per_click.
CloudEdgeCostScenario: Serving a network of sites from the cloud (pay per image) or from a device at each site (buy up front).
CohortAttemptCostScenario: One configuration’s cohort of tasks, one bounded attempt each, all charges settled.
CompactionPaybackScenario: One compaction of a billed trajectory: a summary resent fresh, then shorter cached reads.
ConservedBudgetScenario: A root budget granted to two children; the second stops with a remote job billed late.
DedicatedBreakEvenScenario: Renting a matched-capability API against owning capacity at a fixed hourly cost.
DisclosurePenaltyScenario: Penalties for an incomplete account: days_withheld at daily_maximum each, plus others (name -> amount), all in USD.
ExplanationLoadScenario: Reasons owed for every denial: decisions_per_day at denial_share, each explained by a sampling attributor of samples model evaluations or by exact Shapley over features.
FeatureHistoryScenario: Full-snapshot feature history: entities x features values every update_interval, kept for retention, each row a value, an entity key, and timestamps timestamps.
IdleCapacityCostScenario: gpus accelerators held idle for duration at device_hour_rate.
KingmanQueueScenario: One server under Kingman’s approximation at two utilizations, with a holding price.
LifecycleTcoScenario: Monthly lifecycle cost in four terms (training, inference, data, iteration), each counted once.
ModelCascadeScenario: A tiered cascade over a completed cohort, every exit under one gate, against the top tier alone.
OperationalLoadScenario: Assumed operational-load shapes for N models: alerts a N, deployments N ln N, and pairwise conflicts c N^2 against one team’s team_capacity.
OptimizationPaybackScenario: An optimization costing implementation_cost that cuts a monthly_bill by reduction.
OwnVsRentScenario: Owning gpus accelerators against renting them at rent_rate per GPU-hour for utilization of every hour, over years.
PlatformBenefitScenario: A shared platform costing platform_cost per month that saves each of models model teams hours_saved per month at engineer_rate.
ResendCacheBillScenario: An append-only trajectory (TrajectoryResendScenario) billed under one tariff, with and without reuse.
RetryPolicyScenario: A cheap attempt retried up to a cap, run as a batch, or one stronger attempt.
RevenueRegressionScenario: A metric regression that cuts revenue in proportion for undetected (or for alerted with an alert and containment); revenue is weekly_revenue per week.
ReviewStaffingScenario: Substantive human review: appeal_rate of decisions_per_day at time_per_case each, staffed in shift-long shifts; optionally against a reported compare_cases handled at compare_time_per_case.
RolloutExposureScenario: Users exposed until rollback under an all-at-once cutover against a canary share, with the same request rate, harm, and time to rollback.
SerialEpisodeScenario: One serial episode as disjoint intervals; the model’s intervals sped up by model_speedup.
ServiceLifecycleCostScenario: A service’s multi-year cost in three terms: repeated training cycles, recurring inference, and operations, with a GPU-hour carbon factor.
ServingCostScenario: One model version’s training spend against its first year of serving.
ServingInstanceCostScenario: Instances with an hourly price and a saturated request rate: cost per request, and when the small instance sized to the load undercuts one large instance.
SpeculativeEpisodeScenario: Speculative decoding on a serial episode’s model time, at two draft acceptance levels.
SpotEffectiveCostScenario: Spot capacity priced per hour of retained progress.
SpotRunScenario: A training run of run_duration on fleet, on demand against spot capacity.
SupervisionLaborScenario: The person-hours a supervised fleet creates in one operating_day: an assistant staffed the whole day (busy at queue’s utilization, watching otherwise) plus sweeps corridor sweeps.
TokenPriceComparisonScenario: Two cohort configurations under one acceptance contract: does the cheaper token win?
TrainingCampaignCostScenario: runs_per_year training runs of run_low to run_high on an owned cluster (ownership) against renting the same GPUs only while each run lasts.
TrajectoryAdmissionScenario: A stationary admitted population of trajectories against a token-per-minute quota.
UtilizationGainScenario: A fleet of fleet_gpus raised from utilization_before to utilization_after.
WorkloadLeverScenario: Attempt cost by term for several workloads, and three levers on cost per accepted task.

title: BatchWindowScenario
text:
Serving scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/serving.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
Requests arriving as a Poisson stream into a batching window of length window.
The window collects lambda W arrivals on average; a request waits half the window on average; the batch a request finds itself in is size-biased, 1 + lambda W on average, and its tail_quantile is 1 plus that quantile of the Poisson count.


Equation: The calculation members below define mean_arrivals, arrival_spread, empty_share, count_at_least, mean_wait, budget_share, seen_batch_mean, seen_batch_tail.
Assumptions: Arrivals follow a homogeneous Poisson process and positions in a fixed window are uniform.
Excludes: Worker backlog, service time, and arrival correlations.



Derivation: Requests arriving as a Poisson stream into a batching window of length window. Each member records the corresponding algebra or named physics function.



Evaluate the named configuration and display a modeled result.
>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> case = Scenarios.BatchWindow10ms
>>> value = case.mean_wait
>>> print(f"{value:.3g~}")
5 ms

Calculation: mlsysim.physics.statistics.calc_poisson_tail.



engine.scenario_types.BatchWindowScenario.empty_share(arrival_rate)
Probability of no arrivals, exponential of minus the mean count.
Equation: _math.exp(-mean_arrivals(arrival_rate)).

Expected arrivals in the window, arrival rate times duration, dimensionless count.
Equation: (arrival_rate * window).to('').magnitude.

Expected tagged-request batch size, the request itself plus expected additional arrivals.

Tagged-request batch count threshold via calc_poisson_reserve under the stated tail quantile.

physics.numerics
Number formats: the range a binary floating-point or two’s-complement format holds.
The limits follow from the bit layout alone (IEEE 754-2019 for binary floating point; two’s complement for signed integers), so they are computed here rather than stored (added 2026-10-20).

physics.numerics.calc_accumulator_headroom(operand_bits, accumulator_bits)
Estimate worst-case positive-product accumulator headroom.











Name
Type
Description
Default




operand_bits
int
Signed operand width in bits, at least two.
required


accumulator_bits
int
Signed accumulation register width in bits, at least two.
required














Name
Type
Description





int
Approximate number of positive-maximum products fitting the sign-bit budget.






Equation: headroom = 2**(accumulator_bits-1) // (2**(operand_bits-1)-1)**2.
Assumptions: Products use the largest positive signed operands; numerator uses the power-of-two boundary.
Excludes: Negative minimum operands, bias terms, and an exact overflow-safe count at the signed maximum.
About how many worst-case products of two signed operand_bits codes fit in a signed accumulator_bits register: 2^(a-1) // (2^(b-1) - 1)^2 (127 times 127 at INT8; about 133,000 in INT32).



Derivation: Divide the modeled accumulation budget by one maximum positive product.



>>> calc_accumulator_headroom(4, 8)
2




physics.numerics.calc_affine_scale(alpha, beta, bits)
Compute the step of an affine integer quantization grid.











Name
Type
Description
Default




alpha
float
Lower clipping endpoint in the same units as the modeled values.
required


beta
float
Upper clipping endpoint, greater than alpha.
required


bits
int
Integer code width in bits; at least two for signed maxima, otherwise one.
required









Name
Type
Description





float
Value-unit spacing between neighboring codes.






Equation: scale = (beta-alpha)/(2**bits-1).
Assumptions: Both clipping endpoints are grid endpoints.
Excludes: Calibration of clipping thresholds and quantization error distributions.
Step of an asymmetric (affine) integer grid over the clipping range [alpha, beta]: s = (beta - alpha) / (2^b - 1).



Derivation: Divide endpoint span by the number of intervals between 2**bits codes.



>>> calc_affine_scale(-1.0, 2.0, 2)
1.0

Excludes: Padding, alignment, headers, and incomplete final blocks.

physics.numerics.calc_float32_bit_flip(value, bit)
Flip one bit of a stored binary32 value.











Name
Type
Description
Default




value
float
Input magnitude in arbitrary consistent scalar units.
required


bit
int
Zero-based bit index in [0, 31], counting from the least significant bit.
required














Name
Type
Description





tuple of float
Original binary32 stored value and value after the bit flip.






Equation: corrupted_word = stored_word XOR (1 << bit).
Assumptions: struct packs the input to binary32 before corruption.
Excludes: Fault probabilities, error correction, and arithmetic after corruption.
value stored as an IEEE 754 binary32 word, read back after bit bit flips.
Bit 31 is the sign, bits 30 to 23 the exponent, bits 22 to 0 the fraction. Returns (stored, corrupted): the value as stored, and the value after the flip. For a normal value whose encoded exponent is in 1..126, flipping bit 30 raises that exponent by 128 and preserves a finite normal value with the same sign and fraction. Encoded exponent 127 instead becomes the all-ones exponent: a zero fraction produces infinity and a nonzero fraction produces NaN. Zero, subnormals, and values whose exponent already has its high bit set require interpreting the resulting bits directly; there is no universal finite-multiplier rule.



Derivation: Exclusive-or toggles exactly the selected bit of the packed word.



>>> calc_float32_bit_flip(1.0, 31)
(1.0, -1.0)
>>> import math
>>> math.isfinite(calc_float32_bit_flip(0.5, 30)[1])
True
>>> math.isinf(calc_float32_bit_flip(1.0, 30)[1])
True
>>> math.isnan(calc_float32_bit_flip(1.5, 30)[1])
True

Estimate decimal precision from binary significand width.











Name
Type
Description
Default




fraction_bits
int
Stored fraction-field width in bits, at least one.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Equivalent decimal digits, not an integer round-trip guarantee.






Equation: digits = (fraction_bits+1)*log10(2).
Assumptions: Normal values include one implicit leading bit.
Excludes: Decimal serialization guarantees and subnormal precision loss.
Decimal digits a binary float keeps: (f + 1) log10 2 for f stored fraction bits plus the implicit leading bit (about 7.2 for FP32, 3.3 for FP16, 2.4 for BF16; added 2026-10-20).



Derivation: Equate 2**precision_bits with 10**decimal_digits and take logarithms.



>>> round(calc_float_decimal_digits(3), 3)

physics.numerics.calc_float_range(exponent_bits, fraction_bits)
Compute the finite range of a binary floating-point format.











Name
Type
Description
Default




exponent_bits
int
Exponent-field width in bits, at least two.
required


fraction_bits
int
Stored fraction-field width in bits, at least one.
required














Name
Type
Description





tuple of float
Largest finite, smallest normal, and smallest subnormal positive values.






Equation: Bias b = 2**(e-1)-1; limits are (2-2**(-f))*2**b, 2**(1-b), and 2**(1-b-f).
Assumptions: Biased exponent, implicit leading bit for normals, reserved top exponent.
Excludes: Alternative exponent encodings; host overflow for extremely wide formats.
Largest finite, smallest normal, and smallest subnormal magnitude of a binary float.
bias              = 2^(e-1) - 1
largest finite    = (2 - 2^-f) 2^bias
smallest normal   = 2^(1 - bias)
smallest subnormal= 2^(1 - bias - f)
Returns (largest, smallest_normal, smallest_subnormal).



Derivation: Binary positional notation with reserved zero and top exponents.



>>> calc_float_range(3, 2)
(14.0, 0.25, 0.0625)




physics.numerics.calc_float_round(value, exponent_bits, fraction_bits)
Round a scalar to the modeled binary floating-point format.











Name
Type
Description
Default




value
float
Input magnitude in arbitrary consistent scalar units.
required


exponent_bits
int
Exponent-field width in bits, at least two.
required


fraction_bits
int
Stored fraction-field width in bits, at least one.
required









Name
Type
Description





float
Rounded scalar; overflow becomes signed infinity.






Equation: Round abs(value)/step to even, multiply by step, and restore the sign.
Assumptions: Subnormal spacing is fixed; Python round supplies ties-to-even.
Excludes: Exception flags, directed rounding, and exact host-independent arithmetic.
value stored in a binary float format, rounded to nearest (ties to even).
A magnitude below half the smallest subnormal flushes to zero (underflow); one that rounds above the largest finite value becomes infinity (overflow).



Derivation: Rounding to the nearest point of the binade grid defined by calc_float_range.



>>> calc_float_round(1.3, 3, 2)
1.25




physics.numerics.calc_float_spacing(value, exponent_bits, fraction_bits)
Compute the magnitude-binade spacing of a binary float.











Name
Type
Description
Default




value
float
Input magnitude in arbitrary consistent scalar units.
required


exponent_bits
int
Exponent-field width in bits, at least two.
required


fraction_bits
int
Stored fraction-field width in bits, at least one.
required









Name
Type
Description





float
Positive grid spacing in the input scalar units.






Equation: step = 2**(max(floor(log2(abs(value))), emin)-fraction_bits).
Assumptions: Finite nonzero input; fixed spacing below the smallest normal.
Excludes: Zero input and directional neighbor differences at binade boundaries for either sign.
A number in the binade [2^E, 2^(E+1)) has neighbors 2^(E - f) apart; below the smallest normal the spacing stays at the subnormal step. A perturbation smaller than half the distance to the neighbor in that direction rounds back to an exactly representable value under nearest rounding, away from midpoint ties. At a binade boundary the upward and downward distances differ; the spacing returned here must not be used as a direction-independent rounding threshold.



Derivation: Adjacent significands differ by one stored fraction unit within a binade.



>>> calc_float_spacing(1.0, 3, 2)
0.25




physics.numerics.calc_float_values(exponent_bits, fraction_bits, ieee=True)
Enumerate nonnegative finite values of a binary format.











Name
Type
Description
Default




exponent_bits
int
Exponent-field width in bits, at least two.
required


fraction_bits
int
Stored fraction-field width in bits, at least one.
required


ieee
bool
Reserve the entire top exponent for special values if True (default).
True









Name
Type
Description





list of float
Sorted represented values, including zero.






Equation: Normals are (1+f/2**F)*2**(e-bias); subnormals are (f/2**F)*2**(1-bias).
Assumptions: Small field widths suitable for exhaustive enumeration; ieee selects the special-value encoding.
Excludes: Negative values, infinities, NaNs, and practical enumeration of wide formats.
Every non-negative finite value of a binary float format, sorted (zero included).
ieee=True reserves the top exponent for infinities and NaNs (IEEE 754, and FP8 E5M2). ieee=False is the “finite” layout of FP8 E4M3 (Micikevicius et al. 2022): the top exponent holds normal values and only its all-ones fraction is NaN, which lifts the largest value from 240 to 448.



Derivation: Enumerate each exponent/fraction code under the selected reserved-code convention.



>>> calc_float_values(2, 1)
[0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0]

Count distinct integer codes of a fixed width.











Name
Type
Description
Default




bits
int
Integer code width in bits; at least two for signed maxima, otherwise one.
required









Name
Type
Description





int
Number of bit patterns.






Equation: levels = 2**bits.
Assumptions: Each bit can independently take two values.
Excludes: Reserved codes and the interpretation of sign.
Distinct codes of a bits-bit integer, 2^b.



Derivation: Multiply two choices for each bit.



>>> calc_int_levels(3)

Compute the largest signed integer for a code width.











Name
Type
Description
Default




bits
int
Integer code width in bits; at least two for signed maxima, otherwise one.
required









Name
Type
Description





int
Largest positive two’s-complement code.






Equation: maximum = 2**(bits-1)-1.
Assumptions: One sign bit and a two’s-complement representation.
Excludes: Saturating arithmetic and unsigned encodings.
Largest value of a signed two’s-complement integer of bits bits, 2^(n-1) - 1.



Derivation: The positive half of the binary code space contains zero and 2**(bits-1)-1 positive values.



>>> calc_int_max(4)

physics.numerics.calc_quantize(x, scale, zero_point, qmin, qmax)
Encode a scalar by rounding and clipping to integer codes.











Name
Type
Description
Default




x
float
Scalar value to encode, in the same units as scale.
required


scale
float
Positive quantization step in value units per integer code.
required


zero_point
int
Integer code representing zero.
required


qmin
int
Lowest code; defaults to zero when omitted.
required


qmax
int
Highest code, at least qmin.
required









Name
Type
Description





int
Clipped integer code.






Equation: code = max(qmin, min(qmax, round(x/scale+zero_point))).
Assumptions: Positive scale and ordered code bounds; ties round to even.
Excludes: Scale calibration, stochastic rounding, and tensor broadcasting.
Code for x: clamp(round(x / s + z), qmin, qmax) (ties to even).

>>> calc_quantize(1.2, 0.5, 0, -7, 7)

    start,
    update,
    repeats,
    exponent_bits,

)
Trace repeated additions with format rounding after each step.











Name
Type
Description
Default

float
Initial scalar value, rounded before the first update.
required

Scalar increment in the same units as start; rounded before reuse.
required

required


fraction_bits

start after adding update repeats times, rounding to the format after every add.
Returns the stored value after each add, starting with start itself (repeats + 1 values). This is how a weight kept in a narrow format accumulates small optimizer updates (added 2026-10-20).

physics.numerics.calc_symmetric_scale(max_abs, bits)
Compute the step of a symmetric signed quantization grid.











Name
Type
Description
Default




max_abs
float
Positive largest absolute represented value.
required


bits
int
Integer code width in bits; at least two for signed maxima, otherwise one.
required









Name
Type
Description





float
Value-unit spacing per code.






Equation: scale = max_abs/(2**(bits-1)-1).
Assumptions: Zero point is zero; the most negative signed code is unused.
Excludes: Asymmetric clipping and selection of max_abs from data.
Step of a symmetric signed grid that reaches max_abs: s = max_abs / (2^(b-1) - 1) (zero-point 0; the code -2^(b-1) goes unused).

>>> calc_symmetric_scale(7.0, 4)
1.0




physics.numerics.calc_zero_point(alpha, scale, qmin=0)
Locate the integer code representing zero on an affine grid.











Name
Type
Description
Default




alpha
float
Lower clipping endpoint in the same units as the modeled values.
required


scale
float
Positive quantization step in value units per integer code.
required


qmin
int
Lowest code; defaults to zero when omitted.
0














Name
Type
Description





tuple of float and int
Unrounded offset -alpha/scale and rounded zero code including qmin.






Equation: offset=-alpha/scale; zero_code=qmin+round(offset).
Assumptions: Positive scale; nearest rounding with ties to even.
Excludes: Clamping the zero point to a valid code interval.
Integer that stands for real zero on an affine grid: qmin + round(-alpha / s).
Returns (exact, zero_point): the unrounded -alpha / s and the stored integer. Rounding is to nearest, ties to even, as Python and PyTorch round.



Derivation: Solve alpha+scale*(code-qmin)=0 and round the resulting offset.



>>> calc_zero_point(-2.0, 0.5)
(4.0, 4)

Zero, subnormals, and values whose exponent already has its high bit set require interpreting the resulting bits directly; there is no universal finite-multiplier rule.



Derivation: Exclusive-or toggles exactly the selected bit of the packed word.



>>> calc_float32_bit_flip(1.0, 31)
(1.0, -1.0)
>>> import math
>>> math.isfinite(calc_float32_bit_flip(0.5, 30)[1])
True
>>> math.isinf(calc_float32_bit_flip(1.0, 30)[1])
True
>>> math.isnan(calc_float32_bit_flip(1.5, 30)[1])
True

A data-parallel job inside one node and across nodes, from its one-device profile.
Every update reduces the full gradient: a ring AllReduce inside each node on the fast link, and, with more than one node, a ring across all devices on the inter-node link. engine.solvers.parallelism.ParallelLayoutModel()
One training step of a TP x PP x DP layout, read through the Fleet Law.
Compute: the step’s 6 P D FLOPs (flops_per_param_token per parameter per token, D tokens per update) spread over every device at a local share of peak. Communication: each data-parallel rank reduces its gradient shard (the full gradient over TP x PP) with a ring AllReduce of about twice the shard; up to overlap_fraction of that transfer hides under the compute window, never more than the window itself. engine.solvers.parallelism.DataParallelScaleOutModel()
A data-parallel job inside one node and across nodes, from its one-device profile.
Every update reduces the full gradient: a ring AllReduce inside each node on the fast link, and, with more than one node, a ring across all devices on the inter-node link. Gradient accumulation runs accumulation_steps local steps per update, so the same exchange serves more compute and the global batch grows. Speedup is the device count times the compute share of each update; training time and cost follow from the one-device run.

engine.solvers.parallelism.ParallelLayoutModel()
One training step of a TP x PP x DP layout, read through the Fleet Law.
Compute: the step’s 6 P D FLOPs (flops_per_param_token per parameter per token, D tokens per update) spread over every device at a local share of peak. title: FanoutDeadlineScenario
text:
Agents scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/agents.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A fan-out whose workers each finish by the deadline with one probability, independently.
An all-results barrier needs every worker (horizon compounding across workers); a quorum contract accepts any required of workers.


Equation: All-results probability is p**workers; quorum probability is the binomial tail at required successes.
Assumptions: Workers have identical independent on-time probabilities supplied externally.
Excludes: Correlated stalls and an inferred latency distribution; deadline labels the supplied probability.

Their contracts supply the underlying equations; property equations show the remaining unit conversions and accounting.

>>> round(float(value), 3)
0.43
