title: ResidualShareScenario
text:
Communication scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/communication.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A residual equal to residual of the one-device step, on devices devices.
Compute divides by N and the residual does not, so the residual’s share of the distributed step, r / ((1 - r)/N + r), is far larger than r: an observed share must not be read as the serial fraction.


Equation: Compose mlsysim.physics.performance.calc_strong_scaling_speedup.
Assumptions: The residual is a fixed fraction of the one-device step; all remaining work scales inversely with device count.
Excludes: Communication or synchronization overhead that grows with fleet size is absent.



Derivation: this scenario binds its input fields to the referenced implementation contracts: mlsysim.physics.performance.calc_strong_scaling_speedup. The methods below identify any additional arithmetic.



>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> case = Scenarios.ResidualOnePercent512
>>> round(case.step_fraction, 4)
0.0119

title: engine.solvers.training
text:
engine.solvers.training
Training memory, checkpointing, and scaling-law solvers.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__); kept per-domain so the logic stays reviewable.





Name
Description




CheckpointModel
Analyzes the storage constraints and I/O burst penalties of saving model states.


ScalingModel
Analyzes the ‘Scaling Physics’ of model training (Chinchilla Laws).


TrainingMemoryModel
Decomposes per-accelerator training memory into teachable components.


TrainingRunModel
Wall-clock time of a training run, from peak throughput to delivered time.


TrainingStateModel
Persistent mixed-precision Adam state and how parallelism shards it.





engine.solvers.training.CheckpointModel()
Analyzes the storage constraints and I/O burst penalties of saving model states.
Training massive models requires saving hundreds of gigabytes (Weights + Optimizer States) to persistent storage. This model calculates the time spent blocked on I/O, subtracting from the cluster’s Model FLOPs Utilization.
Literature Source: 1. Eisenman et al. (2022), “Check-N-Run: A Checkpointing System for Training Large Language Models.”





Name
Description




solve
Estimate synchronous checkpoint size, write time, and stall fraction.





engine.solvers.training.CheckpointModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    optimizer='adam',
    checkpoint_interval_hours=4.0,
    n_writers=1,
    filesystem_limit_gbs=500.0,
)
Estimate synchronous checkpoint size, write time, and stall fraction.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model
Workload
Workload whose parameter count sets the checkpoint payload.
required


hardware
HardwareNode
Device with storage bandwidth in bytes/second. Missing or zero storage bandwidth uses the declared fallback in engine.calibration.
required


optimizer
str
"adam" selects mixed-precision Adam checkpoint bytes; other names use the SGD convention. Gradients are not persisted.
'adam'


checkpoint_interval_hours
float
Hours between checkpoints. A nonpositive interval returns a stall fraction of one; positive intervals use write time divided by interval.
4.0


n_writers
int
Positive number of writers sharing the checkpoint payload.
1


filesystem_limit_gbs
float
Positive aggregate filesystem ceiling in decimal GB/second.
500.0














Name
Type
Description





CheckpointResult
Checkpoint size in GB, write duration in seconds, and a dimensionless stall fraction in mfu_penalty_pct (not multiplied by 100). storage_bottleneck flags writes longer than one minute; it does not certify that a checkpoint schedule fits the interval.






mlsysim.physics.memory.calc_checkpoint_size : Persisted state accounting.



Equation: M = P b; bandwidth = min(n_writers * device_bandwidth, filesystem_limit); write_time = M / bandwidth. The penalty is write_time / checkpoint_interval for a positive interval.
Assumptions: writers partition one payload without duplicated writes; checkpointing synchronously blocks useful training. Byte conventions come from engine.calibration and are separate from storage rates.
Excludes: asynchronous overlap, filesystem metadata, serialization CPU work, network contention, and checkpoint recovery. The penalty can exceed one when a write takes longer than its configured interval.



Derivation: payload size is parameter count times persisted bytes per parameter; elapsed transfer time is payload divided by available rate. The writer minimum is a shared-bandwidth capacity constraint.



>>> from mlsysim import Models, Hardware
>>> result = CheckpointModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B, Hardware.Cloud.H100)
>>> result.checkpoint_size.to("GB").magnitude > 0
True
>>> result.write_time_seconds.to("second").magnitude > 0
True






engine.solvers.training.ScalingModel()
Analyzes the ‘Scaling Physics’ of model training (Chinchilla Laws).
This model determines the optimal model size (P) and dataset size (D) given a compute budget (C), following the compute-optimal training regime where D ≈ 20P.
Literature Source: 1. Hoffmann et al. (2022), “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” 2. Kaplan et al. (2020), “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” 3. McCandlish et al. (2018), “An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training.”





Name
Description




solve
Allocate a training compute budget between parameters and tokens.





engine.solvers.training.ScalingModel.solve(
    compute_budget,
    target_model_size=None,
)
Allocate a training compute budget between parameters and tokens.











Name
Type
Description
Default




compute_budget
Quantity
Finite positive training work in FLOPs, or a finite positive duration interpreted as reference-H100 compute time at the declared sustained efficiency. Any compatible FLOP prefix is accepted and normalized before calculation.
required


target_model_size
Quantity
Finite positive fixed parameter count. If omitted, use the registered compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio.
None














Name
Type
Description





ScalingResult
Modeled parameter and token counts, compute budget, and dimensionless tokens per parameter. The result does not include a quality estimate or a memory-feasibility decision.






Equation: C = k P D, where k is the registered compute coefficient. With D = r P, P = sqrt(C / (k r)); when P is fixed, D = C / (k P). A time input becomes C = duration * reference_peak * reference_MFU.
Assumptions: parameter-dominated dense training work and a constant registered optimal token ratio. The time conversion uses a declared reference accelerator rather than an arbitrary fleet supplied by a user.
Excludes: inference cost, data-quality variation, architecture-dependent loss prediction, attention work, and hardware memory capacity.



Hoffmann et al. (2022), “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556 (bibliography key: hoffmann2022chinchilla). The fixed-ratio allocation is the package’s simplified accounting form.



>>> result = ScalingModel().solve(Q_(1200000, "flop"))
>>> result.optimal_parameters.to("count").magnitude > 0
True
>>> result.optimal_tokens.to("count").magnitude > 0
True






engine.solvers.training.TrainingMemoryModel()
Decomposes per-accelerator training memory into teachable components.
This model answers a different question than SingleNodeModel. Roofline feasibility asks whether a workload’s inference weights fit; training feasibility must also account for gradients, optimizer state, activations, and communication buffers. The accounting follows the common mixed-precision state breakdown used by Megatron-LM and ZeRO.
Literature Source: 1. Shoeybi et al. (2019), “Megatron-LM” (tensor/pipeline parallel state). 2. Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO” (data-parallel state sharding). 3. Korthikanti et al. (2023), activation recomputation accounting.
Formula contract: - parameter states are sharded by TP * PP * EP before ZeRO sharding. - ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state, ZeRO-2 also shards gradients, and ZeRO-3 also shards weights across DP. - activation memory is based on local microbatch, layers per pipeline stage, hidden dimension, and the actual bytes per element for the precision.





Name
Description




solve
Estimate per-accelerator training memory from local state and activations.





engine.solvers.training.TrainingMemoryModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    batch_size,
    seq_len=2048,
    precision='fp16',
    optimizer='adam',
    activation_checkpointing='selective',
    tp_size=1,
    pp_size=1,
    dp_size=1,
    ep_size=1,
    zero_stage=0,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=1,
    trainable_fraction=1.0,
    communication_buffer_fraction=0.05,
    sequence_parallel=True,
)
Estimate per-accelerator training memory from local state and activations.

Type
Description
Default

required

Optimizer storage convention supported by optimizer_state_bytes.
'adam'

Activation retention strategy passed to the activation-memory model.
'none'

Tensor-parallel degree, at least one.
1

Pipeline-parallel degree, at least one.
1

int
Data-parallel degree, at least one.
1

int
Expert-parallel degree, at least one.
1

(0, 1, 2, 3)
Cumulative DP sharding: optimizer state, then gradients, then weights.
0


gradient_accumulation_steps
int
Positive number of sequential microbatches per update.
1


trainable_fraction
float
Fraction in [0, 1] receiving gradients and optimizer state.
1.0


communication_buffer_fraction
float
Gradient staging buffer as a fraction in [0, 1] of local gradients.
0.05


sequence_parallel
bool
If true, split stored activations across the TP group. If false, retain the unsharded activation estimate as a conservative bound.
True














Name
Type
Description





TrainingMemoryResult
Weights, gradients, optimizer state, activations, buffers, and total memory in GB. feasible compares that modeled total with device capacity; it excludes unmodeled runtime reserves.






mlsysim.physics.memory.calc_activation_memory : Activation retention model. mlsysim.physics.memory.optimizer_state_bytes : Optimizer storage convention.



Equation: total = weights + gradients + optimizer + activations + communication_buffers. Parameter state first divides by TP * PP * EP; ZeRO then divides selected terms by DP. Local microbatch is max(1, ceil(global_batch / (DP * accumulation_steps))). Layers per stage are max(1, ceil(layers / PP)). Activation bytes follow calc_activation_memory and divide by TP when sequence parallelism is enabled. Buffers contain a gradient fraction plus send/receive pipeline boundary activations.
Assumptions: balanced parameter sharding and uniform layer geometry. The precision byte count rescales the activation model’s FP16 baseline. ZeRO stages are cumulative. Trainable fraction affects gradients and optimizer state but not resident weights.
Excludes: allocator reserves, implementation workspaces, fragmentation, uneven expert placement, and detailed interleaved pipeline lifetimes. A capacity pass does not guarantee a runnable deployment.



Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models.” https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 (bibliography key: rajbhandari2020). Korthikanti et al. (2023), “Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models.” https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05198 (bibliography key: korthikanti2023).



>>> from mlsysim import Models, Hardware
>>> result = TrainingMemoryModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
...     Hardware.Cloud.H100, batch_size=1, seq_len=128)
>>> result.total_memory.to("GB").magnitude > 0
True
>>> result.feasible == (result.total_memory <= result.available_memory)
True






engine.solvers.training.TrainingRunModel()
Wall-clock time of a training run, from peak throughput to delivered time.
The chain starts from the 6PD training FLOPs at every device’s peak, divides by the local compute efficiency (the compute-only baseline), then by the scaling efficiency (communication and pipeline bubbles), then multiplies by each operational overhead in order (checkpointing, failures and restarts, maintenance), each relative to the subtotal before it.
Literature Source: 1. Kaplan et al. (2020) and Hoffmann et al. (2022), the 6PD rule. 2. Narayanan et al. (2021), scaling efficiency at cluster scale.





Name
Description




solve
Compose compute, scaling, and operational factors into training time.





engine.solvers.training.TrainingRunModel.solve(
    model,
    fleet,
    local_efficiency,
    scaling_efficiency,
    overheads,
    precision='fp8',
    tokens=None,
)
Compose compute, scaling, and operational factors into training time.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model
Workload
Parameter count and, when tokens is omitted, training-token count.
required


fleet
Fleet
Accelerator count and per-device peak compute at the chosen precision.
required


local_efficiency
float
Positive dimensionless fraction of local peak throughput, usually at most one. It acts before cluster scaling losses.
required


scaling_efficiency
float
Positive fraction of compute throughput retained after communication and pipeline effects, usually at most one.
required


overheads
dict
Ordered mapping from stage name to nonnegative fractional time overhead. Each fraction applies to the preceding subtotal.
required


precision
str
Compute precision key; unsupported keys use the hardware’s base peak.
'fp8'


tokens
Quantity
Positive total training-token count overriding model.training_tokens.
None














Name
Type
Description





TrainingRunResult
Work in FLOPs and peak, compute, scaled, intermediate, and total times in hours. Delivered fraction is peak time divided by total time; this calculation does not check model residency.






mlsysim.physics.transformer.calc_transformer_training_flops : Training work. mlsysim.physics.performance.dTime : Work divided by effective compute rate.



Equation: F = 6 P D; T_peak = F / (N peak); T_compute = T_peak / eta; T_scaled = T_compute / scaling_efficiency. Each overhead f multiplies its preceding subtotal by (1 + f).
Assumptions: homogeneous accelerator throughput and supplied efficiencies that already summarize kernel and cluster behavior. The overhead mapping is an ordered accounting scenario, not a measured trace.
Excludes: overlap among overhead stages, explicit communication schedules, activation residency, data starvation, and changing efficiency during a run.



Derivation: work divided by aggregate rate gives elapsed compute time; sequential fractional overheads multiply the running subtotal. Parameter-dominated training work follows the cited contract in mlsysim.physics.transformer.calc_transformer_training_flops.



>>> from mlsysim import Models, Systems
>>> result = TrainingRunModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
...     Systems.Clusters.Research_256, local_efficiency=0.5,
...     scaling_efficiency=0.8, overheads={"checkpoint": 0.1},
...     tokens=Q_(1000, "count"))
>>> result.total_time > result.scaled_time > result.peak_time
True






engine.solvers.training.TrainingStateModel()
Persistent mixed-precision Adam state and how parallelism shards it.
Per parameter: FP16 weights and gradients (2 B each), FP32 master weights (4 B), and two FP32 Adam moments (4 B each), 16 B in all. Tensor parallelism splits every term across the TP group; ZeRO-style sharding further splits the optimizer moments across the data-parallel replicas. Activations are a stated total, not derived (they depend on sequence length, microbatch, and recomputation).
Literature Source: 1. Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO” (16 B/param accounting, sharding). 2. Shoeybi et al. (2019), “Megatron-LM” (tensor parallelism).





Name
Description




solve
Account for mixed-precision Adam state under selected sharding choices.





engine.solvers.training.TrainingStateModel.solve(
    model,
    tp_size,
    dp_size,
    activations,
)
Account for mixed-precision Adam state under selected sharding choices.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model
Workload
Model parameter count; this accounting uses FP16 weights and gradients.
required


tp_size
int
Positive tensor-parallel degree splitting each state term.
required


dp_size
int
Positive data-parallel degree additionally splitting Adam moments in the reported moments-sharded comparison.
required


activations
Quantity
Nonnegative total activation storage in bytes, supplied by the caller rather than derived from a batch shape.
required














Name
Type
Description





TrainingStateResult
Full and per-device state components in GB, including TP-only, offloaded, and moments-sharded comparisons. These totals do not imply device feasibility because no capacity is supplied.






mlsysim.engine.solvers.training.TrainingMemoryModel.solve : Full state budget.



Equation: W = G = 2 P bytes; master = 4 P bytes; moments = 8 P bytes. Persistent state is W + G + master + moments. TP-only total is (persistent + activations) / TP. The moments-sharded term is moments / (TP * DP); weights remain W / TP in that comparison.
Assumptions: uniform dense parameter storage and even sharding. The moments-only comparison does not shard the master copy and must not be read as a complete implementation of every ZeRO state transition.
Excludes: communication buffers, activation recomputation, allocator reserve, offload transfer latency, and a hardware capacity check.



Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models.” https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 (bibliography key: rajbhandari2020). The moments-only output is a declared partial-sharding comparison; TrainingMemoryModel provides cumulative ZeRO-stage accounting.



>>> from mlsysim import Models
>>> result = TrainingStateModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
...     tp_size=2, dp_size=4, activations=Q_(1, "GB"))
>>> result.zero_moments_per_device < result.tp_moments_per_device
True

Checkpoint size in GB, write duration in seconds, and a dimensionless stall fraction in mfu_penalty_pct (not multiplied by 100). storage_bottleneck flags writes longer than one minute; it does not certify that a checkpoint schedule fits the interval.






mlsysim.physics.memory.calc_checkpoint_size : Persisted state accounting.



Equation: M = P b; bandwidth = min(n_writers * device_bandwidth, filesystem_limit); write_time = M / bandwidth. The penalty is write_time / checkpoint_interval for a positive interval.
Assumptions: writers partition one payload without duplicated writes; checkpointing synchronously blocks useful training. Byte conventions come from engine.calibration and are separate from storage rates.
Excludes: asynchronous overlap, filesystem metadata, serialization CPU work, network contention, and checkpoint recovery. The penalty can exceed one when a write takes longer than its configured interval.



Derivation: payload size is parameter count times persisted bytes per parameter; elapsed transfer time is payload divided by available rate. The writer minimum is a shared-bandwidth capacity constraint.



>>> from mlsysim import Models, Hardware
>>> result = CheckpointModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B, Hardware.Cloud.H100)
>>> result.checkpoint_size.to("GB").magnitude > 0
True
>>> result.write_time_seconds.to("second").magnitude > 0
True






engine.solvers.training.ScalingModel()
Analyzes the ‘Scaling Physics’ of model training (Chinchilla Laws).
This model determines the optimal model size (P) and dataset size (D) given a compute budget (C), following the compute-optimal training regime where D ≈ 20P.
Literature Source: 1. Hoffmann et al. (2022), “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” 2. Kaplan et al. (2020), “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” 3. McCandlish et al. (2018), “An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training.”





Name
Description




solve
Allocate a training compute budget between parameters and tokens.





engine.solvers.training.ScalingModel.solve(
    compute_budget,
    target_model_size=None,
)
Allocate a training compute budget between parameters and tokens.











Name
Type
Description
Default




compute_budget
Quantity
Finite positive training work in FLOPs, or a finite positive duration interpreted as reference-H100 compute time at the declared sustained efficiency. Any compatible FLOP prefix is accepted and normalized before calculation.
required


target_model_size
Quantity
Finite positive fixed parameter count. If omitted, use the registered compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio.
None














Name
Type
Description





ScalingResult
Modeled parameter and token counts, compute budget, and dimensionless tokens per parameter. The result does not include a quality estimate or a memory-feasibility decision.






Equation: C = k P D, where k is the registered compute coefficient. With D = r P, P = sqrt(C / (k r)); when P is fixed, D = C / (k P). A time input becomes C = duration * reference_peak * reference_MFU.
Assumptions: parameter-dominated dense training work and a constant registered optimal token ratio. The time conversion uses a declared reference accelerator rather than an arbitrary fleet supplied by a user.
Excludes: inference cost, data-quality variation, architecture-dependent loss prediction, attention work, and hardware memory capacity.



Hoffmann et al. (2022), “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556 (bibliography key: hoffmann2022chinchilla). The fixed-ratio allocation is the package’s simplified accounting form.



>>> result = ScalingModel().solve(Q_(1200000, "flop"))
>>> result.optimal_parameters.to("count").magnitude > 0
True
>>> result.optimal_tokens.to("count").magnitude > 0
True






engine.solvers.training.TrainingMemoryModel()
Decomposes per-accelerator training memory into teachable components.
This model answers a different question than SingleNodeModel. Roofline feasibility asks whether a workload’s inference weights fit; training feasibility must also account for gradients, optimizer state, activations, and communication buffers. The accounting follows the common mixed-precision state breakdown used by Megatron-LM and ZeRO.
Literature Source: 1. Shoeybi et al. (2019), “Megatron-LM” (tensor/pipeline parallel state). 2. Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO” (data-parallel state sharding). 3. Korthikanti et al. (2023), activation recomputation accounting.
Formula contract: - parameter states are sharded by TP * PP * EP before ZeRO sharding. - ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state, ZeRO-2 also shards gradients, and ZeRO-3 also shards weights across DP. - activation memory is based on local microbatch, layers per pipeline stage, hidden dimension, and the actual bytes per element for the precision.

mlsysim.physics.memory.calc_activation_memory : Activation retention model. mlsysim.physics.memory.optimizer_state_bytes : Optimizer storage convention.



Equation: total = weights + gradients + optimizer + activations + communication_buffers. Parameter state first divides by TP * PP * EP; ZeRO then divides selected terms by DP. Local microbatch is max(1, ceil(global_batch / (DP * accumulation_steps))). Layers per stage are max(1, ceil(layers / PP)). Activation bytes follow calc_activation_memory and divide by TP when sequence parallelism is enabled. Buffers contain a gradient fraction plus send/receive pipeline boundary activations.
Assumptions: balanced parameter sharding and uniform layer geometry. The precision byte count rescales the activation model’s FP16 baseline. ZeRO stages are cumulative. Trainable fraction affects gradients and optimizer state but not resident weights.
Excludes: allocator reserves, implementation workspaces, fragmentation, uneven expert placement, and detailed interleaved pipeline lifetimes. A capacity pass does not guarantee a runnable deployment.



Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models.” https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 (bibliography key: rajbhandari2020). Korthikanti et al. (2023), “Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models.” https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05198 (bibliography key: korthikanti2023).

>>> result.total_memory.to("GB").magnitude > 0
True
>>> result.feasible == (result.total_memory <= result.available_memory)
True






engine.solvers.training.TrainingRunModel()
Wall-clock time of a training run, from peak throughput to delivered time.
The chain starts from the 6PD training FLOPs at every device’s peak, divides by the local compute efficiency (the compute-only baseline), then by the scaling efficiency (communication and pipeline bubbles), then multiplies by each operational overhead in order (checkpointing, failures and restarts, maintenance), each relative to the subtotal before it.
Literature Source: 1. Kaplan et al. (2020) and Hoffmann et al. (2022), the 6PD rule. 2. Narayanan et al. (2021), scaling efficiency at cluster scale.





Name
Description

None

Work in FLOPs and peak, compute, scaled, intermediate, and total times in hours. Delivered fraction is peak time divided by total time; this calculation does not check model residency.






mlsysim.physics.transformer.calc_transformer_training_flops : Training work. mlsysim.physics.performance.dTime : Work divided by effective compute rate.



Equation: F = 6 P D; T_peak = F / (N peak); T_compute = T_peak / eta; T_scaled = T_compute / scaling_efficiency. Each overhead f multiplies its preceding subtotal by (1 + f).
Assumptions: homogeneous accelerator throughput and supplied efficiencies that already summarize kernel and cluster behavior. The overhead mapping is an ordered accounting scenario, not a measured trace.
Excludes: overlap among overhead stages, explicit communication schedules, activation residency, data starvation, and changing efficiency during a run.



Derivation: work divided by aggregate rate gives elapsed compute time; sequential fractional overheads multiply the running subtotal. Parameter-dominated training work follows the cited contract in mlsysim.physics.transformer.calc_transformer_training_flops.



>>> from mlsysim import Models, Systems
>>> result = TrainingRunModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
...     Systems.Clusters.Research_256, local_efficiency=0.5,
...     scaling_efficiency=0.8, overheads={"checkpoint": 0.1},
...     tokens=Q_(1000, "count"))
>>> result.total_time > result.scaled_time > result.peak_time
True






engine.solvers.training.TrainingStateModel()
Persistent mixed-precision Adam state and how parallelism shards it.
Per parameter: FP16 weights and gradients (2 B each), FP32 master weights (4 B), and two FP32 Adam moments (4 B each), 16 B in all. Tensor parallelism splits every term across the TP group; ZeRO-style sharding further splits the optimizer moments across the data-parallel replicas. Activations are a stated total, not derived (they depend on sequence length, microbatch, and recomputation).
Literature Source: 1. Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO” (16 B/param accounting, sharding). 2. Shoeybi et al. (2019), “Megatron-LM” (tensor parallelism).





Name
Description




solve
Account for mixed-precision Adam state under selected sharding choices.

    model,
    tp_size,
    dp_size,
    activations,
)
Account for mixed-precision Adam state under selected sharding choices.











Name
Type
Description
Default

Workload
Model parameter count; this accounting uses FP16 weights and gradients.
required


tp_size
int
Positive tensor-parallel degree splitting each state term.
required


dp_size
int
Positive data-parallel degree additionally splitting Adam moments in the reported moments-sharded comparison.
required


activations
Quantity
Nonnegative total activation storage in bytes, supplied by the caller rather than derived from a batch shape.
required














Name
Type
Description





TrainingStateResult
Full and per-device state components in GB, including TP-only, offloaded, and moments-sharded comparisons. These totals do not imply device feasibility because no capacity is supplied.






mlsysim.engine.solvers.training.TrainingMemoryModel.solve : Full state budget.



Equation: W = G = 2 P bytes; master = 4 P bytes; moments = 8 P bytes. Persistent state is W + G + master + moments. TP-only total is (persistent + activations) / TP. The moments-sharded term is moments / (TP * DP); weights remain W / TP in that comparison.
Assumptions: uniform dense parameter storage and even sharding. The moments-only comparison does not shard the master copy and must not be read as a complete implementation of every ZeRO state transition.
Excludes: communication buffers, activation recomputation, allocator reserve, offload transfer latency, and a hardware capacity check.



Rajbhandari et al. (2020), “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models.” https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 (bibliography key: rajbhandari2020). The moments-only output is a declared partial-sharding comparison; TrainingMemoryModel provides cumulative ZeRO-stage accounting.



>>> from mlsysim import Models
>>> result = TrainingStateModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
...     tp_size=2, dp_size=4, activations=Q_(1, "GB"))
>>> result.zero_moments_per_device < result.tp_moments_per_device
True

Equation: last = s0 + delta (H - 1); total = H s0 + delta H (H - 1) / 2.
Assumptions: Every request resends the full earlier context; append size is constant.
Excludes: Prefix caching, compaction, request-window limits, and output-token billing.



Derivation: Sum the arithmetic progression s0, s0 + delta, …, s0 + (H - 1) delta.



>>> last, total = calc_append_only_context(10, 2, 3)
>>> (last, total) == (10 + 2 * 2, sum([10, 12, 14]))
True

>>> calc_bounded_liability(10, 5, 2, 3) == 10 * 2 + 5 * 3

Excludes: Interactions between quality and price, and clipping an unattainable target to 1.



Derivation: Equate C / p_new with C (1 - cut share) / p_accept and cancel C.

>>> kept, mass, probs = calc_nucleus([0.5, 0.25, 0.25], 0.5)

>>> from mlsysim.core.units import ureg

Equation: L = P_defect * consequence * (1 - r).
Assumptions: One defect event and a specified mean recoverable share; an upstream check can supply r = detection * rollback fidelity.
Excludes: Tail-risk bounds, repeated defects, and proof of recovery effectiveness.



Derivation: Multiply the event probability by the unrecoverable portion of its conditional loss.



>>> calc_expected_irreversible_loss(0.5, 8, 0.25) == 0.5 * 8 * 0.75
True




physics.agents.calc_expected_max_std_normal(n, lo=-10.0, hi=10.0, steps=40000)
Integrate the expected maximum of independent standard normals.











Name
Type
Description
Default




n
int
Positive number of independent standard-normal draws.
required


lo
float
Lower integration limit in standard deviations; default -10.
-10.0


hi
float
Upper integration limit greater than lo; default 10.
10.0


steps
int
Positive trapezoid count; default 40000.
40000














Name
Type
Description





float
Approximate expected maximum, in units of the normal standard deviation.






Equation: E[max] = integral x n phi(x) Phi(x) ** (n - 1) dx over [lo, hi].
Assumptions: Independent standard-normal score errors and a finite uniform integration grid.
Excludes: Tail mass outside the bounds, quadrature error, correlated errors, and unequal candidate means.



Derivation: The maximum CDF is Phi(x) ** n; differentiating gives n phi(x) Phi(x) ** (n - 1).



>>> abs(calc_expected_max_std_normal(1, steps=1000)) < 1e-10

physics.agents.calc_first_horizon_below(step_success, threshold)
Find the first whole horizon below a success threshold.











Name
Type
Description
Default




step_success
float
Per-step success probability strictly between 0 and 1.
required


threshold
float
Task success threshold strictly between 0 and 1.
required














Name
Type
Description





int
First positive whole-step horizon with task success below threshold.






Equation: n = floor(log(threshold) / log(step_success)) + 1.
Assumptions: Identical independent step success and an exact strict inequality.
Excludes: Correlations and numerical ambiguity when logarithms lie near an integer.



Derivation: Solve p ** n < threshold for n; log(p) is negative, so n must exceed the log ratio.



>>> n = calc_first_horizon_below(0.5, 0.3)
>>> 0.5 ** n < 0.3 <= 0.5 ** (n - 1)
True




physics.agents.calc_independent_success(acceptance_probability, attempts)
Calculate the chance that at least one independent attempt passes.











Name
Type
Description
Default




acceptance_probability
float
Acceptance probability of each attempt in [0, 1].
required


attempts
int
Nonnegative count of independent attempts.
required









Name
Type
Description





float
Probability of at least one accepted attempt.






Equation: P_any = 1 - (1 - p_accept) ** k.
Assumptions: Identical independent attempts.
Excludes: Shared failure causes, search adaptation, and dependence among attempts.



Derivation: Subtract the probability that every attempt fails from one.



>>> calc_independent_success(0.5, 2) == 1 - 0.5 ** 2
True




physics.agents.calc_injection_exposure(payload_fraction, reads)
Calculate exposure probability across independent untrusted reads.











Name
Type
Description
Default




payload_fraction
float
Fraction of independently read items carrying a payload, in [0, 1].
required


reads
float
Nonnegative number of reads; whole counts describe discrete items.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Probability of encountering at least one payload, not probability of compromise.






Equation: P_exposure = 1 - (1 - q) ** n.
Assumptions: Identically distributed independent reads; q may include a specified screening miss fraction.
Excludes: Attack success conditional on exposure, correlated items, and adaptive attackers.



Derivation: Exposure is the complement of all n reads being payload-free.



>>> calc_injection_exposure(0.5, 2) == 1 - 0.5 ** 2
True




physics.agents.calc_injection_read_budget(payload_fraction, target_exposure)
Find the largest read budget within an exposure limit.











Name
Type
Description
Default




payload_fraction
float
Per-read payload probability strictly between 0 and 1.
required


target_exposure
float
Maximum exposure probability in [0, 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





int
Largest whole read count satisfying the modeled exposure limit.






Equation: n_max = floor(log(1 - target) / log(1 - q)).
Assumptions: Independent identically distributed payload presence on each read.
Excludes: Correlated exposure, compromise probability, and floating-point errors near integer boundaries.



Derivation: Invert 1 - (1 - q) ** n <= target and take the integer floor.



>>> n = calc_injection_read_budget(0.5, 0.6)
>>> calc_injection_exposure(0.5, n) <= 0.6 < calc_injection_exposure(0.5, n + 1)
True

    model=None,

    n_kv_heads=None,

)

Type

TransformerWorkload or AgentArchitecture

Quantity or int
Bytes per stored cache element; default 2 represents FP16/BF16 storage.

Type

Bytes stored for one sequence token across all layers.






Equation: m_token = 2 L H_kv d_head b, where b is bytes per element.
Assumptions: One key tensor and one value tensor share the stated shape and precision.
Excludes: Allocator metadata, padding, fragmentation, and compressed latent-attention caches.



Derivation: Count L H_kv d_head elements separately in keys and values, then multiply by element width.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
>>> result = calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token(n_layers=2, n_kv_heads=3, head_dim=4)
>>> result == 2 * 2 * 3 * 4 * 2 * ureg.byte

Calculate the probability that a group contains both outcomes.

Per-attempt success probability in [0, 1].
required

Positive number of attempts.
required

Type
Description

Probability of observing both a success and a failure.






Equation: P_mixed = 1 - (1 - p) ** k - p ** k.
Assumptions: Independent attempts with identical pass probability.
Excludes: Correlated attempts, reward magnitudes, and usefulness of the resulting training signal.



Derivation: Exclude the disjoint all-failure and all-success groups from the full outcome space.



>>> calc_mixed_outcome_fraction(0.5, 2) == 0.5
True




physics.agents.calc_nucleus(probabilities, top_p)
Select and renormalize the top-p probability nucleus.











Name
Type
Description
Default

iterable of float
Nonnegative normalized token probabilities with positive total mass.
required


top_p
float
Target retained mass in (0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





tuple
Retained count, original retained mass, and normalized probabilities sorted from largest to smallest.






Equation: Keep the smallest prefix k with sum_{i=1}^k p_sorted_i >= top_p; return p_i / retained_mass.
Assumptions: The input is a probability distribution and highest-probability tokens are retained first.
Excludes: Token identities, tie-breaking identities, temperature scaling, and quality guarantees.



Derivation: A descending cumulative sum finds the shortest prefix reaching the threshold; division renormalizes it.



>>> kept, mass, probs = calc_nucleus([0.5, 0.25, 0.25], 0.5)
>>> (kept, mass, probs) == (1, 0.5, [1.0])
True




physics.agents.calc_pass_at_k_unbiased(samples, passing, k)
Estimate the probability that a size-k sample contains a pass.





Name
Type
Description
Default




samples
int
Positive count n of graded samples.
required


passing
int
Passing sample count c in [0, n].
required


k
int
Subset size in [1, n].
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Unbiased estimate of the probability at least one of k draws passes.






Equation: pass_at_k = 1 - C(n - c, k) / C(n, k), or 1 if n - c < k.
Assumptions: Exchangeable independent draws from a fixed task distribution.
Excludes: Dependence among samples, uncertainty intervals, and changing graders.



Derivation: Count all-failing subsets among all size-k subsets and subtract their fraction from one; this is the combinatorial estimator described by Chen et al. (2021).
Chen et al. (2021), “Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code.” https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374 (bibliography key: chen2021evaluating).



>>> calc_pass_at_k_unbiased(4, 2, 1) == 0.5
True




physics.agents.calc_pass_posterior(
    defect_rate,
    false_accept_rate,
    valid_accept_rate,
)
Calculate the defective share of passing candidates.

Type
Description
Default

float
Prior defective fraction in [0, 1].
required


false_accept_rate
float
Probability of passing conditional on defect, in [0, 1].
required


valid_accept_rate
float
Probability of passing conditional on validity, in [0, 1]; total pass probability must be positive.
required









Name
Type
Description





float
Defective share among passing candidates.






Equation: P(defect | pass) = q f / (q f + (1 - q) v).
Assumptions: Binary validity and fixed conditional checker rates.
Excludes: Distribution shift, uncertainty in checker estimates, and zero-pass populations.



Derivation: Bayes rule divides the joint defect-and-pass probability by total pass probability.



>>> calc_pass_posterior(0.5, 0.25, 0.75) == 0.25
True

Estimate the chance that every run in a size-k sample passes.

required

required

Type

Equation: pass_pow_k = C(c, k) / C(n, k), or 0 if c < k.
Assumptions: Exchangeable independent draws from a fixed task distribution.
Excludes: Sample dependence, grader uncertainty, and confidence intervals.



Derivation: Count all-passing subsets among all size-k subsets; its expectation under independent draws is p ** k.
Yao et al. (2024), “tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains.” https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045 (bibliography key: yao2024taubench).

Count proposed search nodes with and without independent pruning.

Type
Description
Default

int
Nonnegative child count proposed per retained node.
required


rejection_rate

Independent rejection probability in [0, 1].
required


depth
int
Nonnegative number of child levels, excluding the root.
required














Name
Type
Description





tuple
Unpruned node count and expected proposed node count with pruning; neither includes the root.






Equation: unpruned = sum_d b ** d; pruned = sum_d b [b (1 - r)] ** (d - 1).
Assumptions: Constant branching, independent rejection, and no expansion of rejected nodes.
Excludes: Checker execution cost, adaptive branching, and variance in realized tree size.



Derivation: At each level the expected retained-parent count grows by b (1 - r), then each parent proposes b children.



>>> full, pruned = calc_pruned_tree_nodes(2, 0.0, 3)
>>> full == pruned
True




physics.agents.calc_repair_break_even(repair_cost, fallback_cost)
Find the repair success rate that breaks even with fallback.

Type
Description
Default

Nonnegative cost of one repair attempt.
required


fallback_cost
Quantity or float
Positive fallback cost in the same units as repair_cost.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Repair success probability at equal expected cost; above one means repair cannot win on this axis.






Equation: p_star = C_repair / C_fallback.
Assumptions: A failed repair leaves the fallback available at unchanged cost.
Excludes: Irreversible damage, repair repetitions, and joint optimization across unlike units.



Derivation: Equate C_repair + (1 - p) C_fallback with C_fallback, then solve for p.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
>>> calc_repair_break_even(1 * ureg.second, 4 * ureg.second) == 0.25
True

    repair_cost,
    fallback_cost,
    success_probability,
)

required

required


success_probability

Repair success probability in [0, 1].
required

Equation: E[C] = C_repair + (1 - p) C_fallback.
Assumptions: Every attempt pays repair cost; only repair failure incurs fallback.
Excludes: Repeated repairs, changed fallback cost, and consequences outside the chosen cost dimension.



Derivation: Weight the successful and unsuccessful branches by p and 1 - p.



>>> calc_repair_first_expected_cost(1, 4, 0.5) == 1 + 0.5 * 4

Count newly prefetched tokens with full prefix reuse.

required

required

Nonnegative fresh tokens appended on each later request.
required

Total newly prefetched prompt tokens across requests.






Equation: S_fresh = S0 + (H - 1) D.
Assumptions: All earlier prefix KV state remains compatible and available at every subsequent call.
Excludes: Cache eviction, prefix edits, lookup overhead, and generated output tokens.



Derivation: Charge the initial prompt once and only the appended suffix on each remaining request.

Calculate the setup share of serial call time.











Name
Type
Description
Default

Nonnegative setup time, in any time unit.
required


work
Quantity
Nonnegative useful-work time; setup + work must be positive.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Dimensionless share of elapsed time consumed by setup.






Equation: share = T_setup / (T_setup + T_work).
Assumptions: Setup and useful work execute serially with no overlap.
Excludes: Pipelining, shared setup across calls, and concurrent execution.



Derivation: Partition total serial elapsed time into setup and useful-work components.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
>>> calc_setup_share(1 * ureg.second, 3 * ureg.second) == 0.25

physics.agents.calc_short_circuit_cost(pass_probabilities, check_costs)
Calculate the cost and survival share of ordered checks.











Name
Type
Description
Default




pass_probabilities
sequence of float
Pass probabilities in [0, 1], ordered by execution.
required


check_costs
sequence of Quantity or float
Nonempty nonnegative finite costs in compatible units, with the same length as pass_probabilities.
required














Name
Type
Description





tuple
Expected checking cost in the shared cost unit and dimensionless all-pass probability.






Equation: E[C] = sum_i c_i product_{j<i} p_j; P_pass = product_i p_i.
Assumptions: Each check has fixed conditional pass probability given earlier passes; independent checks may use their marginal probabilities.
Excludes: Reordering optimization and input-dependent costs. Inputs must contain the same nonzero number of checks.



Derivation: A check incurs cost only on the fraction of records reaching it, found by multiplying preceding conditional pass rates.



>>> cost, passing = calc_short_circuit_cost([0.5, 0.5], [2, 4])
>>> (cost, passing) == (2 + 0.5 * 4, 0.5 * 0.5)
True

required

int

required

Probability that the task appears on both sides of the run-level split.






Equation: P_straddle = 1 - f ** k - (1 - f) ** k.
Assumptions: Runs are split independently; task identity is shared across the runs.
Excludes: Task-grouped splitting, stratification, and estimates of downstream evaluation bias.



Derivation: The disjoint alternatives to straddling are all-training and all-held-out assignments.



>>> calc_split_straddle(0.5, 2) == 1 - 0.5 ** 2 - 0.5 ** 2

physics.agents.calc_step_error_for_target(target_success, horizon)
Find the per-step error rate allowed by a task success target.

Type
Description
Default

Target task success probability in [0, 1].
required


horizon

Positive number of unchecked steps.
required

Type
Description

Dimensionless maximum per-step error under the independent-step model.






Equation: epsilon = 1 - target_success ** (1 / horizon).
Assumptions: Each step has an identical, independent error probability.
Excludes: Error dependence, checking, recovery, and finite-precision root error.



Derivation: Invert target = (1 - epsilon) ** H; for small epsilon, H epsilon approximates -ln(target).

title: solvers.EfficiencyModel
text:
solvers.EfficiencyModel()
Models the gap between peak and achieved FLOPS (Wall 3: Software Efficiency).
This model quantifies the software efficiency of a workload — the fraction of peak hardware FLOPS that the software stack actually converts into useful computation. It decomposes Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) by workload type, accounting for kernel fusion efficiency, SM occupancy, and memory access patterns.
Literature Source: 1. Chowdhery et al. (2022), “PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways.” (First systematic MFU reporting for large Transformers.) 2. Dao et al. (2022), “FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.” (FlashAttention MFU improvement.) 3. NVIDIA (2023), “Hopper Architecture Tuning Guide.” (SM Occupancy model.)





Name
Description




solve
Estimate achievable MFU and FLOPS for a given workload type.





solvers.EfficiencyModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    workload_type='ffn',
    use_flash_attention=False,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
)

MFU estimate, achievable FLOPS, and overhead breakdown.






Equation: achieved_rate = peak_rate * eta, where eta is a workload lookup scaled by efficiency / 0.5 and clipped by the configured cap. >>> bool(0 <= r.mfu <= 1 and r.achievable_flops <= r.peak_flops)
True

title: engine.solvers.reliability
text:
engine.solvers.reliability
Reliability and checkpoint-interval solvers.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (the public import path, derived from engine.solvers.__init__); kept per-domain so the logic stays reviewable.





Name
Description




CheckpointIntervalModel
Young-Daly checkpoint interval and the share of wall time it wastes.


RecoveryBudgetModel
Cold-restart budget for one failure, and its cost per day at a failure interval.


ReliabilityModel
Calculates Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and optimal checkpointing intervals.


SeriesFailureModel
Failure interval of a synchronous job built from heterogeneous components.





engine.solvers.reliability.CheckpointIntervalModel()
Young-Daly checkpoint interval and the share of wall time it wastes.
tau* = sqrt(2 * write_time * MTBF) balances the write share write_time / tau against the rework share tau / (2 * MTBF); at the optimum the two are equal. Literature: Young (1974); Daly (2006). Added 2026-10-20.





Name
Description




solve
Balance checkpoint write time against expected rework.





engine.solvers.reliability.CheckpointIntervalModel.solve(write_time, mtbf)
Balance checkpoint write time against expected rework.











Name
Type
Description
Default




write_time
Quantity
Positive checkpoint write pause in time units.
required


mtbf
Quantity
Positive job mean time between failures in time units.
required














Name
Type
Description





CheckpointIntervalResult
Write duration in seconds, MTBF in hours, optimal interval, and dimensionless write, rework, and total waste shares.






mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_young_daly_interval : Balance checkpoint writing and lost work. mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_checkpoint_waste : Sum write and rework overhead fractions.



Equation: tau = sqrt(2 write_time MTBF); write_share = write_time/tau; rework_share = tau/(2 MTBF); waste = write_share + rework_share.
Assumptions: First-order periodic checkpointing, failures uniformly placed within an interval, and checkpoint cost small enough for the approximation to be useful.
Excludes: Checkpoint overlap, recovery time, correlated failures, and higher-order scheduling corrections.



Derivation: Differentiating write_time/tau + tau/(2 MTBF) and setting its derivative to zero yields tau; the two contributions are equal at that point.



>>> r = CheckpointIntervalModel().solve(Q_(10, "s"), Q_(1000, "s"))
>>> abs(r.write_share - r.rework_share) < 1e-12
True






engine.solvers.reliability.RecoveryBudgetModel()
Cold-restart budget for one failure, and its cost per day at a failure interval.
The budget is detection + restart + checkpoint load + warmup (RecoveryProfile.cold_restart_time); a job that fails every failure_interval pays it 1 day / failure_interval times a day, on every one of its n_devices. Rework since the last save is charged to checkpoint waste, not here. Added 2026-10-20.





Name
Description




solve
Price serial cold-restart phases at a given failure frequency.





engine.solvers.reliability.RecoveryBudgetModel.solve(
    checkpoint_bytes,
    recovery,
    failure_interval,
    n_devices,
)
Price serial cold-restart phases at a given failure frequency.











Name
Type
Description
Default




checkpoint_bytes
Quantity
Nonnegative checkpoint size in bytes.
required


recovery
RecoveryProfile
Detection, restart, warmup, and positive checkpoint bandwidth profile.
required


failure_interval
Quantity
Positive interval between job failures in time units.
required


n_devices
int
Nonnegative number of reserved job devices.
required














Name
Type
Description





RecoveryBudgetResult
Phase and total restart times, failures/day, lost minutes/day, dimensionless day share, and device-hours lost per day.






Equation: reload = checkpoint_bytes / bandwidth; total = detect + restart + reload + warmup; failures_per_day = one_day / failure_interval; daily_loss = total * failures_per_day.
Assumptions: All phases execute serially, their durations are fixed, and the whole job waits for recovery.
Excludes: Rework since the checkpoint, concurrent recovery, retry failures, and overlapping incidents.



Derivation: Adding serial phase durations gives one recovery budget; multiplying by event frequency and device count gives expected device-time loss.



>>> r = RecoveryBudgetModel().solve(Q_(1, "GB"), Reliability.Recovery, Q_(1, "day"), 4)
>>> r.failures_per_day == 1 and r.lost_per_day == r.total
True






engine.solvers.reliability.ReliabilityModel()
Calculates Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and optimal checkpointing intervals.
This model handles the reliability modeling of massive clusters, helping determine the ‘Goodput’ of long-running training jobs. It identifies the probability of a job failure before completion and calculates the Young-Daly optimal interval to minimize wasted compute time.
Literature Source: 1. Young (1974), “A First-Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” 2. Daly (2006), “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart-Dump Strategy.”





Name
Description




solve
Estimate fleet failure exposure and a checkpoint interval.





engine.solvers.reliability.ReliabilityModel.solve(
    fleet,
    job_duration_hours,
    checkpoint_time_s=60.0,
    avg_recovery_time_s=300.0,
)
Estimate fleet failure exposure and a checkpoint interval.











Name
Type
Description
Default




fleet
Fleet
Cluster configuration with positive node count and per-node device counts.
required


job_duration_hours
float
Nonnegative planned job duration in hours.
required


checkpoint_time_s
float
Positive write pause per checkpoint in seconds; default 60.
60.0


avg_recovery_time_s
float
Nonnegative recovery duration per failure in seconds; default 300, including reload, restart, and warmup.
300.0














Name
Type
Description





ReliabilityResult
Fleet MTBF and checkpoint interval with time units, failure probability, expected failure count, and dimensionless goodput estimate.






mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_mtbf_node : Sum independent component failure rates. mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_young_daly_interval : Balance checkpoint writing and lost work.



Equation: lambda_node = n_gpu / MTBF_gpu + n_nic / MTBF_nic + n_psu / MTBF_psu; M = 1 / (fleet.count * lambda_node); P(failure) = 1-exp(-job_duration/M); tau = sqrt(2 checkpoint_time M). The reported goodput is max(0, 1-checkpoint_time/tau-recovery_time/M).
Assumptions: Independent exponential component failures and a synchronous series system. Nonredundant PSU counts come from the node; component lifetimes come from the Reliability registry.
Excludes: Correlated failures, repair contention, and explicit re-execution loss in the reported goodput. The goodput expression charges checkpoint writes and recovery only, even though the checkpoint interval balances write and rework costs.



Derivation: Series-system hazard rates add. The no-failure survival function is exponential. The checkpoint helper minimizes the first-order write-plus-rework approximation; the goodput subtraction is the implementation’s separate overhead convention.



>>> from mlsysim import Systems
>>> r = ReliabilityModel().solve(Systems.Clusters.Research_256, 24)
>>> 0 <= r.failure_probability <= 1 and r.fleet_mtbf.m_as("hour") > 0
True






engine.solvers.reliability.SeriesFailureModel()
Failure interval of a synchronous job built from heterogeneous components.
Any single component failure stops the job, so failure rates add (a series system with independent, exponentially distributed failures). Each component is stated per node, with its MTTF and its count per node; its share per device is count / devices_per_node / MTTF. A redundant part that cannot fail the node singly (an N+M power supply) enters with count 0. Added 2026-10-20.





Name
Description




solve
Aggregate heterogeneous component hazards for a synchronous job.





engine.solvers.reliability.SeriesFailureModel.solve(
    n_devices,
    devices_per_node,
    component_mttf,
    per_node,
)
Aggregate heterogeneous component hazards for a synchronous job.











Name
Type
Description
Default




n_devices
int
Positive accelerator count in the job.
required


devices_per_node
int
Positive accelerator count per node.
required


component_mttf
dict of str to Quantity
Positive component MTTFs in hours or compatible units.
required


per_node
dict of str to int
Nonnegative component counts per node, with the same keys as component_mttf. Use zero for parts whose single failure cannot stop the node.
required














Name
Type
Description





SeriesFailureResult
Per-device component rates, total device and system rates in inverse hours, MTBF in hours, and failures per day.






Equation: component_rate[k] = per_node[k] / (devices_per_node * MTTF[k]); system_rate = n_devices * sum(component_rate); MTBF = 1/system_rate.
Assumptions: Independent exponential component failures; any included component failure stops the entire job. At least one component rate must be positive.
Excludes: Fault correlation, shared infrastructure, and explicit redundant failure combinations.



Derivation: Summing independent exponential hazards gives the series-system rate. Per-node rates are divided by devices per node and multiplied by the job’s device count.



>>> r = SeriesFailureModel().solve(8, 4, {"gpu": Q_(100, "hour")}, {"gpu": 4})
>>> r.mtbf == Q_(12.5, "hour")
True

engine.solvers.reliability.CheckpointIntervalModel()
Young-Daly checkpoint interval and the share of wall time it wastes.
tau* = sqrt(2 * write_time * MTBF) balances the write share write_time / tau against the rework share tau / (2 * MTBF); at the optimum the two are equal. Literature: Young (1974); Daly (2006). Added 2026-10-20.





Name
Description




solve
Balance checkpoint write time against expected rework.





engine.solvers.reliability.CheckpointIntervalModel.solve(write_time, mtbf)
Balance checkpoint write time against expected rework.











Name
Type
Description
Default




write_time
Quantity
Positive checkpoint write pause in time units.
required


mtbf
Quantity
Positive job mean time between failures in time units.
required














Name
Type
Description





CheckpointIntervalResult
Write duration in seconds, MTBF in hours, optimal interval, and dimensionless write, rework, and total waste shares.






mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_young_daly_interval : Balance checkpoint writing and lost work. mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_checkpoint_waste : Sum write and rework overhead fractions.



Equation: tau = sqrt(2 write_time MTBF); write_share = write_time/tau; rework_share = tau/(2 MTBF); waste = write_share + rework_share.
Assumptions: First-order periodic checkpointing, failures uniformly placed within an interval, and checkpoint cost small enough for the approximation to be useful.
Excludes: Checkpoint overlap, recovery time, correlated failures, and higher-order scheduling corrections.



Derivation: Differentiating write_time/tau + tau/(2 MTBF) and setting its derivative to zero yields tau; the two contributions are equal at that point.



>>> r = CheckpointIntervalModel().solve(Q_(10, "s"), Q_(1000, "s"))
>>> abs(r.write_share - r.rework_share) < 1e-12
True






engine.solvers.reliability.RecoveryBudgetModel()
Cold-restart budget for one failure, and its cost per day at a failure interval.
The budget is detection + restart + checkpoint load + warmup (RecoveryProfile.cold_restart_time); a job that fails every failure_interval pays it 1 day / failure_interval times a day, on every one of its n_devices. Rework since the last save is charged to checkpoint waste, not here. Added 2026-10-20.

    failure_interval,
    n_devices,
)

RecoveryBudgetResult
Phase and total restart times, failures/day, lost minutes/day, dimensionless day share, and device-hours lost per day.






Equation: reload = checkpoint_bytes / bandwidth; total = detect + restart + reload + warmup; failures_per_day = one_day / failure_interval; daily_loss = total * failures_per_day.
Assumptions: All phases execute serially, their durations are fixed, and the whole job waits for recovery.
Excludes: Rework since the checkpoint, concurrent recovery, retry failures, and overlapping incidents.



Derivation: Adding serial phase durations gives one recovery budget; multiplying by event frequency and device count gives expected device-time loss.



>>> r = RecoveryBudgetModel().solve(Q_(1, "GB"), Reliability.Recovery, Q_(1, "day"), 4)
>>> r.failures_per_day == 1 and r.lost_per_day == r.total
True






engine.solvers.reliability.ReliabilityModel()
Calculates Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and optimal checkpointing intervals.
This model handles the reliability modeling of massive clusters, helping determine the ‘Goodput’ of long-running training jobs. It identifies the probability of a job failure before completion and calculates the Young-Daly optimal interval to minimize wasted compute time.
Literature Source: 1. Young (1974), “A First-Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” 2. Daly (2006), “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart-Dump Strategy.”





Name
Description




solve
Estimate fleet failure exposure and a checkpoint interval.





engine.solvers.reliability.ReliabilityModel.solve(
    fleet,
    job_duration_hours,
    checkpoint_time_s=60.0,
    avg_recovery_time_s=300.0,
)
Estimate fleet failure exposure and a checkpoint interval.











Name
Type
Description
Default

Fleet
Cluster configuration with positive node count and per-node device counts.
required


job_duration_hours
float
Nonnegative planned job duration in hours.
required


checkpoint_time_s
float
Positive write pause per checkpoint in seconds; default 60.
60.0


avg_recovery_time_s
float
Nonnegative recovery duration per failure in seconds; default 300, including reload, restart, and warmup.
300.0














Name
Type
Description





ReliabilityResult
Fleet MTBF and checkpoint interval with time units, failure probability, expected failure count, and dimensionless goodput estimate.






mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_mtbf_node : Sum independent component failure rates. mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_young_daly_interval : Balance checkpoint writing and lost work.



Equation: lambda_node = n_gpu / MTBF_gpu + n_nic / MTBF_nic + n_psu / MTBF_psu; M = 1 / (fleet.count * lambda_node); P(failure) = 1-exp(-job_duration/M); tau = sqrt(2 checkpoint_time M). The reported goodput is max(0, 1-checkpoint_time/tau-recovery_time/M).
Assumptions: Independent exponential component failures and a synchronous series system. Nonredundant PSU counts come from the node; component lifetimes come from the Reliability registry.
Excludes: Correlated failures, repair contention, and explicit re-execution loss in the reported goodput. The goodput expression charges checkpoint writes and recovery only, even though the checkpoint interval balances write and rework costs.



Derivation: Series-system hazard rates add. The no-failure survival function is exponential. The checkpoint helper minimizes the first-order write-plus-rework approximation; the goodput subtraction is the implementation’s separate overhead convention.



>>> from mlsysim import Systems
>>> r = ReliabilityModel().solve(Systems.Clusters.Research_256, 24)
>>> 0 <= r.failure_probability <= 1 and r.fleet_mtbf.m_as("hour") > 0
True






engine.solvers.reliability.SeriesFailureModel()
Failure interval of a synchronous job built from heterogeneous components.
Any single component failure stops the job, so failure rates add (a series system with independent, exponentially distributed failures). Each component is stated per node, with its MTTF and its count per node; its share per device is count / devices_per_node / MTTF. A redundant part that cannot fail the node singly (an N+M power supply) enters with count 0. Added 2026-10-20.

title: Training Scenarios
text:
Scenario contracts

ActivationLogicCostScenario: Logic cost of two activation datapaths, in transistor equivalents (an illustrative budget).
ActivationMemoryScenario: Activation memory of workload at a microbatch, under each recomputation strategy.
AdversarialTrainingPassesScenario: Work per batch of adversarial training, in standard forward-backward passes (equal cost, no reuse).
AlignmentMemoryScenario: PPO and DPO alignment of policy with critic-sized reward and value models.
AttentionTilingScenario: One head’s attention at seq_len tokens, whole or in square tiles, and what each kernel stores.
CenteredRewardScenario: Binary terminal rewards centered on a fixed baseline.
ContinuationForkCostScenario: A trajectory whose value is sampled by forking continuations at chosen turns.
ConvLayerScenario: One kernel-by-kernel convolution, stride one, over a height-by-width-by-in_channels input to out_channels feature maps; values of bytes_per_value each.
CrossEntropyScenario: Cross-entropy losses for named predicted probabilities of the correct class, among classes.
DataParallelScaleOutScenario: A data-parallel job of workload on nodes nodes, from a one-device profile.
DenseLayerScenario: One dense layer: in_features inputs to out_features outputs, bytes_per_weight each.
DenseNetworkScenario: A dense network of layer_widths at batch_size: parameters, FLOPs, traffic, memory.
DenseScalingSweepScenario: Dense networks between a fixed input and output, swept in hidden width and in depth.
DpSgdRunScenario: Inputs a DP-SGD privacy accountant needs for one Poisson-sampled run on dataset_size examples; this type does not estimate epsilon.
DpTrainingPlanScenario: An illustrative differential-privacy planning scenario for one training run of base_cost.
ElementwiseIntensityScenario: An unfused elementwise operation: flops_per_element FLOPs while operands_moved values of bytes_per_value each are read or written.
EpochOverheadScenario: One training epoch of network on a host CPU and an accelerator: work against fixed overhead.
FederatedUplinkScenario: A week of raw captures against compressed model updates sent at named round cadences.
ForkValueScenario: Binary continuations forked before and after one turn, with their pass counts.
FrameRateHeadroomScenario: workload at frame_rate on an accelerator of peak_rate that sustains a utilization_low to utilization_high share of peak; alternative_flops is a heavier model per frame.
GradientChainScenario: The activation-slope factor a gradient keeps after depth layers, at each slope’s peak.
GroupBarrierScenario: The rollout latencies of one synchronous group.
GroupCoefficientsScenario: The rewards of one group of rollouts and the coefficient convention applied to them.
KernelShareScenario: One kernel class’s multiply-adds against a whole model’s, per example.
LayerStackScenario: Weight-only count of a network built from convolution and dense layers, input first (biases omitted).
LengthNormalizationScenario: Two rollouts with one group coefficient and different lengths, averaged per rollout.
LossNormalizationScenario: A long trajectory split into focus_pieces records, batched with other_examples short ones.
LowRankUpdateScenario: A rank-rank update to one out_dim by in_dim weight matrix.
ParadigmCostScenario: One input classified three ways: hand-written rules, engineered features, and a learned network.
ParallelLayoutScenario: workload trained on a TP x PP x DP layout: step time, efficiency, and state per device.
PerExampleGradientScenario: Naive DP-SGD keeps one gradient per example: bytes_per_param per parameter of each named model, batch_size copies per step.
PerInvocationSerializationScenario: A turns-turn trajectory stored as one example per model call, each turn adding tokens_per_turn.
PersonalizationStorageScenario: contexts personalized models stored as full copies or as one backbone plus adapters.
PipelineScheduleScenario: A synchronous pipeline of stages stages fed microbatches microbatches per step.
PowerLawScenario: A power-law term A R^-alpha and the resource multiple that halves it.
PreferencePairScenario: Log-probability sums over a preferred and a dispreferred record’s selected tokens.
PublishedRunScenario: A published training run: its total compute spread over its accelerators and days.
RatioClipScenario: One token’s old probability under a symmetric ratio clip.
RecurrentStepScenario: One step of a recurrent layer: input_dim inputs, a hidden_dim state, and gates affine maps per step (one for a plain RNN, four for an LSTM); steps steps in a sequence.
ReferenceTrainingStepScenario: One optimizer step of a reference pretraining job, fixed once for every chapter that quotes it.
RepeatedVerificationScenario: A timing-sensitive check repeated on one candidate, with an all-pass rule.
ResidualAdapterScenario: Residual bottleneck adapters of width to bottleneck, one at each of sites.
RewardCompositionScenario: One update’s rollouts scored by a verifier that accepts some failures.
RolloutSlotCycleScenario: Sandbox slots running one episode at a time, with a cold and a snapshot reset.
RolloutStepBudgetScenario: One update’s tasks, group size, rollout length, and the policy’s pass rate on the mix.
ScalingOverheadScenario: A planned speedup when communication and coordination take a share of the scaled step.
SequencePackingScenario: Stored example lengths against capacity-token buffers.
SustainedThroughputScenario: A run budgeted from peak throughput, then run at its sustained share of peak.
TargetMaskScenario: One serialized training example by segment, and the responses kept as context only.
TensorParallelLayerScenario: One layer of workload split tp_size ways: compute against the exchange on each link.
TokenizedBatchFeedScenario: A host that tokenizes each batch and copies it to the accelerator, against the device’s step.
TrainingRunScenario: Training workload on fleet: peak time to delivered wall-clock time.
TrainingStateFitScenario: Weights, gradients, and optimizer state of workload at one precision, against hardware’s memory.
TrainingStateScenario: Persistent mixed-precision Adam state of workload and its shards.
UpdateWorkingSetScenario: A full on-device update with Adam: its working set and the DRAM bytes of one step.
VerifierPoolScenario: Completed trajectories arriving in batches, each verified by repeated trials.
ZeroShardingScenario: workload’s training state per device at each ZeRO stage over n_devices.

title: solvers.EconomicsModel
text:
solvers.EconomicsModel()
Calculates Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) including Capex and Opex.
Combines hardware costs, energy consumption, and maintenance into a single financial model for the fleet.
Literature Source: 1. Barroso et al. (2018), “The Datacenter as a Computer: An Introduction to the Design of Warehouse-Scale Machines.” 2. Patterson (2004), “Latent Bugs in Common-Case Software.” (TCO Foundations) 3. Meta (2024), “Sustainable AI Infrastructure at Meta Scale.”
Formula contract: - energy OpEx delegates to SustainabilityModel so cost, carbon, and water share the same PUE and grid assumptions. - hardware CapEx = unit cost * accelerator count * infrastructure multiplier. - period CapEx and maintenance are prorated by duration over the amortization window.





Name
Description




solve
Calculate the TCO for a fleet over a specified duration.





solvers.EconomicsModel.solve(
    fleet,
    duration_days,
    kwh_price=None,
    datacenter=None,
    grid=None,
    mfu=1.0,
    amortization_years=3.0,
    infrastructure_multiplier=cal.DEFAULT_INFRASTRUCTURE_MULTIPLIER,
)
Calculate the TCO for a fleet over a specified duration.











Name
Type
Description
Default




fleet
Fleet
The hardware cluster configuration.
required


duration_days
float
Operation duration in days.
required


kwh_price
float
Price of electricity per kWh.
None


datacenter
Datacenter
A specific datacenter profile.
None


grid
GridProfile
A specific grid profile.
None


mfu
float
Model FLOPs Utilization (0.0 to 1.0) impacting energy footprint.
1.0


amortization_years
float
Straight-line CapEx depreciation horizon (default 3 years). The period is charged total_capex / amortization_years * duration_days / 365 — a 365-day year, matching the book’s 8,760 h/yr convention.
3.0


infrastructure_multiplier
float
CapEx multiplier for networking/cooling/facility/staff (default 1.0 = hardware only; 2.0-2.5 approximates full datacenter TCO).
cal.DEFAULT_INFRASTRUCTURE_MULTIPLIER














Name
Type
Description





EconomicsResult
Financial metrics including CapEx, OpEx, and total TCO. Energy OpEx is facility-level (PUE-loaded via SustainabilityModel); maintenance accrues on FULL CapEx, not the amortized slice.






Equation: TCO = amortized CapEx + energy OpEx + maintenance. Period CapEx = unit_cost * accelerator_count * infrastructure_multiplier * duration_days / (365 * amortization_years). Maintenance uses full CapEx; energy uses SustainabilityModel.
Assumptions: Constant prices and straight-line amortization over a positive horizon; missing accelerator price is treated as zero and must be supplied for procurement use. Excludes: Financing, resale, tax, demand charges, and measured fleet billing.



Derivation: Allocate purchase cost uniformly over the amortization horizon, charge maintenance on the full asset value, and add energy purchased during the period. All cost fields are in USD.



>>> from mlsysim import Q_, Systems
>>> result = EconomicsModel().solve(Systems.Clusters.Research_256, duration_days=1)
>>> result.tco_usd >= result.opex_energy_usd
True

title: engine.solvers.retrieval
text:
engine.solvers.retrieval
Retrieval solvers: what a read from long-term memory stages, ranks, streams, and maintains.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated counts: whole serialized records in a token allowance, one BM25 term in two documents, the bandwidth floor of an exact vector scan, the resident bytes of approximate indexes, an exact tree’s neighborhood against an allowance, the write-path cost of keeping an index current, the auxiliary bytes and re-index time of two stores, cost per accepted task with store upkeep, and the words two texts share. None models a tokenizer, a trained encoder, cache effects, or a real code graph’s cycles.

Description

One query term’s BM25 score in a short and a long document of one corpus.

The time floor of an exact scan: every eligible vector streamed once.

A typed traversal’s neighborhood, as an exact tree, against a token allowance.

Who pays to keep an index current after an edit.

engine.solvers.retrieval.AnnFootprintModel()
Resident bytes of two approximate indexes over the same vectors.
A navigable-small-world graph keeps every vector plus M links per node; product quantization replaces each vector with m codes of one byte and scores through a lookup table of m x centroids entries per query.

Description

    dimension,
    bytes_per_value,
    links_per_node,
    link_bytes,
    subvectors,
    centroids,
    code_bytes,
    table_entry_bytes,
)

required

Type

Raw, graph, and code storage; lookup-table KB; dimensionless compression and integer subspace width.






Equation: raw=N*d*b; graph=N*M*link_bytes; codes=N*m*code_bytes; lookup=m*centroids*table_entry_bytes.
Assumptions: Fixed-degree graph representation and equal-width product-quantization codes. Subspace width uses integer division.
Excludes: Index headers, graph hierarchy, allocator overhead, codebooks, recall, and query runtime.



Derivation: each layout is a sum of fixed-width fields multiplied by its record count. This storage accounting does not model an ANN search algorithm.



>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = AnnFootprintModel().solve(100, 16, Q_("4 byte"), 4, Q_("4 byte"), 4, 16, Q_("1 byte"), Q_("4 byte"))
>>> result.graph_total > result.raw > result.codes
True

The same IDF multiplies both; term-frequency saturation (k1) and length normalization (b) decide the order. Lengths and frequencies are analyzer-term counts, not model tokens.

mlsysim.physics.retrieval.calc_bm25_term_score : One-term BM25 score under the selected normalizer.



Equation: score = IDF*f*(k1+1)/(f+k1*(1-b+b*length/average_length)); IDF = log(1+(N-n+0.5)/(n+0.5)).
Assumptions: Both documents use one corpus and analyzer. The nonnegative IDF variant is an implementation convention.
Excludes: Multiple query terms, tokenizer differences, learned relevance, and a probability interpretation of scores.



Robertson and Zaragoza (2009), The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond. https://doi.org/10.1561/1500000019 This solver uses the stated nonnegative IDF variant.



>>> result = Bm25PairModel().solve(100, 10, 50, 25, 2, 100, 2, 1.2, 0.75)
>>> result.short_score > result.long_score
True






engine.solvers.retrieval.ExactScanFloorModel()
The time floor of an exact scan: every eligible vector streamed once.
N d b bytes cross memory and 2 N d FLOPs score them, so the intensity is 2 / b FLOP per byte at any corpus size. Below the host’s ridge point bandwidth sets the floor, t >= N d b / B. A floor, not a forecast: query encoding, record fetches, and caches are left out.





Name
Description




solve
Compute separate bandwidth and arithmetic floors for an exact vector scan.

    host,
    vectors,
    dimension,
    bytes_per_value,
    searches=None,
    filtered_vectors=None,
    budget=None,
)

Type

Default

None














Name
Type
Description





ExactScanFloorResult
Storage bytes, FLOPs, FLOP/byte intensity, separate times in milliseconds, and optional aggregate time in seconds.






Equation: bytes = N*d*b; work = 2*N*d; stream_time = bytes/BW; math_time = work/peak.
Assumptions: Every eligible dense vector is read once, a dot product uses two FLOPs per value, and peak bandwidth/compute rates apply separately.
Excludes: Query encoding, launch overhead, cache reuse, result fetches, and a claim that stream_time alone predicts total latency.



Derivation: count dense dot-product operations and compulsory input bytes; divide each resource demand by its peak service rate.



>>> from mlsysim import Hardware, Q_
>>> result = ExactScanFloorModel().solve(Hardware.Cloud.H100, 100, 16, Q_("2 byte"))
>>> result.flops.magnitude == 2 * 100 * 16
True






engine.solvers.retrieval.GraphNeighborhoodModel()
A typed traversal’s neighborhood, as an exact tree, against a token allowance.
Every node has c children and no node repeats, so depth d reaches (c^(d+1) - 1) / (c - 1) nodes; each serializes to a fixed size plus one envelope for edges. Real code graphs have cycles and hubs, so the count bounds distinct nodes from above.





Name
Description




solve
Compare an exact tree neighborhood with a serialized context budget.

    window,
    output_reserve,
    other_input,
    children,
    depth,
    node_tokens,
    envelope_tokens,
)

Default

required

required

Nonnegative tokens consumed by other input roles.
required

required

required

required
