required














Name
Type
Description





GraphNeighborhoodResult
Integer node counts, token demands by depth, and token-budget packing capacity.






mlsysim.physics.retrieval.calc_full_tree_nodes : Geometric count of nodes through a fixed depth.



Equation: nodes(d)=sum(children^j for j=0..d); required(d)=nodes(d)*node_tokens+envelope_tokens.
Assumptions: No node is revisited and every node has exactly children descendants. A graph upper-bound interpretation additionally requires children to bound out-degree.
Excludes: Cycles, deduplication, variable degree, and an upper-bound claim when children is merely an average.



Derivation: sum each tree level as a geometric series, then apply fixed serialization bytes in token units to each reached node.



>>> result = GraphNeighborhoodModel().solve(100, 10, 10, 2, 2, 5, 5)
>>> result.nodes > result.shallow_nodes and result.packed <= result.allowance
True






engine.solvers.retrieval.IndexMaintenanceModel()
Who pays to keep an index current after an edit.
Synchronous re-indexing parses each changed file, updates postings per chunk, and embeds the chunks (in local batches, one remote request per batch, or one remote request per file) before the write returns. Exclusion records one entry per changed file and adds one lookup per candidate at query time. Durable commit and coordination, which both strategies share, are excluded.





Name
Description




solve
Account for synchronous re-indexing versus exclusion-list maintenance.





engine.solvers.retrieval.IndexMaintenanceModel.solve(
    files,
    chunks_per_file,
    parse_time,
    postings_time,
    local_batch_time,
    batch,
    remote_request_time,
    exclusion_write_time,
    candidates,
    exclusion_check_time,
)
Account for synchronous re-indexing versus exclusion-list maintenance.

Type
Description
Default

required

required

Quantity
Nonnegative parsing duration per file in seconds.
required

required

Quantity
Nonnegative embedding duration per local batch in seconds.
required


batch
int
Positive maximum chunks per embedding batch.
required


remote_request_time
Quantity
Nonnegative remote embedding duration per request in seconds.
required


exclusion_write_time
Quantity
Positive exclusion-write duration per edited file in seconds.
required


candidates
int
Nonnegative retrieved candidates to check against exclusions.
required


exclusion_check_time
Quantity
Nonnegative exclusion lookup duration per candidate in seconds.
required














Name
Type
Description





IndexMaintenanceResult
Integer work counts, milliseconds for batched paths, seconds for per-file remote path, and microseconds for exclusion work.






Equation: chunks=files*chunks_per_file; batches=ceil(chunks/batch); reindex=files*parse+chunks*postings+batches*embed; exclusion_write=files*write.
Assumptions: Costs add serially. A remote per-file request embeds all chunks of that file; a batched request follows the supplied batch limit.
Excludes: Durable commit, concurrent workers, request queueing, and retrieval-quality effects of exclusion.



Derivation: enumerate parsing, postings, and embedding operations on the write path; exclusion instead charges a per-file write and per-candidate read.



>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> t = Q_("1 ms")
>>> result = IndexMaintenanceModel().solve(2, 3, t, t, t, 4, t, t, 5, t)
>>> result.chunks == 6 and result.batches == 2
True






engine.solvers.retrieval.RetrievalPayloadModel()
Whole serialized records in the retrieval allowance of one model call.
The allowance is what the window leaves after the output reserve and every other input role: S_max - K_max - S_other. The envelope is paid once; each record pays its body and its metadata, so the count is floor((allowance - envelope) / (body + metadata)). A count of bodies alone, floor(allowance / body), overshoots once serialized.





Name
Description




solve
Fit serialized retrieval records into one model-call allowance.





engine.solvers.retrieval.RetrievalPayloadModel.solve(
    window,
    output_reserve,
    other_input,
    envelope,
    body,
    metadata,
    metadata_scale=None,
)

Type

required

required


other_input

required

int
Nonnegative tokens for shared serialization structure; must fit the remaining allowance.
required

required

required

None














Name
Type
Description





RetrievalPayloadResult
Integer token counts, whole-record capacity, and overshoot of body-only accounting.






mlsysim.physics.context.calc_observation_budget : Context left after answer and other-input reserves. mlsysim.physics.retrieval.calc_records_that_fit : Whole records admitted after fixed serialization overhead.



Equation: allowance = window-output_reserve-other_input; records = floor((allowance-envelope)/(body+metadata)).
Assumptions: Fixed token counts from a caller-selected tokenizer and identical record sizes. Inputs leave room for the shared envelope.
Excludes: Tokenization, variable record lengths, relevance ranking, and clamping overcommitted envelopes to zero records.



Derivation: reserve fixed context terms, then divide the remaining integer token budget by the serialized record size.



>>> result = RetrievalPayloadModel().solve(100, 20, 10, 5, 10, 5)
>>> result.used <= result.allowance and result.body_only_used > result.allowance
True

Auxiliary bytes and re-index time of a lexical-plus-graph store and a lexical-plus-dense store over the same files.

Storage quantities, integer passage counts, re-indexing milliseconds, and dimensionless storage/time amplification ratios.






Equation: postings=files*tokens_per_file*postings_per_token; chunks=floor(total_tokens/passage_tokens); graph_layout=postings+edges; dense_layout=postings+vectors+links.
Assumptions: Fixed per-file sizes; serial lexical-plus-parse or lexical-plus-embedding work; positive auxiliary-storage and time denominators. Passage counts are taken over aggregate tokens.
Excludes: Per-file boundary padding, overlapping passages, compression, concurrency, and retrieval effectiveness.



Derivation: sum stored field widths for each layout and divide changed work counts by the caller-supplied serial service rates.



>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> b = Q_("1 byte")
>>> result = StorageAmplificationModel().solve(10, 100, 1000*b, b, 2, 4*b, 50, 16, 4*b, 4, 4*b, 2, 10.0, 5.0, 2.0)
>>> result.chunks == 10 * 100 // 50
True

A typed traversal’s neighborhood, as an exact tree, against a token allowance.
Every node has c children and no node repeats, so depth d reaches (c^(d+1) - 1) / (c - 1) nodes; each serializes to a fixed size plus one envelope for edges. Real code graphs have cycles and hubs, so the count bounds distinct nodes from above.

engine.solvers.retrieval.IndexMaintenanceModel()
Who pays to keep an index current after an edit.
Synchronous re-indexing parses each changed file, updates postings per chunk, and embeds the chunks (in local batches, one remote request per batch, or one remote request per file) before the write returns. Exclusion records one entry per changed file and adds one lookup per candidate at query time. Durable commit and coordination, which both strategies share, are excluded.

mlsysim.physics.context.calc_observation_budget : Context left after answer and other-input reserves. mlsysim.physics.retrieval.calc_records_that_fit : Whole records admitted after fixed serialization overhead.

title: physics.fairness
text:
physics.fairness
Fairness arithmetic: error-rate identities, the bias feedback model, and gap sample sizes.
Added 2026-10-20. The closed forms a fairness release gate rests on:

Chouldechova’s identity, which fixes a group’s false positive rate from its base rate, positive predictive value, and false negative rate;
the bias feedback model, a disparity multiplied by a feedback factor at each retraining cycle, and the cycle at which it crosses a release gate;
the per-group sample size that pins a gap between two groups’ rates.






Name
Description




calc_cycles_to_gate
Find the fractional cycle at which a growing disparity reaches a gate.


calc_feedback_disparity
Propagate a disparity through repeated multiplicative feedback.


calc_fpr_from_ppv
Infer a false-positive rate from prevalence, precision, and false negatives.


calc_gap_samples_per_group
Plan equal group sizes for a normal-approximation rate-gap interval.





physics.fairness.calc_cycles_to_gate(launch_gap, factor, gate)
Find the fractional cycle at which a growing disparity reaches a gate.











Name
Type
Description
Default




launch_gap
float
Initial positive disparity, below gate, in the same units as gate.
required


factor
float
Dimensionless multiplicative growth per cycle, greater than one.
required


gate
float
Positive disparity threshold, greater than launch_gap.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Continuous cycle count at equality. Failure under a strict greater-than gate occurs at the next whole cycle above this value.






Equation: k = ln(gate/launch_gap) / ln(factor).
Assumptions: A positive disparity grows monotonically by a constant factor.
Excludes: Discrete-cycle rounding and empirical estimation of feedback strength.



Derivation: take logarithms of gate = launch_gap * factor**k.



>>> calc_cycles_to_gate(0.01, 2, 0.08)
3.0




physics.fairness.calc_feedback_disparity(launch_gap, factor, cycles)
Propagate a disparity through repeated multiplicative feedback.











Name
Type
Description
Default




launch_gap
float
Initial rate difference, expressed as a fraction.
required


factor
float
Dimensionless multiplicative feedback factor per cycle, nonnegative.
required


cycles
int
Number of retraining cycles, nonnegative.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Modeled rate difference after the specified cycles, in the same units as launch_gap; not clamped to a probability interval.






Equation: gap(k) = gap(0) * factor**k.
Assumptions: The same feedback factor applies each cycle; factors above one grow the disparity and factors below one reduce it.
Excludes: Observed feedback dynamics, saturation, and sampling error.



Derivation: apply the recurrence gap(k+1) = factor * gap(k) repeatedly.



>>> calc_feedback_disparity(0.02, 2, 3)
0.16




physics.fairness.calc_fpr_from_ppv(base_rate, ppv, fnr)
Infer a false-positive rate from prevalence, precision, and false negatives.











Name
Type
Description
Default




base_rate
float
Positive-class prevalence p, dimensionless, in (0, 1).
required


ppv
float
Positive predictive value, dimensionless, in (0, 1].
required


fnr
float
False-negative fraction, dimensionless, expected in [0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Implied false-positive fraction. An inconsistent input triple can yield a value above one; this function does not clamp the result.






Equation: FPR = p/(1-p) * (1-PPV)/PPV * (1-FNR).
Assumptions: All rates describe the same population and classifier threshold.
Excludes: Estimation uncertainty, threshold selection, and compatibility checks for the supplied rates.
Equal PPV with unequal base rates prevents simultaneously equal false-positive and false-negative rates, except in degenerate cases.



Chouldechova (2017), “Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact.” https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.00056 (bibliography key: chouldechova2017).



>>> round(calc_fpr_from_ppv(0.2, 0.8, 0.1), 5)
0.05625




physics.fairness.calc_gap_samples_per_group(rate, half_width, z_critical)
Plan equal group sizes for a normal-approximation rate-gap interval.











Name
Type
Description
Default




rate
float
Assumed common Bernoulli probability p, dimensionless, in [0, 1].
required


half_width
float
Desired positive half-width of the difference in rates, as a fraction.
required


z_critical
float
Positive normal critical value for the chosen confidence level.
required














Name
Type
Description





int
Rounded-up number of independent observations required in each group.






Equation: n = ceil(2*z_critical**2*p*(1-p)/half_width**2).
Assumptions: Independent Bernoulli observations, equal group sizes, the same planning rate in both groups, and an adequate normal approximation.
Excludes: Exact finite-sample coverage, paired groups, and unequal allocation.



Derivation: the independent difference has variance 2*p*(1-p)/n; solve z*sqrt(variance) = half_width for n and round up.



>>> calc_gap_samples_per_group(0.5, 0.1, 2)
200

title: solvers.CheckpointModel
text:
solvers.CheckpointModel()
Analyzes the storage constraints and I/O burst penalties of saving model states.
Training massive models requires saving hundreds of gigabytes (Weights + Optimizer States) to persistent storage. This model calculates the time spent blocked on I/O, subtracting from the cluster’s Model FLOPs Utilization.
Literature Source: 1. Eisenman et al. (2022), “Check-N-Run: A Checkpointing System for Training Large Language Models.”





Name
Description




solve
Estimate synchronous checkpoint size, write time, and stall fraction.





solvers.CheckpointModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    optimizer='adam',
    checkpoint_interval_hours=4.0,
    n_writers=1,
    filesystem_limit_gbs=500.0,
)
Estimate synchronous checkpoint size, write time, and stall fraction.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model
Workload
Workload whose parameter count sets the checkpoint payload.
required


hardware
HardwareNode
Device with storage bandwidth in bytes/second. Missing or zero storage bandwidth uses the declared fallback in engine.calibration.
required


optimizer
str
"adam" selects mixed-precision Adam checkpoint bytes; other names use the SGD convention. Gradients are not persisted.
'adam'


checkpoint_interval_hours
float
Hours between checkpoints. A nonpositive interval returns a stall fraction of one; positive intervals use write time divided by interval.
4.0


n_writers
int
Positive number of writers sharing the checkpoint payload.
1


filesystem_limit_gbs
float
Positive aggregate filesystem ceiling in decimal GB/second.
500.0














Name
Type
Description





CheckpointResult
Checkpoint size in GB, write duration in seconds, and a dimensionless stall fraction in mfu_penalty_pct (not multiplied by 100). storage_bottleneck flags writes longer than one minute; it does not certify that a checkpoint schedule fits the interval.






mlsysim.physics.memory.calc_checkpoint_size : Persisted state accounting.



Equation: M = P b; bandwidth = min(n_writers * device_bandwidth, filesystem_limit); write_time = M / bandwidth. The penalty is write_time / checkpoint_interval for a positive interval.
Assumptions: writers partition one payload without duplicated writes; checkpointing synchronously blocks useful training. Byte conventions come from engine.calibration and are separate from storage rates.
Excludes: asynchronous overlap, filesystem metadata, serialization CPU work, network contention, and checkpoint recovery. The penalty can exceed one when a write takes longer than its configured interval.



Derivation: payload size is parameter count times persisted bytes per parameter; elapsed transfer time is payload divided by available rate. The writer minimum is a shared-bandwidth capacity constraint.



>>> from mlsysim import Models, Hardware
>>> result = CheckpointModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B, Hardware.Cloud.H100)
>>> result.checkpoint_size.to("GB").magnitude > 0
True
>>> result.write_time_seconds.to("second").magnitude > 0
True

"adam" selects mixed-precision Adam checkpoint bytes; other names use the SGD convention. Gradients are not persisted.
'adam'

float
Hours between checkpoints. A nonpositive interval returns a stall fraction of one; positive intervals use write time divided by interval.
4.0

int

float

Name
Type
Description





CheckpointResult
Checkpoint size in GB, write duration in seconds, and a dimensionless stall fraction in mfu_penalty_pct (not multiplied by 100). storage_bottleneck flags writes longer than one minute; it does not certify that a checkpoint schedule fits the interval.






mlsysim.physics.memory.calc_checkpoint_size : Persisted state accounting.



Equation: M = P b; bandwidth = min(n_writers * device_bandwidth, filesystem_limit); write_time = M / bandwidth. The penalty is write_time / checkpoint_interval for a positive interval.
Assumptions: writers partition one payload without duplicated writes; checkpointing synchronously blocks useful training. Byte conventions come from engine.calibration and are separate from storage rates.
Excludes: asynchronous overlap, filesystem metadata, serialization CPU work, network contention, and checkpoint recovery. The penalty can exceed one when a write takes longer than its configured interval.



Derivation: payload size is parameter count times persisted bytes per parameter; elapsed transfer time is payload divided by available rate. The writer minimum is a shared-bandwidth capacity constraint.

text:
Robotics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/robotics/site_limits.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A series spring sized so machine’s arm stays under site’s declared latch floor.
The arm’s stop is held to what the guarded approach on the rigid plate needs (calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile); at the fast approach the series stiffness must keep tripwire force plus driven stroke under the floor (calc_passive_compliance_stiffness_bound), and the spring element is the stiffness that gives it in series with the plate. Coasting peaks price the case where the response cuts torque at the tripwire instead (calc_coasting_contact_peak_force).


Equation: The stopping and compliance helpers bound driven stroke and effective stiffness; complementary series stiffness determines the added spring.

title: physics.communication
text:
physics.communication
Collective communication time models (α–β).
All collectives here are pure communication models: the local reduction compute term (γ in Thakur et al. 2005) is deliberately omitted, matching the book’s α–β pedagogical treatment.





Name
Description




calc_all_to_all_time
Estimate an equal-partition ring-style All-to-All exchange.


calc_alpha_beta_crossover
Find the message size where startup and transfer costs are equal.


calc_bisection_bandwidth
Sum effective link capacity across a specified partition cut.


calc_double_binary_tree_allreduce_time
Approximate a double-tree collective with declared overhead factors.


calc_fat_tree_hosts
Count hosts in the modeled nonblocking fat-tree.


calc_fat_tree_path_switches
Count switch traversals on the longest fat-tree path.


calc_fat_tree_switches
Count switches in the modeled full fat-tree.


calc_hierarchical_allreduce_time
Compose local scatter, inter-node reduction, and local gather.


calc_hop_latency
Sum fixed latency over identical sequential hops.


calc_oversubscription_effect
Estimate throughput after stretching the communication portion of a step.


calc_point_to_point_time
Estimate startup plus serialization time for one transfer.


calc_ring_allreduce_data_factor
Return per-rank ring AllReduce traffic in message equivalents.


calc_ring_allreduce_latency_steps
Count startup terms in ring AllReduce.


calc_ring_allreduce_latency_time
Compute the startup-only component of ring AllReduce.


calc_ring_allreduce_time
Estimate ring AllReduce communication time.


calc_ring_attention_min_chunk
Estimate the token chunk needed to hide a ring-attention transfer.


calc_ring_collective_data_factor
Return a single ring-phase traffic multiplier.


calc_ring_tree_crossover_size
Estimate a large-rank ring/tree crossover payload.


calc_torus_bisection_links
Count links in a planar cut through a regular torus.


calc_torus_diameter
Count hops in the longest shortest path of a regular torus.


calc_tree_allreduce_time
Estimate reduction and broadcast over a binary tree.


ring_allreduce_data_factor_latex
Format the ring AllReduce data factor as LaTeX.





physics.communication.calc_all_to_all_time(
    message_bytes,
    n_gpus,
    bandwidth_bytes_s,
    latency_s,
)
Estimate an equal-partition ring-style All-to-All exchange.











Name
Type
Description
Default




message_bytes
Quantity or float
Nonnegative message size M; bare values are bytes.
required


n_gpus
int
Participant count N, at least one; intended to be integral.
required


bandwidth_bytes_s
Quantity or float
Positive unidirectional bandwidth B; bare values are bytes/second.
required


latency_s
Quantity or float
Nonnegative startup latency alpha; bare values are seconds.
required














Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Exchange time in seconds; zero for one participant.






Equation: T = (N - 1) M/(N B) + (N - 1) alpha.
Assumptions: M is the per-rank total send buffer, divided into N equal destination chunks; one chunk stays local.
Excludes: Unequal expert routing, fabric contention, local packing, and reduction compute.



Derivation: Each rank sends N - 1 chunks of size M/N in sequential exchange rounds.



>>> calc_all_to_all_time(1024, 1, 1024, 0).m_as("s") == 0
True




physics.communication.calc_alpha_beta_crossover(alpha_s, bandwidth_bytes_s)
Find the message size where startup and transfer costs are equal.











Name
Type
Description
Default




alpha_s
Quantity or float
Nonnegative startup latency alpha; bare values are seconds.
required


bandwidth_bytes_s
Quantity or float
Positive unidirectional bandwidth B; bare values are bytes/second.
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Crossover message size in bytes.






Equation: M_cross = alpha B.
Assumptions: Constant startup latency and size-independent bandwidth.
Excludes: Protocol thresholds, contention, and collective round counts.



Derivation: Solve alpha = M/B for M in the point-to-point alpha-beta model.



>>> m = calc_alpha_beta_crossover(Q_("1 us"), Q_("1 GB/s"))
>>> (m / Q_("1 GB/s")).to("us") == Q_("1 us")
True




physics.communication.calc_bisection_bandwidth(
    num_ports,
    link_bandwidth,
    oversubscription_ratio=1.0,
)
Sum effective link capacity across a specified partition cut.











Name
Type
Description
Default




num_ports
int
Count of links crossing the cut, at least one; not all fabric ports.
required


link_bandwidth
Quantity or float
Positive capacity per crossing link; bare values are bytes/second.
required


oversubscription_ratio
float
Positive capacity divisor; default one means no reduction.
1.0









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Effective cut bandwidth in bytes/second.






Equation: B_cut = num_ports B_link / r.
Assumptions: Identical crossing links; the specified ratio captures the shared upstream capacity.
Excludes: Routing imbalance and traffic not crossing the selected cut.
For a nonblocking fabric with N endpoints, N/2 links may cross the chosen cut; counting all ports would overstate this cut capacity.



Derivation: Add parallel crossing-link capacities and divide by the supplied sharing factor.



>>> calc_bisection_bandwidth(4, Q_("1 GB/s"), 2) == 2 * Q_("1 GB/s")
True

Equation: T = 2[(g - 1) M/(g B_local) + (g - 1) alpha_local] + T_ring(M/g, n, B_network, alpha_network).
Assumptions: Local ReduceScatter and AllGather surround g concurrent inter-node rings; each local GPU has its own NIC capacity.
Excludes: Shared-NIC contention, phase overlap, packing, and local reduction arithmetic.
If all local GPUs share one NIC, the inter-node traffic term needs an aggregate-capacity treatment; this independent-NIC model understates that contention.



Derivation: Each local ring phase moves (g - 1)/g of M. Each GPU then reduces its M/g shard across nodes before local gathering.

physics.communication.calc_ring_attention_min_chunk(
    element_bytes,
    sustained_flops,
    link_bandwidth,
)
Estimate the token chunk needed to hide a ring-attention transfer.











Name
Type
Description
Default

required

required

Type

Equation: n_min = s R / (2 B).
Assumptions: Tile compute is 4 n^2 d FLOPs and key/value transfer is 2 n d s bytes, with perfect overlap; d cancels.
Excludes: Kernel launch costs, softmax overhead, link startup, and discrete tile constraints.



Derivation: Set tile compute time 4 n^2 d/R greater than or equal to tile transfer time 2 n d s/B and cancel n d.
Liu et al. (2023), “Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context.” https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01889 (bibliography key: liu2023ringAttention). The threshold above is the stated ideal-overlap tile accounting, not an empirical latency fit.

title: Optimization Scenarios
text:
Scenario contracts

AcceleratedFractionScenario: Amdahl’s law with a path gain set by two rates: fraction of the baseline time runs accelerated_rate / baseline_rate times faster.
AcceleratorComparison: candidate against baseline: peak, power, and peak per watt.
AcceleratorGenerationsScenario: Peak compute against memory bandwidth across accelerators, first to last.
AcceleratorPodScenario: A pod envelope of pod.chips copies of accelerator: aggregate peak and memory.
AmdahlScenario: A sequential request path whose stage is made speedup times faster.
ClusterExpansionScenario: A synchronous job grown from n_devices to factor times as many on the same checkpoint tier.
ClusterTrainingTimeScenario: Training workload on n_devices x hardware at one end-to-end utilization (compute-bound).
CompileBreakevenScenario: Eager against compiled execution: the work that repays compile_time.
ConvBnReluFusionScenario: A convolution, batch norm, and ReLU on one feature map, run as three kernels or one.
DailyUploadScenario: A site’s daily captures sent over its uplink inside a working window, against compact summaries.
DiurnalLendingScenario: A fleet split between a serving reservation and a training base, static against lent.
DominantShareScenario: Dominant-resource fairness by progressive filling of indivisible bundles on capacity.
ElasticResizeScenario: Three ways to run one job over window: start small, wait for the full size, or step up.
ElementwiseOpScenario: An element-wise or normalization kernel over elements values, run unfused.
ExpertWeightTrafficScenario: Weight bytes of the mixture-of-experts workload, resident and read per token, against a dense model of dense_parameters that reads every weight each step.
FrameCompressionScenario: A per-frame model against a camera frame rate: the full model and a channel-pruned variant, run in floating point on the CPU and in integers on the accelerator.
GrowthGapScenario: Compute doubling every compute_doubling_period against bandwidth growing bandwidth_growth a year.
HostDispatchScenario: The host’s work to issue one eager step against device_time of accelerator work.
HostInputPipelineScenario: A data loader feeding one accelerator over its host link.
InputSpaceScenario: Every possible input of dataset’s image shape: levels values per channel element.
IronLawScenario: The iron law’s three terms for one task, and an upgrade to the memory or compute term.
IterationBudgetScenario: Two teams in one development window: a slow cycle against a fast one, with assumed gains per run.
JacobianScenario: The full Jacobian of one layer from input_width inputs to output_width outputs.
KernelFusionScenario: A chain of chain_length element-wise operations, run as one kernel each or fused into one.
LateConstraintScenario: A model built without its deployment limit, the day the limit surfaces, and the repair it forces.
MatmulTileScenario: C = A B with A m x k and B k x n, computed one tile_m x tile_n output tile at a time, stepping through the reduction tile_k elements per step.
MemoryRoundTripScenario: A tensor of tensor_bytes crossing to and from memory trips times at energy_per_byte (a layer boundary writes it and the next layer reads it back).
MlpTrainingStepScenario: One eager training step of a one-hidden-layer MLP, operator by operator.
NodePackingScenario: Jobs of job_gpus GPUs packed on nodes nodes of gpus_per_node.
OffloadDeadlineScenario: One input sent over an uplink to a remote model, against a per-frame deadline (lower bound).
OperationEnergyComparisonScenario: A wide and a narrow format’s energy per add, multiply, and multiply-accumulate, and one memory read against the narrow multiply-accumulate. The narrow MAC accumulates in a wider integer, so its add is accumulate_add.
ParameterBandwidthGrowthScenario: Dense-model parameter growth against per-device memory-bandwidth growth.
PeakRatioRangeScenario: One peak rate against a baseline stated as a range, baseline_low to baseline_high.
PipelineSpeedupScenario: Serial pipeline stages; one stage is made speedup times faster (Amdahl’s law).
PreemptionTaxScenario: Forced preemptions of an n_devices job whose checkpoint is checkpoint_bytes.
QuantizationGridScenario: Values stored on a bits-bit integer grid over a clipping range.
QuantizedDeploymentProfileScenario: A float model and its INT8 version on one accelerator, judged against acceptance limits.
QuotaLendingScenario: A team guaranteed guarantee GPUs that uses used_share of them; the rest can be lent.
RooflinePointScenario: A workload of intensity on hardware’s roofline: attainable rate and share of peak.
ScreeningRequirementsScenario: A screener’s release floors and device budget, with measured slices checked against the floor.
SelfContainedReplicaScenario: The smallest model replica of workload whose training state fits without sharding.
ServingConsolidationScenario: Small and large serving models on whole devices, exclusive against shared in pairs.
SingleNodeInferenceScenario: One inference of workload on hardware (roofline profile from SingleNodeModel).
SparseFlashFitScenario: workload pruned until its surviving values total surviving_bytes, stored with one index_bytes position index per value, against a flash_budget.
SpeedupCompositionScenario: Independent paper speedups multiplied together, against the measured speedup.
StagedCompressionScenario: A teacher pruned and distilled into a compact student, then quantized, with the task accuracy after each stage and the loss when quantization comes first.
SystolicReuseEnergyScenario: Energy per MAC with every operand from off-chip memory, against a systolic array.
WakeWordFleetScenario: Wake-word detection for a device fleet: stream everything to the cloud, or detect on device.
WeightReadScenario: Every weight of workload read once from hardware’s memory at bytes_per_weight.
WorkLatencyGapScenario: A cut in work (parameters or FLOPs) against the latency cut it delivered.

text:
Robotics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/robotics/stopping.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A machine at speed that must stop: travel during delay, then braking at deceleration.
clear_distance closes the budget when one is stated. speed_at_delay_end replaces constant-speed delay travel with the trapezoid between two recorded speeds; braking is still from speed. With a site (an embodied site scenario), the deceleration and clear distance default to the site’s, and its localization bound and protective margin join the required distance. added_delay prices one more delay step as travel at speed. The finished budget adds three optional terms: jerk (the resident S-curve stop’s jerk bound), tracking_bound (the tracking inset), and approach_speed (a person closing the gap through delay and stop).

Assumptions: The selected braking limit, clearance, and site margins are credible scenario inputs; the stopping solver determines the kinematic budget.
Excludes: The calculation is not a safety certification, and unmodeled traction or control failures remain outside it.

title: engine.dse.DSE
text:
engine.dse.DSE(space, objective, constraints=None)
Declarative Design Space Exploration (DSE) Engine.
A unified interface for navigating ML system trade-offs through an exhaustive grid search over a defined parameter space, filtering by constraints and ranking by objective.





Name
Description




search
Enumerate a finite design grid and rank accepted evaluations.





engine.dse.DSE.search(evaluator_fn)
Enumerate a finite design grid and rank accepted evaluations.











Name
Type
Description
Default




evaluator_fn
callable
Function receiving one parameter dictionary and returning a result object or dictionary. Objective and constraint paths must resolve to comparable numeric scalars; Pint values are compared by magnitude without unit normalization.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Best parameters, scalar objective, original best result, and up to five ranked candidate records. Ties retain enumeration order; an empty accepted set raises ValueError.






Candidates are the Cartesian product of the configured parameter lists. Retain passing constraints and feasibility status PASS when present; sort objective magnitudes ascending for minimize and descending for maximize.
The evaluator uses identical metric meaning and units for every candidate. Constraint expressions use a three-token metric/operator/numeric-threshold form.
The method does not provide continuous optimization, automatic unit conversion, uncertainty, and causal interpretation of rankings. Evaluator exceptions skip candidates. Malformed constraints, unsupported operators, and non-finite thresholds raise ValueError before any candidate is evaluated. Supported operators are <, >, <=, >=, and ==. An unknown objective or constraint metric path raises ValueError on the first feasible result that lacks it.



>>> search = DSE({"x": [1, 2, 3]}, "minimize: cost", ["cost >= 4"])
>>> result = search.search(lambda p: {"cost": p["x"] ** 2})
>>> result["best_params"]
{'x': 2}

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
Sustainability scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/sustainability.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
workload run once per period on hardware at its peak precision rate, idling between runs.
Active power is the board’s tdp and idle power its tdp_min; average power weights each by its share of the period (DutyCycledPowerModel). energy_cut (optional) divides the energy of each inference, to show how little a cheaper inference moves a duty-cycled average.


Equation: Composition of mlsysim.solvers.DutyCycledPowerModel.solve.
Assumptions: One inference occurs per period; peak FLOPs bound execution time and registry TDP values proxy active/idle power.
Excludes: Measured board energy, wake-up cost, memory-bound latency, and a period shorter than inference time.



Derivation: This scenario binds named inputs to DutyCycledPowerModel. The linked solver contracts own equations, sources, and result-unit definitions.



Evaluate the named configuration and display a modeled result.

>>> case = Scenarios.KeywordSpottingOnEsp32S3
>>> value = case.average_power
>>> print(f"{value:.3g~}")
52.9 mW

Equation: (workload.inference_flops / hardware.compute.precision_flops[precision]).to('ms').



engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.duty
Active fraction of the period, inference time divided by period; no clamping.
Equation: (inference_time / period).to('').magnitude.

Registry TDP used as the active-power assumption, a power quantity.
Equation: hardware.tdp.



engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.idle_power

Equation: hardware.tdp_min.



engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.inference_energy
Modeled active energy in mJ, active power times compute-bound execution time.
Equation: (active_power * inference_time).to('mJ').

Evaluate the stated periodic inference power case through DutyCycledPowerModel.solve; returns its typed result and quantity units.

engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.active_contribution
Active state’s duty-weighted average-power contribution in mW.
Equation: result.contributions['active'].to('mW').



engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.idle_contribution
Idle state’s duty-weighted average-power contribution in mW.
Equation: result.contributions['idle'].to('mW').



engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.average_power
Duty-weighted average power in mW from DutyCycledPowerModel.solve.
Equation: result.average_power.to('mW').



engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.idle_share
Idle contribution divided by average power, dimensionless.
Equation: (idle_contribution / average_power).to('').magnitude.



engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.crossover_duty
Active fraction where active and idle energy contributions are equal.
Duty cycle at which active energy equals idle energy.
Equation: (idle_power / (active_power + idle_power)).to('').magnitude.



engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.cut_saving
Average mW saved by reducing active inference energy by energy_cut; idle power unchanged.
Average power saved when each inference costs 1 / energy_cut of its energy.
Equation: (active_contribution * (1 - 1 / energy_cut)).to('mW').



engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.cut_gain
Dimensionless fraction of average power removed by the active-energy reduction.
Equation: (cut_saving / average_power).to('').magnitude.

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
Type: Optional[float].
Declared default: None.

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.inference_time
Peak-compute execution bound in ms, workload FLOPs divided by precision-specific peak rate.
Equation: (workload.inference_flops / hardware.compute.precision_flops[precision]).to('ms').

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.duty
Active fraction of the period, inference time divided by period; no clamping.
Equation: (inference_time / period).to('').magnitude.

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.active_power
Registry TDP used as the active-power assumption, a power quantity.
Equation: hardware.tdp.

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.idle_power
Registry minimum TDP used as the idle-power assumption, a power quantity.
Equation: hardware.tdp_min.

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.inference_energy
Modeled active energy in mJ, active power times compute-bound execution time.
Equation: (active_power * inference_time).to('mJ').

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.result
Evaluate the stated periodic inference power case through DutyCycledPowerModel.solve; returns its typed result and quantity units.
Calculation: mlsysim.solvers.DutyCycledPowerModel.solve.

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.active_contribution
Active state’s duty-weighted average-power contribution in mW.
Equation: result.contributions['active'].to('mW').

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.idle_contribution
Idle state’s duty-weighted average-power contribution in mW.
Equation: result.contributions['idle'].to('mW').

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.average_power
Duty-weighted average power in mW from DutyCycledPowerModel.solve.
Equation: result.average_power.to('mW').

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.idle_share
Idle contribution divided by average power, dimensionless.
Equation: (idle_contribution / average_power).to('').magnitude.

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.crossover_duty
Active fraction where active and idle energy contributions are equal.
Duty cycle at which active energy equals idle energy.
Equation: (idle_power / (active_power + idle_power)).to('').magnitude.

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.cut_saving
Average mW saved by reducing active inference energy by energy_cut; idle power unchanged.
Average power saved when each inference costs 1 / energy_cut of its energy.
Equation: (active_contribution * (1 - 1 / energy_cut)).to('mW').

title: PeriodicInferencePowerScenario
text:
engine.scenario_types.PeriodicInferencePowerScenario.cut_gain
Dimensionless fraction of average power removed by the active-energy reduction.
Equation: (cut_saving / average_power).to('').magnitude.

title: Glossary
text: This page defines every technical term used across the MLSys·im documentation. When a term is first used on any page, it either links here or is defined inline. Terms marked with slide links point to the relevant lecture deck for deeper coverage.

title: Glossary
text:
A

AllReduce

A collective communication primitive in which every device contributes a local tensor and receives the globally reduced (typically summed) result. The dominant synchronization pattern in data-parallel training. Ring-AllReduce and tree-AllReduce are common algorithms; performance is modeled by the Alpha-Beta Model. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training, Vol II Ch 5: Collective Communication

Alpha-Beta Model (\(\alpha\)-\(\beta\))

An analytical model for communication cost: \(T_\text{comm} = \alpha + n\beta\), where \(\alpha\) is the per-message latency (seconds), \(n\) is the message size (bytes), and \(\beta\) is the inverse bandwidth (seconds/byte). Used throughout MLSys·im to estimate collective communication overhead in distributed training. Slides: Vol II Ch 3: Network Fabrics, Vol II Ch 5: Collective Communication

Arithmetic Intensity (AI)

The ratio of floating-point operations to bytes of memory accessed: \(I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{Bytes}\). High arithmetic intensity means the workload reuses data extensively (compute-bound); low arithmetic intensity means it streams data without reuse (memory-bound). Units: FLOP/byte. Determines which side of the Ridge Point a workload falls on in the Roofline Model. Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

title: Glossary
text:
B

Bandwidth (Memory Bandwidth)

The rate at which data can be transferred between memory (DRAM/HBM) and compute units. Measured in GB/s or TB/s. The A100, for example, provides 2.04 TB/s of HBM bandwidth (and the H100 provides 3.35 TB/s). Not to be confused with network bandwidth (inter-node communication rate) or bisection bandwidth (aggregate cross-section throughput of a network fabric). Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure, Vol II Ch 3: Network Fabrics

Batch Size

The number of inputs processed simultaneously in one forward pass. Larger batch sizes increase Arithmetic Intensity, shifting workloads from memory-bound toward compute-bound. In distributed training, the global batch size equals the per-device batch size multiplied by the number of data-parallel replicas. Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 8: Model Training

Bottleneck

The hardware resource that limits performance. For a given workload-hardware pair, either compute or memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, determined by comparing the workload’s Arithmetic Intensity to the hardware’s Ridge Point. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

title: Glossary
text:
C

CapEx (Capital Expenditure)

The upfront cost of purchasing hardware. In TCO analysis, CapEx is amortized over the hardware’s useful lifetime (typically 3–5 years). Slides: Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

Carbon Intensity

The mass of CO2-equivalent emissions per unit of electricity consumed, measured in gCO2e/kWh. Varies widely by region: 20 gCO2e/kWh (Quebec hydro) to 820 gCO2e/kWh (Poland coal). MLSys·im uses per-region carbon intensity values from the sustainability registry to estimate training and inference emissions. Slides: Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

Compute-Bound

A workload whose performance is limited by the hardware’s peak FLOP/s rate rather than memory bandwidth. Occurs when Arithmetic Intensity exceeds the Ridge Point. Remedies include using tensor cores, upgrading to a faster accelerator, or reducing precision. Contrast with Memory-Bound. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

Continuous Batching

A serving optimization that dynamically inserts and retires requests from a running batch, rather than waiting for all sequences in a static batch to finish before starting new ones. Improves GPU occupancy substantially for LLM inference, where sequence lengths vary widely. Also called iteration-level batching. Slides: Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture)

NVIDIA’s programming platform for writing GPU-accelerated programs. A “CUDA kernel” is a function that runs in parallel across thousands of GPU threads. Dispatch Tax is the per-kernel launch overhead inherent to this model. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

title: Glossary
text:
D

Data Parallelism (DP)

A distributed training strategy where the full model is replicated across \(N\) devices, each processing a different shard of the batch. Requires an AllReduce synchronization step after each backward pass to average gradients. Scales well for models that fit in a single device’s memory. See also Tensor Parallelism, Pipeline Parallelism, and 3D Parallelism. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

Dispatch Tax

The constant per-operation overhead of launching a GPU kernel (typically 0.01–0.1 ms for CUDA kernel launch). Becomes significant at small batch sizes where kernel launch time dominates actual compute time. Captured as the additive term in the Iron Law. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking

title: Glossary
text:
F

FLOP/s (Floating-Point Operations per Second)

The rate at which a device can perform floating-point arithmetic. The A100 achieves 312 TFLOP/s (and the H100 achieves 989 TFLOP/s) at FP16 via its Tensor Cores. Also written as TFLOP/s (tera-) or PFLOP/s (peta-). Not to be confused with FLOPs (a count, not a rate). Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking

FLOPs (Floating-Point Operations)

A count of arithmetic operations (multiplies, adds, etc.) required to execute a single inference or training step. A ResNet-50 (25.6M parameters) inference requires 8.2 GFLOPs; a GPT-3 (175B parameters) forward pass requires 350 GFLOPs per token. Not the same as FLOP/s (the rate). Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation

Forward Pass / Backward Pass

In neural network training, the forward pass runs input data through the model to produce a prediction. The backward pass (backpropagation) computes gradients, the direction and magnitude of change needed for each parameter to reduce error. In distributed systems, gradients must be synchronized across all devices after each backward pass via AllReduce. Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 8: Model Training

title: Glossary
text:
G

GQA (Grouped Query Attention)

A transformer attention variant where multiple query heads share a single key-value head, reducing KV-Cache memory by a factor equal to the group size without significantly affecting model quality. Used in Llama 3 (for example, Llama-3 70B uses 8 KV heads for 64 query heads, an 8× reduction) and other modern LLMs. See also KV-Cache. Slides: Vol I Ch 6: Network Architectures, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

title: Glossary
text:
H

HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory)

Stacked DRAM technology used in modern AI accelerators. Provides far higher bandwidth than GDDR (e.g., 2.04 TB/s on A100, 3.35 TB/s on H100) at the cost of limited capacity (80 GiB, or 85.9 GB, per A100/H100 device). The bandwidth ceiling in the Roofline Model is set by HBM. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure

title: Glossary
text:
I

InfiniBand

A high-throughput, low-latency network fabric commonly used in GPU clusters for distributed training. Supports RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) for zero-copy data transfer that bypasses the CPU. NDR InfiniBand provides 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) per port. See also NVLink (intra-node) vs. InfiniBand (inter-node). Slides: Vol II Ch 3: Network Fabrics

Iron Law of ML Systems

The fundamental performance equation: \[T = \max\!\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak} \times \eta},\; \frac{\text{Bytes}}{\text{BW}}\right) + \text{Dispatch\_Tax}\] The \(\max\) captures the Roofline Model insight that performance is limited by whichever resource (compute or memory bandwidth) is the bottleneck. Named by analogy with the Iron Law of processor performance in computer architecture. Slides: Vol I Ch 8: Model Training, Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

ITL (Inter-Token Latency)

The time to generate each successive token after the first during LLM autoregressive decoding. Almost always Memory-Bound; each decode step loads the full model weights plus the KV-Cache. Measured in ms/token. See also TTFT. Slides: Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

title: Glossary
text:
K

Knowledge Distillation

A model compression technique where a smaller “student” model is trained to match the output distribution of a larger “teacher” model. Reduces model size and inference cost while retaining much of the teacher’s accuracy. See also Quantization and Pruning. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression

KV-Cache

The cached Key and Value matrices from the transformer attention mechanism, retained across decoding steps to avoid recomputation. Memory footprint grows linearly with sequence length and batch size: \(\text{Bytes} = 2 \times L \times B \times d \times \text{layers} \times \text{bytes\_per\_param}\). GQA reduces KV-Cache size; PagedAttention manages it more efficiently. Slides: Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

title: Glossary
text:
L

Latency

The wall-clock time to complete one inference or training step. In MLSys·im, latency is the primary output of the Iron Law equation. Measured in ms or \(\mu\)s. Maximizing Throughput often conflicts with minimizing latency. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking, Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving

LLM (Large Language Model)

A transformer-based model trained on large text corpora, typically with billions of parameters. Examples: GPT-4, Llama 3 (8.0B, 70.6B, and 405B parameters), Gemini. Key serving metrics: TTFT and ITL. Key memory bottleneck: KV-Cache. Slides: Vol I Ch 6: Network Architectures

title: Glossary
text:
M

Memory-Bound

A workload whose performance is limited by the hardware’s memory Bandwidth, not its peak FLOP/s. Occurs when Arithmetic Intensity falls below the Ridge Point. Remedies include lower Precision, Operator Fusion, or faster memory (e.g., HBM3). Contrast with Compute-Bound. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

MFU (Model FLOP Utilization)

The fraction of theoretical peak FLOP/s actually achieved: \(\text{MFU} = \text{Achieved FLOP/s} / \text{Peak FLOP/s}\). Well-optimized training achieves 30–50% MFU; poorly optimized code may fall below 10%. MFU is the single most important efficiency metric for large-scale training runs. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

Microbatch

A subdivision of the training batch used in Pipeline Parallelism. Increasing the number of microbatches \(M\) reduces the Pipeline Bubble fraction: \(\text{Bubble} = (P{-}1) / (P{-}1{+}M)\), where \(P\) is the pipeline depth. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)

The average time a component operates before failing. For a fleet of \(N\) identical nodes, \(\text{MTBF}_\text{fleet} = \text{MTBF}_\text{node} / N\). A 1,024-node cluster with 100,000-hour node MTBF has a fleet MTBF of ~98 hours. Input to the Young-Daly Formula. Slides: Vol II Ch 7: Fault Tolerance

title: Glossary
text:
N

NVLink

NVIDIA’s high-bandwidth interconnect for GPU-to-GPU communication within a server. Provides 900 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth per GPU in DGX H100 systems. Required for Tensor Parallelism, where low-latency intra-node communication is critical. Contrast with InfiniBand for inter-node communication. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure, Vol II Ch 3: Network Fabrics

title: Glossary
text:
O

OpEx (Operational Expenditure)

The ongoing costs of running hardware: electricity, networking, cooling, labor. In cloud pricing, OpEx dominates over a 3-year period by 2–5x over CapEx. Slides: Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

Operator Fusion

Combining multiple small GPU kernels into a single larger one to reduce memory transfers between operations. For example, fusing a matrix multiply followed by an activation function avoids writing and re-reading the intermediate result from HBM. A key optimization for reducing Memory-Bound overhead. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

title: Glossary
text:
P

Pipeline Bubble

The fraction of time a pipeline-parallel system spends idle waiting for the first Microbatch to propagate through all stages: \(\text{Bubble} = (P{-}1) / (P{-}1{+}M)\), where \(P\) is pipeline depth and \(M\) is microbatch count. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

Pipeline Parallelism (PP)

A distributed training strategy that splits the model’s layers across devices, each device processing a different “stage.” Introduces a Pipeline Bubble of idle time. Complementary to Data Parallelism and Tensor Parallelism in 3D Parallelism. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

Precision

The numerical format used to represent weights and activations. fp32 (32-bit float) is most accurate; fp16/bf16 (16-bit) halves memory and doubles throughput on Tensor Cores; int8 and int4 further reduce memory at the cost of accuracy. Lower precision increases Arithmetic Intensity by reducing bytes per operation. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression

Progressive Lowering

MLSys·im’s architectural principle: workload specifications (demand) are progressively mapped onto hardware specifications (supply) through a chain of analytical transformations. The reverse of how hardware is typically specified: it starts from the algorithm, not the chip.

Pruning

A model compression technique that removes redundant weights or entire structures (channels, attention heads) from a trained model. Unstructured pruning zeros out individual weights; structured pruning removes whole rows/columns for hardware-friendly speedups. See also Quantization and Knowledge Distillation. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression

PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness)

\(\text{PUE} = \text{Total Facility Power} / \text{IT Equipment Power}\). A PUE of 1.0 is theoretical perfection; hyperscale datacenters achieve 1.1–1.4. Higher PUE means more energy wasted on cooling and facility overhead. Used in MLSys·im’s sustainability solver alongside Carbon Intensity and WUE. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure, Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

title: Glossary
text:
Q

Quantization

Reducing the numerical Precision of model weights and/or activations (e.g., FP32 to INT8 or INT4) to shrink memory footprint and increase throughput. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) converts a pre-trained model without retraining; Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) simulates low-precision during training for higher accuracy. Slides: Vol I Ch 10: Model Compression

title: Glossary
text:
R

Ridge Point

The Arithmetic Intensity at which a workload transitions from Memory-Bound to Compute-Bound on a given hardware platform: \(I^* = \text{Peak FLOP/s} / \text{Memory BW}\). For the A100 at FP16: \(I^* = 312 \text{ TFLOP/s} / 2\.04 \text{ TB/s} \approx 153 \text{ FLOP/byte}\) (and for the H100 at FP16: \(989 \text{ TFLOP/s} / 3\.35 \text{ TB/s} \approx 295 \text{ FLOP/byte}\)). Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

Roofline Model

A visual and analytical tool that plots hardware performance ceilings (the “roofline”) and shows where workloads sit relative to them. The sloped region is Memory-Bound; the flat region is Compute-Bound; the inflection point is the Ridge Point. Introduced by Williams, Waterman, and Patterson (2009). MLSys·im implements a generalized roofline via the Iron Law. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

title: Glossary
text:
S

SLA (Service Level Agreement)

A target performance guarantee, typically specifying maximum acceptable latency and minimum throughput. For LLM serving, common SLAs target TTFT < 200 ms and ITL < 50 ms/token. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking, Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving

Speculative Decoding

An inference optimization where a small, fast “draft” model generates candidate tokens that are then verified in parallel by the full model. Reduces ITL by converting sequential autoregressive steps into a single parallel verification pass, at the cost of occasional rejected tokens. Slides: Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

SSoT (Single Source of Truth)

The principle that each specification (chip peak FLOP/s, grid carbon intensity, etc.) has exactly one authoritative location: the MLSys Zoo. All computations derive from the Zoo, eliminating inconsistencies from stale copied values.

Systolic Array

A grid of processing elements that rhythmically pass data to their neighbors, performing a multiply-accumulate at each step. The dominant dataflow architecture in ML accelerators: Google TPUs use systolic arrays for matrix multiplication, and NVIDIA Tensor Cores implement a similar systolic-like pattern. Slides: Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

title: Glossary
text:
T

TCO (Total Cost of Ownership)

The full cost of a system over its lifetime: \(\text{TCO} = \text{CapEx}_{\text{amortized}} + \text{OpEx}\). Includes hardware purchase, electricity, cooling, networking, and labor. MLSys·im’s TCO solver computes this from hardware registry specs and regional energy costs. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure, Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

TDP (Thermal Design Power)

The maximum sustained power a chip is designed to dissipate under load, in Watts. Relevant for datacenter cooling capacity planning. An H100 SXM5 has a TDP of 700 W (an A100 has 400 W). Used in MLSys·im to compute energy consumption and TCO. Slides: Vol II Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure

Tensor Core

A specialized hardware unit in NVIDIA GPUs designed for matrix-multiply-accumulate operations. Achieves much higher throughput than standard CUDA cores for ML workloads. The A100’s 312 TFLOP/s peak (FP16) comes from its tensor cores, not its CUDA cores. Functionally similar to a Systolic Array. Slides: Vol I Ch 5: Neural Network Computation, Vol I Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration

Tensor Parallelism (TP)

A distributed training strategy that splits individual matrix multiplications across devices within a node. Requires high-bandwidth intra-node connectivity (NVLink). Combined with Data Parallelism and Pipeline Parallelism in 3D Parallelism. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

3D Parallelism

The combination of Data Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism, and Pipeline Parallelism to scale training across hundreds or thousands of GPUs. TP operates within a node (over NVLink), PP across a small group of nodes, and DP across the remaining replicas. The standard recipe for training frontier LLMs. Slides: Vol II Ch 6: Distributed Training

Throughput

The number of samples (or tokens) processed per unit time: \(\text{Throughput} = \text{Batch Size} / \text{Latency}\). Maximizing throughput often conflicts with minimizing Latency. Larger batches increase throughput but also increase per-request latency. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking

TTFT (Time to First Token)

The latency from receiving a user query to generating the first output token in an LLM serving system. Determined primarily by the prefill phase, which is Compute-Bound. Target: <200 ms for interactive applications. See also ITL. Slides: Vol I Ch 13: Model Serving, Vol II Ch 10: Inference at Scale

title: Glossary
text:
U

Utilization (\(\eta\))

The fraction of theoretical peak FLOP/s actually achieved in practice. Typical values: 30–50% for well-optimized training, 10–30% for inference. MLSys·im uses \(\eta\) as a parameter in the Iron Law; see the hardware registry for per-device defaults. Closely related to MFU. Slides: Vol I Ch 12: Benchmarking, Vol II Ch 9: Performance Engineering

title: Glossary
text:
W

WUE (Water Usage Effectiveness)

Liters of water consumed per kilowatt-hour of energy. Relevant for datacenters using evaporative cooling. MLSys·im estimates water usage as: \(\text{Water (L)} = \text{Energy (kWh)} \times \text{WUE}\). Slides: Vol II Ch 15: Sustainable AI

title: Glossary
text:
Y

Young-Daly Formula

The optimal checkpoint interval for fault-tolerant distributed training: \(\tau_\text{opt} = \sqrt{2 \times \delta \times \text{MTBF}_\text{fleet}}\), where \(\delta\) is the time to save one checkpoint and MTBF is the mean time between failures of the fleet. Named after Young (1974) and Daly (2006). Slides: Vol II Ch 7: Fault Tolerance



This glossary is updated with each MLSys·im release. If a term is missing, please open an issue.

title: Follow a Calculation Through the Code
text: A named scenario connects an input configuration to a calculation. To understand its result, follow that connection through the implementation. The same route helps a contributor find the file that owns a proposed change.
crumbs: Follow a Calculation Through the Code

title: Follow a Calculation Through the Code
text:
Start from the public call
The named serving case below selects a workload, a device, a context length, and a batch size. Its result property invokes the serving model.

from mlsysim import Scenarios

case = Scenarios.Llama3_70B_ServingH100
result = case.result
print("Scenario type:", type(case).__name__)
print("Result type:", type(result).__name__)
print("Fits modeled memory:", result.feasible)

Scenario type: ServingScenario
Result type: ServingResult
Fits modeled memory: False


Feasibility is part of the result. A latency estimate alone does not establish that the selected workload fits the device. For an introduction to the public interfaces and their different scopes, see Choosing a Python API.
crumbs: Follow a Calculation Through the Code

title: Follow a Calculation Through the Code
section: Find the owner of each part
text:
Find the owner of each part
The serving domain uses the same name across scenario definitions, named configurations, and result schemas. These files have different responsibilities.








Part
File under mlsysim/engine/
What to read




Named inputs
scenario_catalog/serving/foundations.py
Llama3_70B_ServingH100: the selected workload, hardware, and scenario assumptions


Typed scenario
scenario_definitions/serving.py
ServingScenario: its input fields and result property


Solver
solvers/serving.py
ServingModel.solve: the parameters, accounting, validity regime, and exclusions


Result
result_types/serving.py
ServingResult: returned fields, units, and feasibility semantics



ServingScenario.result passes the configured inputs to ServingModel.solve. The solver combines reusable equations and shared serving accounting. Its imports point to the specific owners: transformer work in physics/transformer.py, KV storage in physics/memory.py, and the shared decode calculation in engine/solvers/_decode.py. Read the solver’s docstring before interpreting a helper in isolation; it states which costs the composed estimate includes.
The serving scenario reference links related contracts. Each class page identifies the file that defines it. The domain directory follows the same organization for training, communication, data, and the other modeling subjects.
crumbs: Follow a Calculation Through the Code

title: Follow a Calculation Through the Code
text:
Keep public imports stable
Textbooks and applications continue to import Scenarios, mlsysim.solvers, and the established scenario and result classes. The modules engine/scenario_types.py, engine/scenarios.py, and engine/results.py forward those imports to the domain implementations. They provide compatibility; a calculation has one implementation in its defining module.
Historical class metadata is preserved for serialization compatibility. It may therefore identify the older public module rather than the file that now owns the class. Use the source locations in the generated reference when navigating the implementation.
A domain describes a modeling subject, not a textbook volume. A serving scenario can support several volumes, a lab, and a paper without moving or acquiring a second implementation.
crumbs: Follow a Calculation Through the Code

title: Follow a Calculation Through the Code
text:
Make a change reviewable
First identify whether the proposal changes a specification, a scenario input, an equation, or a result’s presentation. Edit its owner. A hardware specification belongs with its sourced registry data; a different context length belongs in a scenario configuration; a different accounting assumption belongs with the calculation and its documented contract.
For serving behavior, start with tests/test_physical_contracts.py, tests/test_shared_accounting.py, and tests/test_solver_suite.py. tests/test_calculation_scenarios.py exercises named cases. The test directory’s README.md maps these checks to the broader suite. Documentation examples check that the stated calls run; physical contracts check the calculation’s units, accounting, and limiting behavior.
A source move should preserve those behaviors. A numerical correction needs a separate explanation of the changed assumption and its downstream consequences. Run the modeling documentation checks, then compare the affected textbook and paper consumers using the release runbook’s downstream snapshot workflow. Surface changed prose claims for editorial review rather than silently updating their numbers.
