title: Modeling and documentation conventions
text: MLSysIM is the modeling engine for the four-volume ML Systems textbook series. The books are its primary integration consumers; the same public API also serves students, instructors, and engineers working independently of the books. Organize the engine by the system being modeled, not by volume or chapter. A memory equation can serve a single accelerator, a fleet, an agent, or a robot.

title: Modeling and documentation conventions
section: Follow a calculation through the code
text:
Follow a calculation through the code








Layer
Question it answers
Location




Definitions
What hardware, workload, and environment are we modeling?
Registry packages and their data/ directories


Physics
What equation applies, and where does it come from?
mlsysim/physics/


Solvers
How do the equations combine under these constraints?
mlsysim/engine/solvers/


Scenarios
What named configuration are we evaluating?
mlsysim/engine/scenario_catalog/ and scenario_definitions/


Results
What does the answer mean, in which units?
mlsysim/engine/result_types/


Teaching
How does a reader reason about the result?
Quarto guides, textbook cells, and labs



Keep equations in one implementation. A solver composes equations and checks constraints; a scenario supplies inputs. Chapter-specific empirical series and one-off anecdotes remain with the chapter rather than becoming engine constants.
Use descriptive names such as context_tokens and bytes_per_element. Short symbols are appropriate when the adjacent docstring maps them directly to a published equation. Keep units attached until formatting the output.
Split a large module when its domains can be understood independently. Preserve public import paths through explicit re-exports, and compare outputs before and after a move. Keep structural changes separate from changes to equations or defaults.

title: Modeling and documentation conventions
section: Document the calculation where it lives
text:
Document the calculation where it lives
Use NumPy-style docstrings for public equations and solver methods. The first sentence explains the purpose in plain English. Include these standard sections:







Section
Required explanation




Parameters
Meaning, units, valid range, and meaning of defaults


Returns
Quantity or result type, units, and feasibility semantics


Notes
Equation, symbol definitions, unit of work, assumptions, and exclusions


References
A supporting source URL and bibliography key when available, or a concrete algebraic derivation for original accounting


Examples
A small executable example using the public API



Put the reusable equation’s full derivation in its physics function. A solver should explain how it composes those equations and link to the relevant functions using See Also. Avoid copying a derivation into several implementations.
Elementary identities do not need an unrelated citation. Use Derivation: in References to explain how a result follows from its definitions, conservation relationship, or stated construction. A heuristic must identify its assumed relationship and limitations; labeling it a derivation does not make it a physical law. Literature-derived methods should link the supporting source.
An equation or section number belongs in the reference only after checking the source. A citation to a paper is not evidence that every constant in our implementation came from it. Identify each addition as a modeling convention, assumed efficiency, calibrated parameter, or algebraic consequence.
For example, the Roofline principle motivates taking the larger of compute and memory time. An additive per-layer runtime tax is a separate assumption. Report both, rather than attributing the entire implementation to the Roofline paper.
The existing provenance catalog records sources for values. Formula docstrings record the derivation and modeling choices. These complement each other; a verification-date field alone does not establish that an equation is correct.

title: Modeling and documentation conventions
text:
Keep scenario properties concise
Calculation scenarios share their inputs and assumptions across related properties. Put the scenario’s equation or composition map, assumptions, exclusions, sources, and runnable example in its class docstring. A delegated scenario may name a qualified Implementation reference: in References; the checker resolves every linked target so a renamed solver cannot silently leave a broken explanation. Each public calculated property then states what it means, its units, and its equation or the qualified function or solver that owns the calculation. A simple alias can point to that contract instead of repeating a derivation. A property that introduces additional arithmetic must explain that arithmetic locally.
These property explanations are part of the code, not generated substitutes for reading it. An extracted Python expression alone does not explain a unit of work, a valid regime, or why a relation applies.

title: Modeling and documentation conventions
text:
Publish from the same source
The site already uses quartodoc, configured in _quarto.yml. Its NumPy docstring parser turns code documentation into the API reference. The pre-render hook, scripts/build_api.py, regenerates the reference for a full site build and checks public API coverage. Do not edit generated docs/api/ pages. The scenario reference index links class pages with input fields, defaults, calculated properties, and their explanations. Single-page previews do not regenerate the API; rebuild it explicitly when reviewing changed docstrings.
From the package directory, with the development and documentation extras installed:
python docs/scripts/build_api.py
make modeling-docs-check
make docs
Keep conceptual explanations in Quarto guides and implementation contracts in code. Link between them. Generate numerical tables from executable calculations; calibration and validation scope is an example. API coverage checks establish that pages exist, not that every explanation is complete.

title: Modeling and documentation conventions
text:
Enforce the convention
Run make modeling-docs-check from the package directory. This command is also part of make check, the development and release CI workflows, and the local pre-commit hooks. Install the development extra before running it.







Check
What fails




Ruff with the NumPy pydocstyle convention
Missing or incorrectly formatted docstrings in the selected modules


Ruff formatter check
Python formatting that differs from the standard layout


numpydoc validation
Missing or misordered parameters, undocumented returns, malformed sections, or missing examples


MLSysIM contract check
Missing Equation:, Assumptions:, or Excludes: labels in Notes; missing supporting source URL, concrete Derivation:, or qualified Implementation reference: in References


Executable examples
A doctest fails or the examples contain no executable code


Citation-key check
A supplied key does not exist in the repository’s paper bibliography


Equation display
Unquoted multiplication tokens could become Markdown emphasis instead of the written equation


Discovery
A newly added public calculation or scenario lacks its required contract


Scenario trace
A scenario property loses its local equation or link to an underlying contract



The checker discovers public functions in the physics tree, public concrete solver methods and helpers, generic Engine calculations, workload calculations, calculated registry and result properties, serving profiles, constraint-explorer calculations, and scenario classes and their public properties from source definitions. New calculations in these modules enter the gate without someone remembering to add an allowlist entry. Scenario definitions and result types are scanned recursively through their domain packages, including base classes and package initializers. The legacy scenario_types.py and results.py import facades remain compatible entry points; imported aliases add no duplicate checks. Discovery follows physical source definitions rather than historical __module__ values retained for serialization compatibility. Private implementation modules, abstract interfaces, and presentation-only summary methods are outside this numerical-contract inventory; their public callers own the documented contract. Imported aliases are checked at the defining function.
[tool.mlsysim.documentation] in pyproject.toml controls optional module-wide Ruff style and formatting checks and the numpydoc exceptions. It does not narrow the discovered scientific-contract scope. Full NumPy contracts apply to equations and solvers; scenario properties use the concise shared-context convention above. Composition and conversion entry points have a separate ordinary NumPy API check: parameters, return semantics, and executable examples, without artificial equations or citations for dispatch and unit conversion. Presentation, serialization, metadata lookup, schema/introspection, abstract interfaces, and optional backend plumbing are not scientific-model contracts. Optional optimizer examples state the required installation extra and are validated separately when it is present.
The only disabled numpydoc rules are the optional extended-summary and See Also requirements. The scientific explanation belongs in Notes; cross-links remain encouraged. The source distribution does not contain the paper bibliography, so checks there explicitly report that key resolution is unavailable. Repository CI checks the bibliography. A citation key existing does not prove that a source supports an equation; that remains a review responsibility.
To apply formatting locally, run python -m ruff format on the affected modules. Checks never rewrite files. The tests exercise both documented APIs and deliberate failures such as an undocumented parameter, an unknown citation key, or an incorrect example result. Tests also add new temporary calculations to prove that discovery includes them, remove a scenario trace, and reject an empty or unexplained source declaration.
The implementation uses standard Ruff NumPy conventions and numpydoc validation. It does not require changing the existing Quarto publishing system.

title: Modeling and documentation conventions
text:
Protect the textbook series
Treat a change to an equation, default, unit, or feasibility decision as a numerical compatibility change even when the Python signature stays the same.

Record the old and new outputs with identical inputs and package versions.
Search consumers in all four volumes, including named scenarios and indirect solver calls. Include labs, slides, the paper, figures, and generated tables.
Execute affected textbook cells and compare the values interpolated into prose. Passing registry lookup tests alone does not check the claims around those values.
Review the surrounding claim: its inequality, bottleneck, comparison, and conclusion may change even when rounding hides a small numerical difference.
Flag prose discrepancies for a separate editorial decision. Do not silently rewrite a teaching claim or tune an equation merely to retain its previous answer.
Before a coordinated release, refresh approved generated artifacts and inspect the affected rendered pages and figures. Report any cells or environments not tested.

A structural cleanup should preserve outputs. A correctness fix may change them; its release notes must explain the change. Neither passing tests nor agreement with calibration cases establishes an accuracy guarantee for unseen workloads.

title: For Students
text: For a student taking a first ML systems course or preparing for industry interviews, MLSys·im offers a way to experiment with real hardware specifications and see why systems behave the way they do. Hardware registry specs come from datasheets where available; outputs are derived from documented equations.

title: For Students
text:
Learning Objectives
Students who work through the MLSys·im tutorials learn to:

Identify bottlenecks: Determine whether a workload is memory-bound or compute-bound on any hardware, and understand why
Reason quantitatively: Use real datasheet numbers (not made-up examples) to calculate latency, throughput, and cost
Build systems intuition: See how batch size, precision, parallelism strategy, and datacenter location each affect performance
Think across the stack: Connect workload characteristics to hardware specs to infrastructure constraints

title: For Students
text:
Prerequisites

Python: Comfortable with functions, loops, and f-strings
Math: Basic algebra (no calculus required; all solver equations are arithmetic)
ML: Familiarity with terms like “model parameters,” “inference,” and “training” (the Glossary defines everything else)

No GPU, no cloud account, and no special hardware are required. Installation is one command:
pip install mlsysim
See the Getting Started guide for development installs. Local install is the supported path; Colab works by running pip install mlsysim in the first cell, but one-click Colab/Binder launch buttons are not available yet.

title: For Students
text:
Quick Start

import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

# Load a model and hardware from the vetted registry
model = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
gpu   = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100

# Solve: is this workload memory-bound or compute-bound?
profile = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=gpu, batch_size=1, precision="fp16", efficiency=1.0)

print(f"Bottleneck: {profile.bottleneck}")
print(f"Latency:    {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")

Bottleneck: Memory
Latency:    0.54 ms

title: For Students
text:
Recommended Study Workflow
For self-study or a course, this workflow maximizes retention:

Read the textbook chapter (or skim the slide deck) to get the conceptual framework
Predict what will happen before running any code, and write it down
Model the setup using MLSys·im to test the prediction against real hardware specs
Explore by changing one parameter at a time (batch size, precision, hardware) and observing the effect
Reflect on where the prediction was wrong, because that gap is where learning happens







NoteSelf-Study vs. Classroom



For self-study, the slide decks include speaker notes with timing guidance, teaching tips, and common misconceptions, written to be useful even without an instructor. In a course, the instructor may assign specific tutorials as homework; the Instructor Guide gives the recommended pairing.

title: Understanding the Efficiency Parameter
text:
Every equation in mlsysim needs one number it cannot derive from first principles. That number is efficiency.




The efficiency parameter, written as eta in equations and efficiency in code, is the ratio of achieved FLOPS to peak FLOPS. MLSys·im exposes it on every solver where the compute term depends on achieved FLOP/s, including Engine.solve(), SingleNodeModel, ServingModel, DistributedModel, ContinuousBatchingModel, ServingCapacityModel, and the optimizers that call those models.
eta = Achieved_FLOPS / Peak_FLOPS
Consider this call:
Engine.solve(model=llama70b, hardware=h100, batch_size=32, precision="fp16", efficiency=0.45)
It tells the model to assume that this workload achieves 45% of the H100’s peak FP16 throughput. The framework uses this to convert theoretical compute time into realistic wall-clock time:
Time = FLOPs / (Peak_FLOPS x eta)
Efficiency is always between 0.0 and 1.0. A value of 1.0 would mean the hardware is computing at its absolute theoretical maximum on every cycle, which never happens in practice.




Efficiency is a single number because it compresses 12+ sub-factors that are impossible to predict analytically for an arbitrary workload on arbitrary hardware. Here is what eta actually absorbs:







Sub-factor
What it means




Kernel launch overhead
Each CUDA kernel launch has microseconds of latency. CUDA Graphs help amortize this, but eager-mode PyTorch pays it on every op.


SM occupancy
Register pressure and shared memory usage determine how many warps can run concurrently on each streaming multiprocessor. Low occupancy means idle compute lanes.


Memory coalescing
Misaligned or scattered memory accesses waste bandwidth. A perfectly coalesced access pattern can be 10x faster than a naive one.


Instruction-level parallelism
The GPU’s pipeline depth means instructions must be independent to keep all stages busy. Data dependencies create bubbles.


Pipeline bubbles
In pipeline-parallel training, micro-batch scheduling leaves some stages idle while others compute. The bubble fraction depends on the number of micro-batches relative to pipeline stages.


Communication overlap
Modern training overlaps AllReduce with backward computation. How well this overlap works depends on network bandwidth, gradient sizes, and scheduling.


Framework overhead
Python GIL contention, graph compilation time (for torch.compile or XLA), operator dispatch overhead, and autograd bookkeeping all steal cycles from useful compute.


Attention implementation
FlashAttention achieves 2-4x the throughput of naive attention by fusing operations and reducing HBM reads. The choice of attention kernel alone can shift eta by 0.15-0.25.


Quantization runtime overhead
INT8/INT4 kernels may not achieve the same fraction of peak as FP16 GEMM, especially for non-standard shapes or when dequantization is on the critical path.


Data loader stalls
If the CPU cannot tokenize, augment, and transfer data to the GPU fast enough, the GPU sits idle between batches.


Garbage collection pauses
Python’s GC and CUDA’s memory allocator can cause periodic stalls, especially with large batch sizes and frequent tensor allocation.


OS/driver interrupt handling
Context switches, NUMA effects, PCIe configuration space accesses, and driver-level synchronization all introduce non-deterministic latency.



No analytical model can predict the combined effect of all twelve factors for a given workload. Even NVIDIA’s own performance models use empirical calibration. Eta should be measured, not derived.




This is not a new challenge. In Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach (CAQDA), Patterson and Hennessy face the identical issue with CPI (Cycles Per Instruction).
CPI is the average number of clock cycles each instruction takes. It depends on the instruction mix, cache hit rates, branch prediction accuracy, pipeline hazards, memory latency, and a dozen other microarchitectural details. Patterson and Hennessy do not try to predict CPI from first principles. Instead, they:

Measure it on real hardware with real workloads.
Teach students what affects it, so they can reason about why CPI differs across programs and architectures.
Use it as a parameter in the performance equation: Time = Instructions x CPI x Clock_Period

This is exactly what eta is for ML systems. It is our CPI. The performance equation has the same structure:
Time = FLOPs x (1 / Peak_FLOPS) x (1 / eta)
       ^^^^^   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^   ^^^^^^^^^
       work    clock period         CPI equivalent
Just as CAQDA students learn to reason about why a SPEC benchmark has CPI = 1.2 on one processor and CPI = 0.8 on another, mlsysim users learn to reason about why Megatron-LM training achieves eta = 0.50 while eager-mode PyTorch on a small model achieves eta = 0.10.
The value of the framework is not in predicting eta. It is in answering what happens, for a given eta, when the hardware, the model, or the batch size changes.




Use these empirically-grounded ranges as starting points:








Scenario
Efficiency
Rationale




Training (Megatron-LM, large Transformer)
0.40-0.55
Well-optimized GEMM + FlashAttention


Training (PyTorch eager, small model)
0.08-0.15
Kernel launch overhead dominates


Inference decode, batch=1
0.01-0.05
Memory-bound; compute nearly idle


Inference decode, batch=32+
0.15-0.35
Batch amortizes weight loading


Inference prefill, long context
0.30-0.50
Compute-bound GEMM + attention


TinyML (TFLite Micro on ESP32)
0.05-0.15
Interpreter overhead, no tensor cores



These ranges come from published benchmarks (MLPerf, PaLM training reports, Megatron-LM papers) and our own measurements. They are not universal truths; they are informed defaults. If a solver exposes efficiency=0.5, read that as a documented starting point for a well-optimized datacenter workload, not a hidden claim that every workload reaches 50% of peak.




With access to real hardware, eta can be measured directly. This is the gold standard, because it turns the analytical model from an estimation tool into a calibrated prediction tool.


Run the actual training or inference workload on the target hardware. Use the real code, the real data, and the real batch size. Do not use synthetic benchmarks, because they measure a different workload.



Record the achieved throughput in tokens/second (for language models) or samples/second (for vision models). Use steady-state measurements after warmup, excluding the first few batches.



# Your measurements
measured_throughput = 1200  # tokens/sec (from step 2)

# Known quantities
model_flops_per_token = 1.4e12    # FLOPs per token for your model
peak_flops = 989e12               # H100 SXM FP16 peak

# Back-calculate
theoretical_max_throughput = peak_flops / model_flops_per_token
eta = measured_throughput / theoretical_max_throughput

print(f"eta = {eta:.3f}")  # e.g., eta = 0.423



With a grounded eta in hand, use it to explore counterfactuals:
# "What if I moved from H100 to B200?"
result = Engine.solve(
    model=my_model,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.B200,
    batch_size=32,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=0.423  # calibrated from H100 measurement
)
Important caveat: eta does not transfer perfectly across GPU generations (see the fallacies section below), but it transfers much better than having no measurement at all. A calibrated eta from one GPU gives a reasonable starting point for another, which further measurement can then refine.







It is not. The appropriate eta varies by orders of magnitude depending on the workload:

LLM decode at batch=1: eta ~ 0.01-0.05
Optimized large-batch training: eta ~ 0.40-0.55
Small model in eager mode: eta ~ 0.08-0.15

Using eta = 0.5 for decode-phase inference will overestimate throughput by 10-50x. Always match the efficiency to the workload regime.



Not necessarily. A workload running at INT4 precision might report higher hardware utilization (more ops/sec relative to INT4 peak) while producing lower-quality results than the same model at FP16 with lower eta. Efficiency measures hardware utilization, not model quality.
Similarly, a workload that maximizes eta by using enormous batch sizes may achieve high throughput but unacceptable latency for real-time serving. The right eta depends on the objective.



It does not, at least not exactly. Different architectures have different bottleneck profiles:

A100 to H100: The Transformer Engine and higher memory bandwidth on H100 shift many workloads from memory-bound to compute-bound, changing eta significantly.
Dense to sparse: Architectures with hardware sparsity support (like NVIDIA’s 2:4 structured sparsity) achieve different eta for the same workload.
GPU to TPU: Completely different memory hierarchy, interconnect topology, and programming model. An eta measured on GPU says almost nothing about TPU performance.

When moving across architectures, use the calibrated eta as a starting point, then adjust based on known architectural differences.



Eta is a ratio. Buying a faster GPU increases both numerator and denominator. If the bottleneck is software overhead (Python dispatch, kernel launch latency), faster hardware may actually decrease eta because the hardware ceiling rises but the software overhead stays constant.
Improving eta requires optimizing the software stack: better kernels, operation fusion, reduced framework overhead, efficient communication overlap. This is the domain of ML systems engineering.






PaLM Training Report (Chowdhery et al., 2022): Reports MFU of 46.2% for PaLM 540B on TPUv4, one of the most carefully measured large-scale training efficiency numbers published.
Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2020): The reference implementation for efficient large model training. Published efficiency numbers across model sizes and parallelism configurations.
MLPerf Training (mattson et al., 2020): Standardized benchmarks that provide comparable efficiency measurements across hardware platforms.
Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach (Hennessy & Patterson): Chapter 1’s treatment of CPI and the CPU performance equation is the direct intellectual ancestor of how mlsysim treats efficiency.

Optimized large-batch training: eta ~ 0.40-0.55
Small model in eager mode: eta ~ 0.08-0.15

Using eta = 0.5 for decode-phase inference will overestimate throughput by 10-50x. Always match the efficiency to the workload regime.



Not necessarily. A workload running at INT4 precision might report higher hardware utilization (more ops/sec relative to INT4 peak) while producing lower-quality results than the same model at FP16 with lower eta. Efficiency measures hardware utilization, not model quality.
Similarly, a workload that maximizes eta by using enormous batch sizes may achieve high throughput but unacceptable latency for real-time serving. The right eta depends on the objective.



It does not, at least not exactly. Different architectures have different bottleneck profiles:

A100 to H100: The Transformer Engine and higher memory bandwidth on H100 shift many workloads from memory-bound to compute-bound, changing eta significantly.
Dense to sparse: Architectures with hardware sparsity support (like NVIDIA’s 2:4 structured sparsity) achieve different eta for the same workload.
GPU to TPU: Completely different memory hierarchy, interconnect topology, and programming model. An eta measured on GPU says almost nothing about TPU performance.

When moving across architectures, use the calibrated eta as a starting point, then adjust based on known architectural differences.



Eta is a ratio. Buying a faster GPU increases both numerator and denominator. If the bottleneck is software overhead (Python dispatch, kernel launch latency), faster hardware may actually decrease eta because the hardware ceiling rises but the software overhead stays constant.
Improving eta requires optimizing the software stack: better kernels, operation fusion, reduced framework overhead, efficient communication overlap. This is the domain of ML systems engineering.

title: Understanding the Efficiency Parameter
text:
PaLM Training Report (Chowdhery et al., 2022): Reports MFU of 46.2% for PaLM 540B on TPUv4, one of the most carefully measured large-scale training efficiency numbers published.
Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2020): The reference implementation for efficient large model training. Published efficiency numbers across model sizes and parallelism configurations.
MLPerf Training (mattson et al., 2020): Standardized benchmarks that provide comparable efficiency measurements across hardware platforms.
Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach (Hennessy & Patterson): Chapter 1’s treatment of CPI and the CPU performance equation is the direct intellectual ancestor of how mlsysim treats efficiency.

title: Getting Started
text:
NotePrerequisites



MLSys·im assumes basic Python familiarity (variables, functions, pip install). No prior ML or hardware knowledge is required. Key concepts like roofline analysis, memory-bound vs. compute-bound, and FLOP/s are explained in context throughout the tutorials. For a full reference of terms, see the Glossary.

title: Getting Started
text:
Installation
MLSys·im requires Python 3.10+ and installs with pip:
pip install mlsysim
For development or to follow along with tutorials locally:
git clone https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book
cd cs249r_book/mlsysim
pip install -e ".[dev]"
Verify the installation:
python -c "import mlsysim; print(mlsysim.__version__)"






TipLocal install recommended



Tutorials are pure Python and run in any Python 3.10+ environment. The local workflow is the supported path for the current release and matches the commands used throughout the documentation.

title: Getting Started
text:
A First Analysis
For a map of Engine, specialized solvers, and scenarios, see Choosing a Python API. The example below uses the generic single-device Roofline model.
Once MLSys·im is installed, a complete roofline analysis takes five lines. The roofline model is the foundation of ML systems performance reasoning. It determines whether a workload is limited by compute (arithmetic units) or memory (data movement). For a visual walkthrough, see the Hardware Acceleration slide deck (Vol I, Ch 11).

import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

# 1. Load a model and hardware from the vetted Zoo
model    = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
hardware = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100

# 2. Solve -- the Engine applies the roofline model
profile = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=hardware, batch_size=1, precision="fp16", efficiency=1.0)

# 3. Read the results
print(f"Bottleneck: {profile.bottleneck}")
print(f"Latency:    {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"Throughput: {profile.throughput.to('1/s'):~.0f}")

Bottleneck: Memory
Latency:    0.54 ms
Throughput: 1843 / s


The output above is produced by running the code when this page is built, so it always matches the installed version of MLSys·im.






NoteWorking with units



MLSys·im uses the Pint library for physical units. All quantities carry attached units (ms, GB, TFLOP/s, etc.). Use .to('ms') to convert between units. Use .magnitude to extract the raw number for calculations or plotting.

title: Getting Started
text:
Understanding the Output
Engine.solve() returns a PerformanceProfile, a structured result containing everything the roofline model can determine about the workload.

Core fields







Field
What it means




bottleneck
'Memory' or 'Compute': which resource limits performance


latency
Time to process one batch: the roofline bound plus fixed overhead


throughput
Samples per second = batch_size / latency


latency_compute
Time if only compute were the constraint


latency_memory
Time if only memory bandwidth were the constraint


latency_overhead
Fixed dispatch and kernel-launch time added on top of the roofline bound


arithmetic_intensity
Operations per byte, the x-axis of the roofline plot





Extended fields







Field
What it means




energy
Estimated energy consumption (Joules)


memory_footprint
Total memory required for the workload


mfu
Model FLOPs Utilization, the fraction of peak compute achieved


feasible
Whether the workload fits in device memory









TipThe key insight



If latency_memory > latency_compute, the workload is memory-bound, and faster arithmetic units will not help. The remedies are to increase batch size, use a more compute-dense operation (e.g., fused attention), or reduce data movement. When the workload is compute-bound, parallelism and quantization pay off.
This is the same insight taught in the Neural Network Computation slides (Vol I, Ch 5) and the Performance Engineering slides (Vol II, Ch 9).

title: Getting Started
text:
Adjusting the Efficiency Parameter
The efficiency parameter (\(\eta\)) is the parameter that most affects MLSys·im results. It represents the fraction of theoretical peak hardware performance that is actually achieved in practice. Unoptimized single-request inference often runs near 5% of peak, whereas well-tuned training and batched serving workloads reach 30%–50%.

# Default: well-optimized training (η = MfuHigh)
profile_default = Engine.solve(
    model=model, hardware=hardware,
    batch_size=32, precision="fp16", efficiency=mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuHigh
)

# Conservative: typical inference workload (η = 0.35)
profile_inference = Engine.solve(
    model=model, hardware=hardware,
    batch_size=32, precision="fp16", efficiency=0.35
)

print(f"Training estimate:  {profile_default.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"Inference estimate: {profile_inference.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")

Training estimate:  2.20 ms
Inference estimate: 2.92 ms


Typical efficiency ranges:








Scenario
\(\eta\) range
Notes




Well-optimized training (fp16)
0.30–0.50
Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed


Inference (fp16)
0.25–0.40
vLLM, TensorRT-LLM


Inference (int8)
0.20–0.40
Quantized serving



See the Accuracy & Validation page for guidance on choosing η for different scenarios. The gap between theoretical peak and achieved throughput is covered in detail in the Performance Engineering slides (Vol II, Ch 9).

title: Getting Started
text:
Defining Custom Models
Analyses are not limited to Zoo models. Define any model by specifying its parameters and FLOPs:

from mlsysim import ureg
from mlsysim.models.types import TransformerWorkload

my_model = TransformerWorkload(
    name="My-Custom-LLM",
    architecture="Transformer",
    parameters=13e9 * ureg.param,
    layers=40,
    hidden_dim=5120,
    heads=40,
    kv_heads=8,
    inference_flops=2 * 13e9 * ureg.flop  # Rule of thumb: 2 FLOPs per parameter
)

profile = Engine.solve(model=my_model, hardware=hardware, batch_size=1)
print(f"Bottleneck: {profile.bottleneck}")
print(f"Latency:    {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"Feasible:   {profile.feasible}")

Bottleneck: Memory
Latency:    14.44 ms
Feasible:   True


The Model Compression slides (Vol I, Ch 10) explain why parameter count and precision together determine both the memory footprint and the arithmetic intensity of a workload.

title: Hello, Roofline
text:
An engineer has a model and a GPU. Before writing any code, training anything, or renting any cloud instance, which hardware resource will be the bottleneck?
This tutorial teaches the single most important skill in ML systems: using the roofline model to answer that question in under a second.






NotePrerequisites



None. This is the starting point for all MLSys·im tutorials.








TipKey Terms for These Tutorials



Readers new to ML will meet the following terms throughout this tutorial series:







Term
Meaning




Model
A mathematical function with learned parameters (weights) that maps inputs to outputs (e.g., an image to a label)


Parameters
The numbers a model learns during training. A “25M parameter” model stores 25 million numbers


Inference
Running a trained model on new input to get a prediction (as opposed to training, which learns the parameters)


CNN
Convolutional Neural Network, a model architecture for images (e.g., ResNet-50)


LLM
Large Language Model, a model that generates text one token (roughly one word) at a time (e.g., GPT-4, Llama-3)


FP16
16-bit floating point (“half precision”), which uses 2 bytes per parameter. ML often uses reduced precision for speed


FLOP/s
Floating-point operations per second, a measure of compute speed. TFLOP/s = trillion FLOP/s


HBM
High Bandwidth Memory, the fast DRAM attached to a GPU (e.g., HBM2e on A100, HBM3 on H100)


Batch size
How many inputs are processed together in one pass. Larger batches amortize the cost of loading weights



See the Glossary for a complete list of terms.








NoteLearning Objectives




Identify the performance bottleneck (memory-bound vs. compute-bound) for any model-hardware pair
Predict how batch size shifts the operating point along the roofline
Interpret the ridge point as the boundary between two performance regimes
Use Engine.solve as the foundational API for all MLSys·im analyses









TipBackground: The Roofline Model



The roofline model (Williams, Waterman, and Patterson, 2009) is the foundational analytical tool for predicting hardware bottlenecks. Every accelerator has two speed limits:

Compute ceiling: how fast it can do arithmetic (measured in FLOP/s)
Memory bandwidth ceiling: how fast it can load data from memory (measured in bytes/s)

The roofline model reduces to four lines of algebra:
\[T_{\text{compute}} = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak FLOP/s}}
\qquad
T_{\text{memory}} = \frac{\text{Bytes}}{\text{Peak BW}}\]
\[T = \max(T_{\text{compute}},\; T_{\text{memory}})\]
\[\text{Ridge point} = \frac{\text{Peak FLOP/s}}{\text{Peak BW}} \quad [\text{FLOP/byte}]\]
A model’s arithmetic intensity (FLOPs ÷ Bytes) determines which ceiling it hits. Below the ridge point, the workload is memory-bound (starved for data). Above it, the workload is compute-bound (saturating the arithmetic units). This single classification drives every optimization decision downstream.
Caveat: The roofline is an upper bound. Real performance is always below it because of scheduling overhead, memory access patterns, and imperfect utilization. Achieving 40–60% of the roofline ceiling is considered good in practice. The model’s value lies not in predicting exact latency but in identifying the binding constraint (the resource that limits performance).








NoteConventions Used in These Tutorials




FLOP counting: Both the MLSys Zoo and vendor datasheets count one multiply-accumulate (MAC) as 2 FLOPs (one multiply plus one add). Some academic papers count 1 MAC = 1 FLOP, which halves both model FLOPs and hardware peak FLOP/s. Check which convention a paper uses before comparing raw numbers.
Peak vs. sustained specs: Passing efficiency=1.0 to Engine.solve evaluates the theoretical roofline ceiling using vendor-published peak Tensor Core throughput and peak HBM bandwidth. Real workloads typically sustain 40–70% of peak (Engine.solve defaults to efficiency=0.5 when efficiency is omitted).
Units: Q_ creates physical quantities with units (e.g., Q_("2 TB/s")). The ~ in format strings like :~.2f formats abbreviated unit symbols.

title: Hello, Roofline
text:
1. Setup
After pip install mlsysim, the import is two lines:
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

title: Hello, Roofline
section: 2. Pick a Model and a GPU
text:
2. Pick a Model and a GPU
Pull vetted specifications from the MLSys Zoo instead of searching datasheets.

from mlsysim.show import table, info

model = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
hardware = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100

info("Model",
     Name=f"{model.name} ({model.architecture})",
     Parameters=model.parameters,
     FLOPs_per_inf=model.inference_flops)

info("Hardware",
     Name=hardware.name,
     Peak_FP16=hardware.compute.peak_flops.to('TFLOPs/s'),
     HBM_BW=hardware.memory.bandwidth.to('TB/s'))

── Model ───────────────────────────────────
Name:           ResNet-50 (CNN)
Parameters:     25,557,032 param
FLOPs per inf:  8,200,000,000 flop
── Hardware ────────────────────────────────
Name:       NVIDIA A100
Peak FP16:  312 TFLOPs/s
HBM BW:     2.04 TB/s


In the Zoo, ResNet-50 has 25.6M parameters and 8.2 GFLOP per single-image forward pass, while the NVIDIA A100 provides 312 TFLOP/s of FP16 Tensor Core throughput, 2.04 TB/s (2039 GB/s) of HBM2e bandwidth, and 80 GiB of capacity.

title: Hello, Roofline
text:
3. Solve: One Line, One Answer
The Engine.solve method applies the roofline model. It calculates which of the two speed limits the workload hits first and returns latency, throughput, and the bottleneck classification.

# One line: model + hardware + config → theoretical roofline prediction
profile = Engine.solve(
    model=model,
    hardware=hardware,
    batch_size=1,          # Single image inference
    precision="fp16",      # Half-precision (16-bit floating point)
    efficiency=1.0         # Theoretical roofline ceiling
)

info(Bottleneck=profile.bottleneck,
     Arithmetic_Intensity=f"{profile.arithmetic_intensity.to('flop/byte'):~.1f}",
     Latency=profile.latency.to('ms'),
     Throughput=f"{profile.throughput.to('1/s').magnitude:.0f} images/sec")

Bottleneck:            Memory
Arithmetic Intensity:  145.8 flop / B
Latency:               0.543 ms
Throughput:            1843 images/sec


At batch size 1, ResNet-50 performs 8.2 GFLOP and transfers both model weights (51.1 MB at 2 bytes per parameter) and intermediate activations, yielding an arithmetic intensity of 145.8 FLOP/byte. That sits just below the A100’s theoretical ridge point of 153.0 FLOP/byte, making batch-1 inference memory-bound.
Sanity check: The weight-transfer and compute bounds from the Background equations confirm why the two ceilings are nearly balanced at batch size 1:

\(T_{\text{memory (weights)}} = 51\.1\;\text{MB} \div 2\.04\;\text{TB/s} = 0\.025\;\text{ms}\)
\(T_{\text{compute}} = 8\.2\;\text{GFLOP} \div 312\;\text{TFLOP/s} = 0\.026\;\text{ms}\)
Including activation traffic brings total memory time to \(0\.543\;\text{ms} > T_{\text{compute}}\), placing the operating point just on the memory-bound side of the ridge.

ResNet-50 at batch 1 sits right next to the ridge point. When \(T_{\text{compute}} \approx T_{\text{memory}}\), the operating point is near the boundary between the two regimes.
Computing arithmetic intensity from first principles: This ratio extends the analysis to any model, not only those in the Zoo. The formula is FLOPs ÷ Bytes. Compare two different workloads at batch size 1:

ResNet-50 (batch 1): 8.2 GFLOP across weights and activations = 145.8 FLOP/byte → just below the A100 ridge (153.0 FLOP/byte), near the crossover
LLM decode (batch 1): Each token performs 2 FLOPs per parameter and loads 2 bytes per parameter = 1.0 FLOP/byte → deeply memory-bound (explored in Tutorial 2)

For an unfamiliar model, compute this ratio first. It reveals the regime before any code runs.

title: Hello, Roofline
section: 4. Sweep Batch Size: Watch the Regime Shift
text:
4. Sweep Batch Size: Watch the Regime Shift
Increasing the batch size shows when the bottleneck changes. More images per batch means more computation per weight load, which increases arithmetic intensity past the 153.0 FLOP/byte ridge point.

rows = []
for batch in [1, 4, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]:
    p = Engine.solve(
        model=model,
        hardware=hardware,
        batch_size=batch,
        precision="fp16",
        efficiency=1.0
    )
    rows.append([
        batch,
        p.bottleneck,
        f"{p.arithmetic_intensity.to('flop/byte'):~.1f}",
        f"{p.throughput.to('1/s').magnitude:.0f}/s",
        p.latency.to('ms'),
    ])

table(["Batch", "Bottleneck", "Arithmetic Intensity", "Throughput", "Latency"], rows)

Batch  Bottleneck  Arithmetic Intensity  Throughput   Latency
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1          Memory        145.8 flop / B      1843/s  0.543 ms
4         Compute        458.4 flop / B      6450/s  0.620 ms
16        Compute        987.2 flop / B     17103/s  0.936 ms
32        Compute       1222.3 flop / B     23598/s   1.36 ms
64        Compute       1387.5 flop / B     29130/s   2.20 ms
128       Compute       1488.0 flop / B     32997/s   3.88 ms
256       Compute       1543.9 flop / B     35343/s   7.24 ms


The roofline plot below shows where batch-1 ResNet-50 sits relative to the ridge point (the crossover between memory-bound and compute-bound regimes).

from mlsysim.viz.plots import plot_roofline

# The plot_roofline function takes the hardware node and a list of workloads
fig, ax = plot_roofline(hardware, workloads=[model])














ImportantKey Insight



The roofline model predicts performance without running a single experiment. The answer is determined by two ratios: the workload’s arithmetic intensity and the hardware’s ridge point. Batch size is the primary knob that moves a workload along the roofline. At small batches the workload is memory-bound, and at large batches it is compute-bound. The ridge point is the most efficient operating point. Every optimization decision starts with knowing which side of the ridge the workload is on.








WarningPitfall: Assuming Peak FLOP/s Determines Inference Speed



A common mistake is selecting hardware based on peak FLOP/s alone. LLM decode at batch size 1 performs about 1 FLOP per byte loaded, so it is deeply memory-bound, and the 312 TFLOP/s compute ceiling is irrelevant. A GPU with half the FLOP/s but the same bandwidth would deliver identical decode latency. Always check the regime before comparing specs.

title: Tutorials
text:
These tutorials teach quantitative reasoning about ML infrastructure using MLSys·im, the first-principles analytical modeling framework behind the Machine Learning Systems textbook. They are organized by the six domains of the 22 Systems Walls taxonomy.
Each tutorial answers one question. Start at the beginning for a guided path, or jump to any domain of interest.

title: Tutorials
text:
Start Here
Before starting any domain, complete this introduction to the roofline model.


Beginner

0 · Hello, Roofline
Question: How do I predict whether my model is memory-bound or compute-bound?
Five lines of code give one answer. Every later tutorial builds on it. ⏱ ~10 min
Start Tutorial →

title: Tutorials
text:
Cluster 1: Node (Walls 1–3)
One accelerator, one model. Where is the ceiling?
These tutorials explore the three walls that constrain a single accelerator: compute throughput (Wall 1), memory capacity (Wall 2), and memory bandwidth (Wall 3). Understanding which wall binds, and why, is the most fundamental skill in ML systems reasoning.


Beginner

1 · The Memory Wall
Question: Why does 3.2× more FLOP/s not give a 3.2× speedup?
Compare A100 → H100 and discover that for LLM inference, bandwidth (1.6×), not compute (3.2×), is the binding constraint. The most important fallacy in ML systems. ⏱ ~15 min
Start Tutorial →



Intermediate

2 · Two Phases, One Request
Question: Why is LLM serving fundamentally different from CNN inference?
The same model on the same GPU hits two different ceilings: prefill is compute-bound, decode is memory-bound. This is why LLM serving requires its own analysis. ⏱ ~15 min
Start Tutorial →



Intermediate

3 · KV-Cache: The Hidden Tax
Question: What actually limits how many users I can serve concurrently?
At 128K context length, a single user’s GQA KV-cache takes 17.2 GB (16 GiB), exceeding the model weights and capping an 80 GiB GPU at 4 concurrent users. Explore how sequence length, batch size, and paged attention interact to constrain serving capacity. ⏱ ~20 min
Start Tutorial →

title: Tutorials
text:
Cluster 2: Data (Walls 8–10)
The GPU is fast. Is the pipeline faster?
Even the fastest accelerator sits idle if the data pipeline cannot keep up. These walls cover ingestion (Wall 8), transformation (Wall 9), and storage bandwidth (Wall 10).


Intermediate

4 · Starving the GPU
Question: Why is my GPU utilization only 22%?
A100 compute takes 14.0 ms per step, but the CPU augmentation pipeline requires 64 ms. The binding constraint is JPEG decoding, not silicon. ⏱ ~15 min
Start Tutorial →

title: Tutorials
text:
Cluster 3: Algorithm (Walls 11–13)
Can I make the model smaller or the training cheaper?
These walls govern scaling laws (Wall 11), compression and quantization (Wall 12), and architecture efficiency (Wall 13).


Intermediate

5 · Quantization: Not a Free Lunch
Question: Does INT4 always give 4× speedup?
For memory-bound decode: nearly 4×. For compute-bound training: 0×. The regime determines whether quantization helps, and the roofline identifies which regime applies. ⏱ ~20 min
Start Tutorial →

title: Tutorials
text:
Cluster 4: Fleet (Walls 14–16)
Scaling past one machine. Where does efficiency go?
Distributed training introduces three new walls: communication overhead (Wall 14), synchronization cost (Wall 15), and reliability (Wall 16).


Advanced

6 · Scaling to 1000 GPUs
Question: Where does my training efficiency disappear at scale?
At 1024 GPUs, AllReduce communication overhead erodes scaling efficiency. The real hidden cost, however, is reliability: cluster MTBF drops to 36.6 hours, forcing frequent checkpoints that consume 0.1× more wall-clock time than communication itself. ⏱ ~20 min
Start Tutorial →

title: Tutorials
text:
Cluster 5: Ops (Walls 17–20)
What does it cost, in dollars, carbon, and water?
Operational walls cover energy (Wall 17), sustainability (Wall 18), economic cost (Wall 19), and safety (Wall 20). These are the walls that determine whether a technically feasible system is actually deployable.


Intermediate

7 · Geography is a Systems Variable
Question: Does it matter where I train?
Same 256-GPU cluster, same model, same duration: 167.2 tonnes CO₂ in Poland vs. 2.7 tonnes in Québec (62.0 tonnes US average). A 41× grid carbon-intensity gap (61× with PUE) from geography alone. ⏱ ~15 min
Start Tutorial →



Intermediate

8 · The $9M Question
Question: How much does chain-of-thought reasoning actually cost?
K=8 reasoning steps multiply per-query latency and fleet cost by 6.5×, scaling annual 100-QPS serving TCO from $2.9M to $18.7M for Llama-3.1-70B (and from $70M to $455M for unsharded GPT-4). A seemingly simple algorithmic choice becomes a capital expenditure decision. ⏱ ~20 min
Start Tutorial →

title: Tutorials
text:
Cluster 6: Analysis (Walls 21–22)
Cross-cutting diagnostics. Which knob matters most?
These walls provide the tools for sensitivity analysis (Wall 21) and synthesis (Wall 22): the ability to ask “what if?” and “what must be true?”


Advanced

9 · Where to Invest: Sensitivity Analysis
Question: Should I buy more FLOPS or more bandwidth?
\(\partial \ln T / \partial \ln \text{BW} = \-0\.88\) vs. \(\partial \ln T / \partial \ln \text{FLOPS} = 0\.00\). For Llama-3.1-8B decode on NVIDIA A100, a 10% bandwidth increase cuts latency by 8.8%, while more compute yields 0.0%. Then use inverse Roofline to derive the 2.8 TB / s bandwidth floor from a 50 ms SLA. ⏱ ~20 min
Start Tutorial →



Advanced

10 · GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
Question: Can a fundamentally different architecture change which wall binds?
Cerebras eliminates the HBM memory wall entirely, but the binding constraint shifts to injection bandwidth. The result is a qualitative regime change, not only a speedup. ⏱ ~20 min
Start Tutorial →



Advanced

11 · Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE
Question: What should I check after the roofline says a design is plausible?
Break training memory into components, turn QPS and P99 into a first-pass replica count, and model MoE hot-expert imbalance as a bandwidth sensitivity. ⏱ ~25 min
Start Tutorial →



Advanced

12 · Design Space Exploration
Question: How do I search for the best architecture without writing nested loops?
Learn to use the declarative DSE Engine to navigate complex ML trade-offs and filter configurations based on SLA constraints. ⏱ ~20 min
Start Tutorial →

text:
Cluster 7: Capstone
Compose everything. All 22 walls, one analysis.


Advanced

13 · Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
Question: What does a complete systems analysis look like?
Trace LLaMA-70B training through all six domains: Node → Data → Algorithm → Fleet → Ops → Analysis. Twelve of the 22 walls exercised in one coherent analysis. ⏱ ~30 min
Start Tutorial →

title: Quantization: Not a Free Lunch
text:
INT4 quantization reduces model weight size by 4× (from 16.06 GB in FP16 to 4.02 GB in INT4 for Llama-3.1-8B). Intuitively, 4× fewer bytes should mean 4× faster execution. Does INT4 always give a 4× speedup?
Tutorial 1 already supplies the tools to predict the answer: performance is governed by whichever ceiling binds first. When quantization reduces bytes transferred from HBM without increasing arithmetic throughput, it accelerates memory-bound workloads and leaves compute-bound workloads unchanged.
This tutorial makes the prediction, runs the experiment, and shows that the outcome depends entirely on the operating regime.






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall and Tutorial 2: Two Phases, One Request. This tutorial assumes familiarity with memory-bound vs. compute-bound regimes and why LLM decode is memory-bound.








NoteLearning Objectives




Predict whether quantization will help a given workload based on its regime
Measure the speedup from INT8 and INT4 for both memory-bound and compute-bound workloads
Explain why weight-only INT4 yields 3.4× in one regime and 1.0× in another
Evaluate the accuracy-compression trade-off using CompressionModel









TipBackground: What Quantization Actually Does



Quantization reduces the number of bytes per parameter:









Precision
Bytes/Param
Relative to FP16
Llama-3.1-8B Weights




FP16
2
1.0× (baseline)
16.06 GB


INT8
1
0.5×
8.03 GB


INT4
0.5
0.25×
4.02 GB



For memory-bound workloads, performance scales with bytes loaded from HBM per step. Halving bytes nearly halves latency. For compute-bound workloads, performance scales with FLOP/s. Fewer weight bytes do not change the number of FLOPs, so latency stays the same unless the hardware also provides higher-throughput low-precision Tensor Cores.
The key criterion is always which ceiling the workload is hitting.

title: Quantization: Not a Free Lunch
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel, SingleNodeModel
from mlsysim.solvers import CompressionModel

title: Quantization: Not a Free Lunch
section: 2. Memory-Bound Case: LLM Decode at Batch 1
text:
2. Memory-Bound Case: LLM Decode at Batch 1
LLM decoding at batch 1 is the textbook memory-bound workload. Each token generation must reload the entire model from HBM. Fewer bytes per parameter means fewer bytes to load, and therefore lower inter-token latency:

from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel
from mlsysim.show import table, info

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B
hardware = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100
solver = ServingModel()

rows = []
baseline_itl = None
for prec in ["fp16", "int8", "int4"]:
    r = solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=hardware,
        seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, precision=prec
    )
    itl_ms = r.itl.to("ms").magnitude
    if baseline_itl is None:
        baseline_itl = itl_ms
    speedup = baseline_itl / itl_ms
    rows.append([prec, r.itl.to('ms'), r.model_weights_size, f"{speedup:.1f}x"])

table(["Precision", "ITL", "Weights", "Speedup vs FP16"], rows)

Precision      ITL   Weights  Speedup vs FP16
─────────────────────────────────────────────
fp16       5.19 ms  16.06 GB             1.0x
int8       2.76 ms   8.03 GB             1.9x
int4       1.54 ms   4.02 GB             3.4x


INT8 cuts weights from 16.06 GB to 8.03 GB and lowers ITL from 5.19 ms to 2.76 ms, a 1.9× speedup. INT4 cuts weights to 4.02 GB and lowers ITL to 1.54 ms, a 3.4× speedup. The speedup tracks the byte reduction closely (falling slightly short of 2.0× and 4.0× only because per-layer kernel launch overhead does not shrink with weight precision). Every weight byte removed directly reduces HBM transfer time.

title: Quantization: Not a Free Lunch
text:
3. Compute-Bound Case: Large-Batch Execution
The same optimization behaves differently on a compute-bound workload, ResNet-50 at batch 256 on the NVIDIA A100:

from mlsysim.solvers import SingleNodeModel

train_model = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
train_hw = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
train_solver = SingleNodeModel()

rows = []
baseline_lat = None
for prec in ["fp16", "int8", "int4"]:
    p = train_solver.solve(
        model=train_model, hardware=train_hw,
        batch_size=256, precision=prec
    )
    lat_ms = p.latency.to("ms").magnitude
    if baseline_lat is None:
        baseline_lat = lat_ms
    speedup = baseline_lat / lat_ms if lat_ms > 0 else 0
    rows.append([prec, p.latency.to('ms'), f"{p.throughput.magnitude:.0f} img/s", f"{speedup:.1f}x"])

table(["Precision", "Latency", "Throughput", "Speedup"], rows)

Precision   Latency   Throughput  Speedup
─────────────────────────────────────────
fp16       13.97 ms  18323 img/s     1.0x
int8        7.24 ms  35343 img/s     1.9x
int4       13.97 ms  18323 img/s     1.0x


At batch 256, ResNet-50 on the NVIDIA A100 is compute-bound: weight-only INT4 (13.97 ms, 18,323 img/s) delivers 1.0× speedup relative to FP16 (13.97 ms, 18,323 img/s). Because the A100 lacks native INT4 Tensor Cores in the Zoo, weight-only INT4 dequantizes weights to FP16 in registers and executes at the 312 TFLOP/s FP16 compute ceiling; shrinking weight traffic by 4× does nothing when arithmetic is the bottleneck. By contrast, INT8 reaches 7.24 ms (1.9× speedup) only because the A100 provides dedicated INT8 Tensor Cores at 624 TFLOP/s (2× the FP16 compute peak).






WarningNuance: INT8 Tensor Cores vs. Weight-Only INT4



GPUs with dedicated INT8 Tensor Cores (such as the A100 at 624 TFLOP/s INT8 vs. 312 TFLOP/s FP16, a 2× compute boost) raise both the memory ceiling (fewer bytes) and the compute ceiling (more INT ops/sec) when activations and weights are quantized together (W8A8). Weight-only INT4 (W4A16), by contrast, reduces HBM weight traffic by 4× while keeping arithmetic on FP16 Tensor Cores, so it accelerates memory-bound decode (3.4×) while leaving compute-bound steps unchanged (1.0×).

title: Quantization: Not a Free Lunch
section: 4. The Reveal: Same Optimization, Two Regimes
text:
4. The Reveal: Same Optimization, Two Regimes
Placing the results side by side makes the contrast stark:

rows = []

# Memory-bound: LLM decode
decode_row = ["Llama-3 8B decode"]
for prec in ["fp16", "int8", "int4"]:
    r = solver.solve(model=model, hardware=hardware, seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, precision=prec)
    decode_row.append(r.itl.to('ms'))
decode_row.append("Memory-bound")
rows.append(decode_row)

# Compute-bound: large-batch CNN execution
train_row = ["ResNet-50 bs=256"]
for prec in ["fp16", "int8", "int4"]:
    p = train_solver.solve(model=train_model, hardware=train_hw, batch_size=256, precision=prec)
    train_row.append(p.latency.to('ms'))
train_row.append("Compute-bound")
rows.append(train_row)

table(["Workload", "FP16", "INT8", "INT4", "Regime"], rows)

Workload               FP16     INT8      INT4         Regime
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Llama-3 8B decode   5.19 ms  2.76 ms   1.54 ms   Memory-bound
ResNet-50 bs=256   13.97 ms  7.24 ms  13.97 ms  Compute-bound








ImportantKey Insight



Weight-only quantization reduces bytes loaded from memory. For a memory-bound workload, fewer bytes mean proportional speedup. For a compute-bound workload, fewer bytes alone mean no speedup, because compute, not memory, is the ceiling. The regime determines whether byte reduction works: INT4 lowers Llama-3.1-8B decode latency from 5.19 ms to 1.54 ms (3.4× speedup, memory-bound) yet leaves ResNet-50 at batch 256 at 13.97 ms (1.0×, compute-bound). Always check the regime before choosing an optimization.

title: Quantization: Not a Free Lunch
text:
5. The Accuracy Tax: CompressionModel
Quantization is not free; it trades accuracy for speed and memory capacity. The CompressionModel quantifies this trade-off relative to an FP32 baseline:

from mlsysim.solvers import CompressionModel

comp_solver = CompressionModel()

rows = []
for bits in [16, 8, 4]:
    c = comp_solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=hardware,
        method="quantization", target_bitwidth=bits
    )
    rows.append([
        bits,
        c.compressed_size_gb,
        f"{c.compression_ratio:.1f}x",
        f"{c.estimated_accuracy_delta:+.1%}",
        f"{c.memory_savings_pct:.1f}%"
    ])

table(["Bits", "Compressed", "Compression", "Accuracy", "Savings"], rows)

Bits  Compressed  Compression  Accuracy  Savings
────────────────────────────────────────────────
16      16.06 GB         2.0x     +0.0%    50.0%
8        8.03 GB         4.0x     -0.2%    75.0%
4        4.02 GB         8.0x     -2.5%    87.5%


Relative to FP32, 8-bit quantization shrinks Llama-3.1-8B to 8.03 GB (4.0× compression, 75.0% memory savings) with an estimated accuracy change of -0.2%. Going to 4-bit shrinks weights to 4.02 GB (8.0× compression, 87.5% savings) with an estimated accuracy change of -2.5%. The decision is not “always quantize” but “quantize when the workload is memory-bound AND the accuracy cost is acceptable for the application.”






WarningWhen NOT to Quantize




Training: Training is compute-bound at large batch sizes. Weight-only quantization does not help and low-precision gradients can harm convergence.
High-accuracy applications: Medical, financial, and safety-critical systems may not tolerate even a 0.2% to 2.5% accuracy loss.
Already compute-bound inference: An inference workload that runs at large batch sizes (e.g., offline batch processing) is already compute-bound unless hardware supports faster low-precision arithmetic.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
A team has Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters) and a budget for 1024 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Communication overhead (AllReduce, pipeline bubbles) will consume some of the scaling efficiency, as every distributed-training engineer expects. How do communication overhead and cluster reliability evolve as the fleet scales from 8 to 1024 GPUs over a 30-day training run?






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 0: Hello, Roofline and Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall. This tutorial assumes familiarity with memory-bound vs. compute-bound regimes and the roofline model.








NoteLearning Objectives




Calculate scaling efficiency across GPU counts from 8 to 1024
Predict cluster Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) using the reliability model
Compare communication overhead vs. checkpoint overhead over a 30-day training run
Explain how checkpoint I/O and failure rollbacks scale with cluster size









TipBackground: Cluster Reliability and the Young-Daly Formula



At scale, hardware failures are not rare events; they are routine. In the MLSys Zoo, a single GPU has a Mean Time To Failure (MTTF) of 50,000 hours, a NIC has an MTTF of 150,000 hours, and a PSU has an MTTF of 100,000 hours. A cluster of \(N\) GPUs alone has a collective MTBF of \(\text{MTTF} / N\) (97.7 hours at 512 GPUs). Including all node components (8 GPUs, 8 NICs, and 0 non-redundant PSUs per DGX H100 node) lowers the cluster MTBF to 73.2 hours at 512 GPUs and 36.6 hours at 1024 GPUs.
To survive failures, training jobs checkpoint periodically: save the full model state (weights + optimizer) to storage. The Young-Daly formula gives the optimal checkpoint interval that minimizes total wasted time:
\[T_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot \delta \cdot M}\]
where \(\delta\) is the time to write one checkpoint and \(M\) is the cluster MTBF. This assumes failures arrive as a Poisson process (exponentially distributed inter-arrival times) and that on failure, work since the last checkpoint is lost (on average, half the checkpoint interval). The cost of checkpointing is therefore not only the write time but also this rollback time.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
2. Single-Node Baseline
The simplest case is 8 GPUs in a single DGX H100 node (450 GB/s intra-node NVLink per direction), with no cross-node data-parallel traffic. This configuration sets the ceiling for scaling efficiency.

from mlsysim import Models, Systems
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet, Node, NetworkFabric
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
from mlsysim.show import table, info

model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
solver = DistributedModel()

# Single DGX H100 node: 8 GPUs, NVLink interconnect
single_node = Fleet(
    name="Single Node",
    node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
    count=1,
    fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
)

baseline = solver.solve(
    model=model, fleet=single_node,
    batch_size=64, precision="fp16", tp_size=8, pp_size=1
)

info("Single-Node Baseline",
     GPUs=single_node.total_accelerators,
     Compute_latency=baseline.node_profile.latency.to('ms'),
     Communication=baseline.communication_latency.to('ms'),
     Scaling_efficiency=f"{baseline.scaling_efficiency:.1%}")

── Single-Node Baseline ────────────────────
GPUs:                8
Compute latency:     14,037.3 ms
Communication:       2,674.7 ms
Scaling efficiency:  84.0%


With 8 GPUs on a single node at batch size 64, compute takes 14,037.3 ms and intra-node tensor-parallel AllReduce over NVLink takes 2,674.7 ms, yielding a baseline scaling efficiency of 84.0%.
This tutorial uses the three dimensions of 3D parallelism:

TP (Tensor Parallelism) = 8: splits each layer’s weight matrices across 8 GPUs within a node, communicating via NVLink (450 GB/s)
PP (Pipeline Parallelism) = 1: no pipeline stages (the model is not split across sequential stages), so no pipeline bubbles
DP (Data Parallelism) = \(N / 8\): each node processes different data batches, synchronizing gradients via AllReduce over IB NDR (400 Gbps)

Setting PP=1 isolates the communication vs. reliability comparison cleanly. Real production systems often use PP > 1 for models too large to fit on one node with TP alone, which introduces pipeline bubble overhead (idle time proportional to \(1/\text{PP}\) stages).

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
3. Scale Sweep: 8 to 1024 GPUs
The sweep below covers cluster sizes from 8 to 1024 GPUs. At each scale, it measures communication overhead (intra-node TP AllReduce plus inter-node DP AllReduce) and scaling efficiency.

gpu_counts = [8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024]

rows = []
results = {}
for n_gpus in gpu_counts:
    n_nodes = n_gpus // 8
    fleet = Fleet(
        name=f"{n_gpus}-GPU Cluster",
        node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
        count=n_nodes,
        fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
    )
    # Use TP=8 within node, DP across nodes
    r = solver.solve(
        model=model, fleet=fleet,
        batch_size=max(64, n_gpus),
        precision="fp16", tp_size=8, pp_size=1
    )
    results[n_gpus] = r
    rows.append([
        n_gpus, n_nodes,
        f"{r.communication_latency.to('ms').magnitude:.1f}",
        f"{r.pipeline_bubble_latency.to('ms').magnitude:.1f}",
        f"{r.scaling_efficiency:.1%}"
    ])

table(["GPUs", "Nodes", "Comm (ms)", "Bubble (ms)", "Efficiency"], rows)

GPUs  Nodes  Comm (ms)  Bubble (ms)  Efficiency
───────────────────────────────────────────────
8         1     2674.7          0.0       84.0%
32        4     1199.9          0.0       74.5%
64        8      954.1          0.0       64.8%
128      16      998.3          0.0       63.8%
256      32     1020.5          0.0       63.3%
512      64     1031.9          0.0       63.0%
1024    128     1038.0          0.0       62.9%


Once the global batch scales linearly with GPU count from 64 GPUs (954.1 ms AllReduce, 64.8% scaling efficiency) to 1024 GPUs (1,038.0 ms AllReduce, 62.9% scaling efficiency), ring AllReduce bandwidth utilization stabilizes and scaling efficiency degrades gradually. This is Amdahl’s Law in action: if the serial fraction (communication) is \(f\), the maximum speedup at \(N\) GPUs is \(1 / (f + (1-f)/N)\).
This communication analysis, however, assumes that every node stays healthy for the entire 30-day training run. Communication is not the whole story.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
4. The Reliability Reveal
A separate question is how often a 64-GPU, 512-GPU, or 1024-GPU cluster experiences a hardware failure. The ReliabilityModel computes cluster-level MTBF, expected failures, optimal checkpoint intervals, and steady-state goodput.

from mlsysim.solvers import ReliabilityModel

rel_solver = ReliabilityModel()

rows = []
rel_results = {}
for n_gpus in gpu_counts:
    n_nodes = n_gpus // 8
    fleet = Fleet(
        name=f"{n_gpus}-GPU",
        node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
        count=n_nodes,
        fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
    )
    # 30-day training run, 60-second checkpoint write time
    r = rel_solver.solve(fleet=fleet, job_duration_hours=30*24, checkpoint_time_s=60.0)
    rel_results[n_gpus] = r
    mtbf_h = r.fleet_mtbf.to("hour").magnitude
    rows.append([
        n_gpus, n_nodes,
        f"{mtbf_h:.1f} h",
        f"{r.expected_failures:.1f}",
        f"{r.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('hour').magnitude:.1f} h",
        f"{r.goodput_ratio:.1%}"
    ])

table(["GPUs", "Nodes", "Cluster MTBF", "Failures/30d", "Optimal Ckpt", "Goodput"], rows)

GPUs  Nodes  Cluster MTBF  Failures/30d  Optimal Ckpt  Goodput
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8         1      4687.5 h           0.2        12.5 h    99.9%
32        4      1171.9 h           0.6         6.2 h    99.7%
64        8       585.9 h           1.2         4.4 h    99.6%
128      16       293.0 h           2.5         3.1 h    99.4%
256      32       146.5 h           4.9         2.2 h    99.2%
512      64        73.2 h           9.8         1.6 h    98.8%
1024    128        36.6 h          19.7         1.1 h    98.3%


At 64 GPUs, the cluster MTBF is 585.9 h (1.2 expected failures over 30 days, 4.4 h optimal checkpoint interval, 99.6% steady-state goodput). At 512 GPUs, the cluster MTBF drops to 73.2 h (9.8 failures over 30 days, 1.6 h optimal checkpoint interval, 98.8% goodput). At 1024 GPUs, MTBF reaches 36.6 h, with 19.7 expected failures in 30 days, an optimal checkpoint interval of 1.1 h, and 98.3% steady-state goodput. Every checkpoint pauses training, and every failure rolls back to the last checkpoint, discarding all work in between.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
section: 5. The Hidden Cost: Communication vs. Checkpoints
text:
5. The Hidden Cost: Communication vs. Checkpoints
The comparison below tracks how total time lost over a 30-day (720-hour) training run evolves across cluster sizes for both unoverlapped communication overhead and synchronous checkpoint plus rollback overhead.

from mlsysim.solvers import CheckpointModel

ckpt_solver = CheckpointModel()
job_hours = 30 * 24  # 30 days

rows = []
for n_gpus in [64, 256, 512, 1024]:
    dist_r = results[n_gpus]
    rel_r = rel_results[n_gpus]

    # Communication overhead per step as fraction of step time
    comm_fraction = 1.0 - dist_r.scaling_efficiency
    comm_loss_hours = comm_fraction * job_hours

    # Checkpoint overhead: write time per checkpoint + rollback from failures
    ckpt_r = ckpt_solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerator,
        optimizer="adam", checkpoint_interval_hours=rel_r.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to("hour").magnitude
    )
    ckpt_write_s = ckpt_r.write_time_seconds.to("second").magnitude
    ckpt_interval_h = rel_r.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to("hour").magnitude

    # Number of checkpoints in 30 days
    n_checkpoints = job_hours / ckpt_interval_h if ckpt_interval_h > 0 else 0
    total_ckpt_write_h = n_checkpoints * ckpt_write_s / 3600

    # Rollback cost: each failure loses ~half the checkpoint interval on average
    avg_rollback_h = ckpt_interval_h / 2
    total_rollback_h = rel_r.expected_failures * avg_rollback_h

    total_ckpt_loss_h = total_ckpt_write_h + total_rollback_h
    ratio = total_ckpt_loss_h / comm_loss_hours if comm_loss_hours > 0 else 0

    rows.append([n_gpus, f"{comm_loss_hours:.1f}", f"{total_ckpt_loss_h:.1f}", f"{ratio:.2f}x"])

table(["GPUs", "Comm Loss (h)", "Ckpt Loss (h)", "Ckpt/Comm"], rows)

GPUs  Comm Loss (h)  Ckpt Loss (h)  Ckpt/Comm
─────────────────────────────────────────────
64            253.4            9.1      0.04x
256           264.6           18.2      0.07x
512           266.4           25.8      0.10x
1024          267.4           36.4      0.14x








ImportantKey Insight



While ring AllReduce overhead plateaus with cluster size, reliability overhead grows as \(\sqrt{N}\). Between 64 and 1024 GPUs, unoverlapped communication loss changes by only 5.5% (from 253.4 h to 267.4 h over 720 hours), whereas synchronous checkpoint I/O and failure rollback losses grow 4.0× (from 9.1 h at 64 GPUs to 36.4 h at 1024 GPUs, or 14% of the unoverlapped communication loss). When DP communication is overlapped with backward computation, checkpoint I/O and failure recovery become the primary scaling bottleneck.

title: Scaling to 1000 GPUs
text:
6. The Checkpoint Size Problem
Checkpoint overhead is costly because modern models produce large checkpoint files. The cell below computes the checkpoint size for Llama-3.1-70B with the Adam optimizer:

ckpt_result = ckpt_solver.solve(
    model=model,
    hardware=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerator,
    optimizer="adam",
    checkpoint_interval_hours=1.0
)

info("Checkpoint Analysis",
     Model=model.name,
     Checkpoint_size=ckpt_result.checkpoint_size.to('GB'),
     Write_time=ckpt_result.write_time_seconds.to('second'),
     MFU_penalty_1h=f"{ckpt_result.mfu_penalty_pct:.2%}",
     Storage_bottleneck=ckpt_result.storage_bottleneck)

── Checkpoint Analysis ─────────────────────
Model:               Llama-3.1-70B
Checkpoint size:     988.4 GB
Write time:          141.2 s
MFU penalty 1h:      3.92%
Storage bottleneck:  True


A single mixed-precision Adam checkpoint for Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters at 14 bytes per parameter) is 988.4 GB and requires 141.2 s of synchronous storage write time. At a 1-hour interval, checkpoint I/O alone imposes a 3.92% MFU penalty.

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
A 256-GPU cluster (32 DGX H100 nodes) trains a model for 30 days. Where that cluster is located makes no difference to latency or throughput, which the hardware fixes. For carbon emissions, water usage, and total cost of ownership, does geography matter, and if so, by how much?

Quantify the gap between the cleanest and dirtiest electricity grids

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
2. Two-Region Comparison
The first comparison runs the same training job in two locations: Quebec (Hydro) (20 gCO2/kWh, PUE 1.06) and Poland (Coal) (820 gCO2/kWh, PUE 1.58). The 256-GPU fleet, the model, and the 30-day duration are identical. The only variable is where the electricity comes from.

from mlsysim import Systems
from mlsysim.solvers import SustainabilityModel
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet, Node, NetworkFabric
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
from mlsysim.show import table, info

# 256-GPU cluster: 32 DGX H100 nodes
fleet = Fleet(
    name="256-GPU Training Cluster",
    node=Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100,
    count=32,
    fabric=Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
)

solver = SustainabilityModel()

# Quebec: hydroelectric grid
res_quebec = solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet, duration_days=30,
    datacenter=mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec
)

# Poland: coal-heavy grid
res_poland = solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet, duration_days=30,
    datacenter=mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland
)

carbon_q = res_quebec.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude  # tonnes
carbon_p = res_poland.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude
ratio = carbon_p / carbon_q if carbon_q > 0 else 0

table(
    ["Region", "Carbon (tonnes CO2)"],
    [
        ["Quebec (Hydro)", f"{carbon_q:.1f}"],
        ["Poland (Coal)", f"{carbon_p:.1f}"],
    ]
)
info(Ratio=f"{ratio:.0f}x")

Region          Carbon (tonnes CO2)
───────────────────────────────────
Quebec (Hydro)                  2.7
Poland (Coal)                 167.2
Ratio:  61x


Same cluster. Same model. Same 30-day duration. Because Poland’s grid carbon intensity is 41× higher than Quebec’s (820 vs. 20 gCO2/kWh) and its facility PUE is 1.49× higher (1.58 vs. 1.06), the total carbon footprint differs by 61× (167.2 tonnes vs. 2.7 tonnes \(\text{CO}_2\)). The difference comes from a location decision, not from an algorithmic optimization.

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
3. All-Region Sweep
The next sweep expands the comparison to four grid regions in the Infrastructure Zoo, adding energy consumption, water usage, and PUE to the picture.

grids = [
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec,
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Norway,
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg,
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland,
]

region_results = {}
rows = []
for grid in grids:
    r = solver.solve(fleet=fleet, duration_days=30, datacenter=grid)
    energy_mwh = r.total_energy_kwh.magnitude / 1000
    carbon_t = r.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude
    water_kl = r.water_usage_liters / 1000
    region_results[r.region_name] = r
    rows.append([r.region_name, f"{energy_mwh:,.1f}", f"{carbon_t:,.1f}", f"{water_kl:,.1f}", f"{r.pue:.2f}"])

table(["Region", "Energy (MWh)", "Carbon (t)", "Water (kL)", "PUE"], rows)

Region          Energy (MWh)  Carbon (t)  Water (kL)   PUE
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Quebec (Hydro)         136.8         2.7         0.0  1.06
Norway (Hydro)         136.8         1.4         0.0  1.06
US Average             144.5        62.0       260.1  1.12
Poland (Coal)          203.9       167.2       366.9  1.58


Total facility energy varies across regions from 136.8 MWh in Quebec (Hydro) and Norway (Hydro) (PUE 1.06) to 203.9 MWh in Poland (Coal) (PUE 1.58). Water consumption ranges from 0.0 kL in closed-loop cold-climate hydro facilities to 260.1 kL (US Average) and 366.9 kL (Poland (Coal)). Combined with grid carbon intensity, emissions span 1.4 t in Norway (Hydro) and 2.7 t in Quebec (Hydro) up to 167.2 t in Poland (Coal) (61× vs. Quebec and 122× vs. Norway).

title: Geography is a Systems Variable
text:
4. Geography vs. Training Duration
The trade-off between training longer in a clean region and shorter in a dirty region shows up in a comparison of 30 days in Quebec (Hydro) against 10 days in Poland (Coal).

# 30 days in Quebec
res_30d_quebec = solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet, duration_days=30,
    datacenter=mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec
)

# 10 days in Poland (1/3 the training time)
res_10d_poland = solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet, duration_days=10,
    datacenter=mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland
)

c_q = res_30d_quebec.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude
c_p = res_10d_poland.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude

table(
    ["Scenario", "Carbon (tonnes CO2)"],
    [
        ["30 days in Quebec", f"{c_q:.1f}"],
        ["10 days in Poland", f"{c_p:.1f}"],
    ]
)
info(Ratio=f"{c_p/c_q:.1f}x")

Scenario           Carbon (tonnes CO2)
──────────────────────────────────────
30 days in Quebec                  2.7
10 days in Poland                 55.7
Ratio:  20.4x








ImportantKey Insight



Geography is a larger lever than training duration for carbon footprint. Even training for one-third the time (10 days vs. 30 days) in Poland (Coal) emits 55.7 tonnes of \(\text{CO}_2\), which is 20.4× more than the full 30-day run in Quebec (Hydro) (2.7 tonnes). Because grid carbon intensity differs by 41× and total facility emissions per day differ by 61×, no plausible reduction in training time can compensate for a coal-heavy grid. For any organization serious about sustainable AI, datacenter location is not a logistics detail but a first-order systems design decision.
