title: The 22 Laws of ML Systems in Plain English
text: Every equation in mlsysim answers one question. Here is what each one says, why it matters, and how to explain it to anyone in 30 seconds.

title: The 22 Laws of ML Systems in Plain English
section: Domain 1: Node—What One Chip Can Do
text:
Domain 1: Node—What One Chip Can Do

Wall 1: The Compute Wall
Equation: Time = Operations / (Peak_FLOPS × Efficiency)
Plain English: The compute wall sets how long the math takes. Divide the total number of multiply-adds a model needs by how fast the chip can do math (adjusted for real-world inefficiency), and the result is the compute time.
30-second version: “If a 8B-parameter model needs 16 billion operations and the GPU can do 989 trillion per second at 50% efficiency, the math takes 0.03 milliseconds.”
Why it matters: This is the speed limit for any workload. No software optimization can make a model run faster than the hardware can crunch numbers.



Wall 2: The Memory Wall
Equation: Time = Weight_Bytes / Memory_Bandwidth
Plain English: The memory wall sets how long it takes to load the model from memory. A model’s weights sit in HBM (the GPU’s memory). To use them, the GPU must read them through a pipe with a fixed width (bandwidth). Bigger model = longer loading time.
30-second version: “A 16 GB model on a GPU with 3.35 TB/s bandwidth takes 4.8 ms to load the weights, before any computation starts.”
Why it matters: For most LLM inference at batch size 1, this is the bottleneck. The GPU finishes the math long before it finishes reading the weights (the ridge point is 153 FLOP/byte on an A100 at 312 TFLOP/s and 2.04 TB/s, and 295 FLOP/byte on an H100 at 989 TFLOP/s and 3.35 TB/s). This is why memory bandwidth matters more than FLOPS for serving chatbots.



Wall 3: The Software Wall
Equation: MFU = Achieved_FLOPS / Peak_FLOPS
Plain English: MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) measures how much of the chip’s power a workload actually uses: the gap between what the hardware could do and what the software actually achieves. Low MFU means wasted silicon.
30-second version: “If a GPU can do 989 TFLOP/s but training only achieves 450 TFLOP/s, the MFU is 45%. The other 55% is lost to kernel launches, memory stalls, and framework overhead.”
Why it matters: A 50% MFU means paying for twice the hardware actually in use. Improving MFU is often cheaper than buying more GPUs.



Wall 4: The Serving Wall
Equation: TTFT = Prefill_FLOPs / Peak; ITL = Weights / Bandwidth
Plain English: LLM serving has two phases with completely different bottlenecks. Prefill (processing the prompt) is compute-bound, because it does a large amount of math. Decode (generating each token) is memory-bound, because it loads the weights again for every single token. These two phases need different optimizations.
30-second version: “Prefill is like reading a book fast (compute-intensive). Decode is like looking up one word at a time in a dictionary (memory-intensive). That is why the first token takes 50 ms but each subsequent token takes 5 ms.”



Wall 5: The Batching Wall
Equation: KV_cache = 2 × Layers × Heads × Dim × SeqLen × Batch × BytesPerElem
Plain English: Each active request in an LLM server needs its own “memory” of the conversation (the KV cache). This memory grows with sequence length and eats into the GPU’s finite HBM. More concurrent requests = more KV cache = less room for new requests.
30-second version: “Each Llama-3-8B request at 4K context needs 537 MB (512 MiB) of KV cache. An 80 GiB GPU can only serve 130 concurrent requests before running out of memory.”



Wall 6: The Streaming Wall
Equation: Time_per_layer = max(Weight_Injection_Time, Compute_Time)
Plain English: Wafer-scale chips (like Cerebras) flip the normal GPU bottleneck. Instead of weights sitting in memory and being read by compute, weights are streamed from external memory nodes while activations live on-chip in SRAM. The bottleneck shifts from memory bandwidth to the injection interconnect speed.



Wall 7: The Tail Latency Wall
Equation: Erlang C queueing model (M/M/c)
Plain English: When servers are busy, new requests have to wait in line. The waiting time grows non-linearly. At 80% load, the P99 latency might be 2x the average; at 95% load, it can be 10x. This is why servers cannot run at 100%: the tail latency destroys the SLA.
30-second version: “It is like a highway. At 70% capacity, traffic flows. At 95% capacity, everyone is stuck. Servers work the same way.”

title: The 22 Laws of ML Systems in Plain English
section: Domain 2: Data—Whether Storage Can Feed the Pipeline
text:
Domain 2: Data—Whether Storage Can Feed the Pipeline

Wall 8: The Ingestion Wall
Equation: Utilization = Data_Demand / Storage_Supply
Plain English: Storage has to deliver data as fast as the GPU consumes it. If the GPU consumes data faster than the disk can supply it, the GPU sits idle waiting for input. This ratio shows whether the data pipeline is the bottleneck.



Wall 9: The Transformation Wall
Equation: Time = Batch × Sequence / CPU_Throughput
Plain English: Before data reaches the GPU, CPUs must decode images, tokenize text, and apply augmentations. If these CPU operations cannot keep up with GPU consumption, the GPU starves. This is why training pipelines often need 10-100x more CPU cores than one might expect.



Wall 10: The Locality Wall
Equation: Effective_BW = Link_BW × Bisection_Fraction / Oversubscription
Plain English: Not all network bandwidth is created equal. A fat-tree network gives full bisection bandwidth (any node can talk to any other at full speed). A ring or torus does not, because distant nodes communicate through intermediate hops, which reduces effective bandwidth. The topology determines how much of the raw link speed collective communication actually gets.

title: The 22 Laws of ML Systems in Plain English
section: Domain 3: Algorithm—How Much Compute a Model Needs
text:
Domain 3: Algorithm—How Much Compute a Model Needs

Wall 11: The Complexity Wall (Chinchilla Scaling)
Equation: Compute = 6 × Parameters × Tokens; Optimal_Params = √(Budget/120)
Plain English: For a fixed compute budget, model size and training data must be balanced. The Chinchilla scaling law says that, for a fixed compute budget, the optimal model size is proportional to the square root of the budget, and training should use 20 tokens per parameter. Train a too-big model on too-little data = waste. Train a too-small model on too-much data = also waste.
30-second version: “With $10M of compute, the right choice is a ~90B parameter model trained on ~1.8T tokens. Going bigger without more data wastes money.”



Wall 12: The Reasoning Wall [Emerging]
Equation: Time = Steps × Time_per_Step
Plain English: Chain-of-thought reasoning makes models think longer before answering. Each reasoning step costs compute. More steps = better answers but higher cost. This is inference-time scaling: spending more compute at serving time instead of training time.



Wall 13: The Fidelity Wall (Compression)
Equation: Compression = baseline_bits/bits (quantization); Compression = 1/(1-sparsity) (pruning)
Plain English: A model shrinks when it uses fewer bits than a baseline precision (quantization: FP32→INT8 = 4x smaller; FP16→INT4 = 4x for an LLM served from FP16/BF16 weights) or when weights are removed (pruning: 50% sparse = 2x smaller). CompressionModel measures against a configurable baseline_precision that defaults to "fp32"; pass "fp16" for FP16/BF16-served models, or INT4 reads as 8x instead of 4x. Shrinking, however, costs accuracy, and the question is always how much accuracy the application can afford to lose.
Key insight: Storage shrinks for all compression, but inference speedup depends on the method. Unstructured pruning saves storage but gives zero speedup on GPU GEMM. Only structured pruning and N:M sparsity accelerate actual hardware execution.

title: The 22 Laws of ML Systems in Plain English
text:
Domain 4: Fleet—What Happens at Scale

Wall 14: The Communication Wall (AllReduce)
Equation: Time = 2(N-1)/N × Message/Bandwidth + 2(N-1) × Latency
Plain English: Distributed training means every GPU must share its gradients with every other GPU after each training step. This “AllReduce” operation moves data through the network. The time depends on how much data (gradient size) and how fast the network (bandwidth). As more GPUs are added, the communication cost grows, eventually dominating over the compute savings.
30-second version: “1 GB of gradients across 8 GPUs at 50 GB/s NVLink takes 35 ms. That is time the GPUs spend waiting instead of computing.”



Wall 15: The Fragility Wall (Reliability)
Equation: Cluster_MTBF = Component_MTBF / N_components
Plain English: If one GPU fails every 50,000 hours, a 1000-GPU cluster has a failure every 50 hours. At 10,000 GPUs, a failure arrives every 5 hours. This is why large training runs need checkpointing; without it, a single GPU failure wastes days of compute.
30-second version: “At 1000 GPUs, something breaks every 2 days. At 100,000 GPUs, something breaks every 30 minutes.”



Wall 16: The Multi-tenant Wall (Queueing)
Equation: Wait_Time = Utilization / [2 × Service_Rate × (1 - Utilization)]
Plain English: When multiple teams share a cluster, jobs wait in line. The wait time grows non-linearly with cluster load. At 80% cluster load, the average wait is 2x the job duration. This is why shared research clusters feel slow even when they are “only” 80% busy.

title: The 22 Laws of ML Systems in Plain English
text:
Domain 5: Operations—What It Costs

Wall 17: The Capital Wall (TCO)
Equation: TCO = CapEx + OpEx_energy + OpEx_maintenance
Plain English: The total cost of running ML infrastructure is hardware purchase (CapEx, amortized over 3-5 years) plus electricity plus maintenance. A 1024-GPU H100 cluster costs ~$31M in hardware. Electricity is a small share (~8% of total). The dominant cost lever is occupancy, because idle GPUs cost the same as busy ones.



Wall 18: The Sustainability Wall
Equation: Carbon = Energy × PUE × Carbon_Intensity
Plain English: Every GPU-hour converts electricity into carbon emissions. How much depends on three things: how much energy (determined by power and time), how efficiently the datacenter uses it (PUE, where a 1.4 PUE wastes 40% on cooling), and how dirty the grid is (Quebec hydro = 20 gCO₂/kWh and France nuclear = 50 gCO₂/kWh vs Iowa coal/gas = 680 gCO₂/kWh and Poland coal = 820 gCO₂/kWh).
30-second version: “Training the same model in Quebec produces 41x less carbon than training it in Poland (and 34x less than in Iowa). Geography is the biggest lever for sustainable AI.”



Wall 19: The Checkpoint Wall
Equation: MFU_penalty = Write_Time / Checkpoint_Interval
Plain English: Long training runs must periodically save their state to disk in case of failure. This I/O burst interrupts training and reduces effective throughput. The optimal checkpoint frequency balances the cost of saving too often (I/O overhead) against the cost of saving too rarely (wasted compute when failures hit).



Wall 20: The Safety Wall (Privacy)
Equation: Slowdown ∝ 1/ε (DP-SGD)
Plain English: Training with differential privacy (adding noise to protect individual data points) makes training slower. Stronger privacy guarantees (smaller ε) mean more noise, which means more training steps to converge. Privacy is not free; it costs extra compute.

title: The 22 Laws of ML Systems in Plain English
text:
Domain 6: Meta-Analysis—Cross-Cutting Tools

Wall 21: Sensitivity Analysis
Equation: ∂Time/∂parameter (partial derivatives)
Plain English: Sensitivity analysis finds which constraint is actually binding. It perturbs each parameter (bandwidth, FLOPS, network speed) by a small amount and measures how much the total time changes. The parameter with the largest derivative is the bottleneck, and that is where to invest next.



Wall 22: Synthesis (Inverse Roofline)
Equation: Required_BW = Weights / Target_Latency
Plain English: Synthesis starts from a latency target (e.g., “50 ms per token”) and derives the hardware specs needed to meet it. This flips the Roofline model backwards: instead of predicting performance from hardware, it derives the minimum hardware specs from a performance requirement.
30-second version: “A 50 ms decode latency for a 141.2 GB model (70.6B parameters in FP16) requires at least 2.82 TB/s of memory bandwidth. That is more than one A100 provides (2.04 TB/s). One H100 has the bandwidth (3.35 TB/s) but only 80 GiB of memory, so the 141.2 GB model needs tensor parallelism across two H100s.”

title: The 22 Laws of ML Systems in Plain English
text:
The Iron Law (The Master Equation)
Equation: Time = FLOPs / (N × Peak × MFU × η_scaling × Goodput)
Plain English: This one equation governs all of ML systems. Training time equals the total compute divided by how much useful compute the system can actually deliver. Each term in the denominator represents a different loss:








Term
What it means
What reduces it




N
Number of devices
Budget


Peak
Raw hardware speed
GPU generation


MFU
Software efficiency
Kernel optimization, FlashAttention


η_scaling
Communication overhead
Network bandwidth, gradient compression


Goodput
Time lost to failures
Checkpointing, fault tolerance



Every wall in the taxonomy maps to one of these five terms, and together they make up the framework.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text: MLSys·im avoids “black box” heuristics. Every output traces back to one of the equations below. Read this page before the code to understand what the solvers compute and why.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
1. The Roofline Model (Single-Node Performance)
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.SingleNodeModel. Slide Deck: Hardware Acceleration (Vol I, Ch 11)






Intuition: Hardware has two speed limits: how fast it can compute (FLOP/s) and how fast it can feed data to the compute units (bytes/s). Actual throughput is set by whichever limit is reached first. This is why we take the maximum of two terms, not their sum.




1.1 Latency Equation
\[
T = \max \left( \underbrace{\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \eta}}_{\text{compute time}},\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{Bytes}}{\text{Memory\_BW}}}_{\text{memory time}} \right) + \text{Dispatch\_Tax}
\]



Symbol
Meaning
Typical Range




\(\eta\)
Achieved compute efficiency
0.25–0.55 (training); ~0.35 (inference). See Accuracy & Validation.


Dispatch_Tax
Kernel-launch overhead (CUDA, driver)
0.01–0.1 ms





1.2 Arithmetic Intensity and the Ridge Point
The key diagnostic ratio is arithmetic intensity:
\[
I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes Transferred}}
\]
The ridge point is the hardware’s crossover intensity:
\[
I^* = \frac{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s}}{\text{Memory\_BW}}
\]








If…
Regime
Action




\(I > I^*\)
Compute-bound
Faster math units, lower precision, or fewer FLOPs


\(I < I^*\)
Memory-bound
Larger batch size, operator fusion, or higher memory bandwidth









TipWorked Example: Dense Layer on H100





A dense layer with 2048→512, FP16, batch=1:

FLOPs: \(2 \times 2048 \times 512 = 2.1\text{M}\)
Bytes: \(2048 \times 512 \times 2 = 2.1\text{MB}\)
Arithmetic Intensity: \(2.1\text{M} / 2.1\text{MB} = 1\) FLOP/byte
H100 Ridge Point: \(989\text{ TF} / 3.35\text{ TB/s} \approx 295\) FLOP/byte (vs. \(312\text{ TF} / 2.04\text{ TB/s} \approx 153\) FLOP/byte on A100)

At \(I = 1 \ll 295 = I^*\), this workload is deeply memory-bound. The H100 achieves <1% of peak compute. Increasing to batch=64 raises \(I\) to ~64, recovering significant throughput.
Source: Slide deck worked example, Vol I Ch 11.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
2. Distributed Training (3D/4D Parallelism)
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.DistributedModel. Slide Decks: Distributed Training (Vol II, Ch 6) | Collective Communication (Vol II, Ch 5)
Real distributed training involves complex interactions between computation, communication, and scheduling. Empirical profiling requires access to expensive multi-GPU clusters and takes hours per configuration. MLSys·im decomposes the problem into independent overheads, each governed by a closed-form equation, so thousands of parallelism configurations can be evaluated in seconds.

2.1 Parallelism Decomposition
MLSys·im supports 4D parallelism. Given a cluster of \(N\) total GPUs:
\[
\text{DP} = \frac{N}{\text{TP} \times \text{PP} \times \text{EP}}
\]








Dimension
What It Splits
Communication Pattern




Data Parallelism (DP)
Batch across replicas
AllReduce (gradients)


Tensor Parallelism (TP)
Individual layers across GPUs
Point-to-point (intra-node NVLink)


Pipeline Parallelism (PP)
Layer groups across stages
Forward/backward activations


Expert Parallelism (EP)
MoE experts across GPUs
All-to-All (token routing)





2.2 Scaling Efficiency
The solver computes an overall scaling efficiency, the fraction of ideal linear speedup actually achieved:
\[
\eta_{\text{scale}} = \frac{T_{\text{compute}}}{T_{\text{compute}} + T_{\text{dp}} + T_{\text{tp}} + T_{\text{ep}} + T_{\text{bubble}}}
\]
An efficiency of 80% on 256 GPUs delivers the throughput of ~205 GPUs; the rest is lost to communication and pipeline bubbles. For the GPT-3 175B reference job (eight-way tensor and eight-way pipeline parallelism on HDR InfiniBand, fixed GPT-3 batch of 1,536 sequences), the solver predicts about 93% at 64 GPUs, 92% at 256, 86% at 1,024, and 55% at 8,192, where the pipeline bubble dominates. Production systems with larger batches and interleaved pipelines retain more. MegaScale’s 175B MFU falls only from 59.1% to 55.2% between 3,072 and 12,288 GPUs [1].


2.3 Ring All-Reduce (Data Parallelism)
Slide Deck: Collective Communication (Vol II, Ch 5)
After each training step, every GPU must synchronize gradients. The standard algorithm is ring all-reduce, which arranges \(N\) GPUs in a logical ring and passes gradient chunks in two phases (scatter-reduce, then all-gather).
Using the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) communication model (\(\alpha\) = per-message latency, \(\beta\) = bandwidth):
\[
T_{\text{ring}} = 2(N-1) \cdot \alpha \;+\; \frac{2(N-1)}{N} \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}
\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(M\)
Total gradient size in bytes


\(N\)
Number of GPUs in the ring


\(\alpha\)
Per-message startup latency


\(\beta\)
Per-link bandwidth (bytes/s)



Why ring all-reduce scales well: The bandwidth term \(\frac{2(N-1)}{N} \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}\) approaches \(\frac{2M}{\beta}\) as \(N\) grows, so it is asymptotically constant in the number of GPUs. Total data transferred per GPU is always ~\(2M\), regardless of cluster size. The latency term \(2(N-1) \cdot \alpha\) grows linearly, but is negligible for large messages.
MLSys·im also implements tree all-reduce (latency-optimal for small messages):
\[
T_{\text{tree}} = 2 \log_2(N) \cdot \alpha \;+\; 2 \log_2(N) \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}
\]
The crossover point between ring and tree is approximately \(M_{\text{cross}} \approx N \cdot \alpha \cdot \beta\). Below this size, tree wins (latency dominates); above it, ring wins (bandwidth dominates).






TipWorked Example: 140 GB Gradient Sync





A 70B-parameter model in FP16 produces a 140 GB gradient. On a 1,024-GPU cluster with InfiniBand NDR (\(\beta = 50\) GB/s, \(\alpha = 2\;\mu\)s):

Bandwidth term: \(\frac{2 \times 1023}{1024} \times \frac{140}{50} \approx\) 5.6 s
Latency term: \(2 \times 1023 \times 2\;\mu\text{s} \approx 4\) ms (negligible)
Total gradient synchronization time: ~5.6 s, bandwidth-dominated as expected for large messages.

Upgrading from 100 Gb Ethernet (~12.5 GB/s) to NDR (~50 GB/s) recovers 10–30% scaling efficiency.





2.4 Pipeline Parallelism Bubble
Slide Deck: Distributed Training (Vol II, Ch 6)
Pipeline parallelism splits a model’s layers across \(P\) stages. At the start of each batch, downstream stages sit idle while upstream stages produce output. This idle time is the pipeline bubble.






Intuition: The speed of light is fixed, but the software schedule can change. Assigning multiple virtual stages (\(V\)) to each GPU interleaves execution: while a GPU waits for one virtual stage’s next microbatch, it computes a different virtual stage’s microbatch, hiding latency behind useful work.



With \(P\) pipeline stages, \(M\) microbatches, and \(V\) virtual stages per GPU:
\[
\text{Bubble Fraction} = \frac{P - 1}{V \times M + P - 1}
\]



Configuration
Bubble Fraction




\(P=4, M=16, V=1\)
\(3/19 =\) 15.8%


\(P=4, M=16, V=2\)
\(3/35 =\) 8.6%


\(P=8, M=32, V=1\)
\(7/39 =\) 17.9%


\(P=16, M=16, V=1\)
\(15/31 =\) 48.4% (unacceptable)



Keeping the bubble below 5% with standard 1F1B (\(V=1\)) requires \(M \geq 19 \times (P - 1)\) microbatches. Interleaved schedules (\(V \geq 2\)) cut this requirement proportionally.


2.5 Expert Parallelism (Mixture of Experts)






Intuition: Dense Transformers obey a strict “Iron Law”: doubling parameters doubles both memory and compute. Mixture of Experts (MoE) breaks this law by routing tokens to specific expert subnetworks. The memory bound is set by the total parameters, but the compute bound is set by the much smaller active parameters. The physical tradeoff is a network bandwidth tax (All-to-All communication) to route tokens across the cluster.



When \(\text{EP} > 1\), the solver adds an All-to-All communication penalty for token routing:
\[
T_{\text{all-to-all}} = (N-1) \cdot \alpha \;+\; \frac{N-1}{N} \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}
\]
where \(N\) is the EP degree. Compared to AllReduce, All-to-All creates \(O(N^2)\) point-to-point connections, making it latency-sensitive. A 4 KB token routing message is latency-bound, while a 140 GB gradient sync is bandwidth-bound.
MoE routing is rarely perfectly balanced. MLSys·im exposes a single routing-imbalance factor \(\gamma \ge 1\):
\[
E_{\text{active,eff}} = \min(E_{\text{total}}, \gamma \cdot E_{\text{top-k}})
\]
\[
P_{\text{active,eff}} = P_{\text{active}} \cdot \frac{E_{\text{active,eff}}}{E_{\text{top-k}}}
\]
MoERoutingModel reports the effective active experts, effective active parameters, routed bytes, and optional expert-parallel all-to-all latency. This is a first-order hot-expert proxy, not a router simulation; it is intended to capture the load-balancing concern surfaced by sparsely-gated MoE, GShard, and Switch-style systems [2], [3], [4].

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
3. Training Scaling Laws
Used by mlsysim.physics.calc_transformer_training_flops. Slide Deck: Training (Vol I, Ch 8)
The 6PD rule estimates total training FLOPs for a Transformer:
\[
C \approx 6 \times P \times D
\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(C\)
Total training FLOPs


\(P\)
Number of model parameters


\(D\)
Number of training tokens



The factor of 6 is 2 FLOPs per parameter per token (forward pass multiply-accumulate) × 3 passes (forward + backward for weights + backward for activations). Combined with the roofline model (Section 1), this gives training time:
\[
T_{\text{train}} = \frac{6PD}{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \eta}
\]






TipWorked Example: GPT-3 Training Time





GPT-3 175B trained on 300B tokens:

Total FLOPs: \(6 \times 175 \times 10^9 \times 300 \times 10^9 = 3.15 \times 10^{23}\)
On 1,024 A100s (\(312\text{ TF each} \times 0.5\) MFU): \(3.15 \times 10^{23} / (1024 \times 312 \times 10^{12} \times 0.5) \approx 1.97 \times 10^6\text{ s} \approx 23\text{ days}\)

Narayanan et al. estimate about 34 days for this configuration [5]. The gap from 23 days is not a scaling loss. Their estimate counts 8 FLOPs per parameter per token, because activation recomputation repeats the forward pass, and it uses a measured 140 TFLOP/s per GPU (about 45% of peak), which already includes communication and pipeline losses.




3.1 Training Memory Accounting
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.TrainingMemoryModel.
Inference memory is mostly weights plus KV cache. Training memory adds gradients, optimizer state, saved activations, and communication buffers:
\[
M_{\text{train}} =
M_{\text{weights}} + M_{\text{grad}} + M_{\text{opt}} +
M_{\text{act}} + M_{\text{comm}}
\]
For mixed-precision Adam training, the default per-parameter state is:



Component
Default bytes / parameter
ZeRO sharding




Weights
2
Stage 3


Gradients
2
Stage 2+


Adam optimizer state
12
Stage 1+



Tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism first shard the model states across model-parallel ranks. ZeRO then shards data-parallel states [6]. Activation memory scales with local microbatch size, sequence length, hidden dimension, and the chosen activation-checkpointing strategy [7].

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
4. LLM Serving Lifecycle
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.ServingModel. Slide Decks: Model Serving (Vol I, Ch 13) | Inference at Scale (Vol II, Ch 10)
LLM autoregressive inference has two physically distinct phases. Capacity planning depends on knowing which phase dominates.

4.1 Pre-fill Phase (Compute-Bound)
The initial forward pass processes all prompt tokens in parallel:
\[
\text{TTFT} = \frac{2 \times P \times S \times B}{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \eta} + \text{Dispatch\_Tax}
\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(P\)
Number of model parameters


\(S\)
Input sequence length


\(B\)
Batch size



The factor of 2 counts both the multiply and the add in each multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation.


4.2 Decoding Phase (Compute and Memory Bounds)
Each decode step streams model weights and the filled KV cache. The solver compares that memory time with the time needed for linear layers and attention:
\[
T_m = \frac{|W|+M_{\mathrm{KV}}}{\mathrm{BW}}
\]
Here \(|W|\) is the weight payload, \(M_{\mathrm{KV}}\) is filled KV storage, and \(\mathrm{BW}\) is memory bandwidth. With compute time \(T_c\):
\[
\mathrm{ITL}=\max(T_c,T_m)+T_{\mathrm{layer}}.
\]
The compute term divides forward operations by the precision-specific peak FLOP/s times the declared compute efficiency. It includes both attention matrix products. Batch-one decode is commonly memory-limited; larger batches amortize weight reads and can become compute-limited. ServingModel and ContinuousBatchingModel share this accounting. Efficiency does not derate memory bandwidth, and the layer tax is an explicit runtime assumption.






TipWorked Example: Llama-3 70B Decode on H100





Single-token decode, batch=1 (70.6B parameters, 141.2 GB in FP16):

Compute: 2 × 70.6 B ÷ 989 TFLOP/s = 0.14 ms (0.3% of memory time)
Memory: 141.2 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s = 42.1 ms
Weight-only bandwidth floor: ~42 ms/token → ~24 tokens/s

This weight-only floor excludes KV traffic, runtime overhead, and inter-device communication. The model does not fit on a single H100 at this precision, so these terms are a bandwidth illustration, not a feasible single-device serving prediction.
Source: Compute Infrastructure slides (Vol II, Ch 2).





4.3 KV-Cache Size
\[
\text{KV\_Bytes} = 2 \times L \times H_{\text{kv}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times S \times B \times b_{\text{elem}}
\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(L\)
Number of Transformer layers


\(H_{\text{kv}}\)
Number of KV attention heads (equals \(H\) for MHA; smaller for GQA/MQA)


\(d_{\text{head}}\)
Dimension per head


\(S\)
Sequence length


\(B\)
Batch size


\(b_{\text{elem}}\)
Bytes per element (2 for FP16/BF16)



The factor of 2 accounts for both the K and V tensors. With Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), \(H_{\text{kv}} < H\), which reduces cache size. Llama-3 70B uses 8 KV heads vs. 64 query heads, an 8× reduction.






TipWorked Example: KV-Cache Capacity Planning





Llama-3 70B: 80 layers, 8 KV heads (GQA), \(d_{\text{head}} = 128\), FP16:

Per-token: \(2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327.7\text{ KB}\)
Batch=16, seq=4096: \(327.7\text{K} \times 16 \times 4096 = 21.5\text{ GB}\)
Batch=32, seq=4096: \(327.7\text{K} \times 32 \times 4096 = 42.9\text{ GB}\)

Weights (35.3 GB at INT4) + KV-cache (42.9 GB at FP16) = 78.2 GB, which barely fits on an 80 GiB H100. At batch=64 or longer contexts, the model must be sharded across multiple GPUs.
Source: Inference at Scale slides (Vol II, Ch 10).





4.4 Chunked Prefill and Decode Interference
Production serving systems often mix new prefill work with ongoing decode iterations. Long prefills can stall decode unless the scheduler bounds the amount of prefill work admitted per iteration. MLSys·im models this with an optional prefill chunk size. Let \(S_{\text{new}} = S - S_{\text{cache}}\), with \(0 \le S_{\text{cache}} < S\) and \(S_{\text{chunk}} > 0\):
\[
C = \left\lceil \frac{S_{\text{new}}}{S_{\text{chunk}}} \right\rceil
\]
\[
\text{TTFT}_{\text{chunked}} =
\text{TTFT}_{\text{compute}} + C \times \text{Dispatch\_Tax}
\]
\[
\text{Decode\_Stall}_{\max} \approx
\max_i\left(T_{\text{chunk},i}\right)
\]
Here \(T_{\text{chunk},i}\) is the compute time for chunk \(i\) plus one dispatch tax.







Symbol
Meaning




\(C\)
Number of prefill chunks


\(S_{\text{new}}\)
Prompt tokens that still require prefill computation


\(S_{\text{cache}}\)
Prompt tokens already covered by prefix caching


\(S_{\text{chunk}}\)
Maximum prefill tokens admitted per scheduler iteration



This estimates a coarse scheduling proxy used by chunked-prefill systems: smaller chunks do not reduce total prefill compute, but they reduce the largest decode stall caused by a co-scheduled prefill. MLSys·im does not implement Sarathi-Serve’s full scheduler. Disaggregated systems such as Splitwise and DistServe mitigate prefill/decode interference by assigning the phases to separate resources, trading scheduler interference for KV-cache transfer and resource-partitioning costs [8], [9], [10].


4.5 KV Allocation and Batch Capacity
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.ContinuousBatchingModel.
Batching amortizes weight reads across requests, and the KV-cache allocator determines how many requests fit. Throughput gains stop scaling when compute becomes the limiting resource. Let \(M_{\text{KV}}\) be the HBM left after the weights and \(k\) the KV bytes per token (KV-Cache Size). A static allocator reserves the maximum sequence length \(S_{\max}\) for every request. A paged allocator divides the budget into blocks of \(p\) tokens and hands a request of \(S\) tokens \(\lceil S/p \rceil\) of them on demand:
\[
N_{\text{static}} = \left\lfloor \frac{M_{\text{KV}}}{k\,S_{\max}} \right\rfloor
\qquad
N_{\text{paged}} = \left\lfloor \frac{\lfloor M_{\text{KV}} / (k\,p) \rfloor}{\mathbb{E}\left[\lceil S/p \rceil\right]} \right\rfloor
\]
The scheduler’s maximum batch size caps both. Request lengths are \(S = \min(X, S_{\max})\) with \(X\) exponential, scaled so that \(\mathbb{E}[S] = \bar{S}\): most requests are short, and the rare long one is cut off at the context window. Summing tail probabilities gives the expected block count in closed form
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[\lceil S/p \rceil\right] = \sum_{j=0}^{K-1} P(S > jp) = \frac{1 - r^{K}}{1 - r},
\qquad r = e^{-p/\mu},\quad K = \lceil S_{\max}/p \rceil
\]
The unused share of each allocation (internal fragmentation) is \(1 - \bar{S}/S_{\max}\) for static reservation and \(1 - \bar{S}/\left(p\,\mathbb{E}[\lceil S/p \rceil]\right)\) for paging. The paged tail averages about \(p/2\) tokens per request, so page size matters even when \(S_{\max}\) divides evenly by \(p\). Memory-bound decode streams only the tokens requests have filled, so for either allocator
\[
T_m = \frac{|W| + N\,\bar{S}\,k}{\mathrm{BW}}
\]
Using the compute/memory maximum and layer overhead from Decoding Phase,
\[
R_{\text{tok}} = \frac{N}{t_{\text{step}}}
\]
and speedup_vs_static is \(R_{\text{tok}}\) at \(N_{\text{paged}}\) divided by \(R_{\text{tok}}\) at \(N_{\text{static}}\).







Symbol
Meaning




\(M_{\text{KV}}\)
HBM capacity left for the KV cache after the weights


\(k\)
KV bytes per token


\(S_{\max}\)
Longest context a request may reach (max_seq_len)


\(\bar{S}\)
Mean tokens a request fills (mean_request_tokens; defaults to \(S_{\max}\))


\(p\)
Block (page) size in tokens (page_size)


\(\mu\)
Exponential scale chosen so that \(\mathbb{E}[\min(X, S_{\max})] = \bar{S}\)









TipWorked Example: Llama-3 8B on H100 with an 8K Context





FP16 KV costs \(k = 131\,072\) bytes per token, so the H100’s KV budget holds about 532,831 tokens. With \(S_{\max} = 8192\) and \(\bar{S} = 2048\):

Static reservation: \(\lfloor 532\,831 / 8192 \rfloor = 65\) requests, with 75% of every reservation unused
Paged, \(p = 16\): about 128.5 blocks per request, so 259 requests with 0.4% unused
Paged, \(p = 2048\): 165 requests with 36% unused
Decode throughput: paged at \(p = 16\) runs about 1.59× static

Allocation policy matters only when memory binds. If the scheduler caps the batch below 65, both allocators admit the same requests and the speedup is 1.
Source: ContinuousBatchingModel. The Monte Carlo allocators in the KV-cache tutorial admit the same 65 and 259 requests; the tutorial’s throughput ratio is lower because its single random draw happens to give the first 65 requests a below-average length.



Kwon et al. profile contiguous pre-allocation and find that only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV-cache memory holds token states. The rest is reserved slots for future tokens, internal fragmentation from over-provisioning for the maximum length, and external fragmentation from the allocator. PagedAttention limits each request’s waste to one block [11]. The static baseline here is max-length reservation, which captures the first two kinds of waste and is modeled without external fragmentation. Exact-size and power-of-two contiguous allocators, which trade reservation waste for external fragmentation, are not modeled. Sizing both allocators with every request at its full length is a peak-occupancy view: a request mid-generation holds fewer paged blocks, so paged capacity is conservative.


4.6 Serving Capacity Planning
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.ServingCapacityModel.
Capacity planning composes three first-order quantities:

base request latency from ServingModel;
per-replica token throughput from ContinuousBatchingModel;
queueing delay from TailLatencyModel.

For an average response length \(G\) tokens and per-replica decode throughput \(R_{\text{tok}}\), the first-order request capacity is:
\[
Q_{\text{replica}} = \frac{R_{\text{tok}}}{G}
\]
The required replica count is the smallest \(c\) such that traffic intensity remains stable and:
\[
P99_{\text{request}} \approx T_{\text{base}} + P99_{\text{queue}}(Q, Q_{\text{replica}}, c)
\le T_{\text{target}}
\]
Per-replica throughput \(R_{\text{tok}}\) comes from paged allocation in KV Allocation and Batch Capacity, so passing mean_request_tokens below max_seq_len raises the batch each replica can hold. Base latency is then evaluated at the mean request length. This is deliberately a capacity model. It does not simulate request arrivals, preemption, or scheduler internals.


4.7 Serving Cost Dominance
At production scale, serving costs dominate training:
\[
C_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{training}} + C_{\text{serving}} \times T_{\text{deploy}} \times Q_{\text{rate}}
\]
A 70B model costing $2M to train, serving 1M daily users at 50 requests/day, costs ~$18M/year in inference, 9× the training cost in year one. This is why inference optimization (batching, quantization, speculative decoding) has outsized economic impact.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
5. Datacenter Sustainability
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.SustainabilityModel. Slide Deck: Sustainable AI (Vol II, Ch 15)

5.1 Total Energy
\[
E = \text{IT\_Power} \times \text{Hours} \times \text{PUE}
\]
Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) accounts for cooling and facility overhead. A PUE of 1.0 is theoretical perfect efficiency; hyperscale datacenters achieve 1.05–1.10 (liquid-cooled) to 1.4–1.6 (air-cooled). The industry average is 1.58, meaning 37% of energy goes to cooling and power distribution, not computation.


5.2 Carbon Footprint
\[
C = E \times \text{Carbon\_Intensity}
\]
Where \(C\) is in kg CO₂e and Carbon_Intensity is in g CO₂e/kWh, sourced from regional grid data.






TipWorked Example: Training Carbon Footprint





64 GPUs × 400W × 336 hours = 8,602 kWh. With PUE 1.2 = 10,322 kWh.



Grid Region
Carbon Intensity
CO₂ Emissions




Quebec (hydro)
20 g/kWh
206 kg


US Average
429 g/kWh
4,428 kg


Poland (coal)
820 g/kWh
8,464 kg



Geographic choice alone creates a ~41× difference for identical workloads. Combined with hardware choice (5×) and quantization (4×), the total optimization lever is up to 800×.
Source: Sustainable AI slides (Vol II, Ch 15).

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
6. Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.EconomicsModel. Slide Deck: Compute Infrastructure (Vol II, Ch 2)
\[
\text{TCO} = \underbrace{\frac{\text{Hardware\_Cost}}{\text{Depreciation\_Years}}}_{\text{CapEx (amortized)}} + \underbrace{E \times \text{Electricity\_Rate}}_{\text{OpEx (power)}} + \text{OpEx}_{\text{maintenance}}
\]






TipWorked Example: On-Prem vs. Cloud








Metric
On-Prem (H100 Node)
Cloud On-Demand




Unit cost
$350K (amortize over 3 yr)
N/A


Annual cost (80% util)
~$122K/node/yr
~$224K/node/yr


Effective GPU-hour rate
~$2.40
~$4.00



Break-even occupancy: ~55%. Below 55% sustained occupancy, cloud is cheaper. At 20% occupancy, on-prem costs ~$6/GPU-hour, which is more expensive than cloud on-demand.
The right metric is cost per useful TFLOP-hour, not cost per GPU-hour. An H100 delivers 3.2× the FP16 TFLOP/s of an A100 (or 6.3× comparing H100 FP8 to A100 FP16), so a higher sticker price may yield a lower effective cost.
Source: Compute Infrastructure slides (Vol II, Ch 2).

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
7. Cluster Reliability (The Young-Daly Model)
Implemented in mlsysim.solvers.ReliabilityModel. Slide Deck: Fault Tolerance (Vol II, Ch 7)






Intuition: When training on thousands of GPUs for months, hardware failures are a statistical certainty. If a node fails, the job loses all progress since the last checkpoint. Checkpointing too often wastes time writing; checkpointing too rarely wastes time recomputing. The Young-Daly model finds the optimal balance.




7.1 Cluster MTBF
Individual component reliability degrades linearly with scale:
\[
\text{MTBF}_{\text{cluster}} = \frac{\text{MTBF}_{\text{component}}}{N}
\]



Cluster Size (\(N\))
System MTBF (50,000 hr/GPU)




8 GPUs
~8 months


1,000 GPUs
50 hours


10,000 GPUs
5 hours


16,000 GPUs
~3 hours (Llama-3 scale: 419 failures in 54 days)





7.2 Optimal Checkpoint Interval
\[
\tau_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \times \delta \times M}
\]



Symbol
Meaning




\(\delta\)
Time to write one checkpoint


\(M\)
Mean Time Between Failures (cluster MTBF)





7.3 Wasted Compute Fraction
The total overhead from checkpointing has two components:
\[
\text{Waste} = \underbrace{\frac{\delta}{2\tau}}_{\text{checkpoint writes}} + \underbrace{\frac{\tau}{2M}}_{\text{lost work on failure}}
\]
At the optimal \(\tau_{\text{opt}}\), both terms are equal, and waste is minimized.






TipWorked Example: Llama-3 Scale Checkpointing





16,384 GPUs, \(\delta = 2\) min, cluster MTBF \(M = 180\) min:
\[\tau_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \times 2 \times 180} = \sqrt{720} \approx 27\text{ min}\]



Checkpoint Interval
Overhead




10 min (too frequent)
17%


27 min (optimal)
7%


60 min (too rare)
15%



On a cluster costing $10M/month, 7% overhead = $700K/month. Async checkpointing (overlapping writes with computation) can reduce this to ~3%.
Source: Fault Tolerance slides (Vol II, Ch 7).

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
8. Failure Probability
Implemented in mlsysim.physics.calc_failure_probability.
The probability of at least one failure during a job of duration \(T\) follows an exponential model:
\[
P(\geq 1\text{ failure}) = 1 - e^{-T / \text{MTBF}}
\]
For a 30-day training run on a cluster with MTBF of 5 hours: \(P = 1 - e^{-720/5} \approx 1.0\), so failure is virtually certain. This is why checkpointing (Section 7) is not optional at scale.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
9. Effective FLOPS (Fleet Goodput)
Implemented in mlsysim.physics.calc_effective_flops. Slide Deck: Performance Engineering (Vol II, Ch 9)
The actual useful computation delivered by a fleet after all overheads:
\[
\text{Effective\_FLOP/s} = \text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \underbrace{\text{MFU}}_{\text{per-GPU}} \times \underbrace{\eta_{\text{scale}}}_{\text{comm overhead}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\text{Goodput}}{\text{Rawput}}}_{\text{failure waste}}
\]
Each factor in the cascade represents a distinct loss mechanism. Typical values for large-scale training: MFU ≈ 0.3–0.5, \(\eta_{\text{scale}}\) ≈ 0.4–0.85, Goodput/Rawput ≈ 0.85–0.97. The compound effect means a fleet may deliver only 10–35% of its theoretical peak.







NoteLimitations of First-Order Models



These equations are first-order analytical models. They assume: (1) aggregate memory traffic, (2) no explicit cache hierarchy, (3) no network contention under heavy load, and (4) idealized overlap of compute and memory. Batching throughput is bounded by both compute and memory capacity.
Real systems deviate from these assumptions. Use MLSys·im to reason about bottlenecks and compare configurations under stated assumptions. Calibration checks do not establish an accuracy guarantee for unseen workloads. See Calibration and validation scope for executable checks and their limitations.

title: For Instructors
text: MLSys·im provides a framework for assigning analytically grounded problem sets where every answer is deterministic and reproducible, regardless of the hardware students have access to. Combined with the companion lecture slides, it covers the tools needed for an ML systems course.

title: For Instructors
text:
Assignment Ideas

Homework: Hardware Comparison (30 min)

Using Engine.solve(), compare ResNet-50 inference latency on the A100, H100, and Jetson AGX at batch sizes 1, 32, and 256. For each configuration, state whether the workload is memory-bound or compute-bound and explain why the bottleneck shifts with batch size.

Pairs with: HW Acceleration slides (roofline model, ridge point) and Benchmarking slides (measurement methodology).


Homework: Training Memory Budget (30 min)

Using TrainingMemoryModel, calculate the memory required to train GPT-2 (1.5B parameters) in FP16 with Adam optimizer under ZeRO Stage 0, Stage 1, and Stage 3. Explain why each stage reduces memory and what trade-off it introduces.

Pairs with: Model Training slides and Distributed Training slides.


Lab: Carbon-Aware Training (45 min)

Using the SustainabilityModel, calculate the carbon footprint of training GPT-3 on a 256-GPU H100 cluster in Quebec (20 gCO₂/kWh) vs. US Average (429 gCO₂/kWh) vs. Poland (820 gCO₂/kWh, 41× Quebec). Produce a table and a 2-paragraph analysis of why datacenter location matters more than hardware choice for carbon.

Pairs with: Sustainable AI slides (grid carbon intensity, PUE).


Lab: LLM Serving Capacity Planning (45 min)

Using the ServingModel, determine the maximum sequence length at which Llama-3.1-70B can serve a single request on an 8-GPU H100 node without exceeding memory. Then calculate TTFT and ITL at sequence lengths of 1K, 4K, and 16K tokens, and identify the sequence length at which KV-cache pressure dominates.

Pairs with: Model Serving slides and Inference at Scale slides.


Exam Question: Back-of-Envelope

A GPU has 989 TFLOP/s peak dense compute (FP16) and 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth. Compute (a) the ridge point in FLOP/Byte (295 FLOP/Byte), (b) whether a model layer with arithmetic intensity of 50 FLOP/Byte is compute-bound or memory-bound, and (c) which regime a layer with arithmetic intensity of 400 FLOP/Byte occupies and what that implies about the benefit of moving to a GPU with 2× the bandwidth. Show all intermediate steps.

Pairs with: HW Acceleration slides (roofline model, ridge point derivation).


Capstone: Multi-Solver Design Study (1 week)

Design a training cluster for a 70.6B-parameter model. Use the DistributedModel to select a parallelism strategy, the EconomicsModel for TCO over 6 months, the SustainabilityModel to compare three datacenter locations, and the ReliabilityModel to determine checkpoint frequency. Present the analysis as a 3-page technical memo with quantitative justification for each decision.

Pairs with: the full Volume II slide set, covering infrastructure, training, fault tolerance, and sustainability.

title: For Instructors
text:
Grading Notes
Because MLSys·im produces deterministic output from vetted specifications:

Answer keys are stable: the same mlsysim version produces identical numbers for every student, every semester
Partial credit is straightforward: grade the reasoning (which solver, which inputs, which bottleneck explanation), not only the number
Analytical predictions are easy to assess: students can compute analytical bounds from the closed-form equations before running mlsysim to verify their work







NoteVersion Pinning



Pin the exact version in the assignment instructions (pip install mlsysim==<course-version>) so answer keys remain valid even after new releases update specifications.

title: For Instructors
text:
Reproducibility Guarantee
All specifications in the MLSys Zoo are:

Sourced from official manufacturer datasheets and published benchmarks
Typed with pint.Quantity for dimensional correctness, so unit errors are caught at runtime
Frozen per release, so an exact pin such as mlsysim==0.3.0 always produces the same answers

An answer key therefore works for every student, every semester.

title: For Instructors
text:
Jupyter & Quarto Compatibility
All tutorials run in:

Jupyter Notebooks: standard .ipynb workflow
Quarto documents: render to HTML, PDF, or slides with quarto render
Google Colab: pip install mlsysim in the first cell, then run the tutorial

No GPU runtime required. CPU-only environments are sufficient because MLSys·im computes from equations, not from profiling.

title: Choosing a Python API
text: MLSys·im separates specifications, equations, and the solvers that combine them. The same engine serves every textbook volume. Choosing an API depends on the physical question, not on which volume introduces it.

title: Choosing a Python API
text:
Choose the calculation








Question
Start here
What the result represents




How do compute and memory bandwidth constrain one device?
Engine.solve()
A generic Roofline profile with declared traffic and overhead approximations


How do prompt length, KV storage, and batch size affect token generation?
ServingModel().solve()
Separate prefill and decode estimates with KV-aware memory accounting


Does training fit, or how does a fleet scale?
TrainingMemoryModel or DistributedModel
Training-state capacity or distributed training performance


How do named workload and hardware choices perform against a latency target?
Scenario(...).evaluate()
A composed feasibility, performance, and annual economics scorecard


What does one equation imply?
A function in mlsysim.physics
A reusable calculation with an explicit unit and modeling contract



The solver guide maps additional questions to solvers. The resolver guide explains forward models, inverse solvers, and optimizers. These categories describe different calculations; using a more specialized class only helps when its assumptions match the question.

title: Choosing a Python API
text:
A generic single-device profile
Import the main entry point and registries from mlsysim. This example evaluates one batch of a vision model. Its efficiency is an assumed compute-capacity fraction, not a measured end-to-end utilization.

from mlsysim import Engine, Hardware, Models

profile = Engine.solve(
    model=Models.Vision.ResNet50,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    batch_size=8,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=0.5,  # Assumed compute efficiency for this example.
)
print(f"Fits modeled memory: {profile.feasible}")
print(f"Batch latency: {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.3f}")
print(f"Limiting resource: {profile.bottleneck}")

Fits modeled memory: True
Batch latency: 0.643 ms
Limiting resource: Compute


Engine.solve() returns a PerformanceProfile. Its latency is per batch; throughput divides batch size by that latency. A feasibility flag checks the modeled footprint, which does not reserve all production runtime workspaces.
For a language model, the generic engine uses an activation-traffic approximation. It does not become KV-aware autoregressive serving simply because the workload is a transformer. A sweep through this API cannot establish a serving engine’s inter-token latency or continuous-batching capacity.

title: Choosing a Python API
text:
KV-aware language-model serving
Import specialized classes from mlsysim.solvers. ServingModel keeps prompt prefill and decode separate. Decode compares compute time with weight and KV traffic time, then adds the configured layer overhead. Either compute or memory can limit the estimate.

from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

serving = ServingModel().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=2048,
    batch_size=1,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=0.5,  # Derates compute; it does not derate memory bandwidth.
)
print(f"Fits modeled memory: {serving.feasible}")
print(f"Prefill estimate: {serving.ttft.to('ms'):~.3f}")
print(f"Decode step estimate: {serving.itl.to('ms'):~.3f}")
print(f"KV storage: {serving.kv_cache_size.to('GB'):~.3f}")

Fits modeled memory: True
Prefill estimate: 70.970 ms
Decode step estimate: 5.194 ms
KV storage: 0.268 GB


Here seq_len sets the modeled context length. itl is a decode step under those assumptions; it is not a request’s total latency divided by its output length. The default prefill model is compute based. These estimates do not include every kernel, allocator, scheduling, or multi-device communication cost. The serving reference documents the supported options and exclusions.

title: Choosing a Python API
text:
A named scenario and scorecard
A Scenario binds a workload, target system, and declared constraints so a calculation can be reused. This example adds an illustrative latency target to a vision workload; the target is a local assumption, not a hardware specification.

from mlsysim import Hardware, Models, Q_, Scenario

scenario = Scenario(
    name="Vision latency exercise",
    description="Evaluate a vision batch against an illustrative latency target.",
    workload=Models.Vision.ResNet50,
    system=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    sla_latency=Q_("10 ms"),
)
scorecard = scenario.evaluate(batch_size=8, precision="fp16")
print(f"Feasibility: {scorecard.feasibility.status}")
print(f"Performance: {scorecard.performance.status}")
print(scorecard.performance.summary)

Feasibility: PASS
Performance: PASS
Latency: 0.64 ms (Target: 10 ms)


The current generic Scenario.evaluate() uses SingleNodeModel for one device and DistributedModel for a fleet. It does not select ServingModel when the workload is a language model. Its feasibility level checks weight residency and any configured input data rate; its performance level checks the latency target. Its macro level uses annual economics defaults. It is not a check of every constraint exposed elsewhere in the package. For explicit serving costs, training-memory breakdowns, or custom economics assumptions, call those solvers directly and compose their results.
Scenario is the class for a local case. Scenarios is the registry of named, reusable cases and analytical inputs. Inspect an entry’s type and documentation: not every registry entry has the generic class’s evaluate() method.

text:
Follow a result into the code








Layer
Source location
What to inspect




Specifications

Typed fields, units, and provenance for selected inputs

Reusable formulas, assumptions, exclusions, and references

How a domain solver combines equations and accounts for costs

Typed inputs and their calculations, grouped by domain


Named configurations

Reusable choices of inputs exposed through Scenarios

Result schemas, units, and constraint traces in the same domains


Presentation

Formatting and interaction around those results



Some domain-specific calculations live directly in a solver or a private shared helper. Follow its source link rather than assuming every equation is in physics/. The modeling conventions describe the calculation documentation contract; the API reference is built from the package docstrings.
The code walkthrough follows one serving case through these layers. Browse scenarios by domain for related calculations, or use the alphabetical index for a known class name.
Use the public imports shown above in textbook cells and applications. Internal paths explain where implementation lives, but callers do not need to depend on private helpers or the layout beneath engine/solvers/. This separation allows internal cleanup while preserving the public entry points.
engine/scenario_types.py, engine/scenarios.py, and engine/results.py preserve the established imports. Their definitions live in the domain packages listed above; the compatibility modules do not own a second implementation.

title: Extending the Engine
text:
MLSys·im is designed to be fully extensible. Researchers and students can add custom analytical tools to resolve new constraints or search new design spaces.
All extensions must follow the 3-Tier API Contract, which requires each extension to declare what kind of math it does.

title: Extending the Engine
text:
The 3-Tier API Contract
Before writing code, decide what kind of math the tool does.

1. ForwardModel: The Physics Engine

The Math: \(Y = f(X)\). Forward propagation.
When to use: To evaluate a physical or logical state. Given a fixed hardware config and a fixed workload, a Model predicts latency, cost, memory footprint, or energy.
Rule: A Model cannot make decisions or loop through options. It must be a deterministic calculation of a single state.



2. BaseSolver: The Math Engine

The Math: \(X = f^{-1}(Y)\) or \(\nabla f\). Algebraic inversion or calculus.
When to use: Given a specific target (like a latency SLA or a memory budget), solve algebraically for the exact hardware or model parameter required to hit it.
Rule: A Solver should yield a mathematically precise answer derived from inverting a Model’s equations.



3. BaseOptimizer: The Engineering Engine

The Math: \(\max_{x \in X} f(x) \text{ s.t. } g(x) \le c\). Constrained optimization.
When to use: To search a design space (discrete or continuous) for the “best” configuration, balancing competing trade-offs (e.g., maximizing throughput while minimizing carbon).
Rule: An Optimizer must internally call Models to evaluate candidates. It must return an OptimizerResult tracking the objective value and the size of the search space.

title: Extending the Engine
text:
1. Building a Custom Model
Every resolver follows the same pattern: declare inputs (requires), declare outputs (produces), and implement solve().
The following example builds a custom PowerEfficiencyModel that calculates TFLOPs per Watt.
from mlsysim.solvers import ForwardModel
from mlsysim.engine.results import SolverResult
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
from mlsysim.hardware.types import HardwareNode
from mlsysim.core.types import Quantity

# 1. Define the strictly typed Output
class PowerEfficiencyResult(SolverResult):
    flops_per_watt: Quantity
    is_efficient: bool

# 2. Implement the Model
class PowerEfficiencyModel(ForwardModel):
    """Evaluates the compute efficiency per watt of an accelerator."""
    requires = ("hardware",)
    produces = PowerEfficiencyResult

    def solve(self, hardware: HardwareNode) -> PowerEfficiencyResult:
        if hardware.tdp is None:
            raise ValueError(f"{hardware.name} has no TDP specified.")

        fpw = hardware.compute.peak_flops / hardware.tdp

        threshold = Q_("1 TFLOPs/s / W")
        is_eff = fpw > threshold

        return PowerEfficiencyResult(
            flops_per_watt=fpw.to("TFLOPs/s/W"),
            is_efficient=is_eff
        )

title: Extending the Engine
text:
2. Building a Custom Solver
A solver algebraically inverts an equation. For example, if \(T = \frac{W}{BW}\), and we have a target \(T\), we solve for \(BW = \frac{W}{T}\).
from mlsysim.solvers import BaseSolver
from mlsysim.engine.results import SolverResult
from mlsysim.models.types import Workload
from mlsysim.core.types import Quantity

class RequiredBandwidthResult(SolverResult):
    required_bw: Quantity

class RequiredBandwidthSolver(BaseSolver):
    """Solves for the exact memory bandwidth needed to hit an SLA."""
    requires = ("workload", "target_latency")
    produces = RequiredBandwidthResult

    def solve(self, model: Workload, target_latency: Quantity) -> RequiredBandwidthResult:
        weight_bytes = model.size_in_bytes()
        t_target = target_latency.to("s")

        # Algebraic inversion
        required_bw = (weight_bytes / t_target).to("GB/s")

        return RequiredBandwidthResult(required_bw=required_bw)

title: Extending the Engine
text:
3. Building a Custom Optimizer
An Optimizer explores a design space. It MUST inherit from BaseOptimizer and its result MUST inherit from OptimizerResult.
The following example builds a CheapestHardwareOptimizer that searches the HardwareZoo for the cheapest chip that satisfies a minimum TFLOP requirement.
from mlsysim.solvers import BaseOptimizer
from mlsysim.engine.results import OptimizerResult
from mlsysim.hardware.registry import Hardware
from typing import Dict, Any

# Inherit from OptimizerResult, which requires specific fields
class CheapestHardwareResult(OptimizerResult):
    cheapest_cost: float
    hardware_name: str

class CheapestHardwareOptimizer(BaseOptimizer):
    requires = ("min_tflops",)
    produces = CheapestHardwareResult

    def solve(self, min_tflops: float) -> CheapestHardwareResult:
        candidates = []
        target = Q_(min_tflops, "TFLOPs/s")

        # 1. Define Search Space
        for hw in Hardware.list():
            if hw.unit_cost is None:
                continue

            # 2. Evaluate Constraint
            if hw.compute.peak_flops >= target:
                candidates.append({
                    "name": hw.name,
                    "cost": hw.unit_cost.magnitude
                })

        if not candidates:
            raise ValueError("No hardware meets the requirement.")

        # 3. Optimize Objective (Minimize cost)
        best = min(candidates, key=lambda x: x["cost"])

        # 4. Return standard OptimizerResult structure
        return CheapestHardwareResult(
            objective_value=best["cost"], # Standard field
            best_config={"hardware": best["name"]}, # Standard field
            total_searched=len(Hardware.list()), # Standard field
            cheapest_cost=best["cost"],
            hardware_name=best["name"]
        )

title: Extending the Engine
text:
4. Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
MLSys·im does not evaluate models only in isolation. It uses a Composable Pipeline architecture, in which custom solvers snap into a pipeline and execute sequentially, with outputs from earlier stages passing automatically to later stages.
from mlsysim.engine.pipeline import Pipeline
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel, EconomicsModel

# Build a pipeline with your custom solver in the middle
my_pipeline = Pipeline([
    DistributedModel(),
    PowerEfficiencyModel(), # Your custom model
    EconomicsModel()
])

# Run the pipeline
results = my_pipeline.run(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Frontier_8K,
    duration_days=30
)

# Access individual stage results
print(results["PowerEfficiencyModel"].flops_per_watt)

Callbacks (Middleware)
A callback intercepts pipeline execution to log metrics to MLOps platforms like Weights & Biases or Datadog.
class WandbLogger:
    def on_stage_end(self, stage_name: str, result: SolverResult):
        # Example pseudo-code
        wandb.log({f"{stage_name}/{k}": v for k, v in result.dict().items()})

my_pipeline.register_callback(WandbLogger())

title: Extending the Engine
text:
5. Registering a Custom Resolver (Plugins)
Custom models do not require a fork of mlsysim. Package the code as a standard Python module and register it via pyproject.toml entry points. When a user installs the package, mlsysim automatically discovers and loads its custom solvers into the engine.
In the plugin’s pyproject.toml, add:
[project.entry-points."mlsysim.solvers"]
power_efficiency = "my_custom_package.solvers:PowerEfficiencyModel"
required_bandwidth = "my_custom_package.solvers:RequiredBandwidthSolver"
cheapest_hardware = "my_custom_package.solvers:CheapestHardwareOptimizer"
After installation via pip install ., check that mlsysim has discovered the models by running:
from mlsysim.engine.resolver_factory import ResolverFactory

# This will now include 'PowerEfficiencyModel', etc.
print(ResolverFactory.list_available().keys())

title: Extending the Engine
text:
6. Testing an Extension
Every custom resolver should have at least one unit test that verifies dimensional correctness and expected output:
import pytest
from mlsysim import Hardware

def test_power_efficiency_h100():
    model = PowerEfficiencyModel()
    result = model.solve(hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100)

    assert result.flops_per_watt.units == "TFLOPs/s/W"
    assert result.flops_per_watt.magnitude > 0
    assert isinstance(result.is_efficient, bool)

def test_power_efficiency_no_tdp():
    """Hardware without TDP should raise ValueError."""
    from mlsysim.hardware.types import HardwareNode, ComputeCore, MemoryHierarchy
    from mlsysim.core.units import Q_

    hw = HardwareNode(
        name="NoTDP",
        release_year=2024,
        compute=ComputeCore(peak_flops=Q_("100 TFLOPs/s")),
        memory=MemoryHierarchy(capacity=Q_("80 GB"), bandwidth=Q_("2 TB/s")),
        tdp=None,
    )
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="has no TDP"):
        PowerEfficiencyModel().solve(hardware=hw)
Run tests with:
pytest tests/test_my_extension.py -v

title: Extending the Engine
text:
Why Strict Typing
By forcing inputs and outputs to use pint.Quantity, MLSys·im guarantees dimensional consistency. The Pipeline module uses these class signatures (requires and produces) to automatically stitch different Models, Solvers, and Optimizers together into a single execution DAG.
As a result, a custom extension automatically works with:

Engine.sweep(): sweep the model across hardware
SystemEvaluator.evaluate(): include the model in the full scorecard
The CLI: expose the extension via mlsysim eval with YAML input
Schema tooling: validate configuration files before they reach the solver

title: The Sensor Zoo
text: The Sensor Zoo lists every sensor in the mlsysim.Sensors registry. Each entry carries units and a provenance record, so the timing and bandwidth numbers that feed information-age and ingestion budgets trace back to a datasheet.

title: The Sensor Zoo
text:
Where these numbers are used
Sensor timing sets the floor on how stale an observation is by the time the system acts on it. The Volume IV chapters use these entries for information-age budgets (half the exposure plus readout, transport, and processing) and for multi-camera ingestion bandwidth. The underlying formulas are in physics.robotics.perception.

title: The Model Zoo
text: The Model Zoo defines the Computational Demand placed on the hardware. Every workload is pulled from the mlsysim.Models registry and characterized by its FLOPs, parameter count, and architecture type, independent of any specific hardware.

title: The Model Zoo
text:
Workload Types
MLSys·im supports five workload architectures, each with distinct scaling characteristics:









Type
Architecture
Key Characteristic
Example Models

NoteActive vs. Total Parameters



For Sparse/MoE models, parameters refers to total parameters (used for memory sizing), while active_parameters refers to the subset active per token (used for FLOP counting). This distinction matters: DeepSeek-V3 stores 671B total parameters but activates 37B per token, and Mixtral-8x7B stores 46.7B total parameters while activating 12.9B per forward pass.

title: The Model Zoo
section: How to Read the Model Zoo
text:
How to Read the Model Zoo

Parameters vs. Inference FLOPs
These two numbers measure different things:

Parameters determine memory footprint: at fp16, each parameter is 2 bytes. Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters) needs 141.2 GB for the weights alone, more than a single 80 GiB (85.9 GB) A100 holds.
Inference FLOPs determine compute time: the total floating-point operations for one forward pass. Higher FLOPs means more work for the GPU’s compute cores.

The ratio of FLOPs to memory accessed (the arithmetic intensity) determines whether a workload is compute-bound or memory-bound. At small batch sizes, most models are memory-bound because the weights must be loaded regardless of batch size.


Matching Models to Hardware
As a rough guide:

TinyML MCUs (192 KiB–4 MiB memory): only Tiny models fit (DS-CNN, MicroSpeech, WakeVision)
Edge devices (Jetson, 8–64 GiB): small Vision and Language models at int8
Single Cloud GPU (80–141 GiB): models up to ~30B parameters at fp16 on an 80 GiB GPU
Multi-GPU clusters: 70.6B+ models in fp16 require distributed serving or training



Textbook Connection
The Model Training and Model Serving chapters use these workload profiles to demonstrate roofline analysis and serving cost estimation. The Model Compression chapter shows how quantization reduces both parameter memory and inference FLOPs.







NoteAdding a custom model



Custom workloads are straightforward to define: extend the registry, or define a TransformerWorkload (or CNNWorkload, SSMWorkload, DiffusionWorkload) object directly in code. Learn more in the Contributing Guide and the Models API Reference.








TipCLI Access



Browse the Model Zoo from the terminal: mlsysim zoo models


For dynamic memory footprint and KV-cache calculations, see the API Reference.

title: The Actuator Zoo
text: The Actuator Zoo lists every entry in the mlsysim.Actuators registry: strain-wave (harmonic) joints, quasi-direct-drive modules, servos, frameless motors, and wheel hub motors. Each value carries units and a provenance record.

title: The Actuator Zoo
text:
Where these numbers are used
Reflected inertia grows with the square of the gear ratio, so the same motor reflects about 31 times as much rotor inertia behind a 50:1 strain-wave gear as behind a 9:1 quasi-direct-drive stage. The Volume IV planning and enforcement chapters use these entries for torque-jump and stopping budgets. The underlying formulas are in physics.robotics.actuation.

title: The Infrastructure Zoo
text: The Infrastructure Zoo provides the Environmental Context for ML deployments: the carbon intensity of regional electricity grids and datacenter efficiency profiles. Every value is sourced from published government energy data and IEA reporting.

title: The Infrastructure Zoo
section: How to Read the Infrastructure Zoo
text:
How to Read the Infrastructure Zoo

Carbon Intensity: The Biggest Lever
The single most impactful decision for ML sustainability is where a model is trained. Carbon intensity varies by 41× across the grids above. Quebec’s hydro-dominated grid produces 20 gCO₂/kWh, while Poland’s coal-dominated grid produces 820 gCO₂/kWh. The same model on the same hardware therefore carries a vastly different environmental cost.


PUE: The Hidden Multiplier
Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) measures how much energy the datacenter wastes on cooling and overhead. Quebec’s typical PUE of 1.06 means 6% facility overhead, whereas Poland’s typical PUE of 1.58 means 58% of IT energy is added for cooling and power delivery. Modern liquid-cooled facilities (1.06) are substantially more efficient than older air-cooled ones (1.58).


Connecting to TCO
Infrastructure specifications feed directly into both the SustainabilityModel (carbon and water footprint) and the EconomicsModel (electricity costs in TCO). Regional electricity prices vary as much as carbon intensity, a factor the TCO model accounts for.


Cloud and storage pricing anchors
Illustrative list-price anchors for TCO analyses live under Infrastructure.Pricing:

gpu_hr = mlsysim.Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.GpuTrainingPerHour
egress = mlsysim.Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.EgressPerGB
s3 = mlsysim.Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.S3StandardPerTbMonth

print(f"{gpu_hr.name}: {gpu_hr.rate:~P}")
print(f"{egress.name}: {egress.rate:~P}")
print(f"{s3.name}: {s3.rate:~P}")

Cloud GPU training: 4.0 dollar/h
Cloud egress: 0.09 dollar/GB
S3 standard: 23.0 dollar/TB/month


Each PricePoint carries metadata.provenance pointing at the book economics appendix.


Textbook Connection
The Sustainable AI chapter uses these grid profiles to quantify the carbon footprint of training runs. The Compute Infrastructure chapter connects PUE to total facility cost. Try the Geography Tutorial to explore these tradeoffs interactively.

Note: For carbon and water usage formulas, see the SustainabilityModel API Reference.

title: The MLSys Zoo
text:
System Composition Hierarchy
ML systems are structurally composed of smaller parts. The mlsysim registry reflects this physical reality. Before a workload can be evaluated, the structural components are combined into a coherent system.
Here is how the components in the Zoo relate to each other:



The Physical Composition of ML Systems in MLSys·im



HardwareNode (Silicon): The fundamental unit of compute (e.g., an H100 GPU or a DGX Spark GB10 superchip). It provides FLOPs and Memory Bandwidth.
Node: A single server chassis. It contains one or more HardwareNodes connected by a high-speed intra-node bus (like NVLink).
RackProfile: A physical rack composition. It can aggregate node count, accelerator count, accelerator power, and non-accelerator support power.
NetworkFabric: The inter-node networking (e.g., InfiniBand NDR or 100GbE) that allows servers to communicate.
Fleet (Cluster): A collection of Nodes connected by a NetworkFabric. This is the top-level entity used for distributed training and cluster reliability models.
Datacenter & GridProfile (Infrastructure/Regions): The physical facility and regional power grid that hosts the Fleet. It dictates the Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and the carbon intensity of the electricity consumed.

title: The MLSys Zoo
text:
Accessing Zoo Entries in Code
All Zoo entries follow the same registry pattern. This block runs when the site builds, so every name below is guaranteed to exist:

import mlsysim

# Hardware
a100  = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
jetson = mlsysim.Hardware.Edge.JetsonOrinNX

# Models
resnet = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
llama  = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B

# Infrastructure
quebec = mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec
virginia = mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg

# Systems (nodes/racks/fleets)
node = mlsysim.Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
rack = mlsysim.Systems.Racks.DGX_H100_4Node
cluster = mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Frontier_8K

# Agents & Embodied (Autonomous systems & robotics)
agent_runner = mlsysim.Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner
agent_platform = mlsysim.Agents.Platforms.Cloud_DGX_H100
robot = mlsysim.Embodied.Quadruped.Spot

# Platforms (deployment paradigms)
cloud_latency = mlsysim.Platforms.Cloud.latency_range_ms
mobile_ram = mlsysim.Platforms.Mobile.ram

# Literature & Ops (cited anchors, not silicon specs)
chinchilla = mlsysim.Literature.Chinchilla.TokensPerParam
psi_warn = mlsysim.Ops.Monitoring.PsiWarnThreshold

# Reusable scenario anchors (problem settings, not physical systems)
corpus_tokens = mlsysim.ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TrainingTokens

# Solver calibration (engine tuning, not zoo hardware)
ref_mfu = mlsysim.engine.calibration.REFERENCE_MFU_SUSTAINED







NoteType Safety



All quantities (FLOPs, bandwidth, capacity) are pint.Quantity objects. They convert between compatible units, and MLSys·im catches dimensional errors at runtime:

import mlsysim
hw = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
print(hw.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s"))
print(hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s"))
try:
    hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TFLOPs/s")
except Exception as err:
    print(f"{type(err).__name__}: bandwidth cannot become a FLOP rate")

312.0 TFLOPs/s
2.039 TB/s
DimensionalityError: bandwidth cannot become a FLOP rate

title: The Silicon Zoo
text: The Silicon Zoo is the authoritative registry for physical hardware in mlsysim. Every specification is typed (pint.Quantity), provenance-tracked, and validated against official datasheets and MLPerf baselines, so a figure such as the A100’s bandwidth (2.04 TB/s) has one agreed value.

title: The Silicon Zoo
section: How to Read the Silicon Zoo
text:
How to Read the Silicon Zoo

The Three Numbers That Matter
For roofline analysis, focus on three columns:

Peak Performance (TFLOP/s): the compute ceiling. This determines how fast compute-bound workloads run (e.g., large-batch training, LLM pre-fill).
Memory Bandwidth (TB/s): the memory ceiling. This determines how fast memory-bound workloads run (e.g., small-batch inference, LLM token decoding).
Capacity (GB): the memory wall. If the model plus activations exceed this, the workload is infeasible on a single device.



The Ridge Point
The ratio of Peak Performance to Memory Bandwidth gives the ridge point (in FLOP/byte), such as 153 FLOP/byte on the A100 and 295 FLOP/byte on the H100. Workloads with arithmetic intensity below the ridge point are memory-bound; above it, compute-bound. See the Math Foundations page for the full derivation.


Common Patterns

Cloud GPUs (A100, H100, H200) have 80–141 GiB of HBM with high bandwidth (2.04–4.80 TB/s). They are designed for throughput.
Edge devices (NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX at 25 W) trade peak performance for lower power budgets, making TDP per TFLOP a useful comparison metric.
TinyML MCUs (STM32F4 at 192 KiB, nRF52840 at 1 MiB) have KB- to MB-scale memory, so only the smallest quantized models fit. Use the Model Zoo to find matching workloads.



Textbook Connection
These specifications are used throughout Volumes 1 and 2 of the textbook. The Hardware Acceleration chapter uses them for roofline construction, and the Compute Infrastructure chapter uses them for fleet sizing and TCO analysis.







NoteAdding a device



Custom hardware specs can be defined on the fly in Python, and new vetted specs can be contributed to the registry. See the Contributing Guide for how to add persistent specs, or the Hardware API Reference for defining custom HardwareNode objects.








TipCLI Access



Browse the Silicon Zoo from the terminal: mlsysim zoo hardware


For full technical specs and validation details, see the API Reference.

mlsysim.core.units: pint units, byte/bit widths, precision map.
mlsysim.physics.*: physical constants and formulas.
Literature.*: cited appendix scalars (MFU bands, Chinchilla, communication, batch-size anchors).
Scenarios.*: executable workload + system + constraint bundles, suitable for Scenario.evaluate().
ReferenceStats.*: non-executable sourced anchors for real-world scenario and case-study statistics.
Systems.Reliability / Orchestration: MTTF, recovery, scheduling assumptions.
Ops.Monitoring / TrainingRunOverheads: PSI, KS, drift thresholds, training goodput-loss profiles.
mlsysim.engine.calibration: solver/engine default kwargs (not appendix tables).
Infrastructure.Pricing: cloud, storage, labeling, fleet economics (PricePoint.rate).
Regional carbon / PUE / fleet / fabrics: Infrastructure.Grids, FacilityCooling, Systems.Clusters, Systems.Fabrics.




MLSys·im is used to generate textbook calculations, so registry and CLI data are validated before they reach solver equations.

Explicit units are required for physical quantities. A capacity must be written as 80 GB or 80 GiB, not 80. A model size must be bytes, a power value must be watts, and a latency value must be time.
Compute work carries its own dimension. FLOPs (and integer-op rates such as TOPS) live on a dedicated [flop] pint dimension (2026-06-06), so 1 TFLOP/s can never silently add to or convert into 900 GB/s; pint itself raises DimensionalityError. Bytes, counts, parameters, and dollars remain dimensionless aliases, and MLSys·im’s unit-family checks keep those semantically distinct at every schema boundary.
Precision names are closed vocabulary. Use the precision names in core.units.PRECISION_MAP; unsupported values fail instead of silently using FP16 storage.
Distributed topology must divide exactly. Tensor, pipeline, and expert parallel groups must divide total accelerators without flooring. CLI fleet plans must likewise specify topology that divides cleanly.

title: The $9M Question
text:
A team wants to add chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to its production serving pipeline. The accuracy improvement is clear: \(K=8\) reasoning steps (400 reasoning tokens vs. 50 tokens at \(K=1\)) measurably improve answer quality on hard queries. The open matter is what \(K=8\) costs, measured not in tokens but in dollars, GPUs, and annual infrastructure budget. Is this an algorithm decision or a capital expenditure decision?






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 2: Two Phases, One Request and Tutorial 3: The KV Cache Wall. This tutorial assumes familiarity with TTFT, ITL, and the two-phase serving model.








NoteLearning Objectives




Calculate per-query latency and energy cost across reasoning depths \(K=1\) to \(K=16\)
Compose InferenceScalingModel with EconomicsModel for annualized fleet cost
Quantify the cost multiplier of \(K=8\) reasoning at 100 QPS fleet scale
Evaluate a routing strategy that sends easy queries to a smaller model and hard queries to an expensive reasoning model









TipBackground: Inference-Time Compute Scaling



Standard LLM inference generates one answer directly: prefill the prompt (TTFT), then decode tokens one at a time (ITL). Chain-of-thought reasoning changes this: the model generates \(K\) intermediate “thinking” steps, each producing 50 tokens, before the final answer. The cost model becomes:
\[T_{\text{reason}} = \text{TTFT} + K \times T_{\text{step}}\]
where \(T_{\text{step}} = \text{tokens\_per\_step} \times \text{ITL}\). Each step is memory-bound (decoding), so the cost scales linearly with \(K\) at the decode rate, which belongs to the memory-bandwidth-limited phase. A seemingly algorithmic choice (add more reasoning) translates directly into GPU-hours and dollars.
