title: The $9M Question
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

title: The $9M Question
text:
2. Baseline Serving: Single-Query Cost
The baseline is GPT-4 (1,760B parameters) served on NVIDIA H100 at context length 2048 with no multi-step reasoning. It gives the per-query TTFT and ITL that everything else builds on.

from mlsysim import Models, Hardware
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel
from mlsysim.show import table, info

model = Models.Language.GPT4
hardware = Hardware.Cloud.H100

serving = ServingModel()
baseline = serving.solve(
    model=model, hardware=hardware,
    seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, precision="fp16"
)

info("Baseline Serving",
     Model=f"{model.name} ({model.parameters.to('Bparam').magnitude:.0f}B params)",
     Hardware=hardware.name,
     TTFT=baseline.ttft.to('ms'),
     ITL=baseline.itl.to('ms'),
     Memory_Used=f"{baseline.memory_utilization:.0%}",
     Feasible=f"{baseline.feasible}")

── Baseline Serving ────────────────────────
Model:        GPT-4 (1760B params)
Hardware:     NVIDIA H100
TTFT:         14,645.0 ms
ITL:          1,056.8 ms
Memory Used:  4117%
Feasible:     False


For GPT-4 on NVIDIA H100, prefill TTFT is 14,645.0 ms and per-token decode ITL is 1,056.8 ms. Every reasoning step generates 50 tokens at this decode rate (52,837.7 ms per step), so the latency and energy costs accumulate in decode.

title: The $9M Question
text:
3. CoT Sweep: K=1 to K=16
The next cell sweeps reasoning depth \(K \in \{1, 4, 8, 16\}\) with the InferenceScalingModel. Each step generates 50 tokens of intermediate reasoning, and the cost multiplier grows with \(K\).

from mlsysim.solvers import InferenceScalingModel

cot_solver = InferenceScalingModel()
K_values = [1, 4, 8, 16]

baseline_time = None
results = {}
rows = []

for K in K_values:
    result = cot_solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=hardware,
        reasoning_steps=K, context_length=2048, precision="fp16"
    )
    total_ms = result.total_reasoning_time.to("ms").magnitude
    energy_j = result.energy_per_query.to("J").magnitude

    if baseline_time is None:
        baseline_time = total_ms

    multiplier = total_ms / baseline_time
    results[K] = result

    rows.append([K, f"{total_ms:.1f}ms", result.tokens_generated, f"{energy_j:.1f} J", f"{multiplier:.1f}x"])

table(["K", "Total Time", "Tokens", "Energy (J)", "Multiplier"], rows)

K   Total Time  Tokens  Energy (J)  Multiplier
──────────────────────────────────────────────
1    67482.7ms      50   47237.9 J        1.0x
4   225995.8ms     200  158197.1 J        3.3x
8   437346.6ms     400  306142.6 J        6.5x
16  860048.2ms     800  602033.8 J       12.7x


Going from \(K=1\) (50 tokens, 67,482.7 ms, 47,237.9 J) to \(K=8\) (400 tokens, 437,346.6 ms, 306,142.6 J) multiplies per-query time and energy by 6.5× (and by 12.7× at \(K=16\) with 800 tokens). The multiplier is slightly below \(K\) because each query pays one fixed TTFT (14,645.0 ms) plus \(K\) decode steps (52,837.7 ms per step).

title: The $9M Question
text:
4. Annualized Fleet Cost
Per-query cost explains the mechanism, while fleet-level cost drives the budget. The cell below computes the annual infrastructure cost of serving 100 queries per second across \(K=1\), \(K=4\), \(K=8\), and \(K=16\).

from mlsysim.solvers import EconomicsModel
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet, Node, NetworkFabric
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_

econ = EconomicsModel()
target_qps = 100

fleet_results = {}
fleet_objects = {}
rows = []
for K in K_values:
    r = results[K]
    qt_s = r.total_reasoning_time.to("s").magnitude

    # Each GPU serves one query at a time (batch_size=1)
    qps_per_gpu = 1.0 / qt_s if qt_s > 0 else 0
    gpus_needed = int(target_qps / qps_per_gpu) + 1

    # Build fleet: 8 GPUs per node
    fleet = Fleet(
        name=f"K={K} Serving",
        node=Node(
            name="H100 Node",
            accelerator=hardware,
            accelerators_per_node=8,
            intra_node_bw=Q_("900 GB/s"),
        ),
        count=max((gpus_needed + 7) // 8, 1),
        fabric=NetworkFabric(
            name="IB NDR",
            bandwidth=Q_("400 Gbps").to("GB/s"),
        )
    )

    tco = econ.solve(fleet=fleet, duration_days=365)
    fleet_results[K] = tco
    fleet_objects[K] = fleet

    rows.append([K, f"{qt_s * 1000:.1f}ms", f"{qps_per_gpu:.2f}", fleet.total_accelerators, f"${tco.tco_usd:,.0f}"])

table(["K", "Query (ms)", "QPS/GPU", "GPUs", "Annual TCO ($)"], rows)

K   Query (ms)  QPS/GPU   GPUs  Annual TCO ($)
──────────────────────────────────────────────
1    67482.7ms     0.01   6752     $70,271,265
4   225995.8ms     0.00  22600    $235,208,915
8   437346.6ms     0.00  43736    $455,181,289
16  860048.2ms     0.00  86008    $895,126,035


At 100 QPS, moving from \(K=1\) to \(K=8\) expands the required fleet from 6,752 GPUs ($70.3M annual TCO) to 43,736 GPUs ($455.2M annual TCO), and to 86,008 GPUs ($895.1M annual TCO) at \(K=16\). That jump propagates through the entire infrastructure stack: more GPUs, more power, more cooling, more network fabric, and more capital expenditure.






ImportantKey Insight



A seemingly algorithmic decision (“add more reasoning steps”) is actually an infrastructure spending decision. \(K=8\) chain-of-thought reasoning multiplies per-query latency by 6.5×, so maintaining 100 QPS scales the fleet from 6,752 to 43,736 GPUs and increases annual TCO from $70.3M to $455.2M. The decision to add CoT reasoning is not only a model architecture choice; it is a capital expenditure decision that belongs in infrastructure budget planning.

title: The $9M Question
text:
5. The Routing Argument
The $455.2M annual TCO at \(K=8\) reframes the conversation from model architecture to capital planning. It also raises the question of whether every query must pay the full reasoning cost.
In production, not every query does, and the optimization that avoids it is routing. A router sends easy queries to a smaller, faster model (Llama-3.1-70B at \(K=1\), 2,764.5 ms per query) and routes only hard queries to the full GPT-4 \(K=8\) reasoning pipeline (437,346.6 ms per query). The cell below models a 70/30 split.

# Scenario: 70% of queries go to Llama-3 70B (no reasoning, K=1)
# 30% go to GPT-4 with K=8 reasoning
model_cheap = Models.Language.Llama3_70B

# Cheap path: Llama-3 70B, K=1
r_cheap = cot_solver.solve(
    model=model_cheap, hardware=hardware,
    reasoning_steps=1, context_length=2048, precision="fp16"
)

# Expensive path: GPT-4, K=8 (already computed)
r_expensive = results[8]

# Weighted average query time
qt_cheap = r_cheap.total_reasoning_time.to("s").magnitude
qt_expensive = r_expensive.total_reasoning_time.to("s").magnitude
qt_blended = 0.70 * qt_cheap + 0.30 * qt_expensive

# Compare: all queries to GPT-4 K=8 vs. routed
qps_blended = 1.0 / qt_blended if qt_blended > 0 else 0
gpus_blended = int(target_qps / qps_blended) + 1

fleet_routed = Fleet(
    name="Routed Serving",
    node=Node(name="H100", accelerator=hardware,
              accelerators_per_node=8, intra_node_bw=Q_("900 GB/s")),
    count=max((gpus_blended + 7) // 8, 1),
    fabric=NetworkFabric(name="IB", bandwidth=Q_("400 Gbps").to("GB/s")),
)

tco_routed = econ.solve(fleet=fleet_routed, duration_days=365)
tco_all_k8 = fleet_results[8]

savings = tco_all_k8.tco_usd - tco_routed.tco_usd
pct_savings = savings / tco_all_k8.tco_usd * 100 if tco_all_k8.tco_usd > 0 else 0

table(
    ["Strategy", "GPUs", "Annual TCO ($)"],
    [
        ["All queries -> GPT-4 K=8", fleet_objects[8].total_accelerators, f"${tco_all_k8.tco_usd:,.0f}"],
        ["70/30 routed", fleet_routed.total_accelerators, f"${tco_routed.tco_usd:,.0f}"],
    ]
)
info(Savings=f"${savings:,.0f} ({pct_savings:.0f}%)")

Strategy                   GPUs  Annual TCO ($)
───────────────────────────────────────────────
All queries -> GPT-4 K=8  43736    $455,181,289
70/30 routed              13320    $138,627,555
Savings:  $316,553,733 (70%)


Routing 70% of traffic to Llama-3.1-70B (\(K=1\)) reduces the fleet from 43,736 GPUs to 13,320 GPUs and cuts annual TCO from $455.2M to $138.6M, saving $316.6M (70%). The 30% of queries that still need full reasoning continue to require dedicated GPU capacity, and the routing classifier itself introduces latency and operational complexity. Routing contains the cost multiplier, while capital planning remains essential.

title: Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
text:
The Engine.evaluate() function serves standard roofline analysis well. Some workflows, however, need to insert a proprietary power model into the middle of the evaluation, or to log every analytical result to a database or an MLOps platform like Weights & Biases.
How do we extend the core framework without forking it?






NoteLearning Objectives




Compose custom execution graphs using the Pipeline class.
Inject custom analytical solvers into the evaluation flow.
Register callback middleware to log or intercept data.

text:

Compose custom execution graphs using the Pipeline class.
Inject custom analytical solvers into the evaluation flow.

title: Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
text:
1. Setup
First, import the necessary modules. This tutorial uses the Pipeline orchestrator directly instead of relying on the high-level Engine.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.engine.pipeline import Pipeline
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel, EconomicsModel

title: Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
text:
2. The Composable Pipeline
The Pipeline object accepts a list of resolvers. Calling .run() executes them in order, and the output of an early solver is automatically made available as input to later solvers.
A standard evaluation pipeline looks like this:

# 1. Define the execution graph
pipe = Pipeline([
    DistributedModel(),
    EconomicsModel()
])

# 2. Provide the initial inputs (Demand & Supply)
results = pipe.run(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Frontier_8K,
    batch_size=32,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=0.45,
    duration_days=30
)

# 3. Access results by stage name
tco = results["EconomicsModel"].tco_usd
print(f"Total Cost of Ownership: ${tco:,.2f}")

Total Cost of Ownership: $7,007,509.16


For Llama-3.1-8B on the 8,192-GPU Frontier Cluster (8192 GPUs) cluster over 30 days, DistributedModel computes a scaling efficiency of 64.4% and feeds into EconomicsModel, which reports a 30-day TCO of $7,007,509.16.

title: Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
text:
3. Injecting Custom Solvers
Because the pipeline is dynamic, it accepts custom analytical solvers. Suppose a custom plugin called PowerEfficiencyModel has been written (as described in the Extending the Engine guide).
It slots directly into the DAG:
# Assuming a custom ForwardModel subclass is defined:
# class PowerEfficiencyModel(ForwardModel): ...

custom_pipe = Pipeline([
    DistributedModel(),
    PowerEfficiencyModel(), # Injected right into the middle
    EconomicsModel()
])

# Use it just like before
# custom_pipe.run(...)

title: Composable Pipelines & Callbacks
text:
4. Callbacks (Middleware)
MLSys·im supports middleware hooks. To log metrics to an external platform (like a database, MLflow, or Weights & Biases), write a Callback class with an on_stage_end method.
The pipeline will trigger this method every time a solver finishes.

class WandbLogger:
    def on_stage_end(self, stage_name: str, result):
        print(f"[W&B Callback] Logging data for {stage_name}...")

        # If the result is a Pydantic model, dump it to a dict
        if hasattr(result, "model_dump"):
            metrics = result.model_dump(exclude_none=True)

            # Example: wandb.log({f"{stage_name}/{k}": v for k, v in metrics.items()})
            print(f"  -> Logged {len(metrics)} keys")

# Attach the logger
pipe.register_callback(WandbLogger())

# Run the pipeline again to see the callback fire
print("Running Pipeline with Callback:")
_ = pipe.run(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Frontier_8K,
    batch_size=32,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=0.45,
    duration_days=30
)

Running Pipeline with Callback:
[W&B Callback] Logging data for DistributedModel...
  -> Logged 12 keys
[W&B Callback] Logging data for EconomicsModel...
  -> Logged 11 keys

title: Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE
text:
Once a roofline analysis is done, three follow-up questions appear in real design reviews:

Why does training need much more memory than inference?
How many replicas does a QPS and P99 target require?
How much does MoE hot-expert imbalance change the communication cost?

These questions are not separate systems. They are different views of the same demand–supply framework: tensors consume memory, requests consume serving capacity, and routed tokens consume network bandwidth.






NoteLearning Objectives




Break training memory into weights, gradients, optimizer state, activations, and communication buffers.
Turn a serving target into a first-pass replica count.
Sweep a simple MoE routing imbalance factor and read the all-to-all cost.
Decide which numbers are direct byte counts and which require calibration.

crumbs: Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE

title: Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE
section: 1. Training Memory Is Not Inference Memory
text:
1. Training Memory Is Not Inference Memory
Inference mainly stores model weights and KV cache. Training also stores gradients, optimizer state, activations, and communication buffers. That is why a model that fits for inference can fail during training.

from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.solvers import TrainingMemoryModel
from mlsysim.show import table

memory = TrainingMemoryModel().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    batch_size=8,
    seq_len=2048,
    dp_size=8,
    zero_stage=2,
)

rows = [
    ["Weights", memory.weights],
    ["Gradients", memory.gradients],
    ["Optimizer", memory.optimizer_state],
    ["Activations", memory.activations],
    ["Buffers", memory.communication_buffers],
    ["Total", memory.total_memory],
]

table(["Component", "Per-GPU Memory"], rows)
print(f"Fits on H100: {memory.feasible}")

Component    Per-GPU Memory
───────────────────────────
Weights            16.06 GB
Gradients           2.01 GB
Optimizer          12.04 GB
Activations         9.13 GB
Buffers            0.100 GB
Total              39.34 GB
Fits on H100: True


The first three terms (16.1 GB of weights, 2.0 GB of gradients, and 12.0 GB of optimizer state per rank under ZeRO-2 across 8 data-parallel ranks) are direct byte counts, bringing total per-GPU demand to 39.3 GB (45.8% of the H100’s 86 GB HBM). Activation memory (9.1 GB) is the term most sensitive to framework behavior because checkpointing changes what the backward pass must store versus recompute.
crumbs: Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE

title: Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE
text:
2. Serving Capacity Combines Three Walls
A serving deployment is not sized by TTFT alone. Sizing also requires base request latency, per-replica token capacity, and queueing pressure under load.

from mlsysim.solvers import ServingCapacityModel

capacity = ServingCapacityModel().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    qps=20,
    target_p99_latency_ms=2000,
    max_seq_len=1024,
    output_tokens=64,
    max_batch_size=16,
    efficiency=0.35,
)

print(f"Required replicas: {capacity.required_replicas}")
print(f"Capacity:          {capacity.qps_capacity:.1f} QPS")
print(f"Utilization:       {capacity.utilization:.1%}")
print(f"Estimated P99:     {capacity.estimated_p99_latency:~.1f}")
print(f"Bottleneck:        {capacity.bottleneck}")

Required replicas: 1
Capacity:          43.4 QPS
Utilization:       46.0%
Estimated P99:     1317.3 ms
Bottleneck:        Feasible


At 20 QPS with a 2000 ms P99 target, 1 H100 replica suffices (43.4 QPS capacity at 46.0% utilization, combining 1154 ms base request latency and 163 ms queueing wait for an estimated P99 of 1317 ms). The efficiency parameter is exposed because the compute-bound part of serving depends on implementation quality. Use the default for quick comparisons; use a measured efficiency value before making a production SLA commitment.
crumbs: Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE

title: Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE
text:
3. MoE Routing Imbalance
Mixture-of-Experts models reduce compute by activating only a subset of experts, but routed tokens create expert-parallel all-to-all traffic. Perfectly balanced routing is an idealization; hot experts increase the effective active work and the routed payload.

from mlsysim import Systems, ureg
from mlsysim.solvers import MoERoutingModel
from mlsysim.models.types import SparseTransformerWorkload

moe = SparseTransformerWorkload(
    name="Toy-MoE-64B",
    architecture="Sparse Transformer",
    parameters=64e9 * ureg.count,
    active_parameters=8e9 * ureg.count,
    experts=8,
    active_experts_per_token=2,
    layers=32,
    hidden_dim=4096,
    heads=32,
)

rows = []
routing_by_gamma = {}
for gamma in [1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 2.0]:
    routing = MoERoutingModel().solve(
        model=moe,
        batch_size=4,
        seq_len=2048,
        ep_size=8,
        routing_imbalance_factor=gamma,
        fleet=Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
    )
    routing_by_gamma[gamma] = routing
    rows.append([
        gamma,
        f"{routing.effective_active_experts:.2f}",
        routing.token_dispatch_bytes,
        routing.all_to_all_latency,
    ])

table(["Imbalance", "Effective Experts", "Routed Bytes", "All-to-All"], rows)

Imbalance  Effective Experts  Routed Bytes  All-to-All
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.00                    2.00      117.4 MB     9.75 ms
1.25                    2.50      146.8 MB    12.09 ms
1.50                    3.00      176.2 MB    14.44 ms
2.00                    4.00      234.9 MB    19.14 ms


This model does not simulate a router. It provides a clean sensitivity knob: if measured routing logs show a 25% hot-expert effect, setting routing_imbalance_factor=1.25 increases the routed payload from 117.4 MB to 146.8 MB and raises all-to-all communication latency from 9.75 ms to 12.09 ms.
crumbs: Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE

title: Training Memory, Serving Capacity, and MoE
text:
4. What Counts as Validation
For these models, validation means matching the level of the approximation:







Output
How to validate




Weight, gradient, optimizer, KV-cache bytes
Compare against direct tensor counts.


Activation memory
Compare against framework memory traces for one model/config.


Serving replica count
Benchmark one deployment point, calibrate efficiency, then sweep.


MoE routing imbalance
Measure tokens per expert and feed the observed imbalance into the model.



MLSys·im should be used to identify the binding constraint and compare design options before benchmarking. It should not replace empirical measurement for a final production SLA.

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
A fundamentally different architecture can change which wall binds. GPUs are weight-stationary: weights live in HBM (80 GiB at 3.35 TB/s on NVIDIA H100), and the bottleneck is HBM capacity and bandwidth. The Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3) takes the opposite approach: it is activation-stationary, holding activations on 44 GiB of on-wafer SRAM (21 PB/s) and streaming weights from external MemoryX nodes (1.2 TB/s). Does this eliminate the memory wall, or does it move the wall somewhere else?






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 0: Hello, Roofline, Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall, and Tutorial 9: Sensitivity Analysis. This tutorial assumes familiarity with roofline analysis, binding constraints, and sensitivity-based investment decisions.








NoteLearning Objectives




Compare GPU and Cerebras architectures on the same workload using different solvers
Identify that the binding constraint shifts from HBM bandwidth to injection bandwidth
Compute the optimal batch size \(B^*\) where injection and compute overlap perfectly
Explain why this is a qualitative regime change, not only a quantitative speedup









TipBackground: Two Philosophies of Memory



Conventional GPUs use a two-level memory hierarchy: fast but small on-chip SRAM (registers, L1/L2 cache) and large but slower off-chip HBM. The central idea of wafer-scale computing is to make the chip large enough that SRAM alone can hold the working set. The Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3) is an entire silicon wafer (46,225 \(\text{mm}^2\) vs. ~800 \(\text{mm}^2\) for an NVIDIA H100 die) with 44 GiB of on-wafer SRAM delivering 21 PB/s of bandwidth and 125 PFLOP/s of peak compute across 900,000 cores.
GPU (weight-stationary): Model weights live in HBM (80 GiB at 3.35 TB/s on NVIDIA H100). At each decode step, the entire model streams from HBM to the compute units. Activations are small and transient. Bottleneck: HBM capacity and bandwidth.
Cerebras WSE-3 (activation-stationary): Activations and KV-cache live on the 44 GiB of on-wafer SRAM. However, 44 GiB cannot hold a 350 GB model (GPT-3 (175B) at FP16), so weights must stream in layer-by-layer from external MemoryX nodes, dedicated memory boxes connected to the wafer via the SwarmX / MemoryX interconnect (1.2 TB/s). Bottleneck: injection bandwidth from MemoryX.
Same model, same math, completely different performance physics.

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import SingleNodeModel
from mlsysim.solvers import WeightStreamingModel, SensitivitySolver

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
2. GPU Baseline: H100 Inference
The workload is GPT-3 (175B) (175B parameters across 96 layers), a model large enough that architectural differences in how weights reach compute become the dominant factor. At batch size 1, each decode step must stream all 350 GB of FP16 weights.

from mlsysim.solvers import SingleNodeModel
from mlsysim.solvers import WeightStreamingModel, SensitivitySolver
from mlsysim.show import table, info, banner

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.GPT3
gpu_hw = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100

gpu_solver = SingleNodeModel()
gpu_result = gpu_solver.solve(
    model=model, hardware=gpu_hw,
    batch_size=1, precision="fp16"
)

info("GPU Baseline",
     Model=f"{model.name} ({model.parameters.to('Bparam').magnitude:.0f}B)",
     Hardware=gpu_hw.name,
     Bottleneck=gpu_result.bottleneck,
     Latency=gpu_result.latency.to('ms'),
     HBM_BW=gpu_hw.memory.bandwidth.to('TB/s'),
     Peak_FLOPS=gpu_hw.compute.peak_flops.to('TFLOPs/s'))

── GPU Baseline ────────────────────────────
Model:       GPT-3 (175B) (175B)
Hardware:    NVIDIA H100
Bottleneck:  Memory
Latency:     6,016.6 ms
HBM BW:      3.35 TB/s
Peak FLOPS:  989 TFLOPs/s


At batch size 1, GPT-3 (175B) performs 2 FLOPs per parameter per token and must stream 175B parameters (350 GB at FP16). Its arithmetic intensity is 0.91 FLOP/byte, far below the NVIDIA H100 ridge point of 295.2 FLOP/byte. Because 350 GB exceeds a single NVIDIA H100’s 80 GiB HBM capacity, single-device execution spills over PCIe (64 GB/s) for a latency of 6,016.6 ms, and even across a multi-GPU node where weights fit in 3.35 TB/s HBM, pure weight transfer requires 104.5 ms while the 989 TFLOP/s compute units take 0.71 ms.

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
section: 3. Cerebras Path: Weight Streaming on WSE-3
text:
3. Cerebras Path: Weight Streaming on WSE-3
The next cell analyzes the same model on the Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3). Instead of loading weights from HBM, the WSE-3 streams them from MemoryX nodes over the 1.2 TB/s SwarmX / MemoryX interconnect.

ws_hw = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.Cerebras_CS3
ws_solver = WeightStreamingModel()

ws_result = ws_solver.solve(
    model=model, hardware=ws_hw,
    seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, precision="fp16"
)

info("Cerebras WSE-3",
     Hardware=ws_hw.name,
     Feasible=ws_result.feasible,
     Bottleneck=ws_result.bottleneck,
     Throughput=f"{ws_result.throughput_tokens_per_sec:.1f} tokens/sec",
     Layer_compute_time=ws_result.layer_compute_time.to('ms'),
     Layer_injection_time=ws_result.layer_injection_time.to('ms'),
     Optimal_batch_size=ws_result.optimal_batch_size,
     SRAM_utilization=f"{ws_result.wafer_memory_utilization:.1%}")

── Cerebras WSE-3 ──────────────────────────
Hardware:              Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3)
Feasible:              True
Bottleneck:            Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound
Throughput:            3.4 tokens/sec
Layer compute time:    1.06e-03 ms
Layer injection time:  3.04 ms
Optimal batch size:    52083
SRAM utilization:      22.5%


The WSE-3 reports two times per layer: how long the wafer takes to compute one layer (1.06 µs at 125 PFLOP/s), and how long it takes to inject that layer’s weights from MemoryX (3.04 ms at 1.2 TB/s). The bottleneck is whichever is slower: at batch size 1, injection takes 2,871× longer than compute.

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
4. Side-by-Side: Where the Wall Shifts

gpu_lat_ms = gpu_result.latency.to('ms').magnitude
# Cerebras total decode: max(inject, compute) per layer * num_layers
ws_layer_time = max(
    ws_result.layer_injection_time.to('ms').magnitude,
    ws_result.layer_compute_time.to('ms').magnitude
)
ws_total_ms = ws_layer_time * model.layers
speedup = gpu_lat_ms / ws_total_ms if ws_total_ms > 0 else 0

table(
    ["Metric", "H100 (GPU)", "CS-3 (WSE)"],
    [
        ["Bottleneck", gpu_result.bottleneck, ws_result.bottleneck],
        ["Total decode time (ms)", f"{gpu_lat_ms:.2f}", f"{ws_total_ms:.2f}"],
        ["Speedup", "1.0x", f"{speedup:.1f}x"],
        ["Optimal batch B*", "N/A", ws_result.optimal_batch_size],
    ]
)

Metric                  H100 (GPU)                    CS-3 (WSE)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Bottleneck                  Memory  Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound
Total decode time (ms)     6016.60                        291.67
Speedup                       1.0x                         20.6x
Optimal batch B*               N/A                         52083


The GPU and WSE-3 hit fundamentally different walls:

GPU (NVIDIA H100): Limited by HBM capacity (80 GiB) and HBM bandwidth (3.35 TB/s)
WSE-3 (Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3)): Limited by MemoryX injection bandwidth (1.2 TB/s, requiring 291.67 ms across 96 layers)

The optimization strategies therefore differ completely. On the GPU, optimization reduces the bytes loaded (quantization, smaller models, tensor parallelism). On the WSE-3, it overlaps injection with compute by increasing batch size toward \(B^* = 52\,083\).






ImportantKey Insight



The binding constraint is not a property of the model but a property of the model-architecture pair. GPUs are bound by HBM capacity and bandwidth (3.35 TB/s on NVIDIA H100). Cerebras CS-3 (WSE-3) eliminates the HBM wall entirely (activations stay in 44 GiB of 21 PB/s on-wafer SRAM) and replaces it with an injection bandwidth wall (1.2 TB/s from MemoryX). This is a qualitative regime change: the wall shifted, it did not disappear. When evaluating any novel architecture, the question is not “is it faster?” but “which wall does it move, and what new wall does it create?”

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
text:
5. The SRAM Ceiling: Finding B*
The WSE-3 has a distinct optimization knob: batch size controls how much compute is performed per weight injection. At the theoretical balance point \(B^* = 52\,083\), per-layer compute time matches the 3.04 ms injection time. Activations and KV-cache, however, must fit in 44 GiB of on-wafer SRAM, and that limit is the SRAM ceiling.

rows = []
for batch in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]:
    r = ws_solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=ws_hw,
        seq_len=2048, batch_size=batch, precision="fp16"
    )
    rows.append([
        batch, r.bottleneck,
        f"{r.throughput_tokens_per_sec:.1f}/s",
        f"{r.wafer_memory_utilization:.1%}",
        "YES" if r.feasible else "OOM"
    ])

table(["Batch", "Bottleneck", "Throughput", "SRAM Util", "Feasible"], rows)

Batch                    Bottleneck  Throughput  SRAM Util  Feasible
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1      Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       3.4/s      22.5%       YES
2      Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       6.9/s      45.0%       YES
4      Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound      13.7/s      90.0%       YES
8      Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s     180.0%       OOM
16     Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s     360.0%       OOM
32     Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s     720.0%       OOM
64     Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s    1440.0%       OOM
128    Interconnect-Bandwidth-Bound       0.0/s    2880.0%       OOM


At sequence length 2048, a single request consumes 22.5% of the 44 GiB on-wafer SRAM (3.4 tokens/s). Increasing batch size to 4 raises throughput to 13.7 tokens/s at 90.0% SRAM utilization, and at batch size 8 the KV-cache demand reaches 180.0% of wafer SRAM (OOM), long before reaching \(B^* = 52\,083\).

title: GPU vs. Wafer-Scale
section: 6. Sensitivity Confirmation: Different Walls, Different Levers
text:
6. Sensitivity Confirmation: Different Walls, Different Levers
Running SensitivitySolver on NVIDIA H100 confirms how the GPU walls behave: for GPT-3 (175B) (350 GB), single-device execution binds on memory_capacity, and for an HBM-resident model (Llama-3.1-8B), it binds on memory_bandwidth (-0.0856).

sens_solver = SensitivitySolver()
gpu_sens = sens_solver.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B, hardware=gpu_hw, precision="fp16"
)

banner(f"GPU Sensitivity ({gpu_hw.name}, HBM-Resident {mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B.name})")
info(Baseline_latency=gpu_sens.baseline_latency.to('ms'),
     Binding_constraint=gpu_sens.binding_constraint)

sens_rows = [[param, f"{val:+.4f}"] for param, val in gpu_sens.sensitivities.items()]
table(["Parameter", "Sensitivity"], sens_rows)

banner("Cerebras WSE-3")
info(Binding_constraint="injection bandwidth (MemoryX -> wafer)",
     Optimization_lever="increase batch size within on-wafer SRAM capacity")

print()
print("Different architectures -> different walls -> different strategies.")


=== GPU Sensitivity (NVIDIA H100, HBM-Resident Llama-3.1-8B) ===
Baseline latency:    5.60 ms
Binding constraint:  memory_bandwidth
Parameter         Sensitivity
─────────────────────────────
peak_flops            +0.0000
memory_bandwidth      -0.0856
memory_capacity       +0.0000

=== Cerebras WSE-3 ===
Binding constraint:  injection bandwidth (MemoryX -> wafer)
Optimization lever:  increase batch size within on-wafer SRAM capacity

Different architectures -> different walls -> different strategies.








WarningThe Deeper Lesson



When evaluating novel architectures (wafer-scale, photonic, analog, neuromorphic), the diagnostic question is not “Is it faster?” but “Which wall does it move, and what new wall does it create?” Every architecture eliminates one bottleneck by introducing another.

title: The Memory Wall
text:
NVIDIA’s H100 has 3.2× more FLOP/s than the A100. Does upgrading deliver a 3.2× speedup?
It does not. For the workloads that matter most in production (LLM inference, recommendation models, any memory-bound task), the speedup is closer to 1.6× (tracking the 1.6× HBM bandwidth ratio). This tutorial shows why, and how to predict the actual speedup before spending a dollar on hardware.






NotePrerequisites

Calculate the actual speedup between two GPUs for a given workload
Explain why the binding constraint determines which spec matters
Predict whether a hardware upgrade will help a specific model

title: The Memory Wall
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

title: The Memory Wall
text:
2. Side-by-Side Hardware Comparison
Load both GPUs from the Silicon Zoo and confirm the specs:

from mlsysim.show import table

a100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
h100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100

flops_a = a100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
flops_h = h100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
bw_a = a100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
bw_h = h100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude

table(
    ["Spec", "A100", "H100", "Ratio"],
    [
        ["Peak FP16 (TFLOP/s)", flops_a, flops_h, f"{flops_h/flops_a:.1f}x"],
        ["HBM BW (TB/s)", bw_a, bw_h, f"{bw_h/bw_a:.1f}x"],
        ["Ridge (FLOP/byte)", f"{ridge_a:.1f}", f"{ridge_h:.1f}", f"{ridge_h/ridge_a:.1f}x"]
    ]
)

Spec                  A100   H100  Ratio
────────────────────────────────────────
Peak FP16 (TFLOP/s)  312.0  989.0   3.2x
HBM BW (TB/s)         2.04   3.35   1.6x
Ridge (FLOP/byte)    153.0  295.2   1.9x


The FLOP/s ratio is 3.2× (989 vs. 312 TFLOP/s), whereas the bandwidth ratio is only 1.6× (3.35 vs. 2.04 TB/s). The theoretical ridge point also shifts from 153.0 to 295.2 FLOP/byte: the H100 has a higher ridge, meaning more workloads fall into the memory-bound regime on the H100 than on the A100.

title: The Memory Wall
text:
3. The Fallacy: LLM Inference Speedup
The “3.2× speedup” claim can be tested with a workload that dominates production today, Llama-3 8B inference at batch size 1:

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B

# Solve on both GPUs
prof_a100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=a100, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")
prof_h100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=h100, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")

lat_a = prof_a100.latency.to("ms").magnitude
lat_h = prof_h100.latency.to("ms").magnitude
speedup = lat_a / lat_h

table(
    ["", "A100", "H100", "Speedup"],
    [
        ["Bottleneck", prof_a100.bottleneck, prof_h100.bottleneck, ""],
        ["Latency", prof_a100.latency.to("ms"), prof_h100.latency.to("ms"), f"{speedup:.1f}x"],
        ["Throughput", prof_a100.throughput, prof_h100.throughput, ""]
    ]
)

                 A100       H100  Speedup
─────────────────────────────────────────
Bottleneck     Memory     Memory         
Latency       9.00 ms    5.60 ms     1.6x
Throughput  111.1 1/s  178.5 1/s         


Both GPUs report memory-bound. The actual speedup is approximately 1.6× (9.00 ms vs. 5.60 ms), close to the 1.6× bandwidth ratio rather than the 3.2× FLOP/s ratio. The remaining 2.0× of the H100’s compute advantage goes unused for this workload.
Sanity check: Llama-3 8B at FP16 has 8.03B parameters × 2 bytes = 16.06 GB of weights. On the A100 (2.04 TB/s), pure weight-streaming latency is 16.06 GB ÷ 2.04 TB/s = 7.9 ms (9.0 ms in Engine.solve after activation traffic and kernel launch tax). On the H100 (3.35 TB/s), pure weight-streaming latency is 16.06 GB ÷ 3.35 TB/s = 4.8 ms (5.6 ms in Engine.solve). The weight-streaming speedup is 7.9 / 4.8 = 1.64×, matching the bandwidth ratio, as expected for a memory-bound workload.

title: The Memory Wall
section: 4. When 3.2× Matters: The Batch Size Crossover
text:
4. When 3.2× Matters: The Batch Size Crossover
The FLOP/s advantage takes effect only once the workload crosses into the compute-bound regime. Sweeping batch size on both GPUs locates the crossover:

rows = []
for batch in [1, 4, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]:
    pa = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=a100, batch_size=batch, precision="fp16")
    ph = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=h100, batch_size=batch, precision="fp16")

    la = pa.latency.to("ms").magnitude
    lh = ph.latency.to("ms").magnitude
    sp = la / lh if lh > 0 else 0
    ai = pa.arithmetic_intensity.to("flop/byte")

    rows.append([batch, f"{ai:~.1f}", pa.bottleneck, ph.bottleneck, f"{sp:.1f}x"])

table(["Batch Size", "Arithmetic Intensity", "A100 Bottleneck", "H100 Bottleneck", "Actual Speedup"], rows)

Batch Size  Arithmetic Intensity  A100 Bottleneck  H100 Bottleneck  Actual Speedup
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1                   0.9 flop / B           Memory           Memory            1.6x
4                   2.9 flop / B           Memory           Memory            1.6x
16                  6.2 flop / B           Memory           Memory            1.6x
32                  7.6 flop / B           Memory           Memory            1.6x
64                  8.6 flop / B           Memory           Memory            1.6x
128                 9.3 flop / B           Memory           Memory            1.6x
256                 9.6 flop / B           Memory           Memory            1.6x


At batch size 256, where both GPUs are compute-bound, the speedup reaches 1.6×, approaching the 3.2× compute ratio. The roofline plot below shows where Llama-3 8B at batch size 1 sits on the H100 relative to its 295.2 FLOP/byte ridge point:

from mlsysim.viz.plots import plot_roofline

# Plot the H100 roofline and see where Llama-3 8B (batch 1) falls
fig, ax = plot_roofline(h100, workloads=[model])














ImportantKey Insight



The binding constraint determines which hardware spec matters. For a memory-bound workload, speedup scales with the bandwidth ratio (1.6×). For a compute-bound workload, speedup scales with the FLOP/s ratio (up to 3.2×). The transition happens at different batch sizes on each GPU because the H100’s higher ridge point (295.2 vs. 153.0 FLOP/byte) means it stays memory-bound longer. In a procurement decision, the first question is not “how many FLOP/s?” but “which regime will the production workload operate in?”

title: The Memory Wall
text:
5. The Procurement Table: Three Generations
Extending the analysis across three GPU generations shows the trend:

gpus = [
    ("V100", mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.V100),
    ("A100", mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100),
    ("H100", mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100),
]

rows = []
for name, hw in gpus:
    p = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=hw, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")
    flops = hw.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
    bw = hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
    ridge = (hw.compute.peak_flops / hw.memory.bandwidth).to("flop/byte").magnitude
    rows.append([name, flops, bw, f"{ridge:.1f}", p.latency.to("ms"), p.bottleneck])

table(["GPU", "TFLOP/s", "BW (TB/s)", "Ridge", "Latency", "Bottleneck"], rows)

GPU   TFLOP/s  BW (TB/s)  Ridge   Latency  Bottleneck
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
V100    125.0     0.9000  138.9  19.97 ms      Memory
A100    312.0       2.04  153.0   9.00 ms      Memory
H100    989.0       3.35  295.2   5.60 ms      Memory


Across three generations (from 125 TFLOP/s and 0.9 TB/s on the V100 to 989 TFLOP/s and 3.35 TB/s on the H100), compute has grown 7.9× while bandwidth has grown 3.7×. The theoretical ridge point rises from 138.9 to 153.0 to 295.2 FLOP/byte, which means more workloads are memory-bound on newer hardware. This is the memory wall, and it is getting steeper with each generation.

title: The Memory Wall
text:

title: Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
text:
What does a complete systems analysis look like? No single solver captures the full picture. Training a 71B-parameter model (Llama-3.1-70B) on 512 NVIDIA H100 GPUs involves compute walls, memory walls, communication overhead, checkpoint I/O, energy costs, and carbon emissions, all simultaneously. This tutorial traces all six taxonomy domains and exercises 12 of the 22 systems walls through a single workload.






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 0: Hello, Roofline, Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall, Tutorial 6: Scaling to 1000 GPUs, and Tutorial 9: Sensitivity Analysis. This tutorial assumes familiarity with roofline analysis, distributed training, and binding constraint identification.








NoteLearning Objectives




Compose six solver families across all taxonomy domains into a holistic analysis
Identify which of the 22 systems walls bind for a real training workload
Quantify the hidden costs: checkpoint overhead, carbon, water, and TCO

title: Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
text:
1. Setup: Build the Fleet
We construct a 512-GPU training cluster: 64 DGX H100 nodes, 8 GPUs per node, NVLink intra-node (900 GB/s), InfiniBand NDR inter-node (400 Gbps), powered by Quebec (Hydro)’s hydroelectric grid (20 g CO2/kWh).
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet, Node, NetworkFabric
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_

from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet, Node, NetworkFabric
from mlsysim.infrastructure.registry import Grids
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B
h100 = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100
ib_ndr = mlsysim.Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR

# Build the DGX H100 node: 8 GPUs connected by NVLink 4.0
node = Node(
    name="DGX H100",
    accelerator=h100,
    accelerators_per_node=8,
    intra_node_bw=h100.nvlink.bandwidth
)

# Build the cluster fabric: InfiniBand NDR
fabric = NetworkFabric(
    name="InfiniBand NDR",
    topology="fat-tree",
    bandwidth=ib_ndr.bandwidth
)

# Build the fleet: 64 nodes = 512 GPUs, Quebec grid
fleet = Fleet(
    name="Training Cluster",
    node=node,
    count=64,
    fabric=fabric,
    region=Grids.Quebec
)

from mlsysim.show import table, info, banner

info("Fleet Configuration",
     Model=f"{model.name} ({model.parameters.to('Bparam'):.1f~})",
     Fleet=f"{fleet.count} nodes x {node.accelerators_per_node} GPUs = {fleet.total_accelerators} GPUs",
     Intra_node=f"NVLink 4.0 ({h100.nvlink.bandwidth.to('GB/s'):.0f~})",
     Inter_node=f"IB NDR ({ib_ndr.bandwidth.to('Gbps'):.0f~})",
     Region=Grids.Quebec.name)

── Fleet Configuration ─────────────────────
Model:       Llama-3.1-70B (70.6 Bparam)
Fleet:       64 nodes x 8 GPUs = 512 GPUs
Intra node:  NVLink 4.0 (900 GB / s)
Inter node:  IB NDR (400 Gbps)
Region:      Quebec (Hydro)

title: Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
text:
2. Node (Walls 1–3): Single-GPU Roofline
The first step evaluates an unsharded Llama-3.1-70B forward pass on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU.

from mlsysim.solvers import SingleNodeModel

node_solver = SingleNodeModel()
node_result = node_solver.solve(
    model=model, hardware=h100,
    batch_size=4, precision="fp16"
)

banner("Domain: Node (Walls 1-3)")
info(Feasible=node_result.feasible,
     Required_memory=node_result.memory_footprint.to('GiB'),
     Available_memory=h100.memory.capacity.to('GiB'),
     Bottleneck=node_result.bottleneck,
     Per_GPU_latency=node_result.latency.to('ms'),
     Throughput=f"{node_result.throughput.to('1/s').magnitude:.1f} samples/s")


=== Domain: Node (Walls 1-3) ===
Feasible:          False
Required memory:   131.5 GiB
Available memory:  80 GiB
Bottleneck:        Memory
Per GPU latency:   3,089.6 ms
Throughput:        1.3 samples/s


At 70.6B parameters, Llama-3.1-70B weights alone require 141.2 GB in FP16, exceeding a single NVIDIA H100’s 80 GiB (85.9 GB) HBM capacity (feasible = False). Because the unsharded model spills across PCIe (64 GB / s), SingleNodeModel reports Memory-bound at 3089.6 ms per step (1.3 samples/s).
Wall 2 (Memory Capacity) and Wall 3 (Memory Bandwidth) immediately rule out unsharded single-GPU execution and force intra-node tensor parallelism (TP=8 in Section 5). The next question is whether the storage and preprocessing pipeline can keep up with 512 GPUs demanding training tokens.

title: Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
section: 3. Data (Walls 8–10): Whether the Pipeline Can Keep Up
text:
3. Data (Walls 8–10): Whether the Pipeline Can Keep Up
The storage and preprocessing pipeline must deliver tokenized batches at least as fast as the cluster consumes them. If it cannot, the GPUs stall.

from mlsysim.solvers import DataModel

# Estimate data demand per step: 4 samples/GPU * 512 GPUs * 2048 tokens * 2 bytes ≈ 8 MB/step
data_demand = Q_("8 MB/s")

data_solver = DataModel()
data_result = data_solver.solve(
    workload_data_rate=data_demand,
    hardware=h100
)

banner("Domain: Data (Walls 8-10)")
info(Data_demand=data_result.demand_bw,
     Data_supply=data_result.supply_bw,
     Utilization=f"{data_result.utilization:.2%}",
     Stalled=data_result.is_stalled,
     Bottleneck=data_result.bottleneck)


=== Domain: Data (Walls 8-10) ===
Data demand:  8.00e-03 GB/s
Data supply:  7 GB/s
Utilization:  0.11%
Stalled:      False
Bottleneck:   Storage


At 8 MB / s demand against 7.0 GB / s storage bandwidth, storage utilization is only 0.11% (is_stalled = False). For text-based training, the data pipeline is rarely the bottleneck because tokenized text is compact; for image or video training, this wall can dominate.
The remaining question is whether the 30-day compute budget on 512 GPUs is allocated optimally according to scaling laws.

title: Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
text:
4. Algorithm (Walls 11–13): Compute-Optimal Budget
The test of whether this training budget is compute-optimal is the Chinchilla scaling law, which prescribes \(D = 20P\) (tokens = \(20\times\) parameters) for optimal allocation.

from mlsysim.solvers import ScalingModel

# MFU (Model FLOP Utilization): the fraction of peak hardware FLOP/s that goes
# to useful model computation (excluding communication, idle time, overhead).
# MFU = 0.4 means 40% of theoretical peak.
gpu_flops = h100.compute.peak_flops.to("flop/s").magnitude
total_flops = fleet.total_accelerators * gpu_flops * 30 * 86400 * 0.4
compute_budget = Q_(total_flops, "flop")

scaling_solver = ScalingModel()
scaling_result = scaling_solver.solve(
    compute_budget=compute_budget,
    target_model_size=model.parameters
)

banner("Domain: Algorithm (Walls 11-13)")
info(Compute_budget=compute_budget.to('EFLOP'),
     Optimal_tokens=f"{scaling_result.optimal_tokens.magnitude:.2e}",
     Tokens_per_parameter=f"{scaling_result.tokens_per_parameter:.1f}",
     Chinchilla_ratio=f"{'OVER' if scaling_result.tokens_per_parameter > 20 else 'UNDER'}-trained")


=== Domain: Algorithm (Walls 11-13) ===
Compute budget:        525,002.3 EFLOP
Optimal tokens:        1.24e+12
Tokens per parameter:  17.6
Chinchilla ratio:      UNDER-trained


With 512 GPUs at 989 TFLOP/s peak FP16 and 40% MFU over 30 days, the compute budget reaches 525002 EFLOP, funding 1.24T tokens (17.6 tokens per parameter, slightly below the Chinchilla 20 tokens/parameter ratio). If the tokens-per-parameter ratio is significantly above or below 20, the training budget is not optimally allocated: over-training wastes compute, while under-training wastes model capacity.

title: Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
text:
5. Fleet (Walls 14–16): Communication and Reliability
Sharding Llama-3.1-70B with TP=8 within each DGX H100 node (PP=1, DP=64 across the 64 nodes) divides the weights across 8 GPUs per replica. The distributed solver models both the replica’s 2,048-token forward-backward pass and the AllReduce communication overhead, while the reliability solver computes cluster MTBF and optimal checkpoint intervals.

from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel, ReliabilityModel

# 3D parallelism: TP=8 (within node), PP=1, DP=64
dist_solver = DistributedModel()
dist_result = dist_solver.solve(
    model=model, fleet=fleet,
    batch_size=2048, precision="fp16",
    tp_size=8, pp_size=1,
    overlap_comm=True, seq_len=2048
)

banner("Domain: Fleet (Walls 14-16)")
info(Replica_bottleneck=dist_result.node_profile.bottleneck,
     Replica_compute_latency=dist_result.node_profile.latency.to('ms'),
     Scaling_efficiency=f"{dist_result.scaling_efficiency:.2%}",
     Step_latency=dist_result.step_latency_total.to('ms'),
     DP_comm_latency=dist_result.dp_communication_latency.to('ms'),
     TP_comm_latency=dist_result.tp_communication_latency.to('ms'),
     Bubble_fraction=f"{dist_result.bubble_fraction:.2%}")


=== Domain: Fleet (Walls 14-16) ===
Replica bottleneck:       Compute
Replica compute latency:  7,019.9 ms
Scaling efficiency:       90.06%
Step latency:             7,794.6 ms
DP comm latency:          695.6 ms
TP comm latency:          670.3 ms
Bubble fraction:          0.00%



# Reliability: 30-day training job
rel_solver = ReliabilityModel()
rel_result = rel_solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet,
    job_duration_hours=30*24,
    checkpoint_time_s=120
)

info(Fleet_MTBF=rel_result.fleet_mtbf.to('hour'),
     Failure_probability=f"{rel_result.failure_probability:.2%}",
     Expected_failures=f"{rel_result.expected_failures:.1f}",
     Optimal_ckpt_interval=rel_result.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('minute'))

Fleet MTBF:             83.71 h
Failure probability:    99.98%
Expected failures:      8.6
Optimal ckpt interval:  141.7 min


With TP=8 across each node, the 2,048-token forward-backward pass is Compute-bound (7019.9 ms replica compute latency), and overlapping DP AllReduce (695.6 ms unoverlapped) with backward compute plus intra-node TP AllReduce (670.3 ms) yields a 7794.6 ms step time and 90.06% scaling efficiency.
At 512 GPUs, however, the cluster MTBF shrinks to 83.7 h, with 8.6 expected failures over the 30-day run (99.98% failure probability) and an optimal Young-Daly checkpoint interval of 141.7 min. Checkpoint overhead and rollback recovery become a non-trivial fraction of wall-clock time—the hidden cost that single-node analysis misses entirely.

title: Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
text:
6. Ops (Walls 17–20): TCO, Energy, Carbon, Water
The economics solver combines CapEx, OpEx, and sustainability into a single financial model.

from mlsysim.solvers import EconomicsModel, SustainabilityModel

# 30-day training run
econ_solver = EconomicsModel()
econ_result = econ_solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet,
    duration_days=30,
    grid=Grids.Quebec,
    mfu=0.4
)

banner("Domain: Ops (Walls 17-20)")
info(CapEx=f"${econ_result.capex_usd:,.0f}",
     OpEx_energy=f"${econ_result.opex_energy_usd:,.0f}",
     OpEx_maintenance=f"${econ_result.opex_maintenance_usd:,.0f}",
     Total_TCO=f"${econ_result.tco_usd:,.0f}")


=== Domain: Ops (Walls 17-20) ===
CapEx:             $350,685
OpEx energy:       $19,038
OpEx maintenance:  $52,603
Total TCO:         $422,325



sust_solver = SustainabilityModel()
sust_result = sust_solver.solve(
    fleet=fleet,
    duration_days=30,
    datacenter=Grids.Quebec,
    mfu=0.4
)

info(IT_Energy=sust_result.it_energy_kwh.to('MWh'),
     Total_Energy_PUE=sust_result.total_energy_kwh.to('MWh'),
     Carbon_footprint=f"{sust_result.carbon_footprint_kg:.0f} kg CO2",
     Water_usage=f"{sust_result.water_usage_liters:.0f} liters",
     PUE=sust_result.pue,
     Region=sust_result.region_name)

IT Energy:         149.7 MWh
Total Energy PUE:  158.6 MWh
Carbon footprint:  3173 kg CO2
Water usage:       0 liters
PUE:               1.06
Region:            Quebec (Hydro)


For the 30-day run, EconomicsModel reports $422,325 in total TCO ($350,685 amortized CapEx, $19,038 energy OpEx, and $52,603 maintenance OpEx). Quebec (Hydro)’s hydroelectric grid (20 g CO2/kWh, PUE 1.06) keeps total emissions to 3,173 kg CO2 (3.2 tonnes across 158.6 MWh of facility energy). The same run in Poland (820 g CO2/kWh, PUE 1.58) produces 193,910 kg CO2 (193.9 tonnes, 61× higher), making infrastructure geography a first-class engineering variable.

title: Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
text:
7. Analysis (Walls 21–22): Sensitivity and Synthesis
Finally, run SensitivitySolver on a single NVIDIA H100 and SynthesisSolver for a 200 ms step latency target.

from mlsysim.solvers import SensitivitySolver, SynthesisSolver

# Sensitivity: check the single-GPU binding constraint for unsharded Llama-3.1-70B
sens_solver = SensitivitySolver()
sens_result = sens_solver.solve(
    model=model, hardware=h100, precision="fp16"
)

banner("Domain: Analysis (Walls 21-22)")
info(Binding_constraint=sens_result.binding_constraint)

sens_rows = [[param, f"{val:+.4f}"] for param, val in sens_result.sensitivities.items()]
table(["Parameter", "Sensitivity"], sens_rows)


=== Domain: Analysis (Walls 21-22) ===
Binding constraint:  memory_capacity
Parameter         Sensitivity
─────────────────────────────
peak_flops            +0.0000
memory_bandwidth      +0.0000
memory_capacity       +0.0000



# Synthesis: minimum hardware specs for a 200 ms single-step target
synth_solver = SynthesisSolver()
synth_result = synth_solver.solve(
    model=model,
    target_latency=Q_("200 ms"),   # per-GPU step target
    precision="fp16"
)

info("Synthesis (200ms step target)",
     Required_BW=synth_result.required_bw.to('TB/s'),
     Required_FLOPS=synth_result.required_flops.to('TFLOPs/s'),
     Required_memory=synth_result.required_memory.to('GB'))

Required BW:      0.706 TB/s
Required FLOPS:   1.41 TFLOPs/s
Required memory:  141.2 GB


On an unsharded single NVIDIA H100, SensitivitySolver identifies memory_capacity as the binding constraint because the 141.2 GB FP16 weight footprint exceeds 80 GiB (85.9 GB), pinning all small local perturbations at PCIe offload bandwidth until model parallelism (TP=8) brings the per-GPU footprint inside HBM.

title: Full-Stack Audit: LLaMA-70B Training
text:
8. Summary Table: The Complete Picture
We have now traced a single workload through all six domains. Each solver answered one question in isolation. The systems engineer’s job, however, is synthesis: seeing the complete picture at once. The table below is that picture, and its most important property is that no single row captures the full story.

mtbf_hours = rel_result.fleet_mtbf.to('hour').magnitude
summary_rows = [
    ["Node",      "SingleNodeModel",      f"Bottleneck: {node_result.bottleneck}",              "Wall 2/3: Memory"],
    ["Data",      "DataModel",            f"Util: {data_result.utilization:.2%}",               "Not binding"],
    ["Algorithm", "ScalingModel",         f"Tok/param: {scaling_result.tokens_per_parameter:.1f}","Wall 11"],
    ["Fleet",     "DistributedModel",     f"Efficiency: {dist_result.scaling_efficiency:.0%}",   "Wall 14: Comm"],
    ["Fleet",     "ReliabilityModel",     f"MTBF: {mtbf_hours:.0f}h",                           "Wall 16: Ckpt"],
    ["Ops",       "EconomicsModel",       f"TCO: ${econ_result.tco_usd:,.0f}",                  "Wall 19: Cost"],
    ["Ops",       "SustainabilityModel",  f"CO2: {sust_result.carbon_footprint_kg:.0f} kg",     "Wall 18: Carbon"],
    ["Analysis",  "SensitivitySolver",    f"Binding: {sens_result.binding_constraint}",         "Wall 21"],
]

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Node       SingleNodeModel            Bottleneck: Memory  Wall 2/3: Memory
Data       DataModel                         Util: 0.11%       Not binding
Algorithm  ScalingModel                  Tok/param: 17.6           Wall 11
Fleet      DistributedModel              Efficiency: 90%     Wall 14: Comm
Fleet      ReliabilityModel                    MTBF: 84h     Wall 16: Ckpt

ImportantKey Insight



No single solver captures the full picture; the systems view emerges from composition. This end-to-end trace exercises 12 of 22 walls through a single model. At the single-GPU level, memory capacity (141.2 GB vs. 80 GiB) forces tensor parallelism (TP=8), where each 8-GPU replica is compute-bound (7020 ms per step at 90% scaling efficiency). The hidden costs only appear at fleet scale: a 83.7 h cluster MTBF forces checkpoints every 142 min, and infrastructure geography (Quebec (Hydro) vs. Poland (Coal)) changes grid carbon intensity by 41× and PUE-adjusted carbon emissions by 61× (as Tutorial 7 demonstrated). A complete systems analysis is not one solver run but the composition of all six domains.

title: The Differential Explainer
text:
1. Setup
Import the necessary modules. The tutorial uses the standard Engine to get the baseline and proposed profiles, and the DifferentialExplainer to compare them.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.engine.engine import Engine
from mlsysim.engine.explainers import DifferentialExplainer

title: The Differential Explainer
text:
2. A Memory-Bound Upgrade (The Disappointment)
The classic scenario is a hardware upgrade for LLM inference at a low batch size. For Llama-3.1-8B at batch size 1, both GPUs sit in the memory-bound regime, so the 1.61× speedup tracks the 1.64× HBM bandwidth ratio rather than the 3.2× compute ratio:

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B

# Get the two profiles
prof_a100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100, batch_size=1)
prof_h100 = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100, batch_size=1)

# Ask the explainer what happened
explanation = DifferentialExplainer.compare_performance(
    baseline=prof_a100,
    proposal=prof_h100
)

print(explanation)

📊 Differential Analysis: Proposal vs. Baseline
• Speedup: 1.61x
• Baseline Regime: Memory
• Proposal Regime: Memory

Analysis: The workload remained Memory Bound. The speedup is constrained strictly by the ratio of HBM bandwidth between the two configurations. Any additional compute capacity (FLOP/s) in the proposal was left unutilized.

title: The Differential Explainer
text:
3. Compute-Bound Scaling and Regime Shifts
For a high-intensity workload such as ResNet-50 at batch size 256, both GPUs operate in the compute-bound regime, giving a 2.94× speedup that approaches the 3.2× peak compute ratio:

cnn = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50

# At batch size 256, both GPUs are compute-bound
prof_a100_batch = Engine.solve(model=cnn, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100, batch_size=256)
prof_h100_batch = Engine.solve(model=cnn, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100, batch_size=256)

explanation_batch = DifferentialExplainer.compare_performance(
    baseline=prof_a100_batch,
    proposal=prof_h100_batch
)

print(explanation_batch)

📊 Differential Analysis: Proposal vs. Baseline
• Speedup: 2.94x
• Baseline Regime: Compute
• Proposal Regime: Compute

Analysis: The workload remained Compute Bound. The speedup is constrained strictly by the ratio of peak arithmetic throughput (FLOP/s) between the two configurations. Additional memory bandwidth was not the limiting factor.


When an upgrade crosses the ridge point—such as ResNet-50 at batch size 1, where the NVIDIA A100 is Compute-bound (0.57 ms) and the NVIDIA H100’s 3.2× higher compute ceiling shifts the bottleneck to Memory (0.53 ms, a 1.08× speedup)—DifferentialExplainer flags the Regime Shift automatically:

prof_a100_b1 = Engine.solve(model=cnn, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100, batch_size=1)
prof_h100_b1 = Engine.solve(model=cnn, hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100, batch_size=1)

print(DifferentialExplainer.compare_performance(baseline=prof_a100_b1, proposal=prof_h100_b1))

📊 Differential Analysis: Proposal vs. Baseline
• Speedup: 1.08x
• Baseline Regime: Compute
• Proposal Regime: Memory

Analysis: Regime Shift. The proposed hardware provided enough compute capacity to lift the compute wall, exposing a memory bandwidth bottleneck. The speedup is a blended result of higher compute and the new memory ceiling.

title: KV-Cache: The Hidden Tax
text:
Llama-3.1-8B is deployed on an 80 GiB (85.9 GB) NVIDIA H100 or NVIDIA A100. The model weights take 16.06 GB (15.0 GiB), leaving 69.8 GB (65.0 GiB) free. Can that GPU serve dozens of users concurrently?
Not if they have long contexts. Every active user requires a KV-cache that grows linearly with sequence length. At 128K context, a single user’s GQA KV-cache takes 17.18 GB (16 GiB), exceeding the model weights and capping concurrency at 4 users (or 1 user at 68.7 GB / 64 GiB without GQA). This tutorial shows where the real memory wall lies and how to push it back.






NotePrerequisites



Complete Tutorial 1: The Memory Wall and Tutorial 2: Two Phases, One Request. This tutorial assumes familiarity with memory-bound vs. compute-bound regimes and the two-phase LLM serving model.








NoteLearning Objectives




Calculate the KV-cache size for any model, sequence length, and batch size
Identify the OOM boundary where KV-cache exhausts GPU memory
Explain why context length, not model size, is the binding memory constraint in serving
Compare static batching vs. paged attention for maximizing concurrent users









TipBackground: The KV-Cache



During LLM decoding, every attention layer stores Key and Value matrices for all tokens generated so far. In data-structure terms, this is memoization applied to the attention mechanism: store computed results instead of recomputing them. The names come from a database-style lookup: the Query is what is searched for, the Key is what it is matched against, and the Value is what is retrieved. Without this cache, the model would need to recompute attention over the entire context at every step, at quadratic cost. The KV-cache trades memory for compute:



Factor
Effect on KV-Cache




More layers
Linear growth (one K + one V per layer)


Longer context
Linear growth (one entry per token)


More users (batch)
Linear growth (independent cache per user)


Lower precision
Proportional reduction (INT8 = half of FP16)



The formula is KV-cache = 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x seq_len x batch x bytes_per_element (or 2 * 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim bytes per token in FP16). At short contexts this is negligible. At long contexts it dominates everything.
Note on GQA (Grouped Query Attention): Modern architectures like Llama-3 use GQA, where kv_heads < num_heads. Llama-3.1-8B has 32 layers and 32 attention heads (head dimension 128), yet only 8 KV-heads, reducing the FP16 KV-cache by 4× compared to standard multi-head attention (MHA): from 524,288 bytes (512 KiB) per token under MHA down to \(2 \times 2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 = 131\,072\;\text{bytes}\) (128 KiB) per token under GQA. Using num_heads instead of kv_heads in the formula is a common source of 4× overestimates.

title: KV-Cache: The Hidden Tax
text:
1. Setup
import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

title: KV-Cache: The Hidden Tax
section: 2. Single-User Baseline: Where the Memory Goes
text:
2. Single-User Baseline: Where the Memory Goes
The starting point is a single user at a modest 2K context, which shows how memory breaks down:

from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B
hardware = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100
solver = ServingModel()

# Single user, 2K context — the easy case
r = solver.solve(model=model, hardware=hardware, seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, precision="fp16")

from mlsysim.show import table, info

info("Memory Breakdown",
     Model_weights=r.model_weights_size,
     KV_cache_1_user=r.kv_cache_size,
     Total_memory=r.total_memory_required,
     Memory_utilization=f"{r.memory_utilization:.1%}",
     KV_as_pct_of_total=f"{(r.kv_cache_size / r.total_memory_required).magnitude * 100:.1f}%")

── Memory Breakdown ────────────────────────
Model weights:       16.06 GB
KV cache 1 user:     0.268 GB
Total memory:        16.33 GB
Memory utilization:  19.0%
KV as pct of total:  1.6%


At 2K context with one user, the KV-cache is 0.268 GB (1.6% of total memory), a small fraction of the 16.06 GB model weights (and at 4K context it is 0.537 GB, or 0.50 GiB). This is why many engineers assume memory pressure comes from model size, an assumption the next two sweeps overturn.

title: KV-Cache: The Hidden Tax
section: 3. Batch Size Sweep: The Concurrency Wall
text:
3. Batch Size Sweep: The Concurrency Wall
Adding users changes the picture. Each concurrent user needs its own KV-cache, so HBM occupancy climbs with batch size:

rows = []
for batch in [1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]:
    r = solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=hardware,
        seq_len=2048, batch_size=batch, precision="fp16"
    )
    rows.append([batch, r.kv_cache_size, r.total_memory_required,
                 f"{r.memory_utilization:.1%}", "OK" if r.feasible else "OOM"])

table(["Batch", "KV-Cache", "Total", "Util", "Feasible"], rows)

Batch  KV-Cache     Total   Util  Feasible
──────────────────────────────────────────
1      0.268 GB  16.33 GB  19.0%        OK
4       1.07 GB  17.13 GB  19.9%        OK
8       2.15 GB  18.21 GB  21.2%        OK
16      4.29 GB  20.35 GB  23.7%        OK
32      8.59 GB  24.65 GB  28.7%        OK
64     17.18 GB  33.24 GB  38.7%        OK
128    34.36 GB  50.42 GB  58.7%        OK


At 2K context, up to 260 concurrent users fit on an 80 GiB (85.9 GB) A100 or H100 (and up to 130 users at 4K context). The KV-cache per user is small enough that batch size scales comfortably. The picture changes sharply, however, once the context grows.

title: KV-Cache: The Hidden Tax
section: 4. Context Length Sweep: The Real Memory Wall
text:
4. Context Length Sweep: The Real Memory Wall
Fix batch size at 8 users and sweep context length from 512 tokens to 128K. This sweep exposes the hidden tax:

rows = []
for ctx in [512, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768, 65536, 131072]:
    r = solver.solve(
        model=model, hardware=hardware,
        seq_len=ctx, batch_size=8, precision="fp16"
    )
    rows.append([ctx, r.kv_cache_size, r.model_weights_size,
                 r.total_memory_required, f"{r.memory_utilization:.1%}",
                 "OK" if r.feasible else "OOM"])

table(["Context", "KV-Cache", "Weights", "Total", "Util", "Status"], rows)

Context  KV-Cache   Weights     Total    Util  Status
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
512      0.537 GB  16.06 GB  16.60 GB   19.3%      OK
2048      2.15 GB  16.06 GB  18.21 GB   21.2%      OK
4096      4.29 GB  16.06 GB  20.35 GB   23.7%      OK
8192      8.59 GB  16.06 GB  24.65 GB   28.7%      OK
16384    17.18 GB  16.06 GB  33.24 GB   38.7%      OK
32768    34.36 GB  16.06 GB  50.42 GB   58.7%      OK
65536    68.72 GB  16.06 GB  84.78 GB   98.7%      OK
131072   137.4 GB  16.06 GB  153.5 GB  178.7%     OOM








ImportantKey Insight



KV-cache grows linearly with sequence length and batch size. It is the hidden memory consumer that determines the maximum number of concurrent users: not model size, not compute, but cache state. At 2K context, the cache is 0.268 GB per user; at 4K context, 0.537 GB (0.50 GiB). At 128K context, a single user’s cache is 17.18 GB (16 GiB), exceeding the 16.06 GB model weights. The same 80 GiB (85.9 GB) GPU that serves 260 users at 2K context (130 at 4K) can serve at most 4 users at 128K context with 4× GQA (and 1 user under standard MHA). The “context length” on the model card is not a feature but a memory bill.


The extreme case is a single user at 128K:

# Single user at 128K context — the extreme case
r_long = solver.solve(
    model=model, hardware=hardware,
    seq_len=131072, batch_size=1, precision="fp16"
)

info("Single User @ 128K Context",
     Context="131,072 tokens (128K)",
     Model_weights=r_long.model_weights_size,
     KV_cache=r_long.kv_cache_size,
     Total=r_long.total_memory_required,

KV cache:            17.18 GB
Total:               33.24 GB
Feasible:            True
KV as pct of total:  52%

title: KV-Cache: The Hidden Tax
section: 5. Paged Attention: Pushing Back the Wall
text:
5. Paged Attention: Pushing Back the Wall
The KV-cache fills memory fast, and at long contexts a GPU runs out of memory with only a handful of users. Buying more memory is not the only option, because the allocation strategy itself wastes space. Most sequences do not use the maximum context length, yet static batching reserves memory for the worst case.
Static batching allocates contiguous memory for the maximum sequence length, wasting space on incomplete sequences. PagedAttention (from vLLM) allocates KV-cache in small, fixed-size pages, in the same way an operating system uses virtual memory paging to avoid physical memory fragmentation. Much as the OS maps virtual pages to physical frames on demand, PagedAttention maps KV-cache blocks to GPU memory on demand, eliminating fragmentation and fitting more concurrent requests.
An experiment tests the claim with two allocators competing for the same memory budget. The worst-case context is fixed at 8K tokens, but request lengths are drawn from a long-tailed distribution in which most requests are far shorter than the worst case, the workload for which static allocation wastes the most memory.
Set up the KV math. Reuse the model and GPU from the Silicon Zoo and compute the cache cost of a single token:

import random
from mlsysim import Q_
from mlsysim.show import table

model = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B
hardware = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100

# KV cache bytes per token (FP16): 2 (K+V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x 2 bytes
head_dim = model.hidden_dim // model.heads
bytes_per_token = 2 * model.layers * model.kv_heads * head_dim * 2
max_seq = 8192  # worst-case context length we must support
kv_budget = hardware.memory.capacity - model.size_in_bytes()  # HBM left after weights
budget_tokens = int(kv_budget.to("byte").magnitude // bytes_per_token)

The two allocators. Static contiguous reserves a full max_seq slot per request, whether the request needs it or not. Paged hands out fixed-size blocks on demand, so a request pays only for the blocks it fills:

def paged_blocks(tokens, page):
    """Whole blocks needed for `tokens` tokens (ceiling division)."""
    return -(-tokens // page)


def sample_lengths(seed, n, mean=2048, cap=max_seq):
    """n request lengths from a long-tailed distribution (avg well below the cap)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [max(1, min(cap, int(rng.expovariate(1 / mean)))) for _ in range(n)]


class StaticAllocator:
    """Static contiguous KV: every request reserves a full max_seq slot up front."""

    def __init__(self, budget_tokens, max_seq):
        self.budget = budget_tokens
        self.max_seq = max_seq
        self.reserved = 0
        self.used_tokens = 0
        self.admitted = []

    def admit(self, tokens):
        if self.reserved + self.max_seq <= self.budget:
            self.reserved += self.max_seq
            self.used_tokens += tokens
            self.admitted.append(tokens)
            return True
        return False


class PagedAllocator:
    """Paged KV: fixed-size blocks handed out on demand from a free-block pool."""

    def __init__(self, budget_tokens, page):
        self.page = page
        self.free_blocks = budget_tokens // page
        self.used_tokens = 0
        self.admitted = []

    def admit(self, tokens):
        need = paged_blocks(tokens, self.page)
        if need <= self.free_blocks:
            self.free_blocks -= need
            self.used_tokens += tokens
            self.admitted.append(tokens)
            return True
        return False

Same memory budget, two strategies. Feed both allocators the same stream of requests in arrival order until the next request no longer fits, and watch where the memory goes:

def fill(alloc, lengths):
    """Admit requests in arrival order; stop at the first one that does not fit."""
    for t in lengths:
        if not alloc.admit(t):
            break
    return alloc


lens = sample_lengths(seed=42, n=10_000)

static = fill(StaticAllocator(budget_tokens, max_seq), lens)
paged16 = fill(PagedAllocator(budget_tokens, 16), lens)
paged64 = fill(PagedAllocator(budget_tokens, 64), lens)
paged256 = fill(PagedAllocator(budget_tokens, 256), lens)


def kv_tokens(alloc):
    if isinstance(alloc, StaticAllocator):
        return alloc.reserved
    return sum(paged_blocks(t, alloc.page) * alloc.page for t in alloc.admitted)


def internal_frag_pct(alloc):
    return 1 - alloc.used_tokens / kv_tokens(alloc)


def decode_throughput(alloc):
    # Memory-bound decode (Tutorial 2): weights + used KV streamed once per token
    step_bytes = model.size_in_bytes().magnitude + alloc.used_tokens * bytes_per_token
    step_sec = step_bytes / hardware.memory.bandwidth.to("byte/s").magnitude
    return len(alloc.admitted) / step_sec


rows = []
for label, alloc in [(f"Static (reserve {max_seq // 1024}K)", static), ("Paged (16 tok)", paged16),
                     ("Paged (64 tok)", paged64), ("Paged (256 tok)", paged256)]:
    rows.append([label, len(alloc.admitted),
                 f"{Q_(kv_tokens(alloc) * bytes_per_token, 'byte').to('GiB'):~.1f}",
                 f"{internal_frag_pct(alloc):.1%}",
                 f"{decode_throughput(alloc):,.0f} t/s"])

table(["System", "Max Users", "KV Allocated", "Int Frag", "Throughput"], rows)

System               Max Users  KV Allocated  Int Frag  Throughput
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Static (reserve 8K)         65      65.0 GiB     77.8%   6,894 t/s
Paged (16 tok)             259      64.8 GiB      0.4%  10,162 t/s
Paged (64 tok)             255      64.4 GiB      1.5%  10,152 t/s
Paged (256 tok)            245      64.8 GiB      6.0%  10,075 t/s








ImportantKey Insight



The same 65 GiB KV budget serves 65 users at 77.8% internal fragmentation with static reservation, or 259 users at 0.4% with 16-token pages. Static pays for the worst case (8K) on every request even though the average request is ~4× shorter; paged pays for what is used. The extra concurrency buys 1.47× decode throughput under the memory-bound model from Tutorial 2.


The second kind of waste: external fragmentation. The static allocator above never suffers from this, because every freed slot is a full max_seq and fits any request. That is the trade it makes, paying in internal waste instead. A contiguous allocator that hands out exact sizes avoids the reservation waste but fragments under churn: requests finish out of order, leaving holes too small for the next long request. Paged allocation never fragments this way. Any free block works, so external fragmentation is ~0:

class FirstFitAllocator:
    """Contiguous exact-size allocation: variable-size chunks, first-fit, holes merge on free."""

    def __init__(self, budget_tokens):
        self.budget = budget_tokens
        self.holes = [(0, budget_tokens)]
        self.allocated = {}
        self._next_id = 0

    def admit(self, tokens):
        for i, (s, sz) in enumerate(self.holes):
            if sz >= tokens:
                self.holes.pop(i)
                if sz > tokens:
                    self.holes.insert(i, (s + tokens, sz - tokens))
                self.allocated[self._next_id] = (s, tokens)
                self._next_id += 1
                return True
        return False

    def free(self, rid):
        s, sz = self.allocated.pop(rid)
        self.holes.append((s, sz))
        self.holes.sort()
        merged = []
        for s, sz in self.holes:
            if merged and merged[-1][0] + merged[-1][1] == s:
                merged[-1] = (merged[-1][0], merged[-1][1] + sz)
            else:
                merged.append((s, sz))
        self.holes = merged

    def external_frag_pct(self):
        free = sum(sz for _, sz in self.holes)
        largest = max((sz for _, sz in self.holes), default=0)
        return 0.0 if free == 0 else 1 - largest / free


class PagedPool:
    def __init__(self, budget_tokens, page):
        self.page = page
        self.free_blocks = budget_tokens // page
        self.admitted = []

    def admit(self, tokens):
        need = paged_blocks(tokens, self.page)
        if need <= self.free_blocks:
            self.free_blocks -= need
            self.admitted.append(tokens)
            return True
        return False

    def free(self, tokens):
        self.free_blocks += paged_blocks(tokens, self.page)


rng = random.Random(777)
first_fit = FirstFitAllocator(budget_tokens)
paged = PagedPool(budget_tokens, 16)

# Fill both pools in arrival order until each is full, then complete every other
# request (finish out of order — the churn that fragments contiguous memory).
# Both pools admit a prefix of the same wave, so index i is the same request in each.
wave = [rng.randint(256, max_seq) for _ in range(400)]
fill(first_fit, wave)
fill(paged, wave)

n_done = min(len(first_fit.allocated), len(paged.admitted))
for i in range(0, n_done, 2):
    first_fit.free(i)
    paged.free(paged.admitted[i])

# A fresh wave of worst-case requests arrives — who can still admit them?
new_reqs = [max_seq] * 10
ff_adm = sum(first_fit.admit(t) for t in new_reqs)
pg_adm = sum(paged.admit(t) for t in new_reqs)
free_ff = int(sum(sz for _, sz in first_fit.holes))
table(["System", "External Frag", "Free Tokens", f"New {max_seq // 1024}K Req. Admitted"],
      [["Contiguous (first-fit)", f"{first_fit.external_frag_pct():.1%}", free_ff, f"{ff_adm}/10"],
       ["Paged (16 tok)", "~0%", int(paged.free_blocks * 16), f"{pg_adm}/10"]])

System                  External Frag  Free Tokens  New 8K Req. Admitted
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Contiguous (first-fit)          97.1%       268270                  1/10
Paged (16 tok)                    ~0%       194080                 10/10


Page size: the fragmentation knob. Page size trades waste against bookkeeping. Small pages leave a smaller unused tail on each sequence; large pages mean fewer block-table entries per sequence but waste more. Sweep the page size and watch both:

rows = []
by_page = {}
for page in [8, 16, 64, 256, 1024]:
    a = fill(PagedAllocator(budget_tokens, page), lens)
    by_page[page] = a
    n = len(a.admitted)
    blocks_per_req = sum(paged_blocks(t, page) for t in a.admitted) / n
    rows.append([page, n, f"{internal_frag_pct(a):.1%}", f"{blocks_per_req:.1f}",
                 paged_blocks(max_seq, page), f"{kv_tokens(a) / budget_tokens:.1%}"])

table(["Page Size", "Max Users", "Int Frag", "Avg Blocks/Req",
       f"Blocks/{max_seq // 1024}K Seq", "Pool Used"], rows)

Page Size  Max Users  Int Frag  Avg Blocks/Req  Blocks/8K Seq  Pool Used
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8                259      0.2%           255.7           1024      99.4%
16               259      0.4%           128.1            512      99.6%
64               255      1.5%            32.3            128      99.0%
256              245      6.0%             8.5             32      99.6%
1024             209     22.0%             2.5              8      99.2%


16-token pages (vLLM’s default) sit at the sweet spot: 0.4% waste, with about 128 blocks for an average request and 512 for a full 8K sequence. Going to 1024-token pages shrinks the block table 64-fold (8 entries for a full 8K sequence) but burns 22.0% of the cache as slack and serves 50 fewer users, the wrong trade for long-tail workloads.
The third trick: sharing. Because blocks are first-class, sequences can share them. Eight requests that begin with the same 1K-token system prompt (or eight beam-search branches that fork from one prefix) can point at the same blocks via reference counts (copy-on-write) instead of storing the prefix eight times:

prefix, gen, n_req = 1024, 512, 8

rows = []
static_kv = n_req * max_seq
no_share = n_req * paged_blocks(prefix + gen, 16) * 16
shared = paged_blocks(prefix, 16) * 16 + n_req * paged_blocks(gen, 16) * 16
for label, kv in [("Static (reserve max)", static_kv),
                  ("Paged, no sharing", no_share),
                  ("Paged + shared prefix", shared)]:
    rows.append([label, f"{Q_(kv * bytes_per_token, 'byte').to('MiB'):~.1f}",
                 f"{kv / static_kv:.1%}"])

table(["Scheme", "KV Allocated", "vs Static"], rows)

Scheme                 KV Allocated  vs Static
──────────────────────────────────────────────
Static (reserve max)     8192.0 MiB     100.0%
Paged, no sharing        1536.0 MiB      18.8%
Paged + shared prefix     640.0 MiB       7.8%


Sharing the prefix cuts peak KV from 1536 MiB to 640 MiB, a 58% saving that grows with the number of concurrent requests sharing the prompt. Production systems call this prefix caching; it is why shared system prompts and few-shot examples are cheap to serve.
Paged attention therefore attacks the memory wall from three directions at once: it eliminates reservation waste (77.8% → 0.4% internal fragmentation), survives churn with ~0 external fragmentation, and shares common prefixes across requests. This is why vLLM and TensorRT-LLM default to paged KV-cache management in production.
