title: For Engineers & Researchers
text: MLSys·im produces quick, type-safe analytical estimates for capacity planning, hardware selection, cost modeling, and sustainability analysis, in seconds and from specifications alone. Equations are documented and tied to the relevant literature; hardware registry specs come from datasheets where available.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Why Use Analytical Models
Before running expensive benchmarks or provisioning cloud instances, an engineer needs directional answers:

Will this model fit in GPU memory? Check before renting the GPU
Why does training fail when inference fits? Separate weights, gradients, optimizer state, and activations
What is the expected TTFT for my LLM? Estimate before building the serving stack
How many replicas do I need for a P99 target? Size serving capacity before benchmarking
What is the MoE routing tax? Sweep expert imbalance before choosing EP topology
How many H100s do I actually need? Model scaling efficiency before buying the cluster
What will this cost per year? TCO analysis before signing the contract
How often will my training job crash? Reliability modeling before committing to a 30-day run
What is the carbon footprint of this deployment? Quantify before the sustainability review

MLSys·im answers these in microseconds using first-order equations. It does not replace profiling, but it shows where to start profiling.






TipTheory Behind the Tools



Each solver implements equations from the Math Foundations page. For the full conceptual framework, see the companion slide decks linked in the Solver-to-Slides Map below.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Quick Start: Roofline Analysis
The Engine implements the Roofline Performance Model (Williams et al. 2009) to classify workloads as compute-bound or memory-bound.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

# Single-node: Is ResNet-50 memory-bound on A100?
profile = Engine.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100,
    batch_size=1, precision="fp16"
)
print(f"{profile.bottleneck}, {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"MFU: {profile.mfu:.1%}, Arithmetic Intensity: {profile.arithmetic_intensity:~.2f}")

Compute, 0.57 ms
MFU: 4.6%, Arithmetic Intensity: 145.84 flop / B


The returned PerformanceProfile reports latency, throughput, bottleneck classification, Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU), arithmetic intensity, energy, and a feasibility flag, which together support a first-pass hardware assessment.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
LLM Serving Analysis
The ServingModel models the two-phase LLM inference lifecycle: compute-bound pre-fill and memory-bound decoding.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

serving = ServingModel()
result = serving.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=4096, batch_size=1
)
print(f"TTFT:       {result.ttft.to('ms'):~.1f}")
print(f"ITL:        {result.itl.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"KV-cache:   {result.kv_cache_size.to('GB'):~.1f}")
print(f"Feasible:   {result.feasible}")
print(f"Mem util:   {result.memory_utilization:.0%}")

TTFT:       1258.5 ms
ITL:        43.35 ms
KV-cache:   1.3 GB
Feasible:   False
Mem util:   166%


The feasibility check shows immediately whether the model plus its KV-cache fit in device memory, before an out-of-memory error appears in production.

for hw in [mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Distributed Training Analysis
The DistributedModel models 3D parallelism (data, tensor, pipeline) with communication overhead from ring all-reduce and pipeline bubbles.

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel

dist = DistributedModel()
result = dist.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
    batch_size=512, precision="fp16",
    tp_size=8, pp_size=4, microbatch_count=16
)
print(f"Scaling efficiency:  {result.scaling_efficiency:.1%}")
print(f"DP all-reduce:       {result.dp_communication_latency.to('ms'):~.1f}")
print(f"TP overhead:         {result.tp_communication_latency.to('ms'):~.1f}")
print(f"Pipeline bubble:     {result.bubble_fraction:.1%}")
print(f"Step latency:        {result.step_latency_total.to('ms'):~.1f}")

Scaling efficiency:  64.3%
DP all-reduce:       618.5 ms
TP overhead:         668.7 ms
Pipeline bubble:     15.8%
Step latency:        5456.6 ms


Tune tp_size, pp_size, and microbatch_count to find the parallelism configuration that maximizes scaling efficiency for a given cluster topology.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Composing Solvers for Real Questions
The core solvers are designed to chain. Three common engineering workflows follow.

Serving Llama-70B on H100s within budget

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel, EconomicsModel

# Step 1: Does it fit and what's the latency?
serving = ServingModel()
result = serving.solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=4096, batch_size=1
)

# Step 2: What does that fleet cost?
econ = EconomicsModel()
cost = econ.solve(
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
    duration_days=365,
    kwh_price=0.08
)
print(f"Annual TCO: ${cost.tco_usd:,.0f}")
print(f"  CapEx:    ${cost.capex_usd:,.0f}")
print(f"  OpEx:     ${cost.total_opex_usd:,.0f}")

Annual TCO: $2,593,987
  CapEx:    $2,133,333
  OpEx:     $460,653




Choosing a training region to minimize carbon

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import SustainabilityModel

sustain = SustainabilityModel()
for grid in [mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec, mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg,
             mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland]:
    r = sustain.solve(
        fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
        duration_days=30,
        datacenter=grid
    )
    carbon_tons = r.carbon_footprint.to("metric_ton").magnitude
    print(f"{grid.name:16s}  {carbon_tons:8.1f} tCO2e  "
          f"PUE={r.pue:.2f}  Water={r.water_usage_liters:,.0f} L")

Quebec (Hydro)         2.7 tCO2e  PUE=1.06  Water=0 L
US Average            62.0 tCO2e  PUE=1.12  Water=260,112 L
Poland (Coal)        167.2 tCO2e  PUE=1.58  Water=366,944 L


For the theory behind PUE, carbon intensity, and the energy hierarchy, see the Sustainable AI slide deck.


Reliability of a 30-day training run on 256 GPUs

import mlsysim
from mlsysim.solvers import ReliabilityModel

rel = ReliabilityModel()
result = rel.solve(
    fleet=mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256,
    job_duration_hours=720,       # 30 days
    checkpoint_time_s=120.0       # 2 minutes per checkpoint
)
print(f"Fleet MTBF:              {result.fleet_mtbf.to('hour'):~.1f}")
print(f"P(failure before done):  {result.failure_probability:.1%}")
print(f"Optimal ckpt interval:   {result.optimal_checkpoint_interval.to('minute'):~.1f}")
print(f"Expected failures:       {result.expected_failures:.1f}")

Fleet MTBF:              146.5 h
P(failure before done):  99.3%
Optimal ckpt interval:   187.5 min
Expected failures:       4.9


This solver implements the Young-Daly checkpoint model, which sets the checkpoint interval for long training jobs.

title: For Engineers & Researchers
For Engineers & Researchers
text:
Type Safety
All quantities are pint.Quantity objects. Unit conversions are explicit, and dimensional errors are caught at runtime:

import mlsysim
hw = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
print(hw.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s"))
print(hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s"))
try:
    hw.memory.bandwidth.to("second")
except Exception as err:
    print(f"{type(err).__name__}: bytes per second can never become seconds")

312.0 TFLOPs/s
2.039 TB/s
DimensionalityError: bytes per second can never become seconds


Pint catches physical-dimension mismatches (bytes per second can never become seconds). Since 2026-06, compute work also has its own pint dimension, so a bare .to("flop/s") on a bandwidth raises DimensionalityError directly, as does adding a FLOP rate to a memory bandwidth:

for label, attempt in [
    ("FLOP rate + bandwidth", lambda: hw.compute.peak_flops + hw.memory.bandwidth),
    ("bandwidth -> TFLOPs/s", lambda: hw.memory.bandwidth.to("TFLOPs/s")),
]:
    try:
        attempt()
        print(f"{label}: accepted (unexpected)")
    except Exception as err:
        print(f"{label}: {type(err).__name__}")

FLOP rate + bandwidth: DimensionalityError
bandwidth -> TFLOPs/s: DimensionalityError


Bytes, counts, parameters, and dollars remain dimensionless aliases, so MLSys·im additionally enforces unit-family checks at every schema boundary (require_unit_family in mlsysim.core.types) to keep those distinct. A field declared as memory bandwidth rejects a count rate, and vice versa.

title: CLI Reference
text:
Exit Codes
The CLI uses semantic exit codes so scripts and CI pipelines can react programmatically:








Code
Meaning
Example




0
Success
Analysis completed, all assertions passed


1
Bad input
Unknown model name, malformed YAML, missing required flag


2
Physics violation
A hard OOMError raised during evaluation


3
SLA violation
A constraints.assert check in the YAML failed



mlsysim eval NoSuchModel H100
echo $?  # → 1 (unknown model name)

mlsysim eval cluster.yaml   # with a constraints.assert block that fails
echo $?  # → 3






NoteFeasibility failures exit 0



A quick evaluation of an infeasible configuration (e.g. mlsysim eval Llama3_70B T4) renders the scorecard with Feasibility [FAIL] and exits 0, because the analysis itself succeeded. Exit code 2 is reserved for hard out-of-memory errors raised inside the engine. To gate CI on feasibility, use a YAML plan with a constraints.assert block (exit code 3 on violation) or parse the -o json output.

version: "1.0"
name: "llama70b-cluster"
workload:
  name: "Llama3_70B"

hardware:

title: The 5-Layer Architecture
text:
MLSys·im organizes the full ML systems domain into five composable layers. Abstract workload demand (Layer A) is progressively mapped onto concrete hardware supply (Layers B–D) through analytical solvers (Layer E). Each layer corresponds directly to chapters in the Machine Learning Systems textbook and its companion lecture slides.
Understanding this stack is the foundation for working with both this library and the textbook it accompanies.

title: The 5-Layer Architecture
text:
The Stack at a Glance






%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%%
%%| fig-cap: "The MLSys·im 5-Layer Stack. Workloads (demand) are lowered onto Hardware (supply) through Infrastructure and Systems layers. Solvers bridge demand and supply to produce analytical profiles."
%%| fig-width: 100%
flowchart TB
    A["<b>Layer A · Workloads</b> — <i>Demand</i><br/>TransformerWorkload · CNNWorkload<br/>Parameters · FLOPs · Arithmetic Intensity"]
    B["<b>Layer B · Hardware</b> — <i>Silicon</i><br/>HardwareNode · ComputeCore · MemoryHierarchy<br/>Peak FLOP/s · Bandwidth · Capacity · TDP"]
    C["<b>Layer C · Infrastructure</b> — <i>Environment</i><br/>GridProfile · Datacenter<br/>Carbon Intensity · PUE · WUE"]
    D["<b>Layer D · Systems</b> — <i>Topology</i><br/>Node · Fleet · NetworkFabric<br/>Topology · Accelerators/Node · Fabric BW"]
    E["<b>Layer E · Solvers</b> — <i>Analysis</i><br/>SingleNode · Distributed · Serving<br/>Economics · Sustainability · Reliability"]
    F["<b>Results</b><br/>PerformanceProfile · Dict[str, Quantity]"]

    A --> E
    B --> D
    C --> D
    D --> E
    E --> F

    style E fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0284c7,stroke-width:2px






The flow reads top-to-bottom: a Workload (the computation to perform) and a System (the available hardware, network, and environment) feed into a Solver (the analytical engine), which returns quantitative results that can guide a design decision.






NotePhysics formulas



Closed-form equations live in mlsysim.physics.* (performance, memory, communication, serving, economics, reliability). Pint units live in mlsysim.core.units. There is no constants module; chip, model, scenario, and system specs live only in their registries. See Math Foundations.








NoteTwo views of the same package



The five layers are the runtime view: how demand meets supply through solvers. The registries that populate Layers A–D are organized as ten zoos (Hardware, Models, Datasets, Platforms, Infrastructure, Systems, Ops, Scenarios, Embodied, Agents) plus support namespaces. That data view is documented in DATA_MODEL.md. Both descriptions are true at different altitudes.

title: The 5-Layer Architecture
text:
Layer A: Workloads (Demand)
A Workload is a hardware-agnostic description of computational demand. It states how many FLOPs and memory bytes Llama-3 requires, not how fast Llama-3 runs.
MLSys·im provides two workload types:

TransformerWorkload: LLMs and attention-based models (GPT, Llama, BERT). Defined by parameter count, layer count, hidden dimension, attention heads, and sequence length. Supports KV-cache size estimation for autoregressive inference.
CNNWorkload: Vision and convolutional models (ResNet, MobileNet, YOLO). Defined by parameter count and total FLOPs per forward pass.

The key step comes when a workload is “lowered” at a specific numerical precision (FP32, FP16, INT8, INT4). This precision lowering determines the Arithmetic Intensity (FLOPs/Byte), the single ratio that decides whether a model will be compute-bound or memory-bound on any given hardware target.






NoteTextbook and slides



Layer A concepts are covered in the following lecture decks:



Deck
Topic
Key Concepts




NN Computation (Vol I, Ch 5)
The math behind the model
FLOPs, parameter counting, activation memory, forward/backward pass cost


NN Architectures (Vol I, Ch 6)
Architecture as infrastructure
Computational signatures of CNNs, RNNs, Transformers; quadratic attention scaling


Model Compression (Vol I, Ch 10)
From benchmark winner to production model
Pruning, distillation, quantization (FP32 to INT4); precision as a workload knob


Model Training (Vol I, Ch 8)
The physics of learning
Iron Law of training, memory breakdown (activations, gradients, optimizer states)





See the Model Zoo for vetted workloads spanning language, vision, recommendation, and TinyML models.

title: The 5-Layer Architecture
text:
Layer B: Hardware (Silicon)
A HardwareNode represents a single physical accelerator, such as an H100 GPU, an Apple M3 chip, a Jetson Orin, or even an ESP32 microcontroller. It provides the raw physical supply:

Compute: Peak throughput (TFLOP/s) across precisions (FP32, FP16, INT8), modeled via ComputeCore.
Memory: HBM or SRAM capacity and transfer bandwidth (TB/s), modeled via MemoryHierarchy.
Power: Thermal Design Power (TDP) in watts.

Every piece of silicon has a ridge point, the ratio of peak compute to memory bandwidth (\(I^* = \text{Peak\_FLOPs} / \text{BW}\)). When a workload’s arithmetic intensity falls below this ridge point, the workload is memory-bound: the compute units starve waiting for data. When above, the workload is compute-bound: memory delivers data faster than the cores can consume it.
This is the Roofline model, the diagnostic framework at the heart of Layer E’s SingleNodeModel.






NoteTextbook and slides



Layer B concepts are covered in the following lecture decks:



Deck
Topic
Key Concepts




Hardware Acceleration (Vol I, Ch 11)
Moving data costs more than computing it
Systolic arrays, tensor cores, Roofline model, accelerator spectrum (GPU to ASIC)


Compute Infrastructure (Vol II, Ch 2)
The physics of the ML fleet
HBM generations, bandwidth hierarchy (HBM to NVLink to InfiniBand), TCO analysis


Benchmarking (Vol I, Ch 12)
Measuring what matters
MLPerf, roofline profiling, statistical rigor, the lab-to-production gap





See the Silicon Zoo for 30+ vetted hardware specs from cloud GPUs to microcontrollers.

title: The 5-Layer Architecture
text:
Layer C: Infrastructure (Environment)
Hardware does not run in a vacuum. It runs in datacenters plugged into regional power grids, cooled by air or liquid systems, and constrained by physical energy budgets.
A GridProfile captures this physical context:

Carbon intensity (g CO₂/kWh) varies about 41× across regions. Quebec’s hydroelectric grid produces about 20 g CO₂/kWh; Poland’s coal-dominated grid produces about 820 g CO₂/kWh.
Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) is the ratio of total facility power to IT equipment power. A PUE of 1.1 means 10% overhead for cooling and infrastructure; 1.6 means 60%.
Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) is the liters of water consumed per kWh, which is determined by cooling technology (air, liquid, evaporative).

A 1000-watt GPU running identical computations in Quebec versus Poland produces vastly different carbon footprints. This layer makes that difference quantifiable.






NoteTextbook and slides



Layer C concepts are covered in the following lecture deck:



Deck
Topic
Key Concepts




Sustainable AI (Vol II, Ch 15)
Energy as a first-class engineering constraint
Lifecycle carbon accounting, PUE modeling, carbon-aware scheduling, the 4 Ms framework





See the Infrastructure Zoo for regional grid profiles and datacenter configurations.

title: The 5-Layer Architecture
text:
Layer D: Systems (Topology)
A single GPU cannot train a 100-billion-parameter model. Layer D composes individual HardwareNodes from Layer B into distributed clusters, connected by the network fabrics that determine communication overhead.
Core system types include:

Node: A single compute server grouping accelerators within a physical chassis (e.g., 8x H100 GPUs connected by 900 GB/s NVLink). Includes intra-node bandwidth and NIC count.
RackProfile: A physical rack composition that aggregates node count, accelerator count, accelerator power, and non-accelerator support power.
NetworkFabric: The inter-node interconnect: topology (fat-tree, rail-optimized), bandwidth (e.g., 400 Gbps InfiniBand NDR), latency, and oversubscription ratio.
Fleet: A collection of Nodes connected by a NetworkFabric, deployed in a specific Datacenter (Layer C). This is the complete system that solvers operate on.

The structure of this system (how many GPUs each node holds, what fabric connects them, and which parallelism strategy runs across them) determines its communication overhead and scaling efficiency.






NoteTextbook and slides



Layer D concepts span four lecture decks covering the full distributed systems stack:

Topic
Key Concepts

\(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) model, topology (fat-tree, dragonfly), RDMA, congestion control, bisection bandwidth

AllReduce algorithms (ring, tree), gradient compression, hierarchical communication, computation-communication overlap


Distributed Training (Vol II, Ch 6)
The physics of scaling
Data/tensor/pipeline parallelism, ZeRO/FSDP, Communication-Computation Ratio (CCR), 3D hybrid strategies


Fleet Orchestration (Vol II, Ch 8)

Slurm vs. Kubernetes, topology-aware scheduling, elastic training, multi-tenancy





See the Fleet Zoo for production cluster topologies from 256-GPU research clusters to 8192-GPU frontier fleets.

title: The 5-Layer Architecture
text:
Layer E: Solvers (Analysis)
The previous four layers are static definitions, the nouns of the stack. Solvers are its verbs: the analytical engines that bridge demand and supply to answer specific questions.
Each solver implements closed-form equations from peer-reviewed systems literature. They require no simulation, no benchmarking, and no hardware.

Scaling efficiency, communication overhead, bubble fraction

Solvers are composable. To find the most sustainable way to serve Llama-70B, chain ServingModel (feasibility and latency) into EconomicsModel (cost) into SustainabilityModel (carbon). Each solver’s typed output feeds naturally into the next.

title: The 5-Layer Architecture
text:
Progressive Lowering in Action
The architecture is best understood through a concrete example. Consider the question: “Can I serve Llama-3-70B on a cluster of 4 H100s within a $50K/year budget while minimizing carbon?”
This single question touches all five layers:
1. Layer A — Llama-3-70B workload: 70.6B parameters, GQA with 8 KV heads,
             ~141 GB at FP16 precision

2. Layer B — H100 hardware: 989 TFLOP/s (FP16), 3.35 TB/s HBM3,
             80 GiB capacity, 700 W TDP

3. Layer C — Infrastructure: choose between Quebec (20 g CO₂/kWh)
             and US Average (429 g CO₂/kWh)

4. Layer D — System: 1 node × 4 H100s, NVLink 900 GB/s intra-node,
             tensor parallelism across 4 GPUs

5. Layer E — Chain three solvers:
             ServingModel  → TTFT, ITL, KV-cache feasibility
             EconomicsModel → TCO over 1 year
             SustainabilityModel → carbon footprint by region
Each layer contributes a different piece of the answer. No single layer is sufficient alone. This is why MLSys·im separates concerns into five composable layers rather than offering a monolithic “predict performance” function.

title: The 3-Tier Resolver Guide
text:
Composing Resolvers
Real-world questions require chaining multiple tiers. Here are three common patterns:

Serving Llama-70B on 4 H100s within budget

from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

serving = ServingModel().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=2048, batch_size=4
)
print(f"TTFT: {serving.ttft.to('ms'):~.1f}, ITL: {serving.itl.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"KV-Cache: {serving.kv_cache_size.to('GB'):~.2f}")

TTFT: 2428.1 ms, ITL: 43.75 ms
KV-Cache: 2.68 GB




The parameter that matters most for Llama-8B latency

from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.solvers import SensitivitySolver

sensitivity = SensitivitySolver().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    precision="fp16",
    perturbation_pct=10.0
)
print(f"Binding constraint: {sensitivity.binding_constraint}")
print(f"BW sensitivity:     {sensitivity.sensitivities['memory_bandwidth']:+.3f}")
print(f"FLOPS sensitivity:  {sensitivity.sensitivities['peak_flops']:+.3f}")

Binding constraint: memory_bandwidth
BW sensitivity:     -0.086
FLOPS sensitivity:  +0.000




The hardware a 50ms SLA requires

from mlsysim import Models
from mlsysim.solvers import SynthesisSolver
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_

synthesis = SynthesisSolver().solve(
    model=Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
    target_latency=Q_("50 ms"),
    precision="fp16"
)
print(f"Required bandwidth: {synthesis.required_bw.to('TB/s'):~.2f}")
print(f"Required FLOPS:     {synthesis.required_flops.to('TFLOPs/s'):~.1f}")

Required bandwidth: 0.32 TB / s
Required FLOPS:     0.6 TFLOPs / s

title: How Much Memory Does Llama-3 70B Actually Need?
text:
Every ML engineer eventually confronts the same capacity problem: whether Llama-3.1-70B (70.6B parameters) fits on the available hardware.
The answer depends on three quantities: precision, KV cache, and batch size. The calculation takes 30 seconds.

title: How Much Memory Does Llama-3 70B Actually Need?
text:
The Weights

import mlsysim

llama70b = mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B

# FP16: 2 bytes per parameter
fp16_size = llama70b.size_in_bytes()
print(f"FP16 weights: {fp16_size.to('GB'):~.1f}")

# INT8: 1 byte per parameter
int8_size = llama70b.size_in_bytes(mlsysim.ureg("1 byte"))
print(f"INT8 weights: {int8_size.to('GB'):~.1f}")

# INT4: 0.5 bytes per parameter
int4_size = llama70b.size_in_bytes(mlsysim.ureg("0.5 byte"))
print(f"INT4 weights: {int4_size.to('GB'):~.1f}")

FP16 weights: 141.2 GB
INT8 weights: 70.6 GB
INT4 weights: 35.3 GB


Result: 141.2 GB in FP16, 70.6 GB in INT8, and 35.3 GB in INT4.
An H100 or A100 has 80 GiB (85.9 GB), so Llama-3.1-70B in FP16 does not fit on one GPU. Serving it requires either tensor parallelism (\(\text{TP}=2\)) or quantization to INT8/INT4.

title: How Much Memory Does Llama-3 70B Actually Need?
text:
The KV Cache
Weights are only part of the total. Each active request also needs a KV cache:

from mlsysim.physics import calc_kv_cache_size

head_dim = llama70b.hidden_dim // llama70b.heads
kv_per_request = calc_kv_cache_size(
    n_layers=llama70b.layers,
    n_heads=llama70b.kv_heads,
    head_dim=head_dim,
    seq_len=4096,
    batch_size=1,
    bytes_per_elem=2,
)
print(f"KV cache per request (4K context): {kv_per_request.to('GB'):~.2f} ({kv_per_request.to('MB'):~.0f})")

KV cache per request (4K context): 1.34 GB (1342 MB)


At 1.34 GB (1,342 MB) per request across 80 layers and 8 GQA KV heads (128-dim per head), an 80 GiB (85.9 GB) H100 serving INT4 Llama-3.1-70B has:

35.3 GB for weights
50.6 GB (50,599 MB) remaining for KV cache
50.6 GB / 1.34 GB \(\approx\) 37 concurrent requests max

At 32K context, the KV cache grows to 10.74 GB per request, which leaves room for at most 4 concurrent requests.

title: How Much Memory Does Llama-3 70B Actually Need?
text:
The Full Picture

from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel

result = ServingModel().solve(
    model=mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B,
    hardware=mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100,
    seq_len=4096,
    batch_size=1,
    precision="fp16",
)
print(f"Feasible:    {result.feasible}")
print(f"Memory util: {result.memory_utilization:.1%}")

Feasible:    False
Memory util: 165.9%


The conclusion: A 70.6B-parameter model needs more than 141.2 GB. It needs 141.2 GB + (\(\text{KV cache} \times \text{concurrent requests}\)). At production batch sizes and long contexts, the KV cache can consume more memory than the weights.

title: How Much Memory Does Llama-3 70B Actually Need?
text:
What To Do About It








Strategy
Memory Impact
Trade-off




INT4 quantization
\(4\times\) smaller weights (141.2 GB \(\to\) 35.3 GB)
~2–5% accuracy loss


GQA (built into Llama-3)
\(8\times\) smaller KV cache (64 \(\to\) 8 KV heads)
None (architectural)


KV cache INT8
\(2\times\) smaller KV cache (1.34 GB \(\to\) 0.67 GB at 4K)
Negligible quality loss


Tensor parallelism (\(\text{TP}=2\))
Split across 2 GPUs (70.6 GB weights/GPU)
Adds NVLink communication


PagedAttention (vLLM)
Eliminates KV fragmentation
~20–40% more concurrent requests

title: How Much Memory Does Llama-3 70B Actually Need?
text:
Reproducing the Calculation
pip install mlsysim
mlsysim serve Llama3_70B H100 --seq-len 4096 --batch-size 1

This analysis was computed with mlsysim, a first-principles analytical modeling framework for ML systems. All specifications are traceable to hardware datasheets and model cards.

text:
Applies to: mlsysim v0.1.x

This document defines which parts of the mlsysim API are stable, which are experimental, and what guarantees code built on top of the framework can rely on.



mlsysim follows Semantic Versioning with one important caveat: we are pre-1.0. Under semver, this means:







Version bump
What it means




0.1.x -> 0.1.y (patch)
Bug fixes only. No API changes. Safe to upgrade.


0.1.x -> 0.2.0 (minor)
Breaking changes allowed. Read the changelog before upgrading.


1.0.0
Full stability guarantee begins. Breaking changes require a major bump.



In practice: code pinned to mlsysim ~= 0.1.0 (any 0.1.x) will not break. Upgrading to 0.2.0 means updating imports and possibly adjusting call signatures.




These interfaces are locked for the entire 0.1.x series. Bug fixes may change return values (e.g., correcting a formula), but signatures and field names will not change.


from mlsysim import Engine

result = Engine.solve(
    model=...,        # ModelSpec or registry name
    hardware=...,     # HardwareSpec or registry name
    batch_size=32,    # int
    precision="fp16", # str: "fp32", "fp16", "bf16", "int8", "int4"
    efficiency=0.45,  # float: 0.0-1.0
)
All five parameters to Engine.solve() are stable. Their names, types, and positions will not change.



from mlsysim import Hardware

gpu = Hardware.Cloud.H100            # All current entries are stable
gpu = Hardware.Cloud.A100
gpu = Hardware.Edge.JetsonOrinNX
# ... every entry shipping in 0.1.x
New entries may be added in patch releases, but existing entries will not be removed or renamed.



from mlsysim import Models

model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B      # All current entries are stable
model = Models.Language.GPT2
# ... every entry shipping in 0.1.x
Same guarantee as Hardware: additions are allowed, removals are not.



Use nested canonical paths in Python:
mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100
mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B
mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
Flat aliases at the registry root (for example bare H100 or ResNet50 leaf names) were removed in the registry migration. The CLI still resolves short names (mlsysim eval Llama3_8B H100) for convenience.
Solvers not listed in mlsysim.__init__ (for example CompressionModel, MoERoutingModel) import from mlsysim.solvers. Workload types import from mlsysim.models.types.



from mlsysim import ReferenceStats, Scenarios
Scenarios.* is the executable scenario registry: each entry composes an existing Models.* workload, a Hardware.* or Systems.* target, and scenario-local constraints such as latency or power budget. ReferenceStats.* holds non-executable sourced anchors, such as mobile power envelopes, Waymo data-rate ranges, and TinyML case-study measurements.
There are no compatibility aliases between these namespaces. Use Scenarios.SmartDoorbell for an executable case and ReferenceStats.MobilePower for sourced non-executable anchors.



The following fields on the result object returned by Engine.solve() are stable:



Field
Type
Description




latency
pint.Quantity
Wall-clock time for one forward pass


throughput
pint.Quantity
Tokens/sec or samples/sec


bottleneck
str
"Compute" or "Memory"


mfu
float
Model FLOPs Utilization (0.0-1.0)


feasible
bool
Whether the workload fits in memory


energy
pint.Quantity
Energy consumption per forward pass






from mlsysim import ureg
The Pint unit registry instance is stable. All quantities returned by the engine use this registry.





These interfaces work today but are not yet finalized. Use them freely for exploration, but do not build production tooling against them without pinning to an exact version.


from mlsysim.solvers import ForwardModel, DistributedModel, ServingModel
The solver class hierarchy, their constructors, and their method signatures may change. The Engine.solve() facade insulates calling code from these changes, so prefer it over direct solver instantiation.
Solver classes are exported from mlsysim.solvers, not the package root. Use from mlsysim.solvers import ServingModel so solver-specific dependencies stay explicit and the root namespace remains reserved for registries, units, and formatting helpers.



Engine.solve(..., is_training=True)  # experimental
The is_training flag will likely be replaced by separate Engine.train() and Engine.infer() methods in v0.2.0, or by a more expressive workload specification.



The API for composing multiple solver stages into a pipeline (e.g., prefill + decode, or TP + PP) is experimental. The abstraction is correct but the interface is still being refined.



The search/sweep API for exploring hardware-model combinations is experimental. Parameter names and result formats may change.



All mlsysim CLI command names, subcommands, and flags are experimental. Shell scripts that call the CLI should pin to an exact version.



Fields on specialized result types (DistributedResult, ServingResult, etc.) beyond the six stable PerformanceProfile fields listed above are experimental. They may be renamed, reorganized, or moved to nested objects.





These interfaces still work in v0.1.x but emit deprecation warnings and will be removed in the next minor release.
No public import path is deprecated in 0.1.2. Deprecations will be listed here and in the changelog before the next minor release.





Pin the dependency: mlsysim ~= 0.1.0 (allows 0.1.x patches, blocks 0.2.0).
Use Engine.solve() as the primary interface. It is the most stable entry point.
Use mlsysim.solvers only when solver-specific features are needed. The engine facade covers most use cases.
Run with warnings enabled (python3 -W default) to catch deprecation notices early.
Read the changelog before any minor version upgrade.

title: Tutorial Slides
text: The MLSys·im tutorial is delivered as a Beamer deck in four modules. The PDFs are built from source on every release (see mlsysim/tutorial/slides/) and published alongside this site.

title: Tutorial Slides
text:
Module 1: Foundations & Architecture
Foundations: the iron law of ML systems, the roofline model, constraint-based systems engineering, dimensional strictness, and the Pydantic registry system.
Download Module 1 (PDF)

title: Tutorial Slides
text:
Module 2: Advanced Single-Node Analysis
Bottlenecks: the data wall (ingestion vs transformation), LLM serving limits (pre-fill vs decoding), algorithmic optimizations (speculative decoding), and the reasoning wall (OpenAI o1 scaling).
Download Module 2 (PDF)

title: Tutorial Slides
text:
Module 3: Scale, Dollars, and Carbon
Fleet dynamics: distributed training, the Amdahl Trap, Total Cost of Ownership (the infrastructure multiplier), and cross-domain carbon accounting.
Download Module 3 (PDF)

title: Tutorial Slides
text:
Module 4: Design Space Exploration & Synthesis
Systems engineering: rapid parametric sweeps, the universality of the roofline (TinyML to Frontier), sensitivity analysis, and SLA-driven hardware synthesis.
Download Module 4 (PDF)

title: Tutorial Slides
text:
Source
The decks live in the mlsysim/tutorial/slides/ directory of the MLSysBook repository. To rebuild locally:
cd mlsysim/tutorial
make
This produces the four PDFs using pdflatex and the shared beamerthememlsys theme. Prerequisites: pdflatex (TeX Live or MacTeX) plus either inkscape or rsvg-convert for SVG conversion.

title: Tutorial Slides
text:
Textbook lecture slides
The 35-deck textbook lecture series covering both volumes of Machine Learning Systems lives at mlsysbook.ai/slides. Those decks are organized by chapter and are independent of the MLSys·im tutorial.

Optimization scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/optimization.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A pod envelope of pod.chips copies of accelerator: aggregate peak and memory.


Equation: Use the dimensional products, ratios, or selection rules documented on the calculated properties below.
Assumptions: The pod envelope contains identical chips; capacities and peaks add arithmetically.
Excludes: Aggregate local memory is not a unified address space, and aggregate peak does not imply achieved scaling.



Derivation: the calculated properties below state their defining arithmetic and units. They are scenario accounting or input-selection rules, not independently measured relationships.



>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> case = Scenarios.TPUv4Pod4096
>>> str(case.peak_flops)
'1126400.0 TFLOPs/s'

pod







Type: object.
Declared default: required.



Type: HardwareNode.
Declared default: required.



engine.scenario_types.AcceleratorPodScenario.peak_flops
Sum of per-chip arithmetic peaks in the pod envelope. Equation: pod.chips * accelerator.compute.peak_flops. Units: FLOP/s; perfect parallel utilization is not implied.

Sum of local chip memory capacities. Equation: pod.chips * accelerator.memory.capacity. Units: bytes; this does not make the memory a single shared address space.

title: ShardedUnlearningScenario
text:
Statistics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/statistics.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
Exact unlearning by sharded retraining (SISA) against a full retrain of workload.
The full retrain runs on n_accelerators of accelerator at mfu and costs full_cost. Planning rounds it to whole days; one request retrains one of shards equal shards, at a proportional share of time and cost. requests_per_day arrive uniformly at random over the shards.


Equation: Uniform occupancy gives the expected touched-shard count; multiply by one-shard retraining cost.
Assumptions: Equal-sized shards, linear retraining cost, uniform independent deletion-to-shard assignment, and fixed MFU.
Excludes: SISA slice mechanics, imbalance, optimizer startup, and exact unlearning verification.



Derivation: Uniform occupancy gives the expected touched-shard count; multiply by one-shard retraining cost. Individual property contracts identify the exact accounting expression or reusable calculation. Registry entries supply the scenario inputs; this class does not turn them into measured outcomes.



Evaluate a named scenario using its declared inputs.
>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> scenario = Scenarios.Gpt3ShardedUnlearning
>>> round(float(scenario.full_retrain_time.magnitude), 4)

engine.scenario_types.ShardedUnlearningScenario.full_retrain_time
Days to perform the stated training FLOPs at aggregate peak FLOP/s times the declared MFU.
Equation: rate = n_accelerators * accelerator.compute.peak_flops * mfu; result = (workload.training_ops / rate).to('day').



engine.scenario_types.ShardedUnlearningScenario.planning_days
Full-retrain time rounded to integer days for the scenario’s planning convention.
The full retrain rounded to whole days, the figure planning quotes.
Equation: round(full_retrain_time.to('day').magnitude).



engine.scenario_types.ShardedUnlearningScenario.shard_share
Fraction of equal-sized training work assigned to one shard.
Equation: 1 / shards.



engine.scenario_types.ShardedUnlearningScenario.shard_cost
USD for one shard retrain under linear equal-shard cost scaling.
Equation: (full_cost * shard_share).to('USD').



engine.scenario_types.ShardedUnlearningScenario.shard_time
Hours per shard retrain using rounded planning days rather than exact full-retrain time.
Equation: (Q_(planning_days, 'day') * shard_share).to('hour').



engine.scenario_types.ShardedUnlearningScenario.p_shard_untouched
Probability one shard receives no deletion requests when requests independently choose shards uniformly.
Chance a given shard receives none of a day’s requests.
Equation: (1 - shard_share) ** requests_per_day.



engine.scenario_types.ShardedUnlearningScenario.shards_touched_per_day
Expected daily count of distinct shards hit by deletion requests.
Equation: shards * (1 - p_shard_untouched).



engine.scenario_types.ShardedUnlearningScenario.daily_batch_cost
Expected USD to retrain each touched shard once in a daily deletion batch.
Cost if every touched shard retrains once a day.
Equation: (shards_touched_per_day * shard_cost).to('USD').

title: solvers.WeightStreamingModel
text:
solvers.WeightStreamingModel()
Analyzes Wafer-Scale inference (e.g., Cerebras CS-3) using Weight Streaming.
Instead of holding weights in HBM and streaming activations (the GPU Memory Wall), this architecture holds massive activation batches on-wafer (SRAM) and streams the model weights from external MemoryX nodes.
The bottleneck shifts from Memory Bandwidth to Injection Interconnect Bandwidth.
Literature Source: 1. Lie et al. (2022), “Cerebras Architecture Deep Dive: First Look Inside the Hardware/Software Co-Design for Deep Learning.”





Name
Description




solve
Estimate layer-wise weight streaming time and on-device state capacity.





solvers.WeightStreamingModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    seq_len,
    batch_size=1,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
    phase='decode',
)
Estimate layer-wise weight streaming time and on-device state capacity.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model
TransformerWorkload
Transformer with positive layer count, parameters, and head geometry.
required


hardware
HardwareNode
Device supplying compute FLOP/s, resident memory bytes, dispatch time, and weight-injection interconnect bytes/s. Missing/zero injection bandwidth uses the fallback in engine.calibration.
required


seq_len
int
Positive resident context length in tokens per request.
required


batch_size
int
Positive simultaneous requests; default one.
1


precision
str
Weight and KV precision; default FP16.
'fp16'


efficiency
float
Compute utilization in (0, 1]; default 0.5.
0.5


phase
str
‘prefill’ processes seq_len tokens; ‘decode’ processes one token. Other strings currently follow the decode branch.
'decode'














Name
Type
Description





WeightStreamingResult
Layer compute/injection times, throughput in tokens/s, memory utilization, optimal linear-work batch, and feasibility. Feasibility checks KV state plus the declared activation allowance only.






Equation: T_layer = max(W_layer/BW_inject, F_layer/(eta*peak)+dispatch). T_step = layers*T_layer. Decode F_layer = 2P_layer*B. Prefill adds 2*H_query*S^2*d*B to 2P_layer*S*B under this model’s approximation. Resident storage is 1.1 times KV bytes; the extra tenth is a declared activation allowance. Weights stream from external storage.
Assumptions: uniform layers and complete injection/compute overlap. The optimal-batch estimate equates injection and linear compute time. Excludes: decode attention work, runtime workspace, detailed communication scheduling, and measured injection efficiency. Prefill uses the causal half-square attention approximation; ServingModel uses a rectangular upper bound over the final context.



Derivation: divide each layer’s weight bytes by injection bandwidth and its operation count by effective compute rate; the slower concurrent resource sets the layer time. The activation allowance is a heuristic.



>>> from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
>>> from mlsysim.solvers import WeightStreamingModel
>>> r = WeightStreamingModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B,
...     Hardware.Cloud.Cerebras_CS3, seq_len=128)
>>> bool(r.feasible and r.layer_compute_time.m_as("ms") > 0)
True

text:
Statistics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/statistics.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A continuous feature fitted as a normal at reference and now: KL divergence of the reference from the current fit.


Equation: The statistics helpers decompose and evaluate KL(reference || current); the trigger compares that value with a threshold.

One step of a recurrent layer: input_dim inputs, a hidden_dim state, and gates affine maps per step (one for a plain RNN, four for an LSTM); steps steps in a sequence.


Equation: Each gate uses H*I input MACs and H*H recurrent MACs; all gates and steps share their matrices.
Assumptions: Dense gates and a retained hidden vector of H values at the declared width.

Statistics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/statistics.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
One board, a host CPU and an attached accelerator: model-only and end-to-end latency, active energy.
The end-to-end times add host preprocessing (and, on the accelerator path, the copy across the host link) to the model time; active energy is the component’s active power times its model-only latency, so it leaves out preprocessing and idle power.


Equation: The calculation members below define frame_budget, int8_speedup, isolated_speedup, end_to_end_speedup, power_ratio, host_energy, accelerator_energy, energy_ratio.
Assumptions: Active energy is power times model-only latency; end-to-end times are supplied separately.
Excludes: Idle energy, host/accelerator overlap, and energy of the surrounding response path.



Derivation: One board, a host CPU and an attached accelerator: model-only and end-to-end latency, active energy. Each member records the corresponding algebra or named physics function.

Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
One head’s attention at seq_len tokens, whole or in square tiles, and what each kernel stores.
Standard attention stores the scores and the probabilities (seq_len squared each) beside Q, K, V, and the output; FlashAttention stores a running maximum and sum per row instead.

title: GroupConfusionScenario
text:
Statistics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/statistics.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
Binary decisions for two or more groups as confusion counts {group: {tp, fp, fn, tn}}.
A positive decision is an approval (or a flag); the positive label is the outcome the decision should select. gap compares the first two groups, first minus second.


Equation: Each metric is the stated confusion-count numerator divided by its corresponding population denominator.
Assumptions: Supplied confusion counts share the same outcome definition and every requested rate has a nonzero denominator.
Excludes: Sampling uncertainty, causal fairness claims, and metrics for unspecified groups.



Derivation: Each metric is the stated confusion-count numerator divided by its corresponding population denominator. Individual property contracts identify the exact accounting expression or reusable calculation. Registry entries supply the scenario inputs; this class does not turn them into measured outcomes.



Evaluate a named scenario using its declared inputs.
>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> scenario = Scenarios.CreditServiceTwoGroups
>>> round(float(scenario.pooled_positive_rate), 4)
0.525






Name
Description




average_odds_difference
Mean of the absolute group TPR and FPR gaps; this is an unsigned disparity summary.


disparate_impact
Smaller divided by larger group positive rate, a dimensionless selection-rate ratio.


first
First group label in insertion order, used as the signed-gap reference group.


groups



overall_accuracy
Correct-decision fraction pooled by decision count across all groups.


pooled_positive_rate
Predicted-positive fraction pooled by decision count across all groups.


second
Second group label in insertion order, used as the signed-gap comparison group.









Name
Description




accuracy
Correct-decision fraction in the named group.


base_rate
Actual-positive fraction among all decisions in the group.


fnr
False-negative fraction among actual positives in the group.


fpr
False-positive fraction among actual negatives in the group.


gap
Signed first-minus-second group difference for the named rate metric.


positive_rate
Predicted-positive fraction among all decisions in the group.


positives
Predicted-positive count in the group, summing true and false positives.


ppv
True-positive fraction among predicted positives in the group.


share
Named group’s fraction of the combined decision population.


size
Total decisions in the named group, summing all confusion-table cells.


tpr
True-positive fraction among actual positives in the group.





engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.accuracy(group)
Correct-decision fraction in the named group.
Share of the group decided correctly (added 2026-10-20).
Equation: c = _c(group); result = (c['tp'] + c['tn']) / size(group).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.base_rate(group)
Actual-positive fraction among all decisions in the group.
Equation: c = _c(group); result = (c['tp'] + c['fn']) / size(group).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.fnr(group)
False-negative fraction among actual positives in the group.
Share of the positive-label members given a negative decision (added 2026-10-20).
Equation: c = _c(group); result = c['fn'] / (c['tp'] + c['fn']).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.fpr(group)
False-positive fraction among actual negatives in the group.
Equation: c = _c(group); result = c['fp'] / (c['fp'] + c['tn']).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.gap(metric)
Signed first-minus-second group difference for the named rate metric.
metric (positive_rate, tpr, fpr, ppv, base_rate) of the first group minus the second’s.
Equation: metric(first group)-metric(second group); metric names select the documented rate methods.



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.positive_rate(group)
Predicted-positive fraction among all decisions in the group.
Share of the group given a positive decision (the demographic-parity quantity).
Equation: positives(group) / size(group).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.positives(group)
Predicted-positive count in the group, summing true and false positives.
Positive decisions (approved or flagged).
Equation: c = _c(group); result = c['tp'] + c['fp'].



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.ppv(group)
True-positive fraction among predicted positives in the group.
Equation: c = _c(group); result = c['tp'] / (c['tp'] + c['fp']).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.share(group)
Named group’s fraction of the combined decision population.
The group’s share of all members (added 2026-10-20).
Equation: size(group) / sum((size(g) for g in groups)).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.size(group)
Total decisions in the named group, summing all confusion-table cells.
Equation: c = _c(group); result = c['tp'] + c['fp'] + c['fn'] + c['tn'].



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.tpr(group)
True-positive fraction among actual positives in the group.
Equation: c = _c(group); result = c['tp'] / (c['tp'] + c['fn']).




Type: Dict[str, Dict[str, float]].
Declared default: required.



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.first
First group label in insertion order, used as the signed-gap reference group.
Equation: list(groups)[0].



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.second
Second group label in insertion order, used as the signed-gap comparison group.
Equation: list(groups)[1].



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.pooled_positive_rate
Predicted-positive fraction pooled by decision count across all groups.
Share of all members, every group pooled, given a positive decision (added 2026-10-20).
Equation: sum((positives(g) for g in groups)) / sum((size(g) for g in groups)).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.overall_accuracy
Correct-decision fraction pooled by decision count across all groups.
Share of all members of all groups decided correctly (added 2026-10-20).
Equation: right = sum((c['tp'] + c['tn'] for c in groups.values())); result = right / sum((size(g) for g in groups)).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.disparate_impact
Smaller divided by larger group positive rate, a dimensionless selection-rate ratio.
Lower positive rate over higher positive rate across the first two groups.
Equation: a, b = (positive_rate(first), positive_rate(second)); result = min(a, b) / max(a, b).



engine.scenario_types.GroupConfusionScenario.average_odds_difference
Mean of the absolute group TPR and FPR gaps; this is an unsigned disparity summary.
Mean of the absolute TPR and FPR gaps.
Equation: 0.5 * (abs(gap('tpr')) + abs(gap('fpr'))).

title: solvers.ContinuousBatchingModel
text:
solvers.ContinuousBatchingModel()
Compares static KV reservation with PagedAttention under continuous batching.
Decode is memory-bound, so the number of requests sharing a step is the throughput lever, and the KV-cache allocator decides how many fit. A static allocator reserves a contiguous slot of max_seq_len tokens for every request; PagedAttention hands out fixed-size blocks on demand. This model sizes both from the same KV budget and a request-length distribution, then compares memory-bound decode throughput at each allocator’s concurrency.
Kwon et al. (2023) profile contiguous pre-allocation (their Orca baselines) and find that only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV-cache memory holds actual token states (Fig. 2). The rest is reserved slots for future tokens, internal fragmentation from over-provisioning for the maximum sequence length, and external fragmentation from the memory allocator (Sec. 3.1, Fig. 3). vLLM limits each request’s waste to one block (Sec. 4.2) and reaches 96.3% token-state usage (Fig. 2).
Scope and assumptions:

The static baseline is max-length reservation, like Kwon’s “Orca (Max)”. It is modeled with no external fragmentation because every slot has the same size, although Kwon et al. still attribute 8.9% of Orca (Max) KV memory to external fragmentation and other overhead. Exact-size and power-of-two contiguous allocators, which trade reservation waste for external fragmentation, are not modeled.
Both allocators are sized with every admitted request at its full length (peak occupancy). A request mid-generation holds fewer paged blocks, so paged capacity is conservative, while static reserves max_seq_len for the whole request lifetime either way.
Request lengths are exponential, cut off at max_seq_len, with mean mean_request_tokens (calc_capped_exponential_scale).

Literature Source: 1. Kwon et al. (2023), “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention,” SOSP ’23. 2. Yu et al. (2022), “ORCA: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.”





Name
Description




solve
Compare static max-length KV reservation with paged allocation.





solvers.ContinuousBatchingModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    max_seq_len,
    mean_request_tokens=None,
    max_batch_size=1,
    page_size=16,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
)
Compare static max-length KV reservation with paged allocation.
With KV budget M_KV (HBM capacity minus weights) and k KV bytes per token:

Static reservation: every request reserves max_seq_len tokens, so N_static = floor(M_KV / (k * S_max)) and the unused share of each reservation is 1 - S_mean / S_max.
Paged allocation: the budget is a pool of floor(M_KV / (k * p)) blocks and a request of S tokens holds ceil(S / p) of them, so N_paged = floor(pool / E[ceil(S / p)]). The unused share is the expected tail of each request’s last block (calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens), which grows with page size.
Both counts are capped by max_batch_size. When the cap binds for both allocators, allocation policy cannot change throughput.
Throughput: each step streams weights plus filled KV tokens (reserved but empty slots are not read). Step latency is the larger of compute and memory time, plus the layer tax, using the same accounting as ServingModel. Tokens/s is N / t_step; paging’s throughput gain can saturate at the compute ceiling.
TTFT is the worst-case prefill of a full scheduler batch (max_batch_size prompts of max_seq_len tokens): linear 2*P*S plus attention 4*L*H*d*S^2 FLOPs, plus the dispatch tax.

mlsysim.physics.memory.calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens : Page rounding. ServingModel.solve : Shared compute/memory decode accounting.



Equation: static concurrency is floor(KV_budget/(k*S_max)); paged concurrency is floor(pool_blocks/E[blocks_per_request]). Both are capped by max_batch_size. Throughput = active_requests/decode_step_time.
Assumptions: capped exponential request lengths, peak resident context per admitted request, fixed-size pages, peak memory bandwidth, and the shared decode Roofline including its layer tax. Excludes: external fragmentation, scheduler traces, arrival transients, workspace, tensor parallelism, and growing-context dynamics. Feasibility means modeled weights plus allocated KV fit, not engine deployability.



Kwon et al. (2023), “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180 (bibliography key: kwon2023). The capped-exponential occupancy distribution is a modeling assumption, not a reproduction of vLLM scheduling.



>>> from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
>>> from mlsysim.solvers import ContinuousBatchingModel
>>> r = ContinuousBatchingModel().solve(Models.Language.Llama3_8B, Hardware.Cloud.H100,
...     max_seq_len=2048, mean_request_tokens=512, max_batch_size=8)
>>> bool(r.feasible and r.max_active_requests <= 8 and r.throughput_tokens_per_sec > 0)
True

title: ServiceLifecycleCostScenario

Economics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/economics.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A service’s multi-year cost in three terms: repeated training cycles, recurring inference, and operations, with a GPU-hour carbon factor.
Inference: daily_users x items_per_user requests a day, each service_time of dedicated accelerator time (unbatched, not overlapped), billed at inference_rate. A training cycle is data preparation and a final run in GPU-hours at training_rate plus a search of search_experiments at search_cost_per_experiment; cycles of them over years. serving_cut and training_cut are fractional savings to compare.


Equation: Lifecycle cost adds repeated preparation/search/training cycles, dedicated inference device-hours, and recurring operations; carbon multiplies device-hours by a supplied coefficient.
Assumptions: Requests use serial unbatched dedicated service time; tariffs, volumes, annual operations, and carbon coefficients stay fixed.
Excludes: Discounting, hardware purchase accounting, dynamic batching, shared capacity, and a measured power/emissions trace.

engine.scenario_types.ServiceLifecycleCostScenario.carbon_ratio

The smallest model replica of workload whose training state fits without sharding.
Tensor parallelism spans one node of fleet; the pipeline depth is the smallest power of two at which each accelerator’s share of the bytes_per_param training state fits its memory. An elastic job that keeps this layout fixed grows or shrinks one whole replica at a time.


Equation: pipeline depth is the first power of two satisfying state / (tensor degree * pipeline depth) <= device memory.
Assumptions: Training-state bytes per parameter are supplied; every shard receives an equal share and tensor parallelism spans one node.
Excludes: Activations, runtime workspace, communication buffers, and layout- performance ranking.

title: PackagingCellScenario
text:
Robotics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/robotics/site_limits.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A packaging cell’s carriage that must stop before a fixed stop line.
The pre-brake delay is a chain of four allocations (event to usable frame, transfer through admission, command delivery, brake onset); the stop is the elementary constant-deceleration budget (StoppingBudgetModel) with the allocated reserve held back from the clearance, so the speed ceiling is the positive root of v tau + v^2/(2a) = clearance - reserve. The supervisory settings (force limiter, thermistor trip, stall timeout, bus overvoltage trip, kinematic-check rate) are selected thresholds, not measured limits.


Equation: Stopping uses v*delay+v**2/(2*deceleration) with reserved clearance; energy uses mass*speed**2/2.
Assumptions: Delay components add serially and braking deceleration is constant and positive.
Excludes: Measured actuator dynamics, traction variation, threshold validation, and a safety certification.

text:
solvers.FailureIntervalModel()
Interval between failures across identical, independent components.
With N components that each fail on average once per MTBF, some component fails on average every MTBF / N (the minimum of N exponentials). Over a run of a given length the expected failure count is the run length divided by that interval.





Name
Description




solve

Default

required














Name
Type
Description





FailureIntervalResult
System interval in hours, dimensionless expected failure count over the run, and failures per day.






mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_mtbf_cluster : Aggregate identical node failure rates.



Equation: interval = component_mtbf / n_components; expected_failures = run_duration / interval; failures_per_day = one_day / interval.

Excludes: Common-cause faults, repair downtime, and redundancy masking component failures.



Derivation: The minimum of independent exponential lifetimes has the sum of their rates; count expectation is rate times duration.

title: solvers.ReliabilityModel
text:
solvers.ReliabilityModel()
Calculates Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and optimal checkpointing intervals.
This model handles the reliability modeling of massive clusters, helping determine the ‘Goodput’ of long-running training jobs. It identifies the probability of a job failure before completion and calculates the Young-Daly optimal interval to minimize wasted compute time.
Literature Source: 1. Young (1974), “A First-Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” 2. Daly (2006), “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart-Dump Strategy.”





Name
Description




solve
Estimate fleet failure exposure and a checkpoint interval.





solvers.ReliabilityModel.solve(
    fleet,
    job_duration_hours,
    checkpoint_time_s=60.0,
    avg_recovery_time_s=300.0,
)
Estimate fleet failure exposure and a checkpoint interval.











Name
Type
Description
Default




fleet
Fleet
Cluster configuration with positive node count and per-node device counts.
required


job_duration_hours
float
Nonnegative planned job duration in hours.
required


checkpoint_time_s
float
Positive write pause per checkpoint in seconds; default 60.
60.0


avg_recovery_time_s
float
Nonnegative recovery duration per failure in seconds; default 300, including reload, restart, and warmup.
300.0














Name
Type
Description





ReliabilityResult
Fleet MTBF and checkpoint interval with time units, failure probability, expected failure count, and dimensionless goodput estimate.






mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_mtbf_node : Sum independent component failure rates. mlsysim.physics.reliability.calc_young_daly_interval : Balance checkpoint writing and lost work.



Equation: lambda_node = n_gpu / MTBF_gpu + n_nic / MTBF_nic + n_psu / MTBF_psu; M = 1 / (fleet.count * lambda_node); P(failure) = 1-exp(-job_duration/M); tau = sqrt(2 checkpoint_time M). The reported goodput is max(0, 1-checkpoint_time/tau-recovery_time/M).
Assumptions: Independent exponential component failures and a synchronous series system. Nonredundant PSU counts come from the node; component lifetimes come from the Reliability registry.
Excludes: Correlated failures, repair contention, and explicit re-execution loss in the reported goodput. The goodput expression charges checkpoint writes and recovery only, even though the checkpoint interval balances write and rework costs.



Derivation: Series-system hazard rates add. The no-failure survival function is exponential. The checkpoint helper minimizes the first-order write-plus-rework approximation; the goodput subtraction is the implementation’s separate overhead convention.



>>> from mlsysim import Systems
>>> r = ReliabilityModel().solve(Systems.Clusters.Research_256, 24)
>>> 0 <= r.failure_probability <= 1 and r.fleet_mtbf.m_as("hour") > 0
True

title: engine.solvers.cost_accounting
text:
engine.solvers.cost_accounting
Agent cost-accounting solvers: what one accepted task costs, and what each lever buys (added 2026-10-20).
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers. Each model is arithmetic on stated inputs: the fitted fall of a fixed capability’s price, cost against score on long-horizon trials, a cohort of one-attempt tasks under a tariff, prefix-cache bills and the payback of one compaction, retry policies under independent attempts, a serial episode under Amdahl’s law and speculative decoding, a tiered model cascade under one gate, admission against a token quota, Kingman’s queue price, renting tokens against owning capacity, a conserved budget across children, architectures with a human fallback, the payback of a one-time adaptation, per-workload levers on cost per accepted task, measured coverage against independent trials, and one server swept across concurrency. None models a particular provider’s billing system.





Name
Description




AdaptationPaybackModel
Tasks until a one-time adaptation repays its data, training, and evaluation.


ArchitectureChoiceModel
Designs priced by automated spend alone and with a human fallback.


CohortAttemptCostModel
One configuration’s cohort: one bounded attempt per task, all charges settled.


CompactionPaybackModel
One compaction priced against keeping the transcript, under one tariff.


ConservedBudgetModel
A root budget kept as settled + reserved + free across two children.


DedicatedBreakEvenModel
Renting tokens from an API against owning capacity with a fixed hourly cost.


KingmanQueueModel
Kingman’s mean wait for one server at two utilizations, and its holding price.


ModelCascadeModel
A tiered cascade under one acceptance gate, priced over a completed cohort.


PrefixCacheBillModel
An append-only trajectory billed at the fresh rate, and with ideal prefix reuse.


RetryPolicyModel
Bounded attempt policies under independent attempts at a fixed all-in cost.


SerialEpisodeModel
One serial episode of disjoint intervals; a faster model shortens only its own.


SpeculativeEpisodeModel
Speculative decoding’s decode-stream speedup, composed with a serial episode.


TrajectoryAdmissionModel
Admitted trajectories against a token quota, in the mean.


WorkloadLeverModel
Cost per accepted task by workload, C_eff = C_attempt / p_acc, and three levers.





engine.solvers.cost_accounting.AdaptationPaybackModel()
Tasks until a one-time adaptation repays its data, training, and evaluation.
Each task’s model usage is steps times (input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price); the break-even count is the investment over the per-task saving, and the first whole task that crosses it.





Name
Description




solve
Calculate task volume needed to recover adaptation investment.

    base,
    adapted,
    data_cost,
    training_cost,
    evaluation_cost,
    monthly_volume,
    low_volume,
)
Calculate task volume needed to recover adaptation investment.

Type

Name
Type
Description





AdaptationPaybackResult
Step, task, investment, and saving USD quantities; fractional and rounded task break-even counts; payback months and cost shares.






Equation: task cost = steps*(input_tokens*input_price + output_tokens*output_price); crossing = investment/(base_task-adapted_task).
Assumptions: Fixed token usage and tariffs; adaptation lowers cost per task; positive volume and investment.
Excludes: Quality changes, model drift, recurring retraining, and discounting.



Derivation: Sum data, training, and evaluation investment. Each completed task repays the difference between baseline and adapted usage bills. Divide investment by this difference, then divide tasks by monthly volume.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
>>> base = dict(steps=2, input_tokens=100, output_tokens=10, input_price=Q_('1 USD/Mtoken'), output_price=Q_('2 USD/Mtoken'))
>>> adapted = dict(base, steps=1)
>>> r = AdaptationPaybackModel().solve(base, adapted, Q_('1 USD'), Q_('1 USD'), Q_('1 USD'), 1000, 100)
>>> r.payback_months_low > r.payback_months
True

Designs priced by automated spend alone and with a human fallback.

Mean concurrent trajectories, call and demand rates in the supplied arrival units, tokens per trajectory, and dimensionless quota shares.

engine.solvers.cost_accounting.WorkloadLeverModel()
Cost per accepted task by workload, C_eff = C_attempt / p_acc, and three levers.
Halving the token price saves half the model share; halving the largest term saves half its share; raising acceptance by dp saves dp / (p + dp) of every term, and also removes the handoffs charged per rejected attempt. Acceptance beats halving tokens whenever the model share is below 2 dp / (p + dp).





Name
Description




solve
Compare token, dominant-cost, and acceptance improvements.

    workloads,
    acceptance_gain,
)

Type
Description
Default

Mapping[str, Mapping[str, float]]
Names mapped to model, environment, assessment, human costs in USD and acceptance in (0,1]; optional handoff replaces human with (1-acceptance)*handoff.
required


acceptance_gain
float
Absolute increase in acceptance probability; keeps each probability at most one.
required














Name
Type
Description





WorkloadLeverResult
Rows with USD attempt and accepted-task costs as floats, the dominant cost-term name, and dimensionless lever savings and shares.






Equation: cost per accepted = sum(attempt costs)/acceptance; each lever recomputes this ratio after changing its specified term.
Assumptions: Positive acceptance and total cost; acceptance_gain keeps acceptance at most one; costs use a common currency.
Excludes: Interactions among levers, causal predictions of acceptance, and changed task mix.



Derivation: Recompute cost per accepted task after halving model cost, halving the largest cost term, or raising acceptance. If human cost is charged per rejection, recompute that term under the changed rejection fraction.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
>>> w = {'x': dict(model=1.0, environment=2.0, assessment=1.0, human=1.0, acceptance=0.5)}
>>> r = WorkloadLeverModel().solve(w, 0.1)
>>> r.rows['x'].largest_term == 'environment'
True

Equation: task cost = steps*(input_tokens*input_price + output_tokens*output_price); crossing = investment/(base_task-adapted_task).
Assumptions: Fixed token usage and tariffs; adaptation lowers cost per task; positive volume and investment.

>>> r.payback_months_low > r.payback_months
True

>>> r.per_call_saving > Q_('0 USD')

Equation: budget = settled + reserved + free at every transition; duplicate delivery of the same settlement identity is applied once.
Assumptions: Two child allocations in common integer budget units; charges fit reservations; nonnegative conserved state.

Assumptions: Single-server stationary renewal approximation; positive service and variability; 0 < low, high < 1.

float
Fraction of reusable prefix charged fresh, in [0,1].

Name
Type
Description





PrefixCacheBillResult
Sent and fresh token counts, cached and uncached USD quantity bills, dimensionless cost ratios, and per-turn USD amounts as floats.






Equation: sent = H*s0 + delta*H*(H-1)/2; fresh = s0 + (H-1)*delta. Cached input costs p_in*(fresh + cached_fraction*(sent-fresh)).
Assumptions: Positive turn count; cached_fraction and miss_fraction lie in [0,1]; only unchanged prefixes are eligible.
Excludes: Cache capacity, eviction, cache-write charges, and changes in generation latency.



Derivation: Sum the arithmetic progression of prompt lengths. Each token is fresh on its first appearance; subsequent appearances form the cached portion. Apply the two tariffs separately, then add generated-token cost.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
>>> r = PrefixCacheBillModel().solve(2, 100, 10, 5, Q_('1 USD/Mtoken'), 0.1, Q_('2 USD/Mtoken'), 0.0)
>>> r.sent_tokens == 210 and r.fresh_tokens == 110
True






engine.solvers.cost_accounting.RetryPolicyModel()
Bounded attempt policies under independent attempts at a fixed all-in cost.
Sequential retry with early stopping covers 1 - (1 - p)^k of tasks in coverage / p attempts on average, so its cost per accepted task is c / p whatever the cap; a batch of k pays for all k.

Description

    pass_probability,
    attempt_cost,
    max_attempts,
    strong_pass_probability,
    strong_attempt_cost,
)
Compare bounded sequential retries with a paid batch.











Name
Type

Quantity

Type
Description





RetryPolicyResult
Coverage probability, expected attempt count, USD quantity spends and costs per accepted task, and dimensionless batch premium.






Equation: coverage = 1-(1-p)**k; expected attempts = sum((1-p)**j for j in range(k)); sequential spend = cost*expected attempts.
Assumptions: Independent trials with constant success probability in (0,1]; positive max_attempts and positive strong_pass_probability.
Excludes: Correlation across retries, changing attempt difficulty, cancellation, and latency.



Derivation: Trial j is reached only if the preceding trials fail. Sum those reach probabilities for expected sequential attempts. A batch pays for every attempt, even when an earlier member would have succeeded.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
>>> r = RetryPolicyModel().solve(0.5, Q_('1 USD'), 2, 0.8, Q_('2 USD'))
>>> r.expected_attempts == 1.5
True

One serial episode of disjoint intervals; a faster model shortens only its own.
T' = T_other + T_model / s (Amdahl’s law); instant model calls bound the episode speedup at 1 / (1 - f).

)

Type

SerialEpisodeResult
Component, total, changed, and saved durations as second quantities; model fraction and achieved/limiting speedups are dimensionless.






Equation: T_new = T_other + T_model/model_speedup; speedup = T_total/T_new.
Assumptions: Nonnegative disjoint intervals; positive speedup and positive non-model time for the finite limiting ratio.
Excludes: Overlap between intervals, queueing, and changes to non-model work.



Derivation: Partition elapsed time into model and non-model intervals. Divide only the model sum by the supplied acceleration; leave other intervals unchanged. Zero model time gives the limiting episode speedup.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_

>>> r.changed_time == Q_('3 s')

Speculative decoding’s decode-stream speedup, composed with a serial episode.
Treats the episode’s model time as pure decode (an optimistic bound): T' = T [(1 - f) + f / S] with S = (m + 1) / (gamma r + 1).

    accepted_low,
)

SpeculativeEpisodeResult
Decode speedups, accepted-token break-even count, episode times as second quantities, and dimensionless episode speedup bounds.






Equation: S = (accepted+1)/(draft_length*draft_cost_ratio+1); T_new = T*((1-f)+f/S).
Assumptions: Constant draft costs and accepted-token means; decode_fraction in [0,1); accepted counts between zero and draft_length.

>>> r.episode_time_high < r.episode_time_low
True

Type

TrajectoryAdmissionResult
Mean concurrent trajectories, call and demand rates in the supplied arrival units, tokens per trajectory, and dimensionless quota shares.






Equation: concurrent = arrival*residence; demand = arrival*calls*tokens_per_call; quota share = demand/quota.
Assumptions: Stationary mean arrivals and fixed work per trajectory; positive quota and tokens per trajectory; acceptance_drop in [0,1).

True






engine.solvers.cost_accounting.WorkloadLeverModel()
Cost per accepted task by workload, C_eff = C_attempt / p_acc, and three levers.
Halving the token price saves half the model share; halving the largest term saves half its share; raising acceptance by dp saves dp / (p + dp) of every term, and also removes the handoffs charged per rejected attempt. Acceptance beats halving tokens whenever the model share is below 2 dp / (p + dp).





Name
Description




solve
Compare token, dominant-cost, and acceptance improvements.





engine.solvers.cost_accounting.WorkloadLeverModel.solve(
    workloads,
    acceptance_gain,
)
Compare token, dominant-cost, and acceptance improvements.











Name
Type
Description
Default




workloads
Mapping[str, Mapping[str, float]]
Names mapped to model, environment, assessment, human costs in USD and acceptance in (0,1]; optional handoff replaces human with (1-acceptance)*handoff.
required


acceptance_gain
float
Absolute increase in acceptance probability; keeps each probability at most one.
required














Name
Type
Description





WorkloadLeverResult
Rows with USD attempt and accepted-task costs as floats, the dominant cost-term name, and dimensionless lever savings and shares.






Equation: cost per accepted = sum(attempt costs)/acceptance; each lever recomputes this ratio after changing its specified term.
Assumptions: Positive acceptance and total cost; acceptance_gain keeps acceptance at most one; costs use a common currency.
Excludes: Interactions among levers, causal predictions of acceptance, and changed task mix.



Derivation: Recompute cost per accepted task after halving model cost, halving the largest cost term, or raising acceptance. If human cost is charged per rejection, recompute that term under the changed rejection fraction.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
>>> w = {'x': dict(model=1.0, environment=2.0, assessment=1.0, human=1.0, acceptance=0.5)}
>>> r = WorkloadLeverModel().solve(w, 0.1)
>>> r.rows['x'].largest_term == 'environment'
True
