physics.robotics.control.calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
    model_weight_memory,
    memory_bandwidth,
    chunk_horizon,
    bus_efficiency=0.7,
)
Calculate the weight-stream floor per chunk and per waypoint.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model_weight_memory
Quantity
Model parameter storage footprint (e.g. GB).
required


memory_bandwidth
Quantity
Peak memory bus bandwidth (e.g. GB/s).
required


chunk_horizon
int
Number of steps predicted per chunk H (>= 1).
required


bus_efficiency
float
Sustained DRAM efficiency fraction eta in (0, 1] (default 0.70). This physical range is a caller requirement, not validated here.
0.7














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: t_stream, f_single, tau_step, f_waypoint_equivalent, f_effective (legacy alias), b_sustained. Times are milliseconds, rates are hertz, and sustained bandwidth is GB/s.






Equation: t = M / (BW eta); waypoint time = t / H.
Under memory-bandwidth bound autoregressive weight streaming: t_stream = M_weights / (BW_peak * eta_bus) f_single = 1 / t_stream tau_step = t_stream / H f_waypoint_equivalent = 1 / tau_step = H * f_single
The waypoint-equivalent rate is an accounting ratio, not the rate at which the model observes the world or generates a fresh action chunk. Decoder work and other inference costs are excluded. f_effective is retained as a legacy alias for callers of this function.
Assumptions: One weight read per chunk and a positive caller-supplied sustained-bandwidth fraction. The default fraction is an assumption.
Excludes: Decoder compute, KV traffic, transport, and fresh-observation frequency.



Derivation: Divide bytes by sustained bytes per second, then allocate that time over H waypoints. The action-chunk paper motivates chunking, not the assumed efficiency.
Zhao et al., “Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware”, arXiv:2304.13705; Volume IV Chapter 3.



>>> result = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(ureg.Quantity("1 GB"), ureg.Quantity("10 GB/s"), 4, bus_efficiency=1.0)
>>> bool(result["tau_step"] * 4 == result["t_stream"])
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_axi_fifo_contention(
    tile_bytes,
    camera_bytes,
    telemetry_bytes,
    safety_read_bytes,
    transaction_bytes,
    bandwidth,
    bank_switches,
    bank_switch_time,
    compute_time,
)
Compare a finite FIFO backlog with priority bypass.











Name
Type
Description
Default




tile_bytes
int
Positive tile-transfer bytes, aligned to transaction_bytes.
required


camera_bytes
int
Positive camera-transfer bytes, aligned to transaction_bytes.
required


telemetry_bytes
int
Positive telemetry-transfer bytes, aligned to transaction_bytes.
required


safety_read_bytes
int
Positive defended-read bytes, aligned to transaction_bytes.
required


transaction_bytes
int
Positive bytes per indivisible transaction.
required


bandwidth
Quantity
Positive transfer bandwidth in bytes per second.
required


bank_switches
int
Nonnegative bank switches charged to FIFO backlog.
required


bank_switch_time
Quantity
Nonnegative time per bank switch.
required


compute_time
Quantity
Nonnegative compute time added after memory service.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Transaction counts and queue/read/total times in microseconds for FIFO and priority-bypass assumptions.






Equation: FIFO wait = (tile + camera + telemetry)/BW + switches switch_time; bypass wait = transaction/BW.
All transfers are aligned multiples of transaction_bytes. The FIFO scenario admits the entire tile, camera transfer, and telemetry transfer ahead of the safety read, then allows no new arrivals. The priority-bypass scenario waits only for one already in-flight transaction. These are controller-policy assumptions, not AXI timing guarantees. Peak bandwidth ignores arbitration, refresh, and protocol overhead, so times are floors.
Assumptions: Aligned transfers, no arrivals after the initial FIFO backlog, and priority bypass blocked only by the current transaction.
Excludes: Refresh, arbitration, protocol overhead, and any AXI latency or safety guarantee.



Derivation: A constructed policy scenario sums service times of bytes ahead of a read; priority bypass retains only one non-preemptible transaction.



>>> result = calc_axi_fifo_contention(tile_bytes=64, camera_bytes=32, telemetry_bytes=16, safety_read_bytes=16, transaction_bytes=16, bandwidth=ureg.Quantity("1 GB/s"), bank_switches=0, bank_switch_time=0 * ureg.nanosecond, compute_time=0 * ureg.nanosecond)
>>> bool(result["total_fifo"] >= result["total_priority_bypass"])
True

    num_axes,
    payload_bytes=8,
    baud_arbitration=None,
    baud_data=None,
    cycle_time=None,
    frames_per_axis=2,
    extended_id=False,
    worst_case_stuffing=True,
)
Calculate serial CAN FD occupancy for a cyclic axis exchange.











Name
Type
Description
Default




num_axes
int
Axes served on this bus (>= 1). Model one bus per call; parallel buses (for example one per limb) are separate calls.
required


payload_bytes
int
Application bytes per frame (default 8: a position-mode setpoint or feedback record). Padded to a valid CAN FD data-field size.
8


baud_arbitration
Quantity
Nominal (arbitration-phase) bit rate (default 1.0 Mbps).
None


baud_data
Quantity
Data-phase bit rate (default 5.0 Mbps).
None


cycle_time
Quantity
Cycle the exchange must fit (default 1.0 ms).
None


frames_per_axis
int
Frames per axis per cycle (default 2, command plus feedback).
2


extended_id
bool
29-bit identifiers (default False).
False


worst_case_stuffing
bool
Charge worst-case dynamic stuff bits (default True).
True














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: t_tx (per frame), t_total_tx, n_frames, utilization, is_schedulable, plus the per-frame bit breakdown of calc_canfd_frame_bits. Times are microseconds, utilization is dimensionless, and counts are integers. is_schedulable checks occupancy only.






Equation: t_frame = b_nom/R_nom + b_data/R_data; occupancy = axes frames_per_axis t_frame / cycle.
Each axis exchanges frames_per_axis frames per cycle (default 2: one command frame from the controller and one feedback frame from the drive; CAN carries them separately, unlike a summation-frame bus such as EtherCAT). Frame bits come from calc_canfd_frame_bits:
t_frame   = bits_nominal / R_nom + bits_data / R_data
n_frames  = num_axes * frames_per_axis
t_total   = n_frames * t_frame
rho       = t_total / cycle_time
rho <= 1 is only a necessary condition: non-preemptive blocking, competing frames, and error retransmissions still need a response-time analysis.
Assumptions: One serial bus, identical frame lengths, positive rates/cycle, and the chosen frame-stuffing policy.
Excludes: Non-preemptive blocking, other traffic, errors, and sufficient schedulability or safety certification.



Derivation: Convert each bit-rate phase to time, sum frames, and divide by the available cycle.
frame format per ISO 11898-1:2015 and Bosch CAN FD Specification 1.0 (2012), via calc_canfd_frame_bits.



>>> one = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(1)
>>> two = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(2)
>>> bool(two["t_total_tx"] == 2 * one["t_total_tx"])
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_canfd_frame_bits(
    payload_bytes=8,
    extended_id=False,
    worst_case_stuffing=True,
)
Count nominal-rate and data-rate bits in one CAN FD frame.











Name
Type
Description
Default




payload_bytes
int
Application bytes to carry (0 to 64). Padded up to the next data-field size a DLC can encode.
8


extended_id
bool
29-bit identifier (extended format) instead of 11-bit.
False


worst_case_stuffing
bool
Include the worst-case dynamic stuff bits (the bound a response-time analysis needs). False gives the unstuffed length.
True














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: data_field_bytes, crc_bits, fixed_stuff_bits, stuff_bits_nominal, stuff_bits_data, bits_nominal, bits_data (all int).






Equation: bits = fixed fields + padded payload bits + selected stuffing bound.
Frame layout (ISO 11898-1:2015 FD base format; extended format adds the SRR bit and the 18-bit identifier extension):
nominal rate, before the switch:  SOF 1, ID 11, RRS 1, IDE 1, FDF 1,
                                  res 1, BRS 1          (17 bits; 36 extended)
data rate, after BRS:             ESI 1, DLC 4, data 8n,
                                  stuff count 4, CRC 17 (n <= 16) or 21,
                                  fixed stuff bits 6 (CRC-17) or 7 (CRC-21)
nominal rate, after the switch:   CRC delimiter 1, ACK slot 1,
                                  ACK delimiter 1, EOF 7, intermission 3
                                                        (13 bits)
Dynamic stuff bits (one after five equal bits) apply from SOF through the end of the data field. The worst case over a stuffed run of L bits is floor((L - 1) / 4); the nominal-rate share is floor((L_nom - 1) / 4) and the rest fall in the data phase. The CRC field uses the fixed stuff bits above instead. BRS and the CRC delimiter straddle the rate switch; both are counted whole at the nominal rate, which slightly overstates the time.
Assumptions: The stated base/extended frame layout, legal DLC padding, and the selected worst-case or unstuffed mode.
Excludes: Error frames, retransmissions, arbitration waits, and measurement of an actual bus.



Derivation: Sum the documented frame fields; bound dynamic stuffing by floor((L-1)/4), with fixed CRC stuffing counted separately.
ISO 11898-1:2015, Road vehicles – Controller area network (CAN) – Part 1: Data link layer and physical signalling (FD frame format, stuff count, fixed stuff bits); Robert Bosch GmbH, CAN with Flexible Data-Rate, Specification Version 1.0, 2012 (dual bit rate, CRC-17/21, fixed CRC stuff bits).



>>> result = calc_canfd_frame_bits(payload_bytes=9)
>>> result["data_field_bytes"] == min(size for size in CANFD_DATA_FIELD_SIZES if size >= 9)
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_cbf_qp_orthogonal_projection(
    u_nom,
    a_vec,
    b_scalar,
)
Project a nominal control vector onto one supplied half-space.











Name
Type
Description
Default




u_nom
array_like
Finite nominal vector in consistent Euclidean control coordinates.
required


a_vec
array_like
Half-space normal with the same length as u_nom; nonzero when correction is needed.
required


b_scalar
float
Finite half-space bound in the units of the dot product a_vec dot u_nom.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Projected vector, correction norm, multiplier lambda_star, and was_modified flag. Units follow the supplied control coordinates.






Equation: u* = u_nom - max(0, (a dot u_nom - b)/(a dot a)) a for nonzero a.
Solves the quadratic program: min 1/2 ||u - u_nom||^2 s.t. a^T u <= b
The caller must derive a and b from its plant and barrier. This arithmetic alone proves neither forward invariance nor a physical stop.
Assumptions: One Euclidean half-space with compatible vector dimensions and a nonzero normal for an active constraint.
Excludes: Plant dynamics, deriving the barrier, forward-invariance proofs, and physical safety certification.



Derivation: The active half-space boundary requires a dot u*=b; minimizing correction length makes the correction parallel to a.



>>> result = calc_cbf_qp_orthogonal_projection([2.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.0], 1.0)
>>> result["u_projected"] == [1.0, 0.0]
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_chunk_renewal_schedule(
    chunk_rate,
    chunk_step,
    chunk_horizon,
    inference_latency,
)
Calculate renewal timing on an aligned setpoint grid.











Name
Type
Description
Default




chunk_rate
Quantity
Renewal rate f_r of the chunk policy (Hz).
required


chunk_step
Quantity
Setpoint spacing Delta t within a chunk (s).
required


chunk_horizon
int
Setpoints per chunk H (>= 1).
required


inference_latency
Quantity
Time from capture to an available chunk t_infer (s), for example a P99 target.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: renewal_period, setpoints_per_renewal (int), open_loop_span, min_supply_setpoints (int), chunk_span, overlapping_chunks (int), renewal_slack (T_r - t_infer). All time values are milliseconds.














Name
Type
Description





ValueError
If the renewal period is not a whole number of setpoint steps, if the inference does not finish within one renewal period, or if one chunk cannot bridge a renewal (H < h_min).






Equation: n = T_r / dt; open age = T_r + t_infer; H_min = ceil(open age / dt).
A chunk policy begins a fresh evaluation every renewal period T_r = 1/f_r and emits H setpoints spaced Delta t apart. With the renewal on the setpoint grid (T_r = n Delta t for a whole number n), every renewal instant falls on a setpoint boundary, so a new chunk replaces its predecessor at a defined setpoint index and temporal ensembling can blend chunks step by step:
n          = T_r / Delta t                  (setpoints per renewal, integer)
T_open     = T_r + t_infer                  (worst evidence age at replacement)
h_min      = ceil(T_open / Delta t)         (setpoints that bridge one renewal)
T_span     = H * Delta t                    (motion one chunk supplies)
n_overlap  = floor(H / n)                   (chunks that cover one step)
T_open is the worst sampling-phase wait plus inference, before transport and admission delays. n_overlap is the number of predictions a temporal ensemble blends at a step in steady state.
Assumptions: Periodic renewal aligned with the setpoint grid and inference finishing before the next renewal.
Excludes: Transport delays, missed renewals, scheduling jitter, and closed-loop stability.



Derivation: Count grid intervals covered by renewal and inference; floor H/n counts complete overlapping chunks.
action chunking and temporal ensembling from Zhao et al., “Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware” (ACT), RSS 2023, arXiv:2304.13705, which queries its policy every step (n = 1). The renewal-on-the-grid requirement, the worst-case age, and the overlap count are arithmetic of this package for n > 1 (Volume IV, Brain chapter, section on action chunking).



>>> result = calc_chunk_renewal_schedule(10 * ureg.hertz, 10 * ureg.millisecond, 20, 20 * ureg.millisecond)
>>> bool(result["open_loop_span"] == result["renewal_period"] + 20 * ureg.millisecond)
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_delay_phase_margin_ceiling(
    phase_margin,
    crossover,
)
Convert nominal phase margin into an ideal pure-delay ceiling.











Name
Type
Description
Default




phase_margin
Quantity
Positive phase margin in angle units, converted to radians.
required


crossover
Quantity
Positive angular gain-crossover frequency in radians per second.
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Delay ceiling in milliseconds.






Equation: phase lost = omega_c tau => tau_max = PM / omega_c
A pure delay leaves the gain unchanged and removes phase in proportion to frequency, so at the gain crossover omega_c it spends the nominal margin PM (radians) at tau_max.
Assumptions: A pure delay preserves gain, and the supplied crossover/margin describe the nominal loop.
Excludes: Robustness to plant uncertainty and certification of closed-loop safety.



Derivation: At crossover, exp(-s tau) consumes angular_crossover times tau radians of phase.
Franklin, Powell, and Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems, 8th ed. (2019), Sec. 6.4 (time delay); the delay margin.



>>> delay = calc_delay_phase_margin_ceiling(1 * ureg.radian, 2 * ureg.radian / ureg.second)
>>> bool(delay * 2 == 1 * ureg.second)
True

dict
Fields: t_tx, t_forward, t_cycle_total, t_margin (microseconds), utilization (dimensionless), and is_schedulable (occupancy test only).






In an EtherCAT daisy-chain ring, a single standard Ethernet frame passes through all slave ESCs (EtherCAT SubDevice Controllers). Each node processes and injects PDO data on-the-fly with hardware forwarding latency hop_delay (typically 0.6 us).
Equation: total_frame_bytes = header_bytes + (num_axes * bytes_per_axis) t_tx = (total_frame_bytes * 8) / baud_rate t_forward = num_axes * hop_delay t_cycle_total = t_tx + t_forward rho = t_cycle_total / cycle_time t_margin = cycle_time - t_cycle_total
Assumptions: One frame carries all supplied process data; each node adds the same forwarding delay. Positive rates/cycle and nonnegative overheads are caller requirements.
Excludes: Extra frames, synchronization jitter, competing traffic, and a sufficient schedulability or safety guarantee.



Derivation: Bytes become wire bits, bits divided by bit rate give serialization time, and serial node delays add.



>>> result = calc_ethercat_cycle_time(2)
>>> bool(result["t_cycle_total"] == result["t_tx"] + result["t_forward"])
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_phase_lag_total(
    crossover_frequency,
    sample_period,
    compute_delay=None,
    transport_delay=None,
    phase_allowance=None,
)
Calculate phase consumed by sampling, compute, and transport.











Name
Type
Description
Default




crossover_frequency
Quantity
Loop crossover frequency f_c (Hz).
required


sample_period
Quantity
Controller sample period T_s.
required


compute_delay
Quantity
Sample-to-output compute delay tau_comp (default 0).
None


transport_delay
Quantity
Command transport delay to the actuator tau_bus (default 0).
None


phase_allowance
Quantity
Phase erosion the design allows at crossover (angle). When given, the allowed delay, the delay margin, and the highest supported crossover are also returned.
None














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: tau_zoh, tau_total (ms); phase_zoh, phase_compute, phase_transport, phase_total (degrees); and, with phase_allowance, tau_allowed, tau_margin (negative when the budget fails), f_crossover_max, within_allowance.






Equation: tau = T_s/2 + tau_compute + tau_bus; phase = 2 pi f_c tau.
A zero-order hold behaves in the baseband like a pure delay of half a sample period. A controller that outputs its command some time after it samples adds that compute delay, and a command that reaches the actuator one bus cycle later adds the transport delay. A pure delay tau removes phase omega * tau at every frequency, so near crossover:
tau_total   = T_s / 2 + tau_comp + tau_bus
dphi_total  = 2 * pi * f_c * tau_total              (radians)
Given a phase allowance dphi_allow, the largest total delay the loop can absorb, and the highest crossover a given total delay supports, are
tau_allow   = dphi_allow / (2 * pi * f_c)
f_c,max     = dphi_allow / (2 * pi * tau_total)
Assumptions: The zero-order-hold half-period approximation applies well below the sampling frequency.
Excludes: Plant/model uncertainty and a proof of closed-loop stability.



Derivation: Add serial delay contributions and apply the phase of exp(-s tau) at the crossover frequency.
Franklin, G. F., Powell, J. D. and Workman, M. L., Digital Control of Dynamic Systems, 3rd ed., Addison-Wesley, 1998 (zero-order hold as a T/2 delay; phase of a pure delay). The half-sample approximation holds only well below the sampling frequency; it is a budget, not a stability proof.



>>> result = calc_phase_lag_total(10 * ureg.hertz, 2 * ureg.millisecond)
>>> bool(result["tau_total"] == result["tau_zoh"])
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_response_time_bound(
    wcet,
    blocking,
    interference,
    deadline=None,
)
Sum declared execution, blocking, and interference bounds.











Name
Type
Description
Default




wcet
Quantity
Nonnegative worst-case execution-time bound in time units.
required


blocking
Quantity
Nonnegative lower-priority blocking bound in time units.
required


interference
Quantity
Nonnegative higher-priority interference bound over the response window.
required


deadline
Quantity
Positive deadline in time units; omit to return only the response bound.
None














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: response; with deadline, margin, meets_deadline, blocking_limit (all times in microseconds).






Equation: R = C + B + I; margin = D - R.
wcet (C) is the task’s worst-case execution time, blocking (B) the longest section in which lower-priority code keeps it from running, and interference (I) the higher-priority work that preempts it inside one response window. The bound holds only as far as each term is itself a bound: a measured execution time can refute a declared C but never establish it. With a deadline D, the margin D - R and the largest blocking that still meets D (D - C - I) are returned as well.
Assumptions: The three supplied terms are valid bounds for the same response window.
Excludes: Deriving interference through scheduling fixed points, empirical certification of WCET, and safety certification.



Derivation: Partition response time into own execution, blocking, and higher-priority interference, then add these disjoint contributions.
Buttazzo, G., Hard Real-Time Computing Systems, 3rd ed., Springer, 2011 (response-time analysis with blocking); Sha, Rajkumar, and Lehoczky, “Priority Inheritance Protocols,” IEEE Trans. Computers 39(9), 1990.



>>> result = calc_response_time_bound(2 * ureg.microsecond, 3 * ureg.microsecond, 4 * ureg.microsecond, 12 * ureg.microsecond)
>>> bool(result["response"] + result["margin"] == 12 * ureg.microsecond)
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_temporal_ensemble_weights(decay, predictions)
Normalize exponential weights over overlapping chunk predictions.











Name
Type
Description
Default




decay
float
Decay constant k per prediction index (>= 0).
required


predictions
int
Number of overlapping predictions n (>= 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: weights (numpy array, sums to 1), oldest_over_newest (w_0 / w_{n-1}), newest_share (w_{n-1}).






Equation: w_i = exp(-decay i) / sum_j exp(-decay j), oldest first.
A chunk policy queried every step holds predictions overlapping predictions for the current step, index 0 the oldest. ACT blends them with exponentially decaying weights
w_i = exp(-k i) / sum_j exp(-k j),   i = 0 .. n - 1,
so the oldest prediction weighs most for k > 0.
Assumptions: The oldest prediction has index zero; decay is nonnegative and the count is positive.
Excludes: Prediction quality, correlations, and whether blending preserves constraints.



Derivation: Normalize nonnegative exponential weights by their sum. A positive decay weights older entries more heavily.
Zhao et al., “Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware” (ACT), RSS 2023, arXiv:2304.13705, and its reference code (imitate_episodes.py, temporal-ensembling branch).



>>> result = calc_temporal_ensemble_weights(0.0, 4)
>>> bool(np.allclose(result["weights"], np.ones(4) / 4))
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_watchdog_lease_bound(
    clearance_distance,
    initial_velocity,
    max_deceleration,
)
Calculate the ideal total delay budget before braking.











Name
Type
Description
Default




clearance_distance
Quantity
Defended physical clearance / sensory safety field ahead of obstacle (e.g. m).
required


initial_velocity
Quantity
Cruise velocity of the vehicle / mobile base v0 (e.g. m/s).
required


max_deceleration
Quantity
Positive emergency-braking deceleration supplied by the caller (e.g. m/s^2); the function does not certify its achievability.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: t_total_delay_max, t_lease_max (legacy alias), d_brake, d_drift_allowable. Delay values are milliseconds and distances are meters.






Equation: d_brake = v^2/(2a); delay = (clearance - d_brake)/v.
Under constant velocity v0 during uncommanded drift, followed by emergency braking at constant deceleration a_max: d_brake = (v0^2) / (2 * a_max) d_drift = d_clear - d_brake T_lease + T_detection + T_brake_onset <= d_drift / v0
The returned ceiling includes every pre-brake delay. A chosen watchdog lease must be shorter after reserving detection, command delivery, and brake-onset time. t_lease_max is retained as a legacy alias for the ideal total ceiling, not a safe standalone lease setting.
Assumptions: Constant positive speed during the delay followed by constant positive deceleration. The caller supplies the achievable deceleration.
Excludes: Detection, transport, and brake-onset reservations; this ceiling alone is not a safe watchdog setting or certification.



Derivation: Integrate constant acceleration to obtain stopping distance, subtract it from clearance, then divide the remaining drift distance by speed.



>>> result = calc_watchdog_lease_bound(2 * ureg.meter, 1 * ureg.meter / ureg.second, 1 * ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)
>>> bool(result["d_brake"] + result["d_drift_allowable"] == 2 * ureg.meter)
True

physics.robotics.control.calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
    model_weight_memory,
    memory_bandwidth,
    chunk_horizon,
    bus_efficiency=0.7,
)
Calculate the weight-stream floor per chunk and per waypoint.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model_weight_memory
Quantity
Model parameter storage footprint (e.g. GB).
required


memory_bandwidth
Quantity
Peak memory bus bandwidth (e.g. GB/s).
required


chunk_horizon
int
Number of steps predicted per chunk H (>= 1).
required


bus_efficiency
float
Sustained DRAM efficiency fraction eta in (0, 1] (default 0.70). This physical range is a caller requirement, not validated here.
0.7














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: t_stream, f_single, tau_step, f_waypoint_equivalent, f_effective (legacy alias), b_sustained. Times are milliseconds, rates are hertz, and sustained bandwidth is GB/s.






Equation: t = M / (BW eta); waypoint time = t / H.
Under memory-bandwidth bound autoregressive weight streaming: t_stream = M_weights / (BW_peak * eta_bus) f_single = 1 / t_stream tau_step = t_stream / H f_waypoint_equivalent = 1 / tau_step = H * f_single
The waypoint-equivalent rate is an accounting ratio, not the rate at which the model observes the world or generates a fresh action chunk. Decoder work and other inference costs are excluded. f_effective is retained as a legacy alias for callers of this function.
Assumptions: One weight read per chunk and a positive caller-supplied sustained-bandwidth fraction. The default fraction is an assumption.
Excludes: Decoder compute, KV traffic, transport, and fresh-observation frequency.



Derivation: Divide bytes by sustained bytes per second, then allocate that time over H waypoints. The action-chunk paper motivates chunking, not the assumed efficiency.
Zhao et al., “Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware”, arXiv:2304.13705; Volume IV Chapter 3.



>>> result = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(ureg.Quantity("1 GB"), ureg.Quantity("10 GB/s"), 4, bus_efficiency=1.0)
>>> bool(result["tau_step"] * 4 == result["t_stream"])
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_axi_fifo_contention(
    tile_bytes,
    camera_bytes,
    telemetry_bytes,
    safety_read_bytes,
    transaction_bytes,
    bandwidth,
    bank_switches,
    bank_switch_time,
    compute_time,
)
Compare a finite FIFO backlog with priority bypass.











Name
Type
Description
Default




tile_bytes
int
Positive tile-transfer bytes, aligned to transaction_bytes.
required


camera_bytes
int
Positive camera-transfer bytes, aligned to transaction_bytes.
required


telemetry_bytes
int
Positive telemetry-transfer bytes, aligned to transaction_bytes.
required


safety_read_bytes
int
Positive defended-read bytes, aligned to transaction_bytes.
required


transaction_bytes
int
Positive bytes per indivisible transaction.
required


bandwidth
Quantity
Positive transfer bandwidth in bytes per second.
required


bank_switches
int
Nonnegative bank switches charged to FIFO backlog.
required


bank_switch_time
Quantity
Nonnegative time per bank switch.
required


compute_time
Quantity
Nonnegative compute time added after memory service.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Transaction counts and queue/read/total times in microseconds for FIFO and priority-bypass assumptions.






Equation: FIFO wait = (tile + camera + telemetry)/BW + switches switch_time; bypass wait = transaction/BW.
All transfers are aligned multiples of transaction_bytes. The FIFO scenario admits the entire tile, camera transfer, and telemetry transfer ahead of the safety read, then allows no new arrivals. The priority-bypass scenario waits only for one already in-flight transaction. These are controller-policy assumptions, not AXI timing guarantees. Peak bandwidth ignores arbitration, refresh, and protocol overhead, so times are floors.
Assumptions: Aligned transfers, no arrivals after the initial FIFO backlog, and priority bypass blocked only by the current transaction.
Excludes: Refresh, arbitration, protocol overhead, and any AXI latency or safety guarantee.



Derivation: A constructed policy scenario sums service times of bytes ahead of a read; priority bypass retains only one non-preemptible transaction.



>>> result = calc_axi_fifo_contention(tile_bytes=64, camera_bytes=32, telemetry_bytes=16, safety_read_bytes=16, transaction_bytes=16, bandwidth=ureg.Quantity("1 GB/s"), bank_switches=0, bank_switch_time=0 * ureg.nanosecond, compute_time=0 * ureg.nanosecond)
>>> bool(result["total_fifo"] >= result["total_priority_bypass"])
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_canfd_bus_utilization(
    num_axes,
    payload_bytes=8,
    baud_arbitration=None,
    baud_data=None,
    cycle_time=None,
    frames_per_axis=2,
    extended_id=False,
    worst_case_stuffing=True,
)
Calculate serial CAN FD occupancy for a cyclic axis exchange.











Name
Type
Description
Default




num_axes
int
Axes served on this bus (>= 1). Model one bus per call; parallel buses (for example one per limb) are separate calls.
required


payload_bytes
int
Application bytes per frame (default 8: a position-mode setpoint or feedback record). Padded to a valid CAN FD data-field size.
8


baud_arbitration
Quantity
Nominal (arbitration-phase) bit rate (default 1.0 Mbps).
None


baud_data
Quantity
Data-phase bit rate (default 5.0 Mbps).
None


cycle_time
Quantity
Cycle the exchange must fit (default 1.0 ms).
None


frames_per_axis
int
Frames per axis per cycle (default 2, command plus feedback).
2


extended_id
bool
29-bit identifiers (default False).
False


worst_case_stuffing
bool
Charge worst-case dynamic stuff bits (default True).
True














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: t_tx (per frame), t_total_tx, n_frames, utilization, is_schedulable, plus the per-frame bit breakdown of calc_canfd_frame_bits. Times are microseconds, utilization is dimensionless, and counts are integers. is_schedulable checks occupancy only.






Equation: t_frame = b_nom/R_nom + b_data/R_data; occupancy = axes frames_per_axis t_frame / cycle.
Each axis exchanges frames_per_axis frames per cycle (default 2: one command frame from the controller and one feedback frame from the drive; CAN carries them separately, unlike a summation-frame bus such as EtherCAT). Frame bits come from calc_canfd_frame_bits:
t_frame   = bits_nominal / R_nom + bits_data / R_data
n_frames  = num_axes * frames_per_axis
t_total   = n_frames * t_frame
rho       = t_total / cycle_time
rho <= 1 is only a necessary condition: non-preemptive blocking, competing frames, and error retransmissions still need a response-time analysis.
Assumptions: One serial bus, identical frame lengths, positive rates/cycle, and the chosen frame-stuffing policy.
Excludes: Non-preemptive blocking, other traffic, errors, and sufficient schedulability or safety certification.



Derivation: Convert each bit-rate phase to time, sum frames, and divide by the available cycle.
frame format per ISO 11898-1:2015 and Bosch CAN FD Specification 1.0 (2012), via calc_canfd_frame_bits.



>>> one = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(1)
>>> two = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(2)
>>> bool(two["t_total_tx"] == 2 * one["t_total_tx"])
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_canfd_frame_bits(
    payload_bytes=8,
    extended_id=False,
    worst_case_stuffing=True,
)
Count nominal-rate and data-rate bits in one CAN FD frame.











Name
Type
Description
Default




payload_bytes
int
Application bytes to carry (0 to 64). Padded up to the next data-field size a DLC can encode.
8


extended_id
bool
29-bit identifier (extended format) instead of 11-bit.
False


worst_case_stuffing
bool
Include the worst-case dynamic stuff bits (the bound a response-time analysis needs). False gives the unstuffed length.
True














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: data_field_bytes, crc_bits, fixed_stuff_bits, stuff_bits_nominal, stuff_bits_data, bits_nominal, bits_data (all int).






Equation: bits = fixed fields + padded payload bits + selected stuffing bound.
Frame layout (ISO 11898-1:2015 FD base format; extended format adds the SRR bit and the 18-bit identifier extension):
nominal rate, before the switch:  SOF 1, ID 11, RRS 1, IDE 1, FDF 1,
                                  res 1, BRS 1          (17 bits; 36 extended)
data rate, after BRS:             ESI 1, DLC 4, data 8n,
                                  stuff count 4, CRC 17 (n <= 16) or 21,
                                  fixed stuff bits 6 (CRC-17) or 7 (CRC-21)
nominal rate, after the switch:   CRC delimiter 1, ACK slot 1,
                                  ACK delimiter 1, EOF 7, intermission 3
                                                        (13 bits)
Dynamic stuff bits (one after five equal bits) apply from SOF through the end of the data field. The worst case over a stuffed run of L bits is floor((L - 1) / 4); the nominal-rate share is floor((L_nom - 1) / 4) and the rest fall in the data phase. The CRC field uses the fixed stuff bits above instead. BRS and the CRC delimiter straddle the rate switch; both are counted whole at the nominal rate, which slightly overstates the time.
Assumptions: The stated base/extended frame layout, legal DLC padding, and the selected worst-case or unstuffed mode.
Excludes: Error frames, retransmissions, arbitration waits, and measurement of an actual bus.



Derivation: Sum the documented frame fields; bound dynamic stuffing by floor((L-1)/4), with fixed CRC stuffing counted separately.
ISO 11898-1:2015, Road vehicles – Controller area network (CAN) – Part 1: Data link layer and physical signalling (FD frame format, stuff count, fixed stuff bits); Robert Bosch GmbH, CAN with Flexible Data-Rate, Specification Version 1.0, 2012 (dual bit rate, CRC-17/21, fixed CRC stuff bits).



>>> result = calc_canfd_frame_bits(payload_bytes=9)
>>> result["data_field_bytes"] == min(size for size in CANFD_DATA_FIELD_SIZES if size >= 9)
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_cbf_qp_orthogonal_projection(
    u_nom,
    a_vec,
    b_scalar,
)
Project a nominal control vector onto one supplied half-space.











Name
Type
Description
Default




u_nom
array_like
Finite nominal vector in consistent Euclidean control coordinates.
required


a_vec
array_like
Half-space normal with the same length as u_nom; nonzero when correction is needed.
required


b_scalar
float
Finite half-space bound in the units of the dot product a_vec dot u_nom.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Projected vector, correction norm, multiplier lambda_star, and was_modified flag. Units follow the supplied control coordinates.






Equation: u* = u_nom - max(0, (a dot u_nom - b)/(a dot a)) a for nonzero a.
Solves the quadratic program: min 1/2 ||u - u_nom||^2 s.t. a^T u <= b
The caller must derive a and b from its plant and barrier. This arithmetic alone proves neither forward invariance nor a physical stop.
Assumptions: One Euclidean half-space with compatible vector dimensions and a nonzero normal for an active constraint.
Excludes: Plant dynamics, deriving the barrier, forward-invariance proofs, and physical safety certification.



Derivation: The active half-space boundary requires a dot u*=b; minimizing correction length makes the correction parallel to a.



>>> result = calc_cbf_qp_orthogonal_projection([2.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.0], 1.0)
>>> result["u_projected"] == [1.0, 0.0]
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_chunk_renewal_schedule(
    chunk_rate,
    chunk_step,
    chunk_horizon,
    inference_latency,
)
Calculate renewal timing on an aligned setpoint grid.











Name
Type
Description
Default




chunk_rate
Quantity
Renewal rate f_r of the chunk policy (Hz).
required


chunk_step
Quantity
Setpoint spacing Delta t within a chunk (s).
required


chunk_horizon
int
Setpoints per chunk H (>= 1).
required


inference_latency
Quantity
Time from capture to an available chunk t_infer (s), for example a P99 target.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: renewal_period, setpoints_per_renewal (int), open_loop_span, min_supply_setpoints (int), chunk_span, overlapping_chunks (int), renewal_slack (T_r - t_infer). All time values are milliseconds.














Name
Type
Description





ValueError
If the renewal period is not a whole number of setpoint steps, if the inference does not finish within one renewal period, or if one chunk cannot bridge a renewal (H < h_min).






Equation: n = T_r / dt; open age = T_r + t_infer; H_min = ceil(open age / dt).
A chunk policy begins a fresh evaluation every renewal period T_r = 1/f_r and emits H setpoints spaced Delta t apart. With the renewal on the setpoint grid (T_r = n Delta t for a whole number n), every renewal instant falls on a setpoint boundary, so a new chunk replaces its predecessor at a defined setpoint index and temporal ensembling can blend chunks step by step:
n          = T_r / Delta t                  (setpoints per renewal, integer)
T_open     = T_r + t_infer                  (worst evidence age at replacement)
h_min      = ceil(T_open / Delta t)         (setpoints that bridge one renewal)
T_span     = H * Delta t                    (motion one chunk supplies)
n_overlap  = floor(H / n)                   (chunks that cover one step)
T_open is the worst sampling-phase wait plus inference, before transport and admission delays. n_overlap is the number of predictions a temporal ensemble blends at a step in steady state.
Assumptions: Periodic renewal aligned with the setpoint grid and inference finishing before the next renewal.
Excludes: Transport delays, missed renewals, scheduling jitter, and closed-loop stability.



Derivation: Count grid intervals covered by renewal and inference; floor H/n counts complete overlapping chunks.
action chunking and temporal ensembling from Zhao et al., “Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware” (ACT), RSS 2023, arXiv:2304.13705, which queries its policy every step (n = 1). The renewal-on-the-grid requirement, the worst-case age, and the overlap count are arithmetic of this package for n > 1 (Volume IV, Brain chapter, section on action chunking).



>>> result = calc_chunk_renewal_schedule(10 * ureg.hertz, 10 * ureg.millisecond, 20, 20 * ureg.millisecond)
>>> bool(result["open_loop_span"] == result["renewal_period"] + 20 * ureg.millisecond)
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_delay_phase_margin_ceiling(
    phase_margin,
    crossover,
)
Convert nominal phase margin into an ideal pure-delay ceiling.











Name
Type
Description
Default




phase_margin
Quantity
Positive phase margin in angle units, converted to radians.
required


crossover
Quantity
Positive angular gain-crossover frequency in radians per second.
required









Name
Type
Description





Quantity
Delay ceiling in milliseconds.






Equation: phase lost = omega_c tau => tau_max = PM / omega_c
A pure delay leaves the gain unchanged and removes phase in proportion to frequency, so at the gain crossover omega_c it spends the nominal margin PM (radians) at tau_max.
Assumptions: A pure delay preserves gain, and the supplied crossover/margin describe the nominal loop.
Excludes: Robustness to plant uncertainty and certification of closed-loop safety.



Derivation: At crossover, exp(-s tau) consumes angular_crossover times tau radians of phase.
Franklin, Powell, and Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems, 8th ed. (2019), Sec. 6.4 (time delay); the delay margin.



>>> delay = calc_delay_phase_margin_ceiling(1 * ureg.radian, 2 * ureg.radian / ureg.second)
>>> bool(delay * 2 == 1 * ureg.second)
True

physics.robotics.control.calc_phase_lag_total(
    crossover_frequency,
    sample_period,
    compute_delay=None,
    transport_delay=None,
    phase_allowance=None,
)
Calculate phase consumed by sampling, compute, and transport.











Name
Type
Description
Default




crossover_frequency
Quantity
Loop crossover frequency f_c (Hz).
required


sample_period
Quantity
Controller sample period T_s.
required


compute_delay
Quantity
Sample-to-output compute delay tau_comp (default 0).
None


transport_delay
Quantity
Command transport delay to the actuator tau_bus (default 0).
None


phase_allowance
Quantity
Phase erosion the design allows at crossover (angle). When given, the allowed delay, the delay margin, and the highest supported crossover are also returned.
None














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: tau_zoh, tau_total (ms); phase_zoh, phase_compute, phase_transport, phase_total (degrees); and, with phase_allowance, tau_allowed, tau_margin (negative when the budget fails), f_crossover_max, within_allowance.






Equation: tau = T_s/2 + tau_compute + tau_bus; phase = 2 pi f_c tau.
A zero-order hold behaves in the baseband like a pure delay of half a sample period. A controller that outputs its command some time after it samples adds that compute delay, and a command that reaches the actuator one bus cycle later adds the transport delay. A pure delay tau removes phase omega * tau at every frequency, so near crossover:
tau_total   = T_s / 2 + tau_comp + tau_bus
dphi_total  = 2 * pi * f_c * tau_total              (radians)
Given a phase allowance dphi_allow, the largest total delay the loop can absorb, and the highest crossover a given total delay supports, are
tau_allow   = dphi_allow / (2 * pi * f_c)
f_c,max     = dphi_allow / (2 * pi * tau_total)
Assumptions: The zero-order-hold half-period approximation applies well below the sampling frequency.
Excludes: Plant/model uncertainty and a proof of closed-loop stability.



Derivation: Add serial delay contributions and apply the phase of exp(-s tau) at the crossover frequency.
Franklin, G. F., Powell, J. D. and Workman, M. L., Digital Control of Dynamic Systems, 3rd ed., Addison-Wesley, 1998 (zero-order hold as a T/2 delay; phase of a pure delay). The half-sample approximation holds only well below the sampling frequency; it is a budget, not a stability proof.



>>> result = calc_phase_lag_total(10 * ureg.hertz, 2 * ureg.millisecond)
>>> bool(result["tau_total"] == result["tau_zoh"])
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_response_time_bound(
    wcet,
    blocking,
    interference,
    deadline=None,
)
Sum declared execution, blocking, and interference bounds.











Name
Type
Description
Default




wcet
Quantity
Nonnegative worst-case execution-time bound in time units.
required


blocking
Quantity
Nonnegative lower-priority blocking bound in time units.
required


interference
Quantity
Nonnegative higher-priority interference bound over the response window.
required


deadline
Quantity
Positive deadline in time units; omit to return only the response bound.
None














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: response; with deadline, margin, meets_deadline, blocking_limit (all times in microseconds).






Equation: R = C + B + I; margin = D - R.
wcet (C) is the task’s worst-case execution time, blocking (B) the longest section in which lower-priority code keeps it from running, and interference (I) the higher-priority work that preempts it inside one response window. The bound holds only as far as each term is itself a bound: a measured execution time can refute a declared C but never establish it. With a deadline D, the margin D - R and the largest blocking that still meets D (D - C - I) are returned as well.
Assumptions: The three supplied terms are valid bounds for the same response window.
Excludes: Deriving interference through scheduling fixed points, empirical certification of WCET, and safety certification.



Derivation: Partition response time into own execution, blocking, and higher-priority interference, then add these disjoint contributions.
Buttazzo, G., Hard Real-Time Computing Systems, 3rd ed., Springer, 2011 (response-time analysis with blocking); Sha, Rajkumar, and Lehoczky, “Priority Inheritance Protocols,” IEEE Trans. Computers 39(9), 1990.



>>> result = calc_response_time_bound(2 * ureg.microsecond, 3 * ureg.microsecond, 4 * ureg.microsecond, 12 * ureg.microsecond)
>>> bool(result["response"] + result["margin"] == 12 * ureg.microsecond)
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_temporal_ensemble_weights(decay, predictions)
Normalize exponential weights over overlapping chunk predictions.











Name
Type
Description
Default




decay
float
Decay constant k per prediction index (>= 0).
required


predictions
int
Number of overlapping predictions n (>= 1).
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: weights (numpy array, sums to 1), oldest_over_newest (w_0 / w_{n-1}), newest_share (w_{n-1}).






Equation: w_i = exp(-decay i) / sum_j exp(-decay j), oldest first.
A chunk policy queried every step holds predictions overlapping predictions for the current step, index 0 the oldest. ACT blends them with exponentially decaying weights
w_i = exp(-k i) / sum_j exp(-k j),   i = 0 .. n - 1,
so the oldest prediction weighs most for k > 0.
Assumptions: The oldest prediction has index zero; decay is nonnegative and the count is positive.
Excludes: Prediction quality, correlations, and whether blending preserves constraints.



Derivation: Normalize nonnegative exponential weights by their sum. A positive decay weights older entries more heavily.
Zhao et al., “Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware” (ACT), RSS 2023, arXiv:2304.13705, and its reference code (imitate_episodes.py, temporal-ensembling branch).



>>> result = calc_temporal_ensemble_weights(0.0, 4)
>>> bool(np.allclose(result["weights"], np.ones(4) / 4))
True




physics.robotics.control.calc_watchdog_lease_bound(
    clearance_distance,
    initial_velocity,
    max_deceleration,
)
Calculate the ideal total delay budget before braking.











Name
Type
Description
Default




clearance_distance
Quantity
Defended physical clearance / sensory safety field ahead of obstacle (e.g. m).
required


initial_velocity
Quantity
Cruise velocity of the vehicle / mobile base v0 (e.g. m/s).
required


max_deceleration
Quantity
Positive emergency-braking deceleration supplied by the caller (e.g. m/s^2); the function does not certify its achievability.
required














Name
Type
Description





dict
Fields: t_total_delay_max, t_lease_max (legacy alias), d_brake, d_drift_allowable. Delay values are milliseconds and distances are meters.






Equation: d_brake = v^2/(2a); delay = (clearance - d_brake)/v.
Under constant velocity v0 during uncommanded drift, followed by emergency braking at constant deceleration a_max: d_brake = (v0^2) / (2 * a_max) d_drift = d_clear - d_brake T_lease + T_detection + T_brake_onset <= d_drift / v0
The returned ceiling includes every pre-brake delay. A chosen watchdog lease must be shorter after reserving detection, command delivery, and brake-onset time. t_lease_max is retained as a legacy alias for the ideal total ceiling, not a safe standalone lease setting.
Assumptions: Constant positive speed during the delay followed by constant positive deceleration. The caller supplies the achievable deceleration.
Excludes: Detection, transport, and brake-onset reservations; this ceiling alone is not a safe watchdog setting or certification.



Derivation: Integrate constant acceleration to obtain stopping distance, subtract it from clearance, then divide the remaining drift distance by speed.



>>> result = calc_watchdog_lease_bound(2 * ureg.meter, 1 * ureg.meter / ureg.second, 1 * ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)
>>> bool(result["d_brake"] + result["d_drift_allowable"] == 2 * ureg.meter)
True

Training scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/training.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
Weights, gradients, and optimizer state of workload at one precision, against hardware’s memory.
bytes_per_value stores each weight and gradient; the optimizer keeps optimizer_bytes_per_parameter (two FP32 values for Adam, one for SGD with momentum). Activations are not included.


Equation: Parameter state sums weights, gradients, optimizer state, and optional master weights; adapter mode keeps base weights frozen.
Assumptions: Bytes per value/state and the activation budget are supplied; activation storage scales linearly with batch.
Excludes: Runtime workspaces, allocator reserve, optimizer-specific extra temporaries, and capacity safety margins.

title: solvers.SustainabilityModel
text:
solvers.SustainabilityModel()
Calculates Datacenter-scale Sustainability metrics.
Handles Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), Carbon Intensity, and Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) across different regional grids. This model simulates the ‘Infrastructure Tax’ — the energy spent on cooling and power delivery rather than on neural computation.
Literature Source: 1. Patterson et al. (2021), “Carbon Emissions and Large Neural Network Training.” 2. Belkhir & Elmeligi (2018), “Assessing ICT Global Emissions Footprint.” 3. Wu et al. (2022), “Sustainable AI: Environmental Implications, Challenges and Opportunities.”
Formula contract: - per-device power = idle_fraction * TDP + dynamic_fraction * TDP * MFU. - IT energy = device power * accelerator count * duration. - facility energy applies PUE; operational carbon applies grid carbon intensity to facility energy; water applies WUE to facility energy.





Name
Description




solve
Calculate energy, carbon, and water footprint for a fleet operation.





solvers.SustainabilityModel.solve(
    fleet,
    duration_days,
    datacenter=None,
    mfu=1.0,
    embodied_carbon_per_device=0.0,
)
Calculate energy, carbon, and water footprint for a fleet operation.
Implements the formula contract in the class docstring: per-device power is an energy-proportionality model (idle_fraction * TDP + dynamic_fraction * TDP * MFU), scaled to the fleet, integrated over the duration, then taxed by PUE for facility energy. Carbon and water apply the regional grid’s carbon intensity and WUE to facility (post-PUE) energy.











Name
Type
Description
Default




fleet
Fleet
The cluster; supplies accelerator count, per-device TDP, and the default datacenter/region when datacenter is not given.
required


duration_days
float
Operation duration in days.
required


datacenter
Datacenter
Override for the fleet’s datacenter (or a bare GridProfile); supplies PUE, carbon intensity, and WUE. Falls back to the fleet region and finally to the US average grid.
None


mfu
float
Model FLOPs Utilization in [0, 1]; drives the dynamic-power term.
1.0


embodied_carbon_per_device
float
Manufacturing/shipping carbon per accelerator in kg CO2e (default 0 = operational carbon only).
0.0














Name
Type
Description





SustainabilityResult
IT and facility energy (kWh), total carbon (kg CO2e, operational plus embodied), water usage (liters), and the PUE applied.






Equation: P = TDP * (idle_fraction + dynamic_fraction * MFU); E_IT = P * devices * duration; E_facility = PUE * E_IT. Carbon is E_facility * grid intensity plus the full supplied embodied amount. Water uses facility energy in this solver, unlike WaterUseModel, whose explicit boundary is IT energy.
Assumptions: Constant utilization, PUE, and regional intensities over the run. Embodied carbon is charged fully rather than amortized. Excludes: Measured power traces, host power beyond the assumed accelerator-based account, and lifetime allocation of embodied carbon.



Derivation: Integrate the assumed idle-plus-utilization power over the fleet duration, apply PUE once, and multiply facility energy by regional carbon and water intensities. This is an energy-accounting convention rather than a meter measurement.



>>> from mlsysim import Q_, Systems
>>> result = SustainabilityModel().solve(Systems.Clusters.Research_256, duration_days=1)
>>> result.total_energy_kwh >= result.it_energy_kwh
True

title: engine.solvers.tool_calls
text:
engine.solvers.tool_calls
Tool-calling solvers: what a retry duplicates, an observation carries, a poll costs, a catalog stages.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated probabilities, counts, and prices: duplicate effects under one blind retry with independent request and reply loss, a raw log against the shaped view later calls carry, the status calls a model makes while a job is pending, descriptor tokens staged per call with and without selection, cost per accepted task for structured tools against one shell tool, and adapters with and without a shared protocol. None models delayed packets, a tokenizer, cache eviction, or a provider’s price schedule.





Name
Description




BlindRetryModel
Timeouts and duplicate effects of calls mutating calls under one blind retry.


ModelPollingModel
Incremental cost of a model that checks a pending job every poll_interval.


ObservationCarryModel
A raw tool output in windows, and the input bill of a shaped view carried by later calls.


ToolCatalogSelectionModel
Descriptor tokens on every call: the whole catalog against a selected subset plus overhead.


ToolkitGranularityModel
Cost per accepted task for a structured toolkit against one general shell tool.





engine.solvers.tool_calls.BlindRetryModel()
Timeouts and duplicate effects of calls mutating calls under one blind retry.
Requests and replies are lost independently and never arrive later; every delivered request executes; each timeout triggers exactly one retry of a non-idempotent call with no deduplication.





Name
Description




solve
Estimate timeouts and duplicate effects from one blind retry.





engine.solvers.tool_calls.BlindRetryModel.solve(request_loss, reply_loss, calls)
Estimate timeouts and duplicate effects from one blind retry.











Name
Type
Description
Default




request_loss
float
Probability a request is permanently lost, in [0, 1].
required


reply_loss
float
Probability an execution reply is permanently lost, in [0, 1].
required


calls
int
Nonnegative original mutating-call count.
required














Name
Type
Description





BlindRetryResult
Dimensionless per-call timeout and duplicate probabilities, original call count, and expected timeout and duplicate counts.






Equation: Timeout probability is request_loss + (1-request_loss)*reply_loss. Duplicate execution probability is (1-request_loss)**2 * reply_loss.
Assumptions: Request and reply losses are independent, including across attempts. Every timeout triggers one retry; every delivered request executes.
Excludes: Idempotency keys, deduplication, late packets, additional retries, and a prediction of workload-specific harm from duplicate execution.



Derivation: A timeout means either a lost request or a delivered request with lost reply. Duplication requires the first request to execute, its reply to vanish, and the retry to execute; multiply those probabilities.



>>> from mlsysim.solvers import BlindRetryModel
>>> result = BlindRetryModel().solve(0.1, 0.2, 100)
>>> result.duplicate_probability < result.timeout_probability
True






engine.solvers.tool_calls.ModelPollingModel()
Incremental cost of a model that checks a pending job every poll_interval.
Checks start one interval after dispatch and stop at completion; each reads context_tokens (a cache_hit share billed at cached_fraction of the input price) and generates output_tokens. The worst detection delay is one interval. Useful calls common to every design are excluded.





Name
Description




solve
Account for extra model calls while a dispatched job is pending.

    job_duration,
    poll_interval,
    context_tokens,
    output_tokens,
    cache_hit,
    input_price,
    cached_fraction,
    output_price,
)

engine.solvers.tool_calls.BlindRetryModel()
Timeouts and duplicate effects of calls mutating calls under one blind retry.
Requests and replies are lost independently and never arrive later; every delivered request executes; each timeout triggers exactly one retry of a non-idempotent call with no deduplication.

required














Name
Type
Description





BlindRetryResult
Dimensionless per-call timeout and duplicate probabilities, original call count, and expected timeout and duplicate counts.






Equation: Timeout probability is request_loss + (1-request_loss)*reply_loss. Duplicate execution probability is (1-request_loss)**2 * reply_loss.
Assumptions: Request and reply losses are independent, including across attempts. Every timeout triggers one retry; every delivered request executes.
Excludes: Idempotency keys, deduplication, late packets, additional retries, and a prediction of workload-specific harm from duplicate execution.



Derivation: A timeout means either a lost request or a delivered request with lost reply. Duplication requires the first request to execute, its reply to vanish, and the retry to execute; multiply those probabilities.



>>> from mlsysim.solvers import BlindRetryModel
>>> result = BlindRetryModel().solve(0.1, 0.2, 100)
>>> result.duplicate_probability < result.timeout_probability
True

Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
The same workload and resource budget served at baseline_rate without a set of controls and at controlled_rate with them.


Equation: Subtract rates for lost throughput and normalize by the baseline for fractional overhead.

title: engine.solvers.reinforcement
text:
engine.solvers.reinforcement
Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards: what a reward measures and what the loop costs.
Domain implementations behind mlsysim.solvers (added 2026-10-20). Each model is arithmetic on stated rates, counts, and durations: the share of an update’s accepted rollouts that failed, binary rewards centered on a fixed baseline, a shaped reward’s ordering condition, a turn valued by forked continuations and the tokens forking costs, group-relative coefficients, the per-token push of length normalization, the rollouts one informative group costs, an all-pass rule over repeated trials, the room a ratio clip leaves, a sandbox slot’s episode cycle, a group barrier, and a verifier pool. None models a trained network’s learning dynamics.





Name
Description




CenteredRewardModel
Binary terminal rewards centered on a fixed baseline: r - b.


ContinuationForkCostModel
Tokens generated when branches continuations are forked at chosen turns.


ForkValueModel
One turn valued by forking k binary continuations before and after it.


GroupBarrierModel
A synchronous group whose step waits for its slowest member.


GroupCoefficientsModel
Group-relative (GRPO) coefficients (r_i - mean) / (std + epsilon) of one group.


LengthNormalizationModel
Per-token push of two rollouts with the same coefficient under per-rollout averaging.


RatioClipModel
The probability ceiling a symmetric ratio clip 1 +/- epsilon sets on one token.


RepeatedVerificationModel
An all-pass rule over n independent trials of one candidate.


RewardCompositionModel
True and false accepts among one update’s rollouts under an imperfect verifier.


RolloutSlotCycleModel
A sandbox slot running one episode at a time, under a cold and a snapshot reset.


RolloutStepBudgetModel
One update’s generated tokens and the rollouts spent per informative group.


VerifierPoolModel
Verification workers for a stationary stream of completed trajectories.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.CenteredRewardModel()
Binary terminal rewards centered on a fixed baseline: r - b.
A positive baseline makes every failure’s centered score negative, so the update pushes every turn of a failed rollout down alike.





Name
Description




solve
Subtract a shared baseline from passing and failing rewards.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.CenteredRewardModel.solve(
    baseline,
    passing_reward,
    failing_reward,
)
Subtract a shared baseline from passing and failing rewards.











Name
Type
Description
Default




baseline
float
Fixed dimensionless reward baseline.
required


passing_reward
float
Dimensionless reward assigned to a passing rollout.
required


failing_reward
float
Dimensionless reward assigned to a failing rollout.
required














Name
Type
Description





CenteredRewardResult
Dimensionless centered scores for passing and failing outcomes.






Equation: score = reward - baseline for each outcome.
Assumptions: A fixed baseline shared by both outcomes.
Excludes: Gradient dynamics, temporal credit assignment, and learned baselines.



Derivation: Centering translates each reward by the same baseline; it changes signs relative to that baseline without changing the difference between rewards.



>>> result = CenteredRewardModel().solve(0.5, 1.0, 0.0)
>>> result.passing_score == -result.failing_score
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.ContinuationForkCostModel()
Tokens generated when branches continuations are forked at chosen turns.
Forking at every boundary costs 1 + m (H - 1) / 2 times the base trajectory, which grows with the square of the horizon in tokens.





Name
Description




solve
Count tokens generated by continuations from selected turn boundaries.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.ContinuationForkCostModel.solve(
    turns,
    tokens_per_turn,
    branches,
    boundaries=None,
)
Count tokens generated by continuations from selected turn boundaries.











Name
Type
Description
Default




turns
int
Positive number of turns in each base trajectory.
required


tokens_per_turn
int
Positive generated-token count per turn.
required


branches
int
Nonnegative continuation count at each selected boundary.
required


boundaries
sequence
Selected turn boundaries; None selects every internal boundary.
None














Name
Type
Description





ContinuationForkCostResult
Generated-token counts and the dimensionless expansion over the base trajectory.






Equation: base=H*a; total=base+sum(m*a*(H-b) for b in boundaries).
Assumptions: Equal token cost per turn and fixed branch count at selected boundaries.
Excludes: Prompt rereads, caching, and variable-length continuations.



Derivation: Each boundary retains its prefix and generates only the remaining turns for each branch. Adding those suffix lengths to the base transcript counts generated work without resending prefixes.



>>> result = ContinuationForkCostModel().solve(4, 10, 2)
>>> result.total_tokens >= result.base_tokens
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.ForkValueModel()
One turn valued by forking k binary continuations before and after it.
Each fork’s sampled mean has standard error at most 1 / (2 sqrt k); the difference of two independent means at most sqrt 2 times that. The difference is resolved when it exceeds two difference bounds.





Name
Description




solve
Compare continuation pass fractions against sampling uncertainty.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.ForkValueModel.solve(
    continuations,
    passes_before,
    passes_after,
)
Compare continuation pass fractions against sampling uncertainty.











Name
Type
Description
Default




continuations
int
Positive number of independent continuations at each fork.
required


passes_before
int
Successful continuations before the turn, between zero and continuations.
required


passes_after
int
Successful continuations after the turn, between zero and continuations.
required














Name
Type
Description





ForkValueResult
Empirical success fractions, standard-error bounds, and the resolution decision.






Equation: v=passes/k; SE<=1/(2*sqrt(k)); threshold=2*sqrt(2)*SE.
Assumptions: Independent Bernoulli continuations in the before and after samples.
Excludes: Paired-sample covariance and a formal confidence-interval decision rule.



Derivation: A Bernoulli variance is at most one quarter; dividing by continuation count bounds each mean variance. Adding the two mean variances gives the comparison standard error.



>>> result = ForkValueModel().solve(100, 20, 80)
>>> result.value_after > result.value_before
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.GroupBarrierModel()
A synchronous group whose step waits for its slowest member.
Every slot is held until the barrier, so the reserved slot time is G x max and the busy share is mean / max.





Name
Description




solve
Measure synchronous group delay and idle slot time.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.GroupBarrierModel.solve(latencies)
Measure synchronous group delay and idle slot time.











Name
Type
Description
Default




latencies
sequence of Quantity
Nonempty sequence of positive, mutually compatible time quantities.
required














Name
Type
Description





GroupBarrierResult
Group count, time-valued extrema and mean, and dimensionless idle-slot fraction.






Equation: barrier=max(latencies); idle_share=1-mean(latencies)/barrier.
Assumptions: All group members begin together and reserve their slots until the barrier.
Excludes: Staggered starts, slot reuse, and distributed synchronization traffic.



Derivation: A barrier releases at the longest latency. Each shorter member idles for the difference; summing those differences and dividing by total reserved slot-time gives idle share.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
>>> result = GroupBarrierModel().solve([Q_("1 s"), Q_("2 s")])
>>> result.fastest <= result.mean <= result.barrier
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.GroupCoefficientsModel()
Group-relative (GRPO) coefficients (r_i - mean) / (std + epsilon) of one group.
Every sampled token of rollout i carries coefficient i. The dispersion divisor (G or G - 1) and the stabilizer are part of the objective; a lone pass in a group of G binary rewards gets sqrt(G - 1) as epsilon goes to zero.





Name
Description




solve
Center and scale rewards within a rollout group.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.GroupCoefficientsModel.solve(
    rewards,
    stabilizer,
    bessel=False,
)
Center and scale rewards within a rollout group.











Name
Type
Description
Default




rewards
sequence of float
Nonempty sequence of dimensionless sampled rewards.
required


stabilizer
float
Nonnegative dimensionless denominator stabilizer.
required


bessel
bool
Use sample standard deviation when True; population deviation otherwise.
False














Name
Type
Description





GroupCoefficientsResult
Group size, reward mean and standard deviation, and dimensionless coefficients.






Equation: coefficient_i=(reward_i-mean)/(std+stabilizer).
Assumptions: One finite reward group; Bessel correction follows the supplied flag.
Excludes: Policy updates, clipping, and the effect of these coefficients on learning.



Derivation: Subtracting the group mean yields centered rewards. Dividing by the chosen standard deviation plus stabilizer defines the normalized update coefficients.



>>> result = GroupCoefficientsModel().solve([0.0, 1.0], 0.1)
>>> abs(result.coefficient_sum) < 1e-12
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.LengthNormalizationModel()
Per-token push of two rollouts with the same coefficient under per-rollout averaging.
Each rollout’s loss is divided by its own length, so the shorter rollout’s tokens each move long / short times as far. A failure is pushed down hardest when it is short, so failures drift long.





Name
Description




solve
Compare per-token weights under equal trajectory weighting.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.LengthNormalizationModel.solve(
    short_tokens,
    long_tokens,
)
Compare per-token weights under equal trajectory weighting.











Name
Type
Description
Default




short_tokens
int
Positive token count of the shorter rollout.
required


long_tokens
int
Positive token count of the longer rollout.
required














Name
Type
Description





LengthNormalizationResult
Dimensionless ratio of the shorter rollout’s per-token coefficient to the longer one.






Equation: per_token_ratio=long_tokens/short_tokens.
Assumptions: Equal rollout coefficients and separate per-rollout mean losses.
Excludes: Actual gradients, reward differences, and predicted sequence-length drift.



Derivation: Equal trajectory weight is divided among its tokens; the ratio of per-token weights is therefore the inverse ratio of trajectory lengths.



>>> result = LengthNormalizationModel().solve(10, 20)
>>> result.per_token_ratio == 20 / 10
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.RatioClipModel()
The probability ceiling a symmetric ratio clip 1 +/- epsilon sets on one token.
A dominant token’s ceiling can exceed 1 (the clip does not bind), while a rare token may rise only epsilon p per update.





Name
Description




solve
Translate a probability-ratio clip into absolute probability headroom.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.RatioClipModel.solve(epsilon, probability)
Translate a probability-ratio clip into absolute probability headroom.











Name
Type
Description
Default




epsilon
float
Nonnegative dimensionless symmetric ratio-clip width.
required


probability
float
Old token probability in [0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





RatioClipResult
Dimensionless probability ceiling and rise, plus whether the ceiling lies below one.






Equation: ceiling=p*(1+epsilon); rise=p*epsilon; binds=(ceiling<1).
Assumptions: A symmetric probability-ratio upper clip for one token.
Excludes: Probability renormalization across tokens and optimizer dynamics.



Derivation: Multiplying the original probability by the upper ratio clip gives its clipped ceiling; subtracting the original probability gives the permitted absolute rise.



>>> result = RatioClipModel().solve(0.2, 0.5)
>>> result.binds
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.RepeatedVerificationModel()
An all-pass rule over n independent trials of one candidate.
Graded once, a group of G incorrect candidates holds at least one false pass with probability 1 - (1 - q_bad)^G. Requiring all n trials to pass accepts an incorrect candidate with q_bad^n and rejects a correct one with 1 - q_good^n. Stopping at the first failed trial runs sum_{j<n} q^j trials on average.





Name
Description




solve
Compute acceptance errors and trial cost for an all-pass rule.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.RepeatedVerificationModel.solve(
    incorrect_pass,
    correct_pass,
    trials,
    group,
)
Compute acceptance errors and trial cost for an all-pass rule.











Name
Type
Description
Default




incorrect_pass
float
Probability an incorrect candidate passes one trial, in [0, 1].
required


correct_pass
float
Probability a correct candidate passes one trial, in [0, 1].
required


trials
int
Positive count of verification trials per candidate.
required


group
int
Number of candidates per group, a positive count.
required














Name
Type
Description





RepeatedVerificationResult
Acceptance and rejection probabilities and expected counts of executed trials.






Equation: false_accept=q_bad**n; true_reject=1-q_good**n; E[trials]=sum(q**j).
Assumptions: Independent identically distributed trials and first-failure termination.
Excludes: Persistent verifier bias and correlated repeated judgments.



Derivation: Independent pass probabilities multiply across required trials. For early rejection, trial j is reached only after the preceding trials pass, so summing those survival probabilities gives expected work.



>>> result = RepeatedVerificationModel().solve(0.1, 0.9, 2, 4)
>>> result.incorrect_accepted < 0.1
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.RewardCompositionModel()
True and false accepts among one update’s rollouts under an imperfect verifier.
tasks x group rollouts pass with probability p; the verifier accepts a pass with probability valid_accept_rate and a failure with false_accept_rate. Expected counts carry no rounding. The false share is Bayes’ rule over the accepts, so it moves with the policy’s pass rate as well as with the verifier.





Name
Description




solve
Separate true and false verifier acceptances in a rollout batch.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.RewardCompositionModel.solve(
    tasks,
    group,
    pass_rate,
    false_accept_rate,
    valid_accept_rate,
)
Separate true and false verifier acceptances in a rollout batch.











Name
Type
Description
Default




tasks
int
Number of tasks in the update, a positive count.
required


group
int
Number of candidates per group, a positive count.
required


pass_rate
float
Underlying binary success probability in [0, 1].
required


false_accept_rate
float
Probability of accepting an incorrect rollout, in [0, 1].
required


valid_accept_rate
float
Probability of accepting a correct rollout, in [0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





RewardCompositionResult
Expected rollout and acceptance counts, plus the dimensionless false-accept share.






Equation: n=tasks*group; true=n*p*v; false=n*(1-p)*f.
Assumptions: Stationary conditional acceptance rates and a nonempty accepted population.
Excludes: Correlated verifier errors and changes in policy quality.



Derivation: Multiply rollout counts by correctness prevalence and conditional acceptance probabilities. The false-accept share divides the false joint count by all accepts, which is Bayes conditioning on acceptance.



>>> result = RewardCompositionModel().solve(2, 4, 0.5, 0.1, 0.9)
>>> result.accepts == result.true_accepts + result.false_accepts
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.RolloutSlotCycleModel()
A sandbox slot running one episode at a time, under a cold and a snapshot reset.
Each episode is decisions x (model + tool) plus an assessment, then a reset. Capacity is slots / cycle. Faster resets raise capacity only by the reset’s share of the cycle (Amdahl’s law); the work floor remains.





Name
Description




solve
Estimate slot occupancy and throughput over rollout-reset cycles.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.RolloutSlotCycleModel.solve(
    slots,
    decisions,
    model_time,
    tool_time,
    assessment_time,
    cold_reset,
    snapshot_reset,
)
Estimate slot occupancy and throughput over rollout-reset cycles.











Name
Type
Description
Default




slots
int
Positive count of independently occupied sandbox slots.
required


decisions
int
Nonnegative number of model/tool decisions per episode.
required


model_time
Quantity
Time quantity per model invocation, nonnegative.
required


tool_time
Quantity
Time quantity per tool invocation, nonnegative.
required


assessment_time
Quantity
Nonnegative time quantity for final assessment.
required


cold_reset
Quantity
Positive time quantity for a cold reset.
required


snapshot_reset
Quantity
Positive time quantity for a snapshot reset.
required














Name
Type
Description





RolloutSlotCycleResult
Work and cycle times in seconds, episodes per hour, and dimensionless capacity ratios.






Equation: work=D*(model+tool)+assessment; capacity=slots/(work+reset).
Assumptions: Serial fixed-duration stages and one episode per slot.
Excludes: Queueing, overlapping stages, startup variance, and resource contention.



Derivation: Serial model and tool stages accumulate over turns, then assessment and reset extend the cycle. Dividing available slots by cycle duration gives the capacity bound.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
>>> result = RolloutSlotCycleModel().solve(2, 3, Q_("1 s"), Q_("2 s"), Q_("1 s"), Q_("2 s"), Q_("1 s"))
>>> result.snapshot_cycle < result.cold_cycle
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.RolloutStepBudgetModel()
One update’s generated tokens and the rollouts spent per informative group.
A group of G independent binary attempts at pass rate p carries reward contrast with probability 1 - p^G - (1 - p)^G; a group without it moves no weights, so each informative group costs G / P(contrast) rollouts (infinite at p = 0 or p = 1, where no group carries contrast).





Name
Description




solve
Count rollout tokens and groups containing both outcome classes.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.RolloutStepBudgetModel.solve(
    tasks,
    group,
    turns,
    tokens_per_turn,
    pass_rate,
)
Count rollout tokens and groups containing both outcome classes.











Name
Type
Description
Default




tasks
int
Number of tasks in the update, a positive count.
required


group
int
Number of candidates per group, a positive count.
required


turns
int
Positive number of turns in each base trajectory.
required


tokens_per_turn
int
Positive generated-token count per turn.
required


pass_rate
float
Underlying binary success probability in [0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





RolloutStepBudgetResult
Rollout and token counts, contrast probability, and rollouts per informative group.






Equation: tokens=tasks*group*turns*tokens_per_turn; contrast=1-p**G-(1-p)**G.
Assumptions: Independent binary outcomes with one shared pass probability.
Excludes: Correlated outcomes, token-length variance, and update effectiveness.



Derivation: Token volume multiplies tasks, rollouts, turns, and tokens per turn. Subtracting all-pass and all-fail group probabilities from one leaves groups with both outcomes.



>>> result = RolloutStepBudgetModel().solve(2, 4, 3, 10, 0.5)
>>> result.step_tokens == result.rollouts * result.rollout_tokens
True






engine.solvers.reinforcement.VerifierPoolModel()
Verification workers for a stationary stream of completed trajectories.
By Little’s law the busy workers are the arrival rate times the service time per trajectory (every trial executes in this sizing case); the pool is that demand over the target utilization, rounded up.





Name
Description




solve
Size a verifier pool from arrival load and utilization target.





engine.solvers.reinforcement.VerifierPoolModel.solve(
    trajectories,
    interval,
    trials,
    trial_time,
    target_utilization,
)
Size a verifier pool from arrival load and utilization target.











Name
Type
Description
Default




trajectories
int
Positive completed-trajectory count in the observation interval.
required


interval
Quantity
Positive observation interval as a time quantity.
required


trials
int
Positive count of verification trials per candidate.
required


trial_time
Quantity
Positive service time quantity per verification trial.
required


target_utilization
float
Target busy fraction in (0, 1].
required














Name
Type
Description





VerifierPoolResult
Arrival rate in inverse seconds, mean busy-worker counts, integer slots, and utilization.






Equation: busy=arrival_rate*trials*trial_time; slots=ceil(busy/target_utilization).
Assumptions: Stationary arrivals, every trial executed, and identical workers.
Excludes: Queueing-tail guarantees, early trial termination, and burst arrivals.



Derivation: Arrival rate times trials per arrival times trial duration gives offered busy-slot demand. Divide by the utilization target and round up to obtain an integer pool size.



>>> from mlsysim.core.units import Q_
>>> result = VerifierPoolModel().solve(10, Q_("1 s"), 2, Q_("0.1 s"), 0.8)
>>> result.utilization <= 0.8
True
