    mission_time,
    replan_rate,
    late_probability,
    mission_budget,
)
Translate repeated deadline misses into a mission exposure budget.











Name
Type
Description
Default




mission_time
Quantity
Positive mission duration, convertible to seconds.
required


replan_rate
Quantity
Positive handoff frequency in hertz; duration times rate must round to at least one handoff.
required


late_probability
float
Per-handoff miss probability in (0, 1]; positive because reciprocal and logarithm are reported.
required


mission_budget
float
Positive mission-level miss-probability budget, normally at most one.
required














Name
Type
Description





HandoffExposureResult
Handoff count, expected misses, dimensionless independent all-on-time probability, and the union-bound per-handoff budget and quantile.






mlsysim.physics.agents.calc_unchecked_success : Multiply independent per-event success probabilities.



Equation: K = round(mission_time * replan_rate), expected_late = K*p, all_on_time = (1-p)**K, and per_handoff_budget = mission_budget/K.
Assumptions: The all-on-time expression assumes independent identical miss probabilities. The budget allocation uses a union bound and does not require independence.
Excludes: Correlated-tail estimation, empirical deadline distributions, recovery, and a mission safety guarantee.



Derivation: Linearity of expectation gives K*p. Multiplying independent on-time probabilities gives (1-p)**K; summing event probabilities bounds any miss by K*p.



>>> from mlsysim.solvers import HandoffExposureModel
>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = HandoffExposureModel().solve(Q_('10 s'), Q_('2 Hz'), 0.01, 0.1)
>>> result.handoffs == 20 and result.design_quantile > 0.9
True






engine.solvers.trajectory.JerkLimitedStopModel()
A delayed jerk-limited (S-curve) stop, beside the constant and polynomial stops it replaces.
The machine travels v tau during the pre-brake delay, then stops along the double-S profile with deceleration bound a and jerk bound j (calc_scurve_stop_distance): above the plateau speed a^2 / j the stop is v^2 / (2 a) of braking plus v a / (2 j) of cruise over half a jerk ramp. Without a stated jerk bound, j is the peak jerk of the reference C2 polynomial stop (calc_c2_stop_suffix) at jerk_reference_speed (the entry speed by default), which stops in 0.75 v^2 / a. A localization bound and a protective margin, when stated, add to every required distance; the speed ceiling is the fastest entry speed whose delayed S-curve stop fits, with the jerk bound held fixed (calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity).

Description

Equation: Required distance is speed*delay + S_curve_distance(speed, deceleration, jerk) + margins. The plateau regime begins at speed = deceleration**2/jerk.
Assumptions: One-dimensional braking with a fixed positive deceleration and jerk limit, zero initial acceleration, and constant speed during delay.
Excludes: Slope, slip, changing traction, sensing distributions, actuator faults, and safety certification.



Derivation: Integrating the piecewise linear acceleration of the S-curve gives its travel and duration. Adding delay travel and explicit distance allowances forms the stopping budget.



>>> from mlsysim.solvers import JerkLimitedStopModel
>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = JerkLimitedStopModel().solve(
...     speed=Q_('1 m/s'),
...     deceleration=Q_('2 m/s^2'),
...     jerk=Q_('4 m/s^3'),
...     clear_distance=Q_('2 m'),
... )
>>> result.fits and result.scurve_travel > result.braking_travel
True






engine.solvers.trajectory.SeamBridgeModel()
A velocity gap at a chunk seam, closed in one servo tick or by a quintic bridge.
Closing a gap of delta in one tick asks the reflected rotor inertia N^2 J_rotor for J delta / dt of torque (calc_seam_acceleration_torque_jump), reached in one tick, a torque rate of J delta / dt^2. The C2 bridge over T, with zero boundary accelerations and an endpoint on the incoming reference, is the quintic q(t) = a3 t^3 + a4 t^4 + a5 t^5 (solved from its 3x3 boundary system); its acceleration peaks at 1.5 delta / T mid-bridge and its jerk at 6 delta / T^2 at both ends, so torque falls as 1 / T and torque rate as 1 / T^2.

mlsysim.physics.robotics.actuation.calc_seam_acceleration_torque_jump : Convert a joint acceleration jump into reflected-inertia torque.



Equation: J = gear_ratio**2*rotor_inertia; step torque = J*velocity_gap/tick. The bridge peaks at 1.5*J*velocity_gap/T in torque and 6*J*velocity_gap/T**2 in torque rate.
Assumptions: Zero correction acceleration at both endpoints, fixed reflected inertia and a quintic endpoint matching velocity gap and half-gap displacement.
Excludes: Gravity, friction, elasticity, actuator bandwidth, saturation response, and full loaded dynamics unless loaded_inertia is supplied.



Derivation: Solve the three endpoint equations for the cubic, quartic and quintic coefficients, differentiate to acceleration and jerk, then multiply by reflected inertia.



>>> from mlsysim.solvers import SeamBridgeModel

>>> result = SeamBridgeModel().solve(
...     gear_ratio=10,
...     rotor_inertia=Q_('0.001 kg*m^2'),
...     rated_torque=Q_('10 N*m'),
...     peak_torque=Q_('20 N*m'),
...     torque_rate_limit=Q_('1000 N*m/s'),
...     velocity_gap=Q_('0.1 rad/s'),
...     tick=Q_('1 ms'),
...     bridge_duration=Q_('20 ms'),
... )
>>> result.peak_torque < result.step_torque

engine.solvers.trajectory.ShoulderSwingModel()
The loaded shoulder: holding torque, effective inertia, and a rest-to-rest swing.
Holding payload m at reach r costs m g r of torque; the payload and the reflected rotor inertia give J = m r^2 + J_refl (link masses omitted, a lower bound). Gravity, held at its horizontal value, makes the torque-limited acceleration (tau_max - tau_g) / J lifting and (tau_max + tau_g) / J braking; the binding acceleration is the smallest of those and the joint limit. The time-optimal (bang-bang) swing of D takes 2 sqrt(D / a) and steps torque by 2 J a at the switch point. A torque-rate limit bounds jerk at taud / J, and the jerk-limited swing is the double-S without cruise (calc_scurve_rest_to_rest_time).

Equation: For the smaller Jacobian singular value sigma, the exact joint-rate norm is v/sigma; at least one of two components is at least that norm/sqrt(2). The damped rate is v*sigma/(sigma**2 + damping**2).
Assumptions: A rigid planar two-link arm; motion lies in its weakest singular direction. Damping is fixed and positive.
Excludes: Joint acceleration, torque, obstacles, tracking dynamics, and other tool-motion directions.



Derivation: The singular-value decomposition reduces inverse kinematics along one direction to scalar division. Adding a squared-rate penalty replaces 1/sigma with sigma/(sigma**2 + damping**2).

engine.solvers.trajectory.BrakingBlendModel()
A bumpless transfer from cruise into braking, beside the step and the resident stop.
At a change of authority the enforcer may blend the base’s command from cruise to the braking deceleration a with the fixed-endpoint quintic smoothstep. Its slope peaks at 1.875, so under the resident stop’s jerk bound j the window is T = 1.875 a / j (calc_smoothstep_blend_window), rounded up to whole permission ticks. The same change taken in one tick asks a jerk of a / tick. During the blend the speed falls by a T / 2 and the base travels v0 T - a T^2 / 7 (calc_smoothstep_braking_blend); full braking follows. The blended stop is set against an ideal step (v0^2 / 2a) and the resident S-curve stop; the reserve a blend uses is the largest growth of travel plus resident stop over its ticks (calc_blend_reserve_use). An arm joint’s torque change under a torque-rate ceiling gives its own window the same way (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




solve
Account for travel and reserve consumed while blending into braking.

    speed,
    deceleration,
    jerk,
    tick,
    torque_change=None,
    torque_rate_limit=None,
)

mlsysim.physics.robotics.actuation.calc_smoothstep_blend_window : Scale the smoothstep derivative to a rate ceiling. mlsysim.physics.robotics.stopping.calc_smoothstep_braking_blend : Integrate speed and travel while acceleration is blended.



Equation: T = 1.875*deceleration/jerk, exit speed = speed-deceleration*T/2, and blend travel = speed*T-deceleration*T**2/7. Constant braking follows the blend.
Assumptions: A fixed-endpoint quintic smoothstep reaches the requested deceleration without reversal. Reserve use is sampled at permission ticks.
Excludes: Actuator lag, changing traction, obstacles, continuous-time reserve maximization, and a safety guarantee.



Derivation: The quintic smoothstep has maximum normalized slope 1.875. Scaling its slope by acceleration change and dividing by the jerk ceiling gives the shortest modeled window; integrating gives speed and travel.

>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = BrakingBlendModel().solve(
...     speed=Q_('2 m/s'),
...     deceleration=Q_('1 m/s^2'),
...     jerk=Q_('10 m/s^3'),
...     tick=Q_('1 ms'),
... )
>>> result.blended_stop > result.step_stop
True

Equation: K = round(mission_time * replan_rate), expected_late = K*p, all_on_time = (1-p)**K, and per_handoff_budget = mission_budget/K.
Assumptions: The all-on-time expression assumes independent identical miss probabilities. The budget allocation uses a union bound and does not require independence.
Excludes: Correlated-tail estimation, empirical deadline distributions, recovery, and a mission safety guarantee.



Derivation: Linearity of expectation gives K*p. Multiplying independent on-time probabilities gives (1-p)**K; summing event probabilities bounds any miss by K*p.

>>> result.handoffs == 20 and result.design_quantile > 0.9

engine.solvers.trajectory.JerkLimitedStopModel()
A delayed jerk-limited (S-curve) stop, beside the constant and polynomial stops it replaces.
The machine travels v tau during the pre-brake delay, then stops along the double-S profile with deceleration bound a and jerk bound j (calc_scurve_stop_distance): above the plateau speed a^2 / j the stop is v^2 / (2 a) of braking plus v a / (2 j) of cruise over half a jerk ramp. Without a stated jerk bound, j is the peak jerk of the reference C2 polynomial stop (calc_c2_stop_suffix) at jerk_reference_speed (the entry speed by default), which stops in 0.75 v^2 / a. A localization bound and a protective margin, when stated, add to every required distance; the speed ceiling is the fastest entry speed whose delayed S-curve stop fits, with the jerk bound held fixed (calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity).

mlsysim.physics.robotics.stopping.calc_scurve_stop_distance : Integrate the bounded-jerk stopping profile. mlsysim.physics.robotics.stopping.calc_c2_stop_suffix : Construct the reference polynomial stopping profile.



Equation: Required distance is speed*delay + S_curve_distance(speed, deceleration, jerk) + margins. The plateau regime begins at speed = deceleration**2/jerk.
Assumptions: One-dimensional braking with a fixed positive deceleration and jerk limit, zero initial acceleration, and constant speed during delay.
Excludes: Slope, slip, changing traction, sensing distributions, actuator faults, and safety certification.



Derivation: Integrating the piecewise linear acceleration of the S-curve gives its travel and duration. Adding delay travel and explicit distance allowances forms the stopping budget.



>>> from mlsysim.solvers import JerkLimitedStopModel

>>> result = JerkLimitedStopModel().solve(
...     speed=Q_('1 m/s'),
...     deceleration=Q_('2 m/s^2'),
...     jerk=Q_('4 m/s^3'),
...     clear_distance=Q_('2 m'),
... )
>>> result.fits and result.scurve_travel > result.braking_travel
True






engine.solvers.trajectory.SeamBridgeModel()
A velocity gap at a chunk seam, closed in one servo tick or by a quintic bridge.
Closing a gap of delta in one tick asks the reflected rotor inertia N^2 J_rotor for J delta / dt of torque (calc_seam_acceleration_torque_jump), reached in one tick, a torque rate of J delta / dt^2. The C2 bridge over T, with zero boundary accelerations and an endpoint on the incoming reference, is the quintic q(t) = a3 t^3 + a4 t^4 + a5 t^5 (solved from its 3x3 boundary system); its acceleration peaks at 1.5 delta / T mid-bridge and its jerk at 6 delta / T^2 at both ends, so torque falls as 1 / T and torque rate as 1 / T^2.

Equation: J = gear_ratio**2*rotor_inertia; step torque = J*velocity_gap/tick. The bridge peaks at 1.5*J*velocity_gap/T in torque and 6*J*velocity_gap/T**2 in torque rate.
Assumptions: Zero correction acceleration at both endpoints, fixed reflected inertia and a quintic endpoint matching velocity gap and half-gap displacement.
Excludes: Gravity, friction, elasticity, actuator bandwidth, saturation response, and full loaded dynamics unless loaded_inertia is supplied.



Derivation: Solve the three endpoint equations for the cubic, quartic and quintic coefficients, differentiate to acceleration and jerk, then multiply by reflected inertia.

engine.solvers.trajectory.ShoulderSwingModel()
The loaded shoulder: holding torque, effective inertia, and a rest-to-rest swing.
Holding payload m at reach r costs m g r of torque; the payload and the reflected rotor inertia give J = m r^2 + J_refl (link masses omitted, a lower bound). Gravity, held at its horizontal value, makes the torque-limited acceleration (tau_max - tau_g) / J lifting and (tau_max + tau_g) / J braking; the binding acceleration is the smallest of those and the joint limit. The time-optimal (bang-bang) swing of D takes 2 sqrt(D / a) and steps torque by 2 J a at the switch point. A torque-rate limit bounds jerk at taud / J, and the jerk-limited swing is the double-S without cruise (calc_scurve_rest_to_rest_time).

Assumptions: A point payload, horizontal gravity torque held constant through the swing, and rest-to-rest symmetric acceleration profiles.
Excludes: Link inertia, changing gravity geometry, friction, velocity-capped replanning, flexibility, and motor electrical limits.



Derivation: Torque balance gives angular acceleration after subtracting gravity. Integrating symmetric acceleration gives the bang-bang time; integrating a bounded-jerk acceleration profile gives the S-curve comparison.

...     velocity_limit=Q_('10 rad/s'),
...     torque_rate_limit=Q_('100 N*m/s'),
... )
>>> result.jerk_limited_time >= result.bang_bang_time

The stop of a machine carrying an open container, whose liquid caps the deceleration.
Under steady deceleration a the free surface tilts until the liquid rises R a / g at the wall; keeping it below the rim’s freeboard h_f caps the deceleration at g h_f / R (calc_quasistatic_spill_acceleration). The stop at that bound keeps the stop’s shape, so its jerk bound is rescaled with the deceleration (the reference polynomial’s peak at the entry speed); the carry speed is the fastest entry speed whose delayed stop fits.

Equation: Allowed deceleration is g*freeboard/inner_radius; rise under unconstrained braking is inner_radius*free_deceleration/g. The constrained stop recomputes the polynomial-derived jerk at that deceleration.
Assumptions: A level open container, quasistatic free surface, fixed geometry and one-dimensional stopping.

Derivation: In the accelerating frame the free-surface slope is acceleration/g. Multiplying the slope by radius gives rim rise and solving the freeboard inequality gives the acceleration ceiling.

engine.solvers.trajectory.TwoLinkJointRateModel()
Joint rates a tool speed asks of a planar two-link arm, exact and damped.
The weakest direction of the Jacobian at elbow angle q2 has singular value sigma_min; a tool speed v along it needs a joint-rate vector of norm v / sigma_min, and with two joints at least one component is that norm divided by sqrt(2). Damped least squares with damping lambda commands v sigma / (sigma^2 + lambda^2), never more than v / (2 lambda), and delivers the fraction sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + lambda^2) of the tool motion.

mlsysim.physics.robotics.kinematics.calc_two_link_singular_values : Compute the two-link Jacobian singular values. mlsysim.physics.robotics.kinematics.calc_dls_joint_rate : Apply the scalar damped inverse along a singular direction.



Equation: For the smaller Jacobian singular value sigma, the exact joint-rate norm is v/sigma; at least one of two components is at least that norm/sqrt(2). The damped rate is v*sigma/(sigma**2 + damping**2).
Assumptions: A rigid planar two-link arm; motion lies in its weakest singular direction. Damping is fixed and positive.
Excludes: Joint acceleration, torque, obstacles, tracking dynamics, and other tool-motion directions.



Derivation: The singular-value decomposition reduces inverse kinematics along one direction to scalar division. Adding a squared-rate penalty replaces 1/sigma with sigma/(sigma**2 + damping**2).



>>> from mlsysim.solvers import TwoLinkJointRateModel
>>> from mlsysim import Q_
>>> result = TwoLinkJointRateModel().solve(
...     upper_arm=Q_('0.5 m'),
...     forearm=Q_('0.5 m'),
...     elbow_angle=Q_('90 deg'),
...     tool_speed=Q_('0.1 m/s'),
...     joint_speed_limit=Q_('2 rad/s'),
...     damping=Q_('0.05 m'),
... )
>>> 0 < result.realized_fraction < 1
True

Serving scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/serving.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
Requests in one batch of fixed membership, one token per iteration.


Equation: Slot work=batch_width*max(output_lengths); continuous scheduling assigns each waiting request to the earliest free slot.
Assumptions: One token per iteration, fixed initial slot count, and arrival-ordered waiting requests; input lists are aligned and nonempty.
Excludes: Prefill costs and variable token times; the request-level comparison starts the entire waiting wave together without a second-wave width check.



Implementation references: mlsysim.physics.serving.calc_padding_waste_fraction. These helper contracts state the source assumptions; the scenario binds their inputs and derives the displayed ratios and budgets.



The named registry scenario supplies the stated inputs; this is a modeled calculation, not a new measurement.

>>> round(scenario.idle_share, 6)
0.375

Description

Initial and waiting output lengths concatenated in arrival order, in token iterations.

Useful token iterations across both initial and waiting requests.


continuous_iterations
Completion iteration of the greedy continuous-batching schedule, taking its latest endpoint.

Fraction of available slot-iterations occupied by useful work under greedy slot reuse.

title: physics.neural
text:
physics.neural
Neural computation: what a dense network costs, and what its activations and loss compute.
A dense (fully connected) network is a list of layer widths [n_0, n_1, ..., n_L]: layer l maps n_{l-1} inputs to n_l outputs with an n_{l-1} by n_l weight matrix and one bias per output. Every count here follows from the widths and the batch size alone (added 2026-10-20).





Name
Description




calc_cross_entropy
Evaluate scalar one-hot cross-entropy in natural-log units.


calc_dense_backward_flops
Count dense weight-gradient and input-gradient matrix work.


calc_dense_biases
Count one bias for each output unit in every layer.


calc_dense_forward_flops
Count forward matrix and elementwise work by layer.


calc_dense_inference_activations
Count peak activation values using adjacent rolling buffers.


calc_dense_macs
Count dense multiply-accumulates for one example.


calc_dense_params
Count weights and biases in a dense network.


calc_dense_saved_activations
Count input and layer-output values retained for backward work.


calc_dense_traffic_values
Count activation values transferred by unfused dense layers.


calc_dense_weights
Count the dense weight matrix entries in each layer.


calc_relu
Apply the scalar rectified linear activation.


calc_sigmoid
Evaluate the logistic sigmoid.


calc_sigmoid_slope
Evaluate the derivative of the logistic sigmoid.


calc_training_state
Separate weight, gradient, and optimizer storage.


calc_training_step_ops
Count launches in the assumed dense ReLU training schedule.





physics.neural.calc_cross_entropy(p_correct)
Evaluate scalar one-hot cross-entropy in natural-log units.











Name
Type
Description
Default




p_correct
float
Probability assigned to the correct class, in (0, 1].
required









Name
Type
Description





float
Loss in nats.






Equation: H = -ln(p_correct).
Assumptions: One-hot target with the correct-class probability already normalized.
Excludes: Label smoothing, class weights, batch reduction, and softmax normalization.



Derivation: In -sum_i y_i ln(p_i), a one-hot target leaves only the correct-class term.



>>> calc_cross_entropy(1.0) == 0.0
True




physics.neural.calc_dense_backward_flops(widths, batch=1)
Count dense weight-gradient and input-gradient matrix work.











Name
Type
Description
Default




widths
sequence of int
Positive layer widths [input, hidden…, output]; at least two entries. Counts are dimensionless.
required


batch
int
Positive number of examples processed together; default 1.
1














Name
Type
Description





tuple of int
Total weight-gradient FLOPs and total input-gradient FLOPs.






Equation: F_weight = sum_l 2 B n_(l-1) n_l; F_input sums the same work except the first layer.
Assumptions: Training does not request a gradient with respect to the original network input.
Excludes: Activation derivatives, bias gradients, loss work, and optimizer updates.



Derivation: F_weight = sum_l 2 B n_(l-1) n_l; F_input sums the same work except the first layer.



>>> calc_dense_backward_flops([2, 3], batch=2) == (2 * 2 * 2 * 3, 0)
True




physics.neural.calc_dense_biases(widths)
Count one bias for each output unit in every layer.











Name
Type
Description
Default




widths
sequence of int
Positive layer widths [input, hidden…, output]; at least two entries. Counts are dimensionless.
required









Name
Type
Description





list of int
Bias parameter counts, one per layer.






Equation: b_l = n_l.
Assumptions: Every dense layer has a bias.
Excludes: Bias-free layers, normalization, and weight matrices.



Derivation: Each output unit adds one independently stored scalar bias; therefore a layer with n_out units contains n_out bias parameters.



>>> calc_dense_biases([2, 3, 1])
[3, 1]




physics.neural.calc_dense_forward_flops(widths, batch=1)
Count forward matrix and elementwise work by layer.











Name
Type
Description
Default




widths
sequence of int
Positive layer widths [input, hidden…, output]; at least two entries. Counts are dimensionless.
required


batch
int
Positive number of examples processed together; default 1.
1














Name
Type
Description





tuple of list of int
Matrix FLOPs and elementwise FLOPs, each indexed by layer.






Equation: F_matrix,l = 2 B n_(l-1) n_l; F_element,l = 2 B n_l.
Assumptions: A multiply-accumulate counts as two FLOPs; bias and activation cost one operation each.
Excludes: Architecture-specific activation costs, fused-kernel savings, and backward work.



Derivation: F_matrix,l = 2 B n_(l-1) n_l; F_element,l = 2 B n_l.



>>> calc_dense_forward_flops([2, 3], batch=2) == ([2 * 2 * 2 * 3], [2 * 2 * 3])
True




physics.neural.calc_dense_inference_activations(widths, batch=1)
Count peak activation values using adjacent rolling buffers.











Name
Type
Description
Default




widths
sequence of int
Positive layer widths [input, hidden…, output]; at least two entries. Counts are dimensionless.
required


batch
int
Positive number of examples processed together; default 1.
1









Name
Type
Description





int
Peak simultaneously resident activation values.






Equation: V_peak = B max_l(n_(l-1) + n_l).
Assumptions: Layers execute serially; consumed buffers can be reused.
Excludes: Skip connections, concurrent execution, weights, and runtime workspace.



Derivation: V_peak = B max_l(n_(l-1) + n_l).



>>> calc_dense_inference_activations([2, 3, 1]) == 2 + 3
True




physics.neural.calc_dense_macs(widths)
Count dense multiply-accumulates for one example.











Name
Type
Description
Default




widths
sequence of int
Positive layer widths [input, hidden…, output]; at least two entries. Counts are dimensionless.
required









Name
Type
Description





int
Multiply-accumulate count per example.






Equation: MACs = sum_l n_(l-1) n_l.
Assumptions: One matrix-vector product is evaluated per layer.
Excludes: Bias additions, nonlinearities, and backward computation.



Derivation: Evaluating a dense layer uses each weight once in a multiply-accumulate for one example; summing the matrix entry counts gives the network MAC count.



>>> calc_dense_macs([2, 3]) == 2 * 3
True




physics.neural.calc_dense_params(widths)
Count weights and biases in a dense network.











Name
Type
Description
Default




widths
sequence of int
Positive layer widths [input, hidden…, output]; at least two entries. Counts are dimensionless.
required









Name
Type
Description





int
Total trainable parameter count.






Equation: P = sum_l (n_(l-1) + 1) n_l.
Assumptions: Every dense connection has a weight and every output has a bias.
Excludes: Normalization parameters, shared weights, and sparsity.



Derivation: P = sum_l (n_(l-1) + 1) n_l.



>>> calc_dense_params([2, 3]) == (2 + 1) * 3
True




physics.neural.calc_dense_saved_activations(widths, batch=1)
Count input and layer-output values retained for backward work.











Name
Type
Description
Default




widths
sequence of int
Positive layer widths [input, hidden…, output]; at least two entries. Counts are dimensionless.
required


batch
int
Positive number of examples processed together; default 1.
1









Name
Type
Description





int
Saved activation value count.






Equation: V = B sum_l n_l, including input width.
Assumptions: Every layer output and the original input remain resident.
Excludes: Recomputation, masks, workspace, and weight or optimizer storage.



Derivation: V = B sum_l n_l, including input width.



>>> calc_dense_saved_activations([2, 3, 1], batch=2) == 2 * (2 + 3 + 1)
True




physics.neural.calc_dense_traffic_values(widths, batch=1)
Count activation values transferred by unfused dense layers.











Name
Type
Description
Default




widths
sequence of int
Positive layer widths [input, hidden…, output]; at least two entries. Counts are dimensionless.
required


batch
int
Positive number of examples processed together; default 1.
1














Name
Type
Description





int
Activation values moved per forward pass, not bytes.






Equation: V = B [n_0 + 2 sum(hidden widths) + n_L].
Assumptions: Each layer reads its input and writes its output to main memory.
Excludes: Weight reads, cache reuse, fusion, and conversion from values to bytes.



Derivation: V = B [n_0 + 2 sum(hidden widths) + n_L].



>>> calc_dense_traffic_values([2, 3, 1]) == 2 + 2 * 3 + 1
True




physics.neural.calc_dense_weights(widths)
Count the dense weight matrix entries in each layer.











Name
Type
Description
Default




widths
sequence of int
Positive layer widths [input, hidden…, output]; at least two entries. Counts are dimensionless.
required









Name
Type
Description





list of int
Parameter counts, one per layer.






Equation: W_l = n_(l-1) n_l.
Assumptions: Every input connects to every output in each layer.
Excludes: Biases, sparsity, shared parameters, and convolutional structure.



Derivation: A fully connected mapping from n_in inputs to n_out outputs has one independently stored weight for every input-output pair, giving n_in times n_out entries.



>>> calc_dense_weights([2, 3]) == [2 * 3]
True




physics.neural.calc_relu(x)
Apply the scalar rectified linear activation.





Name
Type
Description
Default




x
float
Dimensionless scalar activation.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Zero for a negative input; otherwise the unchanged input.






Equation: ReLU(x) = max(0, x).
Assumptions: Scalar input.
Excludes: Leaky variants, derivatives, and tensor execution costs.



Derivation: Rectification preserves a nonnegative scalar and replaces a negative scalar with zero; the maximum with zero implements this piecewise definition.



>>> calc_relu(-2.0)
0.0




physics.neural.calc_sigmoid(x)
Evaluate the logistic sigmoid.











Name
Type
Description
Default




x
float
Dimensionless finite activation; extreme negative inputs may overflow the exponential.
required














Name
Type
Description





float
Dimensionless sigmoid activation between zero and one.






Equation: s(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x)).
Assumptions: Scalar arithmetic using the standard exponential implementation.
Excludes: Vectorization and overflow-stabilized evaluation.



Derivation: s(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x)).



>>> calc_sigmoid(0.0)
0.5




physics.neural.calc_sigmoid_slope(x)
Evaluate the derivative of the logistic sigmoid.











Name
Type
Description
Default




x
float
Dimensionless finite activation; inherits sigmoid exponential limits.
required









Name
Type
Description





float
Dimensionless local derivative.






Equation: s_prime(x) = s(x) [1 - s(x)].
Assumptions: The derivative is evaluated at a single scalar activation.
Excludes: Products across layers and numerical overflow stabilization.



Derivation: Differentiate s(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) by the chain rule.



>>> calc_sigmoid_slope(0.0) == 0.5 * (1 - 0.5)
True




physics.neural.calc_training_state(
    parameters,
    bytes_per_value,
    optimizer_bytes_per_parameter,
)
Separate weight, gradient, and optimizer storage.











Name
Type
Description
Default




parameters
int
Nonnegative trainable parameter count.
required


bytes_per_value
float or Quantity
Bytes per weight and gradient; use matching storage units across both storage inputs.
required


optimizer_bytes_per_parameter
float or Quantity
Additional optimizer bytes per parameter, supplied explicitly.
required














Name
Type
Description





tuple
Weights, gradients, and optimizer storage; unit-bearing inputs retain their units.






Equation: M_weights = M_gradients = P b; M_optimizer = P o.
Assumptions: One common weight/gradient precision; optimizer storage is supplied separately.
Excludes: Activation memory, runtime buffers, and any master weights not included in the optimizer input.



Derivation: M_weights = M_gradients = P b; M_optimizer = P o.



>>> calc_training_state(3, 2, 8) == (3 * 2, 3 * 2, 3 * 8)
True




physics.neural.calc_training_step_ops(layers)
Count launches in the assumed dense ReLU training schedule.





Name
Type
Description
Default




layers
int
Positive number of dense layers.
required














Name
Type
Description





int
Operation-launch count per training step, not FLOPs.






Equation: N = L + 1 + (2L - 1) + (L - 1) + 1 = 4L.
Assumptions: Each forward matrix operation fuses bias and ReLU; loss and optimizer each use one launch. Backward computes all weight gradients and all but the first input gradient.
Excludes: Compiler fusion across layers, communication, and optimizer implementations with multiple launches.



Derivation: N = L + 1 + (2L - 1) + (L - 1) + 1 = 4L.



>>> calc_training_step_ops(3) == 4 * 3
True

Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
An API that returns the top top_k of class_count scores, rounded from from_decimals to to_decimals decimal places.


Equation: Entry fractions count retained scores; log-two level counts express decimal representation sizes in bits.
Assumptions: Positive top-k count and decimal rounding of scores in [0,1].
Excludes: An attack-success model or information-theoretic privacy guarantee.



Derivation: Entry fractions count retained scores; log-two level counts express decimal representation sizes in bits. Individual property contracts identify the exact accounting expression or reusable calculation. Registry entries supply the scenario inputs; this class does not turn them into measured outcomes.



Evaluate a named scenario using its declared inputs.
>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> scenario = Scenarios.ImageNetTop5RoundedScores
>>> round(float(scenario.scores_reduction), 4)
200.0

Training scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/training.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A run budgeted from peak throughput, then run at its sustained share of peak.
Device-hours scale as 1 / sustained_fraction: a plan made from the datasheet rate needs that many times the hours when the workload sustains only part of peak.


Equation: Use the dimensional products, ratios, or selection rules documented on the calculated properties below.
Assumptions: The work budget is fixed and the positive sustained fraction scales delivered arithmetic capacity uniformly.
Excludes: Changes to algorithmic work and time-varying utilization are absent.



Derivation: the calculated properties below state their defining arithmetic and units. They are scenario accounting or input-selection rules, not independently measured relationships.



>>> from mlsysim import Scenarios
>>> case = Scenarios.PeakPlannedTrainingBudget
>>> round(case.required_device_hours, 4)
2500.0

Robotics scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/robotics/demonstrations.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
Raw telemetry of one teleoperated session on machine: its navigation and wrist cameras, external_cameras RGB-D cameras, and the kinematic record at the permission tick.


Equation: Raw bandwidth sums RGB, depth, and kinematic streams; stored bytes=bandwidth*duration.
Assumptions: Uncompressed fixed-rate streams and optional uniform compression ratio; camera geometry comes from the supplied device entries.
Excludes: Codec cost, dropped frames, file framing, and storage replication.



Implementation references: mlsysim.physics.robotics.perception.calc_teleop_ingestion_budget. These helper contracts state the source assumptions; the scenario binds their inputs and derives the displayed ratios and budgets.



The named registry scenario supplies the stated inputs; this is a modeled calculation, not a new measurement.

>>> round((scenario.total_rate).to('MB/s').magnitude, 6)

title: solvers.ServingCapacityModel
text:
solvers.ServingCapacityModel()
Sizes an LLM serving deployment from a QPS and tail-latency target.
The model deliberately composes existing first-order pieces: ServingModel for TTFT/ITL, ContinuousBatchingModel for per-replica token capacity, and TailLatencyModel for queueing pressure. It is a capacity planner, not a request-level scheduler.





Name
Description




solve
Return the minimum replica count that satisfies the target P99.





solvers.ServingCapacityModel.solve(
    model,
    hardware,
    qps,
    target_p99_latency_ms,
    max_seq_len=2048,
    mean_request_tokens=None,
    output_tokens=128,
    max_batch_size=32,
    precision='fp16',
    efficiency=0.5,
    max_replicas=1024,
    service_time_cv=1.0,
)
Return the minimum replica count that satisfies the target P99.
Composes three first-order models and then scans replica counts upward (1, 2, …) until the estimated request P99 meets the target:

ContinuousBatchingModel sizes the per-replica active batch and token throughput under the memory wall, using paged allocation over the request-length distribution;
ServingModel (at that batch and the mean request length) gives TTFT/ITL, so the base request latency is TTFT + ITL * output_tokens;
TailLatencyModel (M/M/c) adds the P99 queue wait at each candidate replica count.

Estimated P99 = base request latency + P99 queue wait. Per-replica QPS capacity = token throughput / output_tokens.











Name
Type
Description
Default




model
TransformerWorkload
The model being served.
required


hardware
HardwareNode
The per-replica accelerator.
required


qps
float
Target aggregate arrival rate in queries per second (> 0).
required


target_p99_latency_ms
float
End-to-end P99 latency target in milliseconds.
required

int
Longest context a request may reach, prompt plus generated tokens.
2048


mean_request_tokens
float
Mean KV tokens a request fills, in (0, max_seq_len]. None means every request fills max_seq_len. Shorter requests raise paged concurrency in ContinuousBatchingModel.

ContinuousBatchingModel.solve : Paged per-replica token capacity. ServingModel.solve : Request prefill and decode time. TailLatencyModel.solve : Queue-wait approximation.



Equation: request_time = TTFT + output_tokens*ITL; replica capacity is paged token throughput/output_tokens. Candidate P99 adds the queue wait to request_time and accepts the first replica count meeting the SLA.
Assumptions: identical replicas, capped exponential request lengths, Poisson arrivals, and the service-variability approximation in TailLatencyModel. Mean request length sets fixed-context decode cost. Excludes: routing overhead, growing decode contexts, admission transients, and runtime workspace. Feasibility is conditional on these assumptions; reaching max_replicas without meeting the SLA returns feasible=False.



Derivation: divide a token budget by tokens per request to obtain QPS, then compose independent request service and queue-wait estimates.

...     qps=1, target_p99_latency_ms=100000, max_replicas=2)
>>> bool(r.feasible and r.required_replicas >= 1)
True

Return the minimum replica count that satisfies the target P99.
Composes three first-order models and then scans replica counts upward (1, 2, …) until the estimated request P99 meets the target:

ContinuousBatchingModel sizes the per-replica active batch and token throughput under the memory wall, using paged allocation over the request-length distribution;
ServingModel (at that batch and the mean request length) gives TTFT/ITL, so the base request latency is TTFT + ITL * output_tokens;
TailLatencyModel (M/M/c) adds the P99 queue wait at each candidate replica count.

Estimated P99 = base request latency + P99 queue wait. Per-replica QPS capacity = token throughput / output_tokens.

title: ConvBnReluFusionScenario
text:
Optimization scenarios · Implementation: mlsysim/engine/scenario_definitions/optimization.py.
Construct this scenario with keyword inputs. The fields below show the types and defaults declared by this class.
A convolution, batch norm, and ReLU on one feature map, run as three kernels or one.
Unfused, each kernel reads its input from device memory and writes its output back (six transfers), and the convolution and norm also read their parameters; fused (the norm folded into the convolution’s weights and bias, the ReLU applied before the write), one read and one write remain. A lower bound on time: traffic over hardware’s memory bandwidth, compute ignored.


Equation: traffic_cut is the worked quantity; each property below states its equation and units.
Assumptions: Batch normalization folds into dense convolution parameters and ReLU fuses before the output write.
Excludes: Compute work, cache hits, workspace, and measured kernel-fusion speedup.

title: MLSys·im
text:
Analytical models of ML systems
Performance, cost, and carbon, estimated from first principles before any hardware is provisioned.
Open source · v0.3.1 · Companion to the Machine Learning Systems textbook
MLSys·im is an analytical modeling framework for the stage before hardware is benchmarked or provisioned. It makes the first-order constraints explicit (memory, compute, network, data, reliability, cost, and carbon), which narrows the design space and shows which experiments are worth running.

Get Started →

  pip install mlsysim
  Copy



Tutorials · The Zoo · API Reference · Tutorial slides · Paper (PDF)

title: MLSys·im
text:
Start from the system question
Each of the four questions below maps to a solver. The analytical answer comes first; the sensitive parameters are then validated on the real stack once hardware is available.


Memory fit
Estimate weights, activations, optimizer state, KV cache, and communication buffers before a job fails at runtime.


The binding constraint
Separate compute, memory bandwidth, network communication, data input, reliability, cost, and carbon constraints.


Serving capacity
Size serving replicas for a QPS and p99 target, including batching and queueing assumptions.


Design-space sweeps
Sweep batch size, precision, parallelism, efficiency, geography, and hardware without needing cluster access.

title: MLSys·im
section: A first analysis in five lines
text:
A first analysis in five lines

from mlsysim import Engine, Models, Hardware

profile = Engine.solve(
    model=Models.Vision.ResNet50,
    hardware=Hardware.Cloud.A100,
    batch_size=1,
    precision="fp16",
    efficiency=1.0,
)

print(f"Bottleneck: {profile.bottleneck}")
print(f"Latency:    {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"Throughput: {profile.throughput.to('1/s'):~.0f}")

Bottleneck: Memory
Latency:    0.54 ms
Throughput: 1843 / s


The engine applies the roofline model [1]: a step takes at least as long as its compute time or its memory-transfer time, whichever is larger.
\[T = \max\!\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak} \times \eta},\ \frac{\text{Bytes}}{\text{BW}}\right) + T_{\text{overhead}}\]
At batch 1 on the theoretical ceiling (\(\eta = 1.0\)), ResNet-50’s arithmetic intensity is 146 FLOP/byte, just under the A100’s ridge point of 153 FLOP/byte. The memory term (0.028 ms) edges out the compute term (0.026 ms), though both are small next to the fixed dispatch overhead of 0.515 ms. The 0.54 ms total is mostly overhead, which is why batching helps so much here. Start from the Model Zoo and Silicon Zoo, or define a custom workload and hardware target.

title: MLSys·im
text:
What MLSys·im models
Every solver takes typed registry objects and returns an analytical estimate with units attached.


Roofline analysis
Compute versus memory bottlenecks, single-node latency and throughput.
Hello Roofline →


LLM serving
Time to first token, inter-token latency, and KV-cache pressure. Llama 3 8B on an H100 with a 2,048-token prompt: 71 ms to first token, 5.2 ms per token after that.
Two Phases of Inference →


Memory and capacity
Training memory breakdowns, serving replicas, and MoE routing imbalance. The same Llama 3 8B needs 15 GiB of weights plus 0.25 GiB of KV cache, out of 80 GiB on the H100.
Memory, Capacity, and MoE →


3D parallelism
Data, tensor, and pipeline parallel scaling, ring all-reduce, and pipeline bubbles.
Scaling to 1000 GPUs →


Total cost of ownership
Capital and operating cost, electricity, and per-query economics over any horizon.
The $9M Question →


Sustainability
Energy, carbon footprint, and water use across datacenter regions.
Geography Matters →


Reliability
Fleet MTBF, failure probability, and the Young-Daly checkpoint interval.
Sensitivity Analysis →


Agents
KV-cache footprints and stranded memory for long-running agent sessions.
The Agent Zoo →


Physical AI
Stopping distances, information age, actuator limits, and fieldbus budgets for robots.
The Embodied Zoo →

title: MLSys·im
text:
Validate the approximation
The outputs are analytical estimates, not measurements. Use them to narrow the design space, expose assumptions, and choose the next experiment.

Check feasibility first. If memory, network, or data movement is infeasible analytically, benchmarking will not rescue the design.
Calibrate efficiency. Compute-heavy solvers expose an efficiency parameter. The defaults are literature-informed starting points; replace them with measured MFU or sustained throughput once those measurements exist.
Compare regimes. The most reliable conclusions are binding constraints, crossover points, and sensitivity rankings.
Escalate fidelity deliberately. Pick the few configurations worth validating with profiling, traces, or production load tests.

See the accuracy and validation guide for how the solvers compare with published measurements.

title: Provenance
text:
Every Tier A number in MLSys·im (registry entries and public sourced scalars) carries structured lineage via the Provenance model. Citation managers and prose live outside the package; MLSys·im stores audit metadata only.
Provenance answers “how do we know this number?” It is not a registry category. A number can have provenance whether it lives under Hardware, Systems, Infrastructure, Ops, Scenarios, or Literature. Literature.* is the registry for cited scalar anchors from papers/tables; those entries use the same provenance machinery as every other sourced value.

Use nested registry paths in Python (Hardware.Cloud.H100, Models.Language.Llama3_8B). The CLI accepts short names (mlsysim eval Llama3_8B H100) via internal lookup. That convenience does not apply to import mlsysim code.

title: Calibration and validation scope
text:
MLSysIM estimates are analytical outputs, not hardware measurements. The table below is generated from engine.empirical; it distinguishes calibrated checks, broad sanity ranges, and formula accounting. Passing these checks does not establish an accuracy percentage for unseen workloads.

resnet50_a100_train_bs256: ResNet-50 training on A100, batch_size=256, efficiency=0.26. The 10% band is intentionally wider than MLPerf run-to-run variation because MLSYSIM uses a first-order roofline plus a calibrated efficiency term.
resnet50_h100_train_bs256: ResNet-50 training on H100, batch_size=256, efficiency=0.13. The calibrated efficiency is lower than A100 because ResNet-50 does not saturate H100 peak tensor throughput in this first-order model.
llama3_8b_h100_bs1_itl: Llama-3-8B serving on H100, seq_len=2048, batch_size=1, efficiency=0.5. Decode is memory-bandwidth dominated; this range is a sanity envelope, not a production SLA for a specific scheduler or prompt distribution.
gpt3_175b_training_flops: 175B parameters, 300B training tokens, 6PD transformer training rule. The tight band is appropriate here because the comparison is formula-level FLOP accounting, not a hardware throughput measurement.




The ResNet efficiencies are calibration inputs, not independently predicted utilization. The H100 reference is a per-accelerator result from a distributed training run, not a matched single-device experiment. The Llama interval is a family sanity range; it does not identify one engine, precision, and request shape. The GPT-3 comparison checks FLOP accounting, not wall-clock performance. Source identities and limitations are recorded in the provenance catalog.
For an external accuracy claim, pin the source revision, hardware topology, model, engine, precision, batch/concurrency, input/output lengths, and metric. Retain the raw timing artifact and declare efficiency assumptions before the comparison. Evaluate held-out configurations separately from calibration. At batch one, decode ITL is (end_to_end_latency - TTFT) / (output_tokens - 1); end-to-end latency divided by output tokens includes prefill and is a different metric. A TTFT prediction must not be checked against an ITL reference.




efficiency derates compute FLOP/s. It does not derate memory bandwidth.
Serving decode uses the larger of compute and weight/KV memory time, plus the configured layer tax. Continuous batching uses the same step accounting.
Prefill is a compute-based estimate, with attention work and dispatch taxes; very short prompts can be memory- or overhead-limited in practice.
A weight-only bandwidth floor remains useful, but is not a complete latency prediction or a serving capacity guarantee.
Runtime workspaces, scheduling interference, and inter-device communication require separate modeling or measurement. Feasible means the modeled state fits; it does not reserve all memory used by a production engine.




From an editable checkout’s mlsysim/ directory:
python scripts/calibration_report.py --check
python -m pytest tests/test_empirical.py
Run the script without --check to regenerate this file. Numerical outputs and reference differences are computed by the script, not entered by hand.
